HEADNOTE: Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section  28(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Penalty - For concealment of income - Whether maximum penalty which can be imposed under section 28(1) of 1922 Act is determined by ascertaining difference between amount of tax on income set out in false return and amount of tax on income in respect of which assessment has been made - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee, who carried on business as money-lenders, returned their assessable income. The ITO, being satisfied ‘that the accounts produced did not contain the whole of the assessees money-lending transaction, and that the assessee had other accounts which were not produced’ assessed their income under section 23(4) of 1922 Act at a much higher amount. Thereafter proceedings were taken under section 28(1) for the purpose of imposing a penalty upon the assessees.

At an enquiry held pursuant to section 28(3) the assessee ‘produced the accounts previously concealed, and the ITO found from the books the assessee’s income and imposed a penalty on the assessees, being ‘difference between the tax on the income declared by the assessee and the tax on the income on which the assessment was made.’ On appeal the Assistant Commissioner gave credit to the assessee in respect of a further sum and reduced the amount of the penalty imposed. The order of the Assistant Commissioner was confirmed by the Commisisoner.

On reference :

HELD: It appeared, that ‘the amount of income-tax which would have been avoided if the income so returned by the assessee had been accepted as the correct income’ was the amount of income-tax which the assessees had been compelled to pay, but which they would not have paid if their false return of assessable income had been accepted as correct. Or, to put the matter in another way, the assessees had in fact paid income-tax on ‘X’ income, while if their false return had been accepted they would have paid income-tax only on ‘Y’ income. By paying income-tax on ‘Y’, therefore, the assessees would have avoided paying income-tax on ‘X’ minus ‘Y’.

The maximum penalty which can be imposed under section 28(1) is determined by ascertaining the difference between the amount of the tax on the income set out in the false return and the amount of the tax on the income in respect of which the assessment has been made.

The construction that was placed upon section 28 in CIT v. A.A.R. Chettiyar Firm [1933] ITR 285 was correct. Therefore, the amount of the penalty imposed in the instant case was properly computed, having regard to the provisions of section 28.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

failure to pay tax is not an offence. Failure to pay even for long time per se does not prove fraudulent conduct. It is the intent to defraud that attracts liability to penalty. The fraudulent evasion creates a right to the Government to claim damages. But the tax payable under section 140A is a civil liability which could not attract any confiscation of property. Any provision enabling confiscation for failure to discharge that liability in time will be unreasonable and infringe article 19(1)(f). It is true that Section 140A(3) could not be attacked on the ground of procedural unreasonableness whether the restrictions imposed by a legislative enactment upon a fundamental right guaranteed by article 19(1) are reasoable within the meaning of Article 19(5) would depend as much on the procedural portion of the law as the substantive part of it. If the penalty under section 140A(3) is confiscatory in nature that could not be taken out of the purview of Article 19(1)(f) by providing procedural safeguards alone.

In testing the standard of reasonableness in order to validate a provision under article 19(5), there are certain basis and well-recognised principles known to law and have been the law and procedure for over a century in the matter of recovery of amounts due to the Government that they have gained the standard of reasonableness. The basic approach in the matter of recovery of Government dues in this country had always been consistent with the law relating to recovery of tax due, contrary to this basic principle, unless substantial grounds are made out for a departure, unreasonable. There are no such substantial grounds for varying this provision of levying interest for delayed payment into one of penalty.

Every citizen has a fundamental right to retain his income after payment of taxes. Any provision in the Act which authorises the taking away of this retained income would be confiscatory unless it is saved under Article 19(5). The penalty levied under section 140A(3) is not compensatory for delayed payment or retention of tax. In the guise of a deterrent provision for enforcing payment of tax due and payable, section 140A(3) authorises confiscation of property. Confiscation of property for non-payment in time of a tax ascertained and payable is an unreasonable restriction on the fundamental right to property of an assessee. Thus, section 140A(3) authorising the levy of penalty for failure to pay within 30 days of the tax payable under section 140A(1) is confiscatory and is not saved under Article 19(5).

While certain provisions in the Act make the Government liable for interest only, for failure of refund within time the excess amount of tax collected, section 140A(9) makes the assessee liable for penalty. The petitioner’s argument that this is an invidious and hostile discrimination against the assessee like them and, therefore, section 140A(3) is violative of Article 14, was not acceptable. Section 140A(3) treats all these persons who fail to pay the tax as provided under section 140A(1) as a class by itself and makes them liable to pay the penalty. There can be no comparison between that class of persons and the Government. Government can be legitimately treated as a class by itself. It is well known that governmental machinery does not move as quickly as non governmental bodies or individuals. Government being an impersonal body, there have to be departmental correspondence, consultations, obtaining sanction, etc., and these necessarily take some time. The Government have to depend on the efficiency and promptness of a team of officials. Loss or damage to the Government is a loss or damage to the public, that is, the community in general. The question whether a State can be treated as a class by itself has been considered in several cases. The Supreme Court in Manna Lal v. Collector of Jhalawar [1961] 1 SCJ 665 held that the Government, even as a banker, can be legitimately put in or separate class; the dues of the Government of a State are the dues of the entire people of the State, and this being the position or law giving special facility for the recovery of such dues cannot, in any event, be said to offend article 14. Therefore, there was no hostile discrimination in Section 140A(3) against the petitioners.

The provision is intended to be a deterrent against failure to pay tax under section 140A(1). The ITO is bound to issue a notice to the assessee before passing any order under that provision. This gives an opportunity to the assessee to bring to the notice of the ITO any grounds in his favour for not levying the penalty or the mitigating circumstances which have to be taken into account in determining the amount of penalty payable by him. Abuse of power is not to be readily assumed. Normally, it is presumed that public officials will discharge their duties honestly and in accordance with law. The discretion vested in the ITO has also to be exercised in a judicial manner. It must be governed by rule and not by whim. Whether in a given case the power has been properly exercised or not is open to question in appeals and further appeals. Thus, there is an effective check on the exercise of the power by the ITO. Therefore, section 140A(3) does not infringe Article 14 on this ground.

HEADNOTE: Section 158BFA of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Block assessment in search cases - Levy of interest and penalty in certain cases - Block period 1-4-1986 to 21-3-1997 - Assessee filed writ submitting that section 158BFA(2) which provides for penalty on heavier terms is oppressive and violative of fundamental rights guaranteed under Constitution of India - Whether since object and purpose of section 158BFA is to provide penalty for concealment of income and act as a deterrent against tax evaders, said provision is not oppressive and violative of fundamental rights guaranteed under Constitution of India - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a builder engaged in the business of construction of commercial buildings and selling or letting out of buildings. The assessee’s premises were searched under section 132 and several incriminating documents were seized. Assessment was proceeded under Chapter XIV- B. On notice under section 158BC to the assessee, he filed a return disclosing income. Assessment was completed under section 158BC whereby total income was determined. Penalty proceeding under section 158BFA(2) was also initiated and, accordingly, penalty was imposed. The assessee’s case was that sub-section (2) of section 158BFA which provides for penalty on heavier terms is illegal, oppressive and violative of fundamental rights guaranteed under Constitution of India.

On petition :

HELD: Chapter XIV-B consists of sections 158B to 158BH which was inserted by the Finance Act, 1995 so as to provide for an assessment of the undisclosed income detected as a result of search, and devised to operate in the separate field of undisclosed income and in addition to the regular assessments covering previous years in the block period. In the instant case, the contention of the assessee that sub-section (2) of section 158BFA was oppressive or in any way violative of any article of the Constitution of India could not be accepted. There was no basis in that contention. [Para 7]

Section 158BFA has been introduced in Chapter XIV-B which deals with special procedure for assessment of search cases. The said provision is intended to act as an effective deterrent against evasion of tax and to put a stop to that practice which the Legislature considers to be against public interest. Merely, because heavy penalty is provided for concealing income and also disclosing of undisclosed and unexplained investment during search conducted, it cannot be said that such a provision is a piece of hostile legislation. Assuming that the provision is harsh since it is a deterrent against tax evaders, provision is not expropriatory. Power to levy tax on income is vested in the Parliament and power to impose penalties to vindicate that particular power of imposition of tax is also with the Parliament. Object and purpose of section 158BFA is to provide penalty for concealment of income and act as a deterrent against tax evaders. Heavy penalty is prescribed to check tax evasion. If Legislature in its wisdom felt that in the matter of search cases such a penalty should be imposed, it cannot be canvassed in a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution of India. [Para 8]

Therefore, there is no infirmity in the said provision. The prayer of the assessee to declare such provision as oppressive and violative of fundamental rights guaranteed under the Constitution could not be sustained.

On reference :

HELD: It is true that the existence of penalties does act as a deterrent and possibly facilitates the ensuring of certain acts to be done by the assessee, but it is impossible to agree that but for such provisions about the imposition of penalties, the assessment or collection of tax would not have any effect. It was quite clear from the scheme of the Acts that the various penalties are by way of punishment, either for concealment of income or refusal or failure to make certain returns, and these punishments are over and above and quite outside the assessment and collection of the taxes themselves. It is, in the circumstances, difficult to agree that when the Parliament used the expression "levy", "assessment" and "collection of income-tax and super-tax", it intended to include the imposition of penalties which could be imposed under the law previously in force. Therefore, the view taken by the Tribunal was upheld and the ITO had no jurisdiction to impose penalty under section 28 of the Patiala Income-tax Act in respect of an assessment for the year 1949-50.

It is true that the question relating to the constitutional validity of a provision of the Act cannot ordinarily be examined in a reference but the position is different when the constitutional validity has already been examined by three High Courts under article 226 of the Constitution and one of them has declared the provision to be invalid. In the circumstances of the instant case, it was not possible to decide the reference without going into the question of the constitutional validity. Section 140A(1) requires the assessee to pay the tax on the basis of the return within thirty days of its furnishing. To make the evasion of this provision unprofitable, section 140A(3) authorises the ITO to impose penalty not exceeding 50 per cent of the amount of tax. It will be seen that the ITO has a discretion which he has to exercise judicially after notice to the assessee. The amount of penalty which the ITO can impose within the maximum limit would depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. Further, the ITO is not abound to impose penalty in every case and if good grounds are shown for not depositing the tax within the time allowed under section 140A(1), he can decide not to impose any penalty. It is well settled that even if a minimum penalty is prescribed, the authority competent to impose the penalty is justified in refusing to impose penalty when there is a technical or venial breach of the provision or where the circumstances show that the assessee in good faith believed that he was not liable to act in the manner prescribed by the statute. Having regard to the discretion conferred upon the ITO, which has to be reasonably exercised, the provision of penalty under section 140A(3) cannot be held to be confiscatory and unreasonable. The penalty is in the nature of additional tax for securing compliance that the tax is paid within the time allowed under section 140A(1). The assessee's income was, no doubt, his property but the assessee can retain that property only subject to right of the State to recover taxes and a reasonable provision made to secure payment of tax on due date cannot be held to be infringement of the right to hold property.

Therefore, section 140A(3) is not unconstitutional. For the above reasons the Tribunal was not right in law in cancelling the penalty.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

In the light of the above observations let us examined as to whether the rule contained in the Explanation can be said to be a rule of substantive law or a rule of procedural law, i.e., whether it is a rule for establishing or dis-establishing a specified substantive right or a rule of evidence merely. Clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271 provides for the payment of certain penalty that may be directed by the ITO or the AAC if he is satisfied that any person has concealed the particulars of his income or furnished inaccurate particulars of such income. Thus a person becomes liable to the penalty, how much that penalty should be we are not concerned with in connection with the enquiry, if he has concealed the particulars of his income or furnished inaccurate particulars of the same. The Explanation only provides that, in certain circumstances, the assessee will be deemed to have concealed the particulars of his income or furnished inaccurate particulars and the burden will then be on him to establish that the failure to return the correct income did not arise from any fraud or any gross or wilful neglect on his part. The condition which raises this presumption is that where the total income returned by the assessee is less than 80% of the total income as assessed under sections 143, 144 and 147 reduced by the expenditure incurred by him for the purpose of making or earning any income included in the total income but which has been disallowed as a deduction, the presumption will arise. Thus if an assessee makes a return and that return is disbelieved and he is assessed to a higher amount than he purports to show in the return and the total income that he has shown in his return is less than 80% of the income for which he is assessed, then the law thinks, as provided by this Explanation, that he has concealed the particulars of his income or furnished inaccurate particulars. Can it be said, in the circumstances, that the existence of the position of the return being less than 80 per cent of the total income assessed is not relevant to the concealment of the particulars of his income by the assessee or his furnishing inaccurate particulars of such income. Clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271 contemplates a certain amount of penalty for concealment of the particulars of income or furnishing inaccurate particulars by an assessee. If the return of an assessee's income is found not to be correct and is less than 80 per cent of the income at which he is ultimately assessed, the Explanation in such a state of affairs provides for the raising of a presumption against the assessee for his having concealed the particulars of his income or having furnished inaccurate particulars of such income. Obviously, applying the test laid down in Izhar Ahmad Khan's case (supra ) the Explanation provides nothing more than a rule of evidence relating to the raising of a rebuttable presumption in certain circumstances. It is not a rule which creates or negatives any substantive right. Such a rule is within the competence of the legislature to create. The question, however, is as to whether by the creation of such a rule the provisions of article 14 of the Constitution have been violated.

Article 14 of the Constitution guarantees to every citizen equality before the law and for the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.

An applicant pleading that article 14 has been violated must make out that not only he had been treated differently from others, but he has been so treated from persons similarly circumstances without any reasonable basis, and such differential treatment is unjustifiably made.

The quantum of penalty being dependent on the tax determined as payable by the assessee, it cannot obviously be fixed until the assessment is completed. If then, penalty cannot be imposed until the assessment order is made, it cannot be said that the classification made for the purpose of imposition of penalty between assessees whose assessments were completed before and after 1-4-1962, is arbitrary and without any basis. The classification made by clauses (f) and (g) of section 297(2) is thus not a mere fanciful classification; it is reasonable and has a reasonable relation to the object to be achieved. The object of penalty proceedings is to curb effectively evasion, and the object to the classification made by clauses (f) and (g) of section 297(2) is not to discriminate against those assessees whose assessments for the year ending on 31-3-1962, or any earlier year had not been completed before 1-4-1962, but to bring them in line with other assessees whose assessments are completed on or after 1-4-1962, in the matter of imposition of penalty. The assessees whose assessments were completed before 1-4-1962, are entitled to a sense of security and certainty in the mater of penalty by the fact that the assessment is completed and the Act of 1961 not having come into force at the date when the assessment was completed. The assessees whose assessments are completed after 1-4-1962, cannot claim the same treatment.

It was clear that if for the purpose of checking evasion the legislature though it fit to apply the penalty provisions contained in the 1961 Act to cases of assessments completed after 1-4-1962, covered by clause (g) instead of the penalty provisions under section 28(1) of the 1922 Act, there can be no justification for striking down clause (g) on the ground that the legislature should have applied the penalty provisions contained in section 28(1) of the 1922 Act. Indeed, such an application would have resulted in discrimination between the assessees whose assessments are completed after 1-4-1962. That discrimination could not have been justified on the ground that the assessee filed his return before the commencement of the Act or that his assessment was for the year ending on 31-3-1962, or any earlier year. What is material for the imposition of penalty is not the assessment year on the date of the filing of the return, but it is the discovery and the satisfaction of the competent authority that the assessee had committed a default attracting penalty. The classification made by clauses (f) and (g) of section 297(2) is based on an intelligible differentia and that differentia has a rational to the object sought to be achieved by the said provisions. It could not therefore, he held that those clauses offend article 14 of the Constitution and are invalid.

It was true that in the present case the return was filed before 1-4-1962, and the assessment was under the 1922 Act, as provided by clause (a) of section 297(2). But the assessment proceedings under the 1922 Act, being by virtue of the provisions of section 297(2)(a) were proceedings under the 1961 Act itself, and, consequently, the satisfaction reached by the ITO about concealment of income on the part of the petitioner attracting penalty was in the course of proceedings under the 1961 Act.

For the foregoing reasons, Courts conclusion was that the order of the IAC upheld by the Tribunal, imposing penalty on the petitioner was valid. Instant petition was, therefore, dismissed.

FACT: For the assessment year 1954-55, the ITO initiated assessment proceedings under section 34(1)(a) of the Act of 1922, and completed the assessment under section 23(3) read with section 34(1)(a) of the Act of 1922. Under section 274(2) read with section 271(1) of the Act of 1961, penal proceedings were commenced and penalty was imposed under section 271(1)(c) read with section 297(2)(g) of the Act of 1961 for deliberate concealment of income.

Appeal against penalty order was pending before the Tribunal.

On writ petition, the petitioner assessee sought quashing of penalty on the ground of violation of article 20(1) of the Constitution and also on the ground that no proceedings could have been started under section 271 of the 1961 Act (new Act,) as, under section 297 of the new Act, proceedings for the imposition of penalty could only be initiated under the repealed Act of 1922.

HELD: As per section 297(2)(g) the proceedings for imposition of penalty in respect of any assessment for the year ending on 31-3-1962, or any earlier year which is completed on or after the 1-4-1962, shall be under the Act. As the assessment was for the assessment year 1954-55, and as it was completed after April, 1962, the proceeding for imposition of penalty under the Act was perfectly competent. Therefore, the proceedings for the imposition of penalty under section 271 of the Act were not open to attack.

As regards violation of article 20(1) of the Constitution, the argument was that as this article prohibited the imposition of a penalty greater than that which might have been imposed upon the petitioner under the law in force on the date of the commission of the offence, she was not liable to be prosecuted, as a penalty had already been imposed upon her on the same facts, and that the petitioner stood in danger of being prosecuted for an offence under section 277 of the Act of 1961.

From section 277 it is clear that, unless a person makes a statement in any verification under the Act or under any rules made thereunder or delivers an account or statement which is false and which he either knows or believes to be false or does not believe to be true, he shall not be punishable. The act of the petitioner was not an offence under the Act. Therefore, a prosecution on the basis that she committed an offence under the provisions of section 277 would not lie. Hence the apprehension of the petitioner that she would be prosecuted under the new Act was an idle one.

The maximum penalty being the same in both the enactments, there was no substance in the contention that the petitioner was being subjected to a greater penalty under the new Act because a minimum is specified in section 271 of the 1961 Act, Penalty is nothing but compensation for damages collected by the State for attempting to evade the provisions of the Act. No conviction for any offence is involved in the imposition of a penalty. Article 20(1) of the Constitution will have application only when a person is subjected to a penalty greater than that which might to have been inflicted under the law in force at the time of the commission of the offence. This would indicate that commission of an offence and a conviction thereof are necessary in order that the provisions of the Article may be attracted.

bypass a constitutional prohibition by employing indirect methods and, therefore, the court has to look behind the form and appearance to discover the true character and nature of legislation: vide Dwarkadas Shrinivas v. Sholapur Spinning and Weaving Co. Ltd. [1954] 24 Comp. Cas 103; [1954] SCR 674; AIR 1954 SC 119 and Hamdard Dawakhana v. Union of India AIR 1960 SC 554. Looking at the substance of section 140A(3), there could be no doubt that it deprives or takes away the owner of his retained income and thus it is confiscatory in nature. That the penalty levied under section 140A(3) is not compensatory or interest for delayed payment of the tax or retention, is clear from the fact that it has no relation to the duration of the delay or the wilful or other nature of the violation to pay or the inability to pay the tax. There is not even a power to extend the time for payment. The moment thirty days given under sub-section (1) of section 140A is over, the liability for penalty is attracted. It is also not related to the quantum of the tax payable except that the penalty is attracted if the tax payable exceeds Rs. 500. Thus this section is not hedged in or circumscribed or limited by any condition other than the lapse of 30 days from the date of furnishing of the return and non-payment of the tax payable within those 30 days in order to attract the liability for penalty.

The revenue contended that, though a discretion is vested in the ITO to levy a penalty for failure to pay tax, having regard to the nature of the provisions, he is expected to exercise a judicial discretion and impose a penalty only in those cases where the failure to pay was wilful by a person who had enough resources to pay but deliberately and fraudulently fails to pay. He also relied on the proviso to sub-section (3) requiring the issue of notice and giving opportunity to the assessee of being heard. This will enable the assessee to bring to the notice of the assessing authority the mitigating circumstances which would have to be taken into account by the assessing authority. In this connection he also relied on a Circular No. 20(LXXVI) D of 1964 dated 7-7-1964, issued by the Central Board of Direct Taxes. Apart from the doubt on the binding nature of this circular, inspite of Section 119, the authority of the ITO under section 140A(3) being quasi-judicial in nature. This instruction could not violate the provision if it is otherwise invalid.

The test is not what is actually done in exercise of the powers under section 140A(3) but what the section enables to be done by the assessing authority. The power to levy penalty under section 140A(3) is very wide and enables levy of penalty even in cases where the delay in payment was bona fide or due to inability or other good reasons and the amount of penalty is also not made dependent on the amount of tax payable or the length of time of the delay.

Though the Supreme Court, in the case of Check Post Officer v. K.P. Abdulla and Bros., [1971] 27 STC 1 (SC) was concerned with the legislative competency of a State legislature under entry 54 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, the ratio of that judgment, is that a provision for confiscation or levy of penalty is not a provision for enforcement of payment of tax. Thus, the provision for confisaction of property for non-payment of tax arrears could not be sustained as a provision ancilliary or incidental for enforcement of payment and, therefore, a reasonable restriction under clause (5) of article 19 of the Constitution. Even as a punishment for failure to pay the tax within time, the legislation could not be sustained from the attack of article 19(1)(f).

The provision of Section 140A(3) has no rationales or intelligent connection with the recovery of the tax itself. Actually, the Act itself does not provide for the issue of a demand notice under section 156 of the Act. If it is intended to be a coercive process it must be to recover the debt itself but not to enhance it. The provision, far from enabling to recover the debt imposes an additional burden. Far from effectuating recovery, the levy of penalty may even frustrate the very object.

Moreover, the liability for penalty arises because of the contumacious or fraudulent conduct of the assessee. Mere failure to pay tax is not an offence. Failure to pay even for long time per se does not prove fraudulent conduct. It is the intent to defraud that attracts liability to penalty. The fraudulent evasion creates a right to the Government to claim damages. But the tax payable under section 140A is a civil liability which could not attract any confiscation of property. Any provision enabling confiscation for failure to discharge that liability in time will be unreasonable and infringe article 19(1)(f).

As already noticed, in the instant appeal, one is not concerned with the assessment that was completed on the assessee but on the penalty that was imposed on him under section 271(1)(c).

■ It will be seen from a perusal of section 271 that it is a specific provision providing for imposition of penalties, and is a complete code in itself, regulating the procedure for the imposition of penalties prescribed. The proceedings are therefore to be conducted in accordance therewith, subject always to the rules of natural justice. The provisions for the assessment and levy of tax will not apply as such for the imposition of penalty, and when there is a specific provision, it is trite that it alone will govern the imposition of penalties. In terms of section 271(1)(c) the penal provision is attracted only when the conditions therein are fulfilled namely, when there is a concealment of the particulars of an assessee's income or when the assessee has furnished inaccurate particulars of such income. The crucial question that arises for consideration is whether on the facts of the instant case those pre-conditions existed for initiating proceedings under section 271. Further, the provisions of section 271(1) mandate that the existence of the conditions precedent for imposition of penalty under section 271(1)(c) must have been noticed by the assessing authority in the course of some proceedings under the Income-tax Act. In other words, the satisfaction of the assessing authority with regard to the existence of either of the conditions warranting the invocation of the provisions of section 271(1)(c) had to be in the course of proceedings initiated by the assessing authority under the Income-tax Act. The reference to proceedings under section 271, on the facts of the instant case, can only be a reference to the proceedings initiated against the assessee in terms of section 148. This is because the call for details and information under section 131 cannot be seen as initiation of any proceedings under the Income-tax Act but is merely a manifestation of the exercise of a power similar to that conferred to civil courts, by the Officers of the I.T. Department. If that be the case, then what we have to examine in the instant case is whether at the time of issuance of notice under section 148, the assessing authority can say that he was satisfied that the assessee had concealed the particulars of his income or furnished inaccurate particulars of such income. It is viewed, in the light of the disclosure made by the assessee, of the income that he had omitted to include in his original return, well before the date on which the notice under section 148 was issued to him by the assessing authority, the assessing authority was effectively estopped from contending that he was satisfied at that point in time, of the assessee having concealed the particulars of his income or furnished inaccurate particulars of such income. Section 271(1)(c) no doubt authorises the imposition of a penalty irrespective of whether the assessee had any mens rea to occasion the default specified therein. The liability in that sense is a strict one as was the case under section 11AC of the Central Excise Act, the scope of which was considered by the Supreme Court in Union of India v.Dharmendra Textiles Processors [2008] 174 Taxman 571/306 ITR 277. It is therefore all the more necessary to strictly construe the provisions of section 271(1)(c) to ensure that only the clear and unambiguous cases of defaults specified therein would attract a penalty. On the facts of this case, one fail to see how an assessee who disclosed his liability to tax, well before the assessing authority himself could determine it, can be seen as having concealed or incorrectly stated the facts leading to his liability. To invoke the penal provisions of the Act against an assessee in such a situation would throw to the winds the elements of fairness in tax administration and discourage assessees from disclosing defects in their tax returns before their assessing authorities. This is more so when, as in the present case, the assessee had also paid the interest on the differential tax to cover the period of delay in payment thereof. The payment of statutory interest having compensated the exchequer adequately, to further penalise the assessee would tantamount to an act of overkill and would be antithetical to the rule of law. The honesty of an assessee cannot attract the penal provisions under the Income-tax Act and that, in the instant case, the essential pre-conditions for the invocation of the provisions of section 271(1)(c) against the assessee were not established.[Para 9]

Under the old Act the ITO was free to determine any penalty within the maximum limit prescribed. In the circumstances, article 20(1) of the Constitution had not been infringed in any manner. As regards violation of article 14 of the Constitution, in enacting section 297(2)(g) of the new Act, in construing the validity of a statute impugned under this article, courts have to bear in mind the well-established principle that the legislature can make class legislation, provided the classification on which it purports to be based is rational and has a reasonable nexus with the object intended to be achieved by it, and so, on the failure of the party to show that the said classification is irrational, or has no nexus with the object intended to be achieved by the impugned Act, the initial presumption of constitutionality would help the state to urge that the failure of the party challenging the validity to rebut the initial presumption goes against his claim that the Act is invalid. In all cases where the material adduced before the court in matters relating to article 14 is unsatisfactory, the court may have to allow the state to lean on the doctrine of initial presumption of constitutionality.

In the instant case no material had been placed to show that this provision had been abused or was capable of being abused in any manner by the taxation authorities. It also could not be said that the legislature had not made a valid classification in drawing a line between assessments which had been completed before the coming into force of the new Act, and those which were completed thereafter. The penalties prescribed under the Income-tax Act for failure to submit returns of income in time are not in the nature of punishment imposed for conviction of an offence. Such penalties are more or less compensatory in character to make good the loss that may be caused to the state revenues on account of late submission of returns of income and in consequence late realization of the tax. Therefore, the provision relating to imposition of penalties can be said to form integral parts of the proceedings relating to assessment. It was, therefore, open to the legislature to make a distinction regarding assessments which were completed before the coming into force of the new Act and those which are to be completed after the coming into force of the new Act. Thus, the distinction made by the legislature was a valid one, and therefore, the provisions were not invalid.

As regards the question as to whether the notice issued under section 22(2) of the old Act could be deemed to be a notice under the new act, reference may be made to section 297 (2)(k) of the new Act. This saving provision applies to the case and the legislature could not have intended that the notices already issued under section 22(1) of the old Act should be taken to be wiped out with the coming into force of the new Act. Section 297(2)(k ) covers agreements, appointments, approval given, recognition granted, direction and instructions, besides the notification, orders or rules issued under any of the old Act. These provisions will, therefore, cover administrative orders and notices and the words "order or rule issued under any provisions" will cover a notice issued under section 22(1) of the old Act. Thus, the notice issued under the old Act can legitimately be considered as good as a notice issued under the new Act for purposes of invoking sections 271 and 274 of the new Act.

Consequently, the instant petition was to be dismissed.

Note : The decision was in favour of revenue.

differentia which distinguishes persons or things that are grouped together from others who are left out of the group, and (2) the differentia must have a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved by the impugned provision. It has also been repeatedly held that the differentia and object are different elements and that the object by itself cannot be the basis of classification. Another principle equally well settled is that article 14 condemns discrimination not by substantive law alone but even by procedural law. The Explanation does not fall in the category of a substantive provision of law but answers the description of procedural law. The Explanation purports to raise a presumption against the assessee if certain facts mentioned therein are proved after assessment has been made, and then shift the burden on the assessee to prove that his case does not fall under clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271. According to the Explanation , if the total income returned by any person is less than eighty per cent of the total income as assessed, that person shall, unless he proves that the failure to return the correct income did not arise from any fraud or any gross or wilful neglect on his part, be deemed to have concealed the particulars of his income or furnished inaccurate particulars of such income for the purpose of clause (c ) of sub-section (1). In other words, if the margin of difference in the case of a particular assessee between the income returned by him and his actual income is more than twenty per cent., then it would be for him to establish that he had not concealed the particulars of his income or furnished inaccurate particulars of that income by reason of fraud or gross or wilful neglect on his part, while in the case of assessees whose returned income reveals less than twenty per cent departure from the actual income, the burden of proving the ingredients of clause (c) shall rest, as before, on the income-tax authorities. Obviously, the main purpose of the Explanation is to place the burden of establishing want of fraud or gross or wilful neglect in the matter of income-tax return filed by an assessee on him where the difference revealed between the returned income and assessed income is more than twenty per cent. Therefore, although the ultimate object of the Explanation may be to provide effective checks against evasion of income-tax, the immediate object of the Explanation appears to be that if an assessee has been apparently guilty of gross deflation of his income as entered in his return compared to his actual income, it shall be for him to establish that he has not merited imposition of penalty under clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271. Briefly put, if the gap between the returned and actual income is more than 20 per cent a presumption of law arises that the assessee's case is covered by clause (c) but that presumption being in rebuttal the assessee is given an opportunity to establish that it is not so.

The classification of the assessees into two varieties as envisaged by the Explanation is founded on intelligible differentia. The two categories of assessee in legislature wisdom are; (1) who, in the opinion of parliament, have been guilty of gross and flagrant violation of ethics benefiting a citizen in the matter of submission of income-tax returns, and (2) the rest of the assessees falling in the category not answering such description. The Explanation is an instance of the legal adage res ipsa loquitur, meaning that the thing speaks for itself. In substance, Parliament wants the income tax authorities to assume if the gap between the returned income and the actual income is so glaring as to the extent of not less than 20 per cent that assessee in question has concealed the particulars of his income or has furnished inaccurate particulars of such income, but in case the difference is less than twenty per cent., then such assumption would not arise and it shall be for the department to establish that the assessee has concealed the particulars of his income or furnished inaccurate particulars of such income. In allocating the burden of proof in one class of cases on the assessee and in the other on the departmental authority, think Parliament has adopted an intelligible differentia dictated by the experience gathered in administering the Act.

It is not for the courts to tell Parliament what sort of classification it should introduce. The function of the courts is only to find out whether the classification actually introduced by Parliament is hit by article 14 of the Constitution. There may be a variety of classifications which can be introduced for achieving a particular object, but if Parliament in its wisdom adopts one in preference to another, the courts cannot take exception to the classification chosen if it is not proved to be obnoxious to the constitutional provision. The classification introduced by the Explanation to section 271(1) does not offend article 14 of the Constitution.

HEADNOTE: Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1983-84 - Assessee’s books of account were seized by department and assessee was not given sufficient time for filing return - Assessee filed provisional return declaring income of Rs. 1,60,000 and after inspecting documents and making copies of accounts, filed another return declaring income of Rs. 2,44,760 - Income was assessed at Rs. 2,57,820 making certain additions relating to cash credits and sales tax liability and latter sale tax addition was deleted on appeal - Assessing Officer initiated penalty proceedings and levied penalty on basis of discrepancy between provisional return and income assessed by department - Whether where Assessing Officer himself had not considered provisional return as valid for assessment purpose, it could not be treated as valid for purpose of levying penalty - Held, yes - Whether mere fact that assessee did not file appeal against cash credit addition, would not automatically mean that penalty could be levied under section 271(1)(c) unless concealment was clearly established by Assessing Officer - Held, yes - Whether since difference between valid return and income assessed by department was only on account of certain petty additions and such additions did not indicate any concealment of income or furnishing of inaccurate particulars of income within meaning of section 271(1)(c), penalty levied was unjustified - Held, yes

FACT: During search operations at the premises of the assessee-company, several books of account and documents were seized. The assessee requested for extension of time for filing return which was granted up to 15-1-1984 only. Request for another extension was refused. Thereafter, the assessee filed a provisional return on 24-3-1984 declaring income of Rs. 1,60,000. Since the books of account were seized by the department, the assessee took some time in inspection of documents and subsequently filed a return on 19-3-1986 declaring total income of Rs. 2,44,760.

The department got the books audited under section 142(2A) and framed the assessment order under section 143(3) computing the total income at Rs. 2,57,820. The discrepancy was due to additions made on account of certain unexplained cash credits and sales tax liability. The addition relating to sales tax was deleted on appeal by the assessee. The Assessing Officer initiated penalty proceedings under section 271(1)( c) and levied penalty treating the assessed income as concealed income presuming that returned income was nil.

The Commissioner (Appeals), however, deleted the penalty so levied as baseless and unwarranted. The Commissioner (Appeals) pointed out that the Assessing Officer could not take double stand, treating the preliminary return as no valid return but relying on same for levying penalty. The revenue contended that since the assessee did not appeal against additions relating to cash credits, the assessee should be deemed to have concealed the particulars of income in respect of that.

On revenue’s appeal :

HELD: No material defect was found in the books of account of the assessee after they were audited under section 142(2A). The IAC (IT) while issuing instructions under section 144A did not agree with the proposed addition to be made by the Assessing Officer. Ultimately the only additions which were considered by the Assessing Officer for the levy of penalty were the three amounts, viz., cash credit, unexplained cash and sales tax liability. It was quite clear that additions related to certain cash credits for which no satisfactory explanation was offered before the Assessing Officer. As regards the addition relating to sales tax liability, it was deleted by the Commissioner (Appeals) in quantum appeal. The assessee-company appeared against the addition relating to sales tax liability only. This led the Assessing Officer to conclude that in respect of cash credits the assessee concealed the particulars of income calling for the levy of penalty. However, the mere fact that the assessee had not filed appeal against the cash credits addition, did not lead to the conclusion that the assessee had concealed the particulars of income. The mere fact that the cash credits had been added under the deeming provisions of section 68, would not automatically mean that penalty could be levied under section 271(1)(c) unless concealment was clearly established by the Assessing Officer.

crept in, was not acceptable. The High Court, accordingly, decided in favour of the revenue.

On appeal to the Supreme Court, the assessee submitted that the Tribunal having arrived at a finding of fact, the impugned judgment of the High Court could not be sustained and that in any event, no specific question having been referred as to whether the Tribunal’s findings were perverse or not, the High Court committed a manifest error in differing with the findings of fact arrived at by the Tribunal. HELD: Reference of the question to the High Court was general in nature. No question was referred as to whether the finding of the Tribunal was perverse or not. Existence of mens rea is essentially a question of fact. The Tribunal alone, as the highest authority empowered to determine the question of fact, would be entitled to go thereinto. However, the same would not mean that the High Court will have no jurisdiction in this behalf. The High Court, it is well-known, should not ordinarily disturb the finding of fact arrived at by the Tribunal. Question of law should generally arise only accepting the finding of fact to be correct. [Para 9]

It is trite that if an explanation given by the assessee with regard to the mistake committed by him has been treated to be bona fide and it has been found as of fact that he had acted on the basis of wrong legal advice, the question of his failure to discharge his burden in terms of Explanation appended to section 271(1)(c ) would not arise. [Para 13]

The expression ‘conceal’ signifies a deliberate act of omission on the part of the assessee. Such deliberate act must be either for the purpose of concealment of income or furnishing of inaccurate particulars. [Para 15]

The term ‘inaccurate particulars’ is not defined. Furnishing of an assessment of value of the property may not by itself be furnishing of inaccurate particulars. Even if the Explanations are taken recourse to, a finding has to be arrived at having regard to clause (A) of Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c) that the explanation offered by an assessee, in the event, he offers one was false. He must be found to have failed to prove that such explanation is not only not bona fide but all the facts relating to the same and material to the income were not disclosed by him. Thus, apart from his explanation being not bona fide, it should be found as of fact that he has not disclosed all the facts which was material to the computation of his income. [Para 16]

The explanation, having regard to the decision of the Supreme Court, must be preceded by a finding as to how and as to in what manner he furnished the particulars of his income. It is beyond any doubt or dispute that for the said purpose the ITO must arrive at its satisfaction in this behalf. [Para 17]

The order imposing penalty is quasi-criminal in nature and, thus, burden lies on the department to establish that the assessee had concealed his income. Since burden of proof in penalty proceeding varies from that in the assessment proceeding, a finding in an assessment proceeding that a particular receipt is income cannot automatically be adopted, though a finding in the assessment proceeding constitute good evidence in the penalty proceeding. In the penalty proceedings, thus, the authorities must consider the matter afresh as the question has to be considered from a different angle. [Para 18]

It is now a well-settled principle of law that the more is the stringent law, more strict construction thereof would be necessary. Even when the burden is required to be discharged by an assessee, it would not be as heavy as in the prosecution case. [Para 19]

The omission of the word ‘deliberate’ in the amended provision of section 271(1)(c) thus, may not be much significance. [Para 20]

Section 271(1)(c ) remains a penal statute. Rule of strict construction shall apply thereto. Ingredients of imposing penalty remains the same. The purpose of the Legislature that it is meant to be deterrent to tax evasion is evidenced by the increase in the quantum of penalty, from 20 per cent under the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 to 300 per cent in 1985. [Para 21]

‘Concealment of income’ and ‘furnishing of inaccurate particulars’ carry different connotations. Concealment refers to deliberate act on the part of the assessee. A mere omission or negligence would not constitute a deliberate act of suppressio veri or suggestio falsi. [Para 22]

The instant case was not a case where penalty had been imposed for breach of contravention of a commercial statute where lack of or intention to contravene or existence of bona fide might not be of much importance. It was also not a case where penalty was mandatorily impossible. It was, therefore, not a case where the enabling provision should have been invoked. [Para 29]

For the reasons aforementioned, the impugned judgment could not be sustained which was to be set aside accordingly. The appeal was to be allowed. [Para 30]

the assessee and held that there was deliberate concealment which had been fully established and, thus, imposed penalty under section 271(1)(c). On appeal, the Tribunal set aside the order of penalty and held that mere estimate of income without any definite basis did not account for any penalty action. Applying the decision of the Supreme Court in CIT v. Anwar Ali [1970] 76 ITR 696 , the Tribunal cancelled the penalty imposed upon the assessee.

On reference: HELD: In the instant case the assessment was completed on 23-3-1967. On the same date penalty proceedings had been initiated. The satisfaction of the ITO that there was concealment of income thus solidified on 23-3-1967. The penalty was, therefore, to be levied in terms of the law applicable on 23-3-1967. The Tribunal was, thus, in error in cancelling the penalty on the basis of the authority laid down in the case of Anwar Ali (supra). There being obvious discrepancy of more than 20 per cent, the obligation to explain the difference was squarely upon the assessee. The assessee did not produce any material to show that his explanation was correct. There was no explanation as to why the assessee showed a figure of sale before the income-tax authority, lower than what he had stated before the sales tax authority. There was, thus, an obvious concealment. Secondly, in regard to assessed income although it was based on estimate, but the estimate was based upon the assessee's own percentage of income from the records of the earlier years. If the rate of sale was higher in earlier years, the income-tax authority was fully justified in holding that the income could not be lower in a subsequent year, as the rate of sale of coal had not come down. These were sufficient to hold that there had been concealment of income. In fact, the Tribunal did not consider these matters with any seriousness, but merely held that the revenue had not brought anything on record to show that the assessee had concealed any income. The concealment of income was writ large on the record. Moreover, even if one brushed aside the Explanation to section 271(1)(c), the concealment would be obvious even upon the authority of the case of Anwar Ali (supra). Thus, the Tribunal was not correct in cancelling the penalty imposed by the IAC under section 271(1)(c) upon the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 297, read with section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 28(1)(c) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Repeals and savings - Assessment year 1959-60 - Whether for purposes of penalty, there is no doubt classification under section 297(g) between assessees who had filed returns of income before 1-4-1962, and whose assessments were completed before that date and assessees who had filed returns of income before 1-4-1962, but whose assessments were completed on or after 1-4-1962 and, this is an intelligible classification - Held, yes - Whether clauses (f) and (g) of section 297(2) is not to discriminate against those assessees whose assessments for year ending on 31-3-1962, or any earlier year had not been completed before 1-4-1962, but to bring them in line with other assessees whose assessments are completed on or after 1-4-1962, in matter of imposition of penalty - Held, yes - Whether, in view of aforesaid, it could be concluded that section 297 (2)(g) was not violative of Article 14 of Constitution of India - Held, yes

FACT: The petitioner, assessee took forest contracts. It ran a saw-mill and also manufactured and sold furniture. It also did stone quarrying business. For the assessment year 1959-60 the petitioner filed a return of its income under section 22(2) of Act, 1922, on 21-10-1959, showing an income of Rs. 7,896. In the assessment proceedings the ITO noticed some discrepancies in the accounts and registers maintained by the assessee of its business and called upon the assessee to explain the discrepancies and furnish certain particulars. Thereupon, the assessee filed a revised return of its income on 17-1-1964, disclosing its total income as Rs. 50,605. The ITO finalized the assessment on 19-3-1964, after taking into consideration the revised return and issued a notice to the petitioner under section 271(1)(c) for concealment of income. The ITO referred the matter to the AAC as penalty intended to imposed by him exceeded Rs. 1,000.

The Inspecting Assistant Commissioner, finding that the assessee had concealed the particular of its income, made the impugned order imposing a penalty of Rs. 25,000 on the petitioner. The petitioner then preferred an appeal before the Tribunal which was dismissed. In the instant writ petition. It was contended by the petitioner that section 297(2)(g) being violative of article 14 of the Constitution is invalid and, therefore, no penalty could be imposed on the petitioner under section 271 and, that under section 271(1) a penalty can be imposed by the Income-tax Officer or the Appellate Assistant Commissioner only if he, in the course of any proceedings under the Act of 1961, is satisfied that any person has committed any of the acts enumerated in clauses (a), (b) or (c) of section 271(1); that, as the assessment against the petitioner was made under the Act of 1922, and not under the Act of 1961, the Income-tax Officer or the Appellate Assistant Commissioner had no jurisdiction to impose any penalty under section 271(1).

HELD: The effect of clauses (a), (f) and (g) of section 297(2) is that where the assessee files a return of income before the commencement of the Act of 1961, that is before 1-4-1962, for any assessment year, then the assessment of that person for that year is under the 1922 Act; any proceeding for the imposition of a penalty in respect of any assessment completed before 1-4-1962, can be initiated and penalty can be imposed under the 1922 Act; any proceedings for the imposition of a penalty in respect of any assessment for the year ending on 31-3-1962 or any earlier year which is completed on or after 1-4-1962 can be initiated and penalty can be imposed under the 1961 Act. In the present case, the petitioner filed a return of income before 1-4-1962, but the assessment was completed on 19-3-1964, that is after 1-4-1962, therefore, clause (g) of section 297(2) was plainly attracted for the initiation of proceedings for imposition of penalty under the Act of 1961.

. An. appellate authority in the case of an assessee whose assessment is completed before 1-4-1962, can reached a finding that there is a concealment of income and such a finding can be reached even after 1-4-1962. Thus, if the completion of assessment has any relevance in determining whereunder and in which circumstances the penal proceedings should be initiated or carried out, it date, 1-4-1962, does not play any important part. It is true that before the classification made by the legislature could be struck down, it is to be established that it is either arbitrary or fanciful or capricious or unjust. The argument that the classification was necessary because initiation of proceedings could not be taken before the assessment was completed was not acceptable. It is true that the ITO or the AAC as the case may be, is required to determine the quantum of penalty with reference to the tax which is determined as payable. But from that circumstances it cannot be held that the very initiation of proceedings is held over until after the completion of the assessment.

Thus, the event which gives a cause of action for initiation of penalty proceedings is not held over until after the completion of assessment proceedings. If the completion of assessment proceedings, therefore, is not relevant to determine whether or not the ITO or the AAC should initiate penalty proceedings, the date on which the assessment is completed in a particular case cannot have any bearing is determining whether the assessment should be governed by one set of provisions of one case and a different set of provisions in the matter of penalty in another case.

If the date of completion of assessment is not a relevant factor in determining whether or not penal proceedings should be initiated or whether the assessee has or has not committed one of the other wrong, there is nothing dividing the two classes of assessee with reference to the date of completion of the assessment proceedings.

The provisions of either sec tion 28 of the 1922 Act or section 271 of the Act of 1961 will show that the infraction of the provisions of the Act takes place as soon as the return is filed.

That such satisfaction is entered by the ITO at a later date shows that the adjudication of the Act or omission of the deliquent assessee is postponed to the date of recording such finding. But, from that it cannot be inferred or legitimately urged that the infraction has not taken place when the returns were filed. Some time must necessarily elapse between the filing of the return and commencement of proceedings for assessment, and during such proceedings the income-tax authority records satisfaction whether there has been failure to comply with the provisions of the Act in respect of matters provided in section 28 of the old Act or section 271 of the new Act.

The date of completion of the assessment makes no difference so far as this aspect of concerned. In fact, it has no impact either on incurring of the liability or for imposition of penalty. Therefore, the classification made by section 297(2)(g) of the Act of 1961 cannot be justified either as relevant or having any relation to the object with which it is concerned. So far as making a provision for imposing a penalty is concerned, there is no difference between the assessees who have filed returns but in whose cases the assessment was completed prior to 1-4-1962, and assessees who have filed returns but in whose cases assessment was not completed or could not be completed till 1-4-1962.

The mere fact that the legislation divides assessees into two classes cannot be itself be its justification. Justification has to be found somewhere else, namely, in a rational nexus between the classification and the object to be achieved. If the respondents are not able to show that nexus, then it is not possible to uphold the contention that classification is rational or just.

That it is arbitrary is obvious when the date of coming into force of the Act is found to have no bearing on the division of assessees into two classes, one governed by one set of provisions and the other governed by anther set of provisions.

The contention that in the instant case, there was no rational nexus between the object with which the provision has been made for imposing penalty and selecting the date for differentiating as to this provision of law by which the proceedings should be governed, was well founded and had not been satisfactorily answered by the respondents.

The contention on behalf of the revenue that if there was no provision like clause (g) of sub-section (2) of section 297, the Income-tax authorities would have no power to initiate penal proceedings for imposition of penalty by having recourse to the provisions of the old Act had no force with regard to assessments completed after 1-4-1962. Assuming that the provisions like clause (g) of sub-section (2) of section 297 were not to be made by the legislature, the provisions of sub-clause (c) of (d) or (e ) of section 6 of the General Clauses Act would have applied and proceedings for imposition of penalty could have been initiated and penalty imposed under the provisions of the repealed Act, i.e., the Income-tax Act, 1922.

HEADNOTE: Explanation-I to section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1972-73 - Since returned income of assessee was less than 80 per cent of assessed income, in penalty proceedings Explanation to section 271(1)(c) became applicable - As assessee failed to furnish any explanation, penalty was imposed under section 271(1)(c) - Whether even though provisions of main section 271(1)(c) were not specifically invoked, penalty was rightly imposed as Explanation to section 271(1)(c) did not give rise to a separate charge as distinguished from substantive provisions of section 271(1)(c) - Held, yes

FACT: For the assessment year 1972-73, since the returned income of the assessee was less than 80 per cent of the assessed income, in penalty proceeding's Explanation to section 271(1)(c) became applicable. Since the assessee was not able to furnish any explanation, penalty was imposed under section 271(1)(c). On appeal, the assessee contended before the Tribunal that Explanation to section 271(1)(c) gave rise to a separate charge as distinguished from the substantive provisions of section 271(1)(c) and that the provisions of the main section 271(1)(c) having not been specifically invoked, penalty could not be levied. The Tribunal rejected the assessee's contention and upheld the imposition of penalty.

On reference:

HELD: The penalty provision is contained in section 271 and on different counts penalty of different amounts is imposable, wherever there is concealment of income. If the concealment is beyond 20 per cent of the returned income, then the Explanation becomes applicable and presumption has to be raised against the assessee which he can rebut but in case concealment does not exceed 20 per cent. the penalty is still leviable but in this situation the onus lies on the department to prove concealment. Therefore, the Explanation has to be read with section 271(1)(c ) and there is no question of considering the Explanation as separate or distinct from it. The law has to be applied to the given facts. Even if in the order specific reference to Explanation is not mentioned but Explanation is applied and onus is placed on the assessee because the returned income is less than 80 per cent of the assessed income, from this inference has to be drawn that the assessing authorities were conscious of the fact that Explanation was applicable. The Tribunal had, therefore, rightly rejected the assessee's claim.

duty to adopt measures to strike at the evil of tax evasion and it must have freedom to choose the class of persons through whom such evasion can be effectively combated and subject such class to a special procedure or treatment. Such legislation cannot be struck down on the ground that it meets out hostile unequal treatment. The petitioners had failed to discharge the heavy burden which laid upon them to sustain the challenge to the impugned provision based on article 14 and the contention urged in that behalf must be rejected. The other argument was that the impugned provision could not be treated as incidental or ancillary to the main provisions and that, therefore, it could not be said to have any rational nexus with the main provisions of the statute.

This is not the case where on the basis of any presumption made by the legislature a penalty such as seizure or confiscation or penalty in lieu of confiscation is sought to be levied. The impugned provision is made on the basis of a well-known fact which is a matter of common knowledge and common report and all that it requires a building contractor to do is to furnish prescribed particulars within the stipulated time limit on the span of penalty with a view to detecting evasion of tax. Such a provision is clearly incidental or ancillary to the power to levy tax because the power to enact a provision for preventing evasion of tax is always an incidental power. In fact, the challenge levelled to the impugned provision on the ground of legislative incompetence has not even been pressed in the instant case. In these circumstances, it could hardly be contended that the impugned provision being not incidental or ancillary to the main power to tax income which is conferred by the Act, it had no nexus with the statute in question.

The petition was, therefore to be dismissed.

Note: The case was decided in favour of the Department.

HEADNOTE: Section 256, read with section 271(1)(c), of the income-tax act, 1961-Reference-question of fact-Ito imposed penalty for concealment of income on assessee on ground that certain household expenses had been underestimated and certain other expenses had not been shown properly-On appeal, penalty was cancelled on ground that as particulars of concealment had not been disclosed to assessee, he was not in position to defend himself and as such he could not be said to have been granted reasonable opportunity of being heard-Tribunal upheld cancellation of penalty-Whether any question of law arose from tribunal's order-Held, no

Section 274(1) of the income-tax act, 1961-Penalty-Opportunity of hearing-Whether where particulars of concealment are not disclosed to assessee while imposing penalty, it would mean that assesses has not been given reasonable opportunity of being heard-Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was assessed by the ITO at an income higher than that declared in the return filed. The ITO held that the assessee had certain concealed income which could be determined from the fact that household expenses had been underestimated and travelling expenses of family and club expenses as well as medical expenses which had been reimbursed, had not been shown properly. The ITO also imposed penalty under section 271(1)(c). On appeal, the penalty was cancelled on the ground that the basis of the penalty proceedings had not been disclosed to the assessee who was put in a difficult position to defend the matter under section 274(1) and was not granted a reasonable opportunity of being heard. On further appeal, the Tribunal confirmed the order cancelling the penalty and rejected the application for reference under section 256(1), holding that the finding regarding lack of reasonable opportunity was a finding of fact.

On application for reference under section 256(2):

HELD: In order to constitute a penalty under section 271(1)(c ) what is required is a concealment, either of the income or of the particulars thereof. In order to enable such a penalty to be imposed, it is necessary to determine which is the income concealed or which are the particulars not disclosed. If a person is accused of a particular offence of which particulars are given to him, he has a chance of giving his defence thereto. If he is generally accused of some offence of an unknown type, he cannot easily defend himself. The additions which were made during the assessment proceedings in the instant case were based on certain surmises and conjectures. In penalty proceedings, it was not only necessary to inform the assessee of the particular concealment but also necessary for the department to prove positively that there was such a concealment. It was the duty of the department to inform the assessee of the particular concealment that had taken place so that he could defend the case. The failure to do so had led to the cancellation of the penalty. No question of law, therefore, arose from the Tribunal's decision since the question whether penalty had been imposed in accordance with proper procedure or in consonance with natural justice, was one of fact.
