HEADNOTE: Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (Corresponding to section 28 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922) - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1954-55 - Whether ITO does not cease to have power to impose a penalty under section 28 of 1922 Act once an appeal has been filed before AAC against assessment which gives rise to initiation of penalty proceedings - Held, yes
Interpretation of statute:
(i) Legislative intent
(ii) Beneficial interpretation

FACT: For the assessment year 1954-55, the ITO made an addition as estimated income for low gross profits and for business income kept outside the account books, and the assessment was completed .Prior to this ITO issued a notice under section 28 in regard to concealment of income.

On appeal, against the quantum assessment, the AAC reduced the addition, and the reduction was confirmed by the Tribunal. Thereafter, the ITO pursued the penalty proceedings initiated earlier and levied penalty.

On second appeal, the Tribunal upheld the penalty.

On reference, the question refereed was as to whether ITO ceased to have power to impose a penalty under section 28, once an appeal had been filed before the AAC against the assessment which gave rise to the initiation of penalty proceedings.

HELD: Tax and penalty, like tax and penal interest, are distinct and different concepts under the Act. Penalty is in addition to the tax determined as payable by the assessee. Penalty, cannot be taken as additional tax for all purposes. The penalty and assessment proceedings are not one and the same proceedings. The findings given in the assessment proceedings would only be relevant and admissible but not final and conclusive in penalty proceedings. In penalty proceedings, further evidence can be led to rebut the findings given in the assessment proceedings. Even in matters which are processed by the ITO, the assessee might not place all the materials before the ITO, with the result he might not be able to detect or find out concealment of income. The AAC, during his enquiry, may come to know additional facts, which are either not disclosed to the ITO, or which escape the attention of the ITO, and those facts might reasonably lead the AAC to a finding that the assessee had concealed income. In such a case, if the AAC has no powers to impose a penalty, the assessee would altogether escape penalty. Therefore, the law has wisely given powers to the AAC and also the Tribunal to impose penalty on the assessee. When the law empowers more than one authority to impose penalty, it would be unreasonable to expect that each one of them would, in his own turn, invoke and impose penalty. At any rate, the assessee can be punished only once in respect of concealment of income and not by all the three authorities simultaneously or one after the other and for the same offence.

It would, therefore, be reasonable to think that when the ITO, having original jurisdiction, and the appellate authorities, i.e. , AAC and the Tribunal, are also invested with powers to impose penalties, it would be wise for the inferior officer to exercise that jurisdiction or power. If section 28 is interpreted in a different manner it would be disadvantageous to the assessee. If the penalty is imposed by the ITO, the assessee would have two opportunities to test the correctness of that penalty order by filing appeals to the AAC and if necessary to the Tribunal. If the power to impose penalty is exercised by the AAC, then the assessee would lose the benefit of one appeal because he could in that case file an appeal only to the Tribunal. If the power to impose penalty is exercised by the Tribunal, then the assessee would altogether lose the right of filing an appeal against the penalty order. If section 28 of the Act is at all to be construed, such construction should be placed on it which would be more advantageous to the assessee.

The language used in section 28 is clear and unambiguous. The section does not under any circumstances oust the jurisdiction of the ITO to impose penalty. If the AAC or the Tribunal imposes penalty on an assessee under section 28(1)(c), he or it is bound under sub-section (5) of section 28, to send a copy thereof to the ITO so that he could not once again impose a penalty upon the assessee for the same concealment.

If the legislature had intended to oust the jurisdiction of the ITO to impose a penalty on an assessee if an appeal was filed against the assessment before the AAC, nothing prevented the legislature from saying so in express language in section 28. There is a general presumption in law against an intention to disturb or oust the jurisdiction or interfere with the jurisdiction, which is given to an officer.

of the business but at the same time to evade income-tax which he would have otherwise been liable to pay. The Income-tax Enquiry Commission of 1936 made certain recommendations to prevent evasion of tax in such cases. The Legislature accepted those recommendations and the loopholes were sought to be plugged by enacting the said sub-section. Sub-section (3)(a)(i) and (ii) was, therefore, enacted for preventing evasion of tax and was well within the competence of the Federal Legislature. The constitutional validity of the said provision was next questioned on the ground that it violated the doctrine of equality before the law enshrined in article 14 of the Constitution. Under the impugned sub-section, an individual is taxed on the income of his wife or his minor children, if he carries on business in partnership with his wife or if he admits his minor sons to the benefits of the partnership, whereas an individual, if he carries on business in partnership with a third party, whether a man or a woman, or even with his major children or if he and his wife or children carry on business separately, will be liable only to pay tax on his share of the partnership income, that, is, for the purpose of this sub-section, the former is put in a category different from the latter. It could not be said that there was no differentia between the two groups. The object of the legislation was to prevent evasion of tax. A similar device would not ordinarily be resorted to by individuals by entering into partnership with persons other than those mentioned in the sub-section, as it would involve a risk of the third party turning round and asserting his own rights. The Legislature, therefore, selected for the purpose of classification only that group of persons who in fact are used as a cloak to perpetrate fraud on taxation.

It was then said that there might be genuine partnerships between an individual and his wife and, therefore, there was no reasonable relation between the classification and the object sought to be achieved, at any rate to the extent of those genuine cases. But there was no classification between genuine and non-genuine cases: the classification was between cases of partnership between husband, wife and/or minor children, whether genuine or not, and partnerships between others. In demarcating, a group, the net was cast a little wider, but it was necessary, as any further sub-classification as genuine and non-genuine partnerships might defeat the purpose of the Act. Hence that contention was rejected.

As to the validity of the provisions based upon article 19(1)(f) and (g) of the Constitution, A combined and plain reading of the provisions of articles 13 and 265 makes it abundantly clear that a law which is inconsistent with any of the provisions of Part III is void. It cannot be denied that a law providing for levy and collection of taxes is a law within the meaning of Part III of the Constitution, and therefore it must stand the test laid down by article 13 of the Constitution. The "law" in article 265 of the Constitution must be a valid law. A law to be valid must not only be one passed by the Legislature in exercise of power conferred on it, but must also be one that does not infringe the fundamental rights declared by the Constitution.

Section 16(3)(a) of 1922 Act must, therefore, pass both the tests and if it violates any of the provisions of article 19, to the extent it is inconsistent with the said provisions, it will be void.

HEADNOTE: Section 140A of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Assessment - Self-assessment - Whether section 140A(3) which provides for levy of penalty for failure to pay self-assessment tax, does not in any way infringe article 19(1)(f) of Constitution of India - Held, yes

FACT: The petitioner did not pay tax due in accordance with the return of income filed by him within stipulated time and, consequently, proceedings for levying penalty under section 140A(3) were commenced by issuing a show-cause notice, to which the petitioner replied contending that inasmuch as on the assessment being completed he had paid the entire tax due, no penalty could be levied under section 140A(3). However, the ITO levied a penalty, which was affirmed in appeal. On writ, the petitioner challenged the constitutional validity of section 140A(3).

HELD: Section 140A which provides for payment of tax due in accordance with the return of income filed by an assessee, within 30 days of the filing of the return is one of the modes/stages of collection of tax devised by Parliament in exercise of its power of taxation.

The principle behind section 140A is that if at the end of the year the assessee is liable to pay any tax according to his own estimate of his income, he shall pay the same within 30 days of the filing of the return. If an assessee is liable to pay advance tax, he would normally pay almost the entire tax in the shape of advance tax, and if he still finds any further tax due at the end of the year, he has to pay it under sub-section (1) of section 140A. In the case of an assessee or in the case of income not liable for payment of advance-tax, the tax due has to be paid within the said 30 days. Obviously, the finalisation of the assessment may take some time and on that occasion, the excess or deficit can be paid or refunded. It is reasonable to presume that every person earning taxable income knows approximately the tax due from him and is expected to and has to pay the same in accordance with law. In other words, the portion of his income due towards income-tax would not be deemed by a prudent and reasonable person to be his "income", properly speaking. In the earlier days, the entire tax was payable, only after the assessment was completed. But when the theory of advance tax was introduced, he had to pay it in certain (now three) instalments as and when he is earning his income. Now, another step is introduced under section 140A, namely, that he has to pay the admitted tax due (i.e., the tax due from him as per his own return) within 30 days of the filing of the return. All these payments towards advance tax and under section 140A(1) are liable to be adjusted at the time of the finalisation of the assessment. There are provisions in the Act providing for levy of penalties for non-compliance with the provisions relating to filing of return, non-furnishing of accounts or particulars, failure to pay advance tax, concealment or evasion of income-tax, etc. Criminal prosecution is also pro-provided for by Chapter 22 in certain cases which, inter alia, include failure to file a return of income, failure to produce accounts and documents, making of false statements and declaration, failure to deduct and pay tax when required to do so. These provisions relating to levy of penalties and criminal prosecutions are twin sanctions provided by law for ensuring compliance with law on the part of the assessees. The object of the two sets of provisions, namely, one levying penalties and the other providing for criminal prosecution, are entirely different.

The provisions made in sub-section (3) is only a measure enacted for ensuring compliance with sub-section (1) of section 140A. The said sub-section merely makes the assessee liable for a penalty which may go up to 50% of the tax payable under sub-section (1). A discretion is conferred upon the ITO in the matter of levying the penalty. In a proper case, he may decline to levy any penalty. The said provision do not compel the ITO to levy such a penalty in each and every case and/or up to the maximum limit. An appeal and a second appeal are provided against his orders and a further reference to the High Court. Further, one cannot assume the case of an assessee "who is not able to pay his taxes". Every person earning taxable income has to provide for payment of taxes. However, certain situations may arise where the assessee may not be able to pay the taxes within 30 days as required by section 140A. But in such cases, if he properly explains the circumstances to the satisfaction of the ITO, he would not levy the penalty.

HEADNOTE: Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessee returned income at Rs. 14,768 but ITO and AAC estimated the same at Rs. 30,000 and imposed penalty of Rs. 15,230 - Tribunal computed total income at Rs. 25,000 but estimated concealed income at Rs. 3,000 with consequential reduction of penalty to Rs. 4,500 - Whether tribunal justified - Held, on facts, yes

FACT: For the assessment year 1970-71, the assessee engaged in the business of assembling pumping sets and manufacturing of canal gates returned its income at Rs. 14,768. The ITO found that in addition to other defects,, the assessee had not incorporated accounts relating to 27 vouchers in his books of account and that, Rs. 2,000 paid in cash to M on 17-3-1970 was recorded in books on 18-3-1970. He consequently estimated income at Rs. 30,000 and levied penalty of Rs. 15,230 for default under section 271(1)( c). The AAC confirmed the ITO's order. On further appeal, the Tribunal held (i) that the recording of cash payment of Rs. 2,000 on a subsequent date was not due to any fraud or gross or wilful neglect on his part; and (ii) that while 12 vouchers were satisfactorily reconciled, the value of Rs. 2,500 represented by the remaining 15 vouchers was not recorded in his books. It, therefore, calculated the concealed income at Rs. 3,000 even though it had estimated the assessee's total income at Rs. 25,000, and reduced the penalty to Rs. 4,500 being 150 per cent of the concealed income.

On reference:

HELD: 1. It is settled that proceedings for penalty are of quasi-criminal nature. While adjudicating on the offence of concealment, the Tribunal is not to be guided by the findings given in the quantum appeal and has to examine the facts afresh to determine the assessee's guilt of concealment and the amount of concealed income for computing the quantum of penalty.

2. The Explanation to section 271(1 )(c) does not have the effect of fixing the quantum of concealment for imposing penalty. The function of fiction created by the Explanation is to convert a case where the assessed income exceeds 80 per cent of the returned income into a case which was covered by section 271 (1)(c), unless the assessee proves that he was not guilty of any fraud or any gross or wilful neglect in filing his return of income. The Explanation exhausts itself once this purpose is achieved. It does not create any further fiction for taking the assessed income as the correct income for levy of penalty under section 271(1)(c)(iii) for which purpose the concerned authority has to independently find the amount of concealed income and may or may not accept the assessed amount as the concealed income. Any other interpretation would make the penalty proceedings completely subservient to the assessment proceedings which does not appear to be the scheme of the Act.

3. Hence, the Tribunal was justified in estimating concealed income at Rs. 3,000, even though the total income had been computed at Rs. 25,000 against returned income of Rs. 14,768 and consequently reducing the quantum of penalty.

Editor's note

The revenue had also argued (i) that the Tribunal had omitted to consider relevant facts while estimating the concealed income at Rs. 3,000 only; and (ii) that, apart from the fact that the assessee had made purchases not shown in the vouchers, there were other irregularities in the accounts to show that he had been carrying on business outside the books: The High Court did not consider these aspects because the question referred did not solicit an enquiry into the validity of the finding regarding estimated concealed income on those scores.

R.K. Gulati and A. Gupta for the Applicant.

Bharatjee Agrawal for the Respondent.

2.

Merely because the legislature in its wisdom decided to give a different treatment to proceedings relating to penalty it is difficult to find discrimination with regard to the classification which has been made in clauses (f) and (g ) which are independent of clauses (a ) and (b). Although penalty has been regarded as an additional tax in a certain sense and for certain purposes it is not possible to hold that penalty proceedings are essentially a continuation of the proceedings relating to assessment where a return has been filed. Further, it is well-settled that in fiscal enactments the legislature has a larger discretion in the matter of classification so long as there is no departure from the rule that persons included in a class are not singled out for special treatment. It cannot be said that while applying the penalty provisions contained in the Act of 1961 to cases of persons whose assessments are completed after 1-4-1962, any class has been singled out for special treatment. It is obvious that for the imposition of penalty it is not the assessment year or the date of the filing of the return which is important but it is the satisfaction of the Income-tax authorities that a default has been committed by the assessee which would attract the provisions relating to penalty. Whatever the stage at which the satisfaction is reached, the scheme of sections 274(1) and 275 of the Act of 1961, is that the order imposing penalty must be made after the completion of the assessment. The crucial date, therefore, for purposes of penalty, is the date of such completion.

As regards the argument that because it rests with the Income-tax Officer to complete the assessment by a particular date it will depend on his fiat whether the penalty should be imposed under the Act of 1922 or under the Act of 1961. It cannot be presumed that officers or authorities who are entrusted with responsible duties under the taxation laws would not discharge them properly and in a bona fide manner. If in a particular case any mala fide action is taken that can always be challenged by an assessee in appropriate proceedings but the mere possibility that some officer may intentionally delay the disposal of a case can hardly be a ground for striking down clause (g) as discriminatory under article 14.

The classification made is based on intelligible differentia having reasonable relation to the object intended to be achieved. The object essentially was to prevent the evasion of tax.

It is true that clause (a) of sub-section (1) of section 271 mentions the corresponding provisions of the Act of 1961 and does not mention provisions of Act of 1922 but that will not make the part relating to payment of penalty inapplicable once it is held that section 297(2)(g ) governs the case. Both sections 271(1) and 297(2)(g) have to be read together and in harmony and so read the only conclusion possible is that for the imposition of a penalty in respect of any assessment for the year ending on 31-3-1962, or any earlier year which is completed after first day of April, 1962, the proceedings have to be initiated and the penalty imposed in accordance with the provisions of section 271 of the Act of 1961. Thus the assessee would be liable to a penalty as provided by section 271(1) for the default mentioned in section 28(1) of the Act of 1922 if his case falls within the terms of section 297(2)(g).

The provision of section 271 of the Act of 1961 will apply mutatis mutandis to proceedings relating to penalty initiated in accordance with section 297(2)(g) of that Act.

As regards challenge to section 271(2) of the Act of 1961 on the ground of contravention of article 14 of the Constitution, it was open to the legislature to say that once a registered firm committed a default attracting penalty, it should be deemed or considered to be an unregistered firm for the purpose of its imposition. No question of discrimination under article 14 can arise in such a situation. There was nothing to prevent the legislature from giving the benefit of a reduced rate to a registered firm for the purpose of tax but withhold the same when it committed a default and became liable to imposition of penalty.

The appeal was dismissed.

Note : The decision was in favour of the revenue.

1-4-1968 - Held, yes

FACT: For the assessment years 1961-62 and 1962-63, the assessee had shown income from house properties in respect of two houses only. After the completion of the original assessment proceedings, the assessments were reopened and during the course of the reassessment proceedings the ITO made certain additions to the income of the house properties, which had been omitted from the original returns filed by the assessee. The ITO issued notice under section 271(1)(c). Since according to the ITO, the minimum penalty which could be imposed under the Act exceeded Rs. 1,000, he, referred the matter to the IAC, who came to the conclusion that the assessee was guilty of concealment and he, therefore, imposed a penalty of Rs. 5,020 in respect of the assessment year 1961-62 and Rs. 7,020 in respect of the assessment year 1962-63. On appeal, before the Tribunal the assessee contended that penalty, if any, must be computed in accordance with the provisions of section 271 as it stood before the amendment and that as the minimum penalty under section 271(1)(c) as it stood before the amendment fell below Rs. 1,000, the ITO had jurisdiction to proceed with the penalty proceedings. These contentions were upheld by the Tribunal. It accordingly, set aside the orders of the Assistant Commissioner in respect of these years and directed that the matter would go back to the ITO for fresh decision according to law.

On reference:

HELD: A comparison of the provisions of section 271 before and after amendment shows that the penalty provisions for concealment of income have been made very stringent and the amount of penalty leviable has been much enhanced. The point for consideration in this case is whether the amended provisions would be applicable to penalty proceedings in respect of assessment years 1961-62 and 1962-63, even though the amendment came into effect on 1-4-1968.

Liability for penalty is incurred by an assessee for concealment of income. The provisions relating to penalty are of a penal character and their object is to punish the assessee so as to deter him from concealing his income in future. Thus, penalty is in the nature of a punishment for the act of concealment, and, therefore, the quantum of penalty must be determined with reference to the law prevailing on the day when the act of concealment was committed and not when the proceedings are initiated or the order is passed.

The provisions of article 20(1) of the Constitution provides that no person shall be subject to a penalty greater than that which might have been inflicted under the law in force at the time of the commission of the offence. Although imposition of penalty under the Income-tax Act is not a punishment for any offence so as to attract article 20 of the Constitution, the principle underlying article 20 would be applicable to instant case, in the absence of any express provision to the contrary.

It is also a settled rule of construction that an amending statute must be given effect to prospectively and not restrospectively unless there in an express provision to that effect. Since, the imposition of penalty is directly related to the act of concealment of the income of the assessee, the material date for the purpose is the date of concealment, and, therefore, the question of penalty must be determined with reference to the law in force on such date.

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1989-90 - Whether addition of Rs. 36,000 was based on estimate, penalty on that account could not be maintained but appropos balance amount, if it could not be said that it was based on estimate, penalty on that account was justified - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1983-84 - Assessee filed return of income declaring certain amount of taxable income - Subsequently, after search, assessee filed returns of income twice for relevant assessment year wherein higher amount of taxable income was disclosed - All authorities below including Tribunal opined that assessee did not voluntarily disclose higher taxable income which remained deposited in assessee's name and, thus, Tribunal confirmed penalty levied under section 271(1)(c) - Whether declaration for purpose of avoiding penalty should be voluntary and before detection of concealed income by department - Held, yes - Whether since, in instant case, assessee had conceded income after department detected same, assessee could not avoid penalty - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1974-75 - Whether where returned income was more than 80 per cent of assessed income, burden of proof to show that penalty was leviable on concealed income, would lie on department - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [as amended by the finance act, 1968, with effect from 1-4-1968] - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1965-66-Return filed on 30-09-1968 - Income concealed-IAC levied penalty almost equal to concealed income applying amended provisions - Tribunal upheld penalty but reduced quantum by applying pre-amended provisions - Whether tribunal was right in law - Held, no

Section 271(1)(c)  read with section 41(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1962-63 - Whether so far as levy of penalty is concerned, there is absolutely no difference between whether income has actually accrued or accrued because of deeming provisions - Held, yes - While filing return, assessee did not disclose income accrued to him under section 41(1) because of repeal of Punjab General Sales Tax (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1960 - ITO having made addition of aforesaid amount imposed penalty under section 271(1)(c) - Tribunal, however held that income having accrued because of deeming provisions of Act, it could not form basis for penalty - Whether, in view of aforesaid legal position, order passed by Tribunal was incorrect and, it was to be set aside - Held, yes [Matter remitted to Tribunal for disposal afresh]

Explanation to section 271(1)(c) of the income-tax act, 1961-Penalty-For concealment of income-ito imposed penalty since difference between returned income and assessed income was more than 20 per cent-tribunal deleted penalty by holding that department had not discharged its burden to prove concealment, but did not give a finding as to whether asseesee had discharged its initial onus under aforesaid explanation-whether tribunal justified-held, no

Section 271(1)(c), read with  section 256, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 28(1), read with  section 66 of the Indian Income-Tax Act, 1922] - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1957-58 - Whether it is not incumbent on officer passing an Order under section 28(1)(c) of 1922 Act to hear assessee or to afford him a fresh opportunity of being heard before passing penalty order even though his predecessor had given reasonable opportunity to assessee of being heard - Held, yes - Whether where Tribunal after knowing fact that concealed income was only Rs. 21,900 thought fit to affirm order of ITO imposing penalty of Rs. 5,000, no question of law arose from its order - Held, yes

Explanation to section 271(1)(c) [as it stood before 1-4-1976] of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Whether even where difference bet-
ween assessed and returned income is less than 20 per cent. Penalty under section 271(1)(c) can be imposed if revenue succeeds in establishing concealment of income -Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment years 1981-82 and 1982-83 - Returns of income were filed after search and seizure operations - Income declared was enhanced by Assessing Officer which was confirmed by Commissioner (Appeals) - Penalty was imposed by treating entire assessed income as concealed income - Commissioner (Appeals) reduced penalty holding that concealment was to be determined with reference to inaccurate particulars furnished in return as case was prior to insertion of Explanation 5 to section 271(1)(c) and that since return of income had been filed after search and seizure operations disclosing major portion of income, there could be no substantive concealment for such income - Whether penalty under section 271(1)(c) could be levied only on income which had not been disclosed in return of income - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c), read with section 256 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1974-75 - penalty levied on assessee under section 271(1)(c) - Tribunal held that there was deemed concealment of income - Whether question as to whether Tribunal had erred in reaching conclusion about deemed concealment of income was question of law to be referred - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c), read with section 256 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1982-83 - Whether findings and conclusion of Tribunal to effect that imposition of penalty in case of assessee was not justified were pure questions of fact and did not give rise to any question of law - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1966-67 - Originally assessee returned an income of Rs. 75,000 but was assessed to tax at Rs. 1,41,595 - Subsequently, assessee in reassessment proceedings initiated under section 147(a) submitted a return on 29-6-1974 declaring an income of Rs. 1,41,595 - Thereafter assessee in view of order of Commissioner in settlement proceedings filed a revised return declaring an income of Rs. 2,25,707 and, was assessed to tax accordingly - Thereafter IAC imposed a penalty of Rs. 1,03,620 upon assessee under section 271(1)(c), dividing in two components: Rs. 19,508 was 20 per cent of difference of tax sought to be evaded on total income of Rs. 2,25,707 and returned income of Rs. 75,000, and Rs. 84,112 was penalty by way of 100 per cent oh income concealed as at 29-6-1974 - However, Commissioner on assessee's admission reduced penalty of Rs. 84,112 to Rs. 40,000-Tribunal upheld order of Commissioner - Whether penalty of Rs. 40,000 imposed on assessee could be said to be in contravention of provisions of Act - Held, no

Section 260A, read with section 271(1)(c), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - High Court, appeal to - Assessment years 1988-89 and 1989-90 - Assessee had claimed deduction of house tax considering actual payment of tax made in years under consideration, in light of proviso to section 23(1) - Commissioner (Appeals) held that such claim would not amount to concealment of income and cancelled penalty - Tribunal upheld order of Commissioner (Appeals) on ground that actual payment having been made and claim having been made for deduction bona fidely, such claim would not amount to concealment for purpose of penalty - Whether once Commissioner (Appeals) had accepted assessee’s explanation in respect of allegation of concealment of income, there was no scope for interference - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c), read with section 256 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1984-85 - Assessee surrendered income when it found it difficult to explain non-disclosure earlier - Income-tax Officer levied penalty under section 271(1)(c) but Tribunal cancelled penalty holding that there was no concealment of income - Whether question of law arose from Tribunal’s order - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income Assessment year 1970-71 - Where in reassessment proceeding assessee filed return showing higher income than one assessed in original assessment, penalty for concealment was justified

Section 220 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Collection and recovery of tax - When tax payable and when assessee deemed in default - Whether where appeal of assessee against assessment order including that of concealed income was pending before Tribunal, recovery of penalty for concealment of income and for non-payment of such penalty was to be stayed - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1983-84 - Assessee’s books of account were seized by department and assessee was not given sufficient time for filing return - Assessee filed provisional return declaring income of Rs. 1,60,000 and after inspecting documents and making copies of accounts, filed another return declaring income of Rs. 2,44,760 - Income was assessed at Rs. 2,57,820 making certain additions relating to cash credits and sales tax liability and latter sale tax addition was deleted on appeal - Assessing Officer initiated penalty proceedings and levied penalty on basis of discrepancy between provisional return and income assessed by department - Whether where Assessing Officer himself had not considered provisional return as valid for assessment purpose, it could not be treated as valid for purpose of levying penalty - Held, yes - Whether mere fact that assessee did not file appeal against cash credit addition, would not automatically mean that penalty could be levied under section 271(1)(c) unless concealment was clearly established by Assessing Officer - Held, yes - Whether since difference between valid return and income assessed by department was only on account of certain petty additions and such additions did not indicate any concealment of income or furnishing of inaccurate particulars of income within meaning of section 271(1)(c), penalty levied was unjustified - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c), read with section 256, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1979-80 - Whether to find out whether any case as contemplated in section 271(1)(c) is made out, one has primarily to see nature of concealment, explanation offered by assessee, his conduct, etc. - Held, yes - Assessing Officer while disallowing assessee’s claim for sales tax, made addition to income and imposed penalty for concealment of income - Tribunal examined entire facts and came to a conclusion that no case of concealment as contemplated under section 271(1)(c) was made out and, accordingly, set aside penalty - Whether any referable question of law arose from Tribunal’s order - Held, no

Section 271(1)(c), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of Income - Assessment year 1968-69 - Assessee-firm filed return showing loss of Rs. 2 lakhs - ITO completed assessment under section 144 on total income of Rs. 50,000/-as against returned loss of Rs. 2 lakhs - IAC considered concealed income at Rs. 2,50,000 and imposed penalty under section 271(1)(c) - Tribunal reduced penalty holding that for purposes of imposition of penalty under section 271(1)(c), income concealed was income actually determined, i.e., Rs. 50,000 - Whether view taken by Tribunal was correct and it was justified in reducing quantum of penalty accordingly - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Whether grant of imposition of penalty on assessee is essentially a question of discussion and if proper explanation is offered and same is accepted by Tribunal, High Court would not disturb such finding in exercise of its jurisdiction conferred under section 256(1) - Held, yes

Section 18(1)(a)  of the Wealth-tax Act, 1957 - Penalty - For failure to furnish returns - Assessment years 1968-69 and 1969-70 - Whether object of section 18(1)(a) is to prevent concealment of wealth and thus, classification of persons, who has failed without reasonable cause to furnish return of net wealth within time, in one category in respect of levy of penalty at uniform rate of one-half per cent on net wealth assessed was an intelligible differentia based on rational relation to object sought to be achieved by statute and, therefore, section 18(1)(a) does not violate article 14 of Constitution - Held, yes - Whether section 18(1)(a) being penal provision intended to prevent evasion of tax and concealment of wealth, it is saved under article 19(5) of Constitution as reasonable restriction on fundamental right of petitioner under article 19(1)(f) of Constitution, in interest of general public and therefore, section 18(1)(a) does not infringe article 19(1)(g) - Held, yes - Whether Parliament lacks legislative competence to enact section 18(1)(a) - Held, no

Section 271(1)(c) , read with section 256 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 28(1), read with section 66 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Penalty - For concealment of income - Whether in matter of imposition of penalty, unless it can be shown that discretion vested in income-tax authorities has been exercised arbitrarily, with no regard to judicial considerations, Court can not require Commissioner to state a case - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 28(1)(c) of Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1960-61 - ITO levied penalty under section 271(1)(c) - Tribunal held that assessment year being 1960-61, provisions of 1922 Act applied and as under relevant provision no minimum penalty had been prescribed, application of provisions of 1961 Act would offend provisions of article 20 of Constitution - Tribunal, therefore, applying section 28(1)(c) of 1922 Act restricted penalty to sum which was less than minimum penalty provided for under section 271(1)(c) of 1961 Act - Whether when penalty proceedings were initiated in 1965, those proceedings would be governed by provisions of 1961 Act - Held, yes - Whether article 20(1) of Constitution is not applicable to proceedings imposing penalty under Act - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, levy of penalty of amount which was less than minimum prescribed under section 271(1)(c) of 1961 Act was not justified - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(iii) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Whether during the period between 1-4-1968 to 31-3-1976 when in place of amount of tax sought to be avoided or evaded the amount of income was made the basis for quantification of the amount of penalty, the term 'income' did not contemplate gross income but contemplated taxable income - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, penalty was to be computed with reference to net capital gains after allowing deductions and not with reference to gross amount of capital gains - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section  28(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1930-31 - Whether maximum penalty that can be imposed under section 28(1) of 1922 Act is a sum representing difference between tax on income declared by assessee and tax on income ascertained under Act in respect of which assessment has been made - Held, yes - Whether in an inquiry under section 28 of 1922 Act, evidence adduced by assessee purporting to disclose real income of assessee is relevant and admissible, not for purpose of varying or affecting assessment made for purpose of imposing tax under Act, but in order to show either that no penalty ought to be imposed, or that amount of penalty ought to be less than maximum prescribed under section 28 - Held, yes

Section 27(1)(c), read with section 256 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1983-84 - Whether question of bona fide mistake in original return of income, rectified in revised return before completion of assessment, could not be termed to be question of law requiring reference to High Court for adjudication under section 256 - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessee voluntarily put in an application for settlement of his tax liability in view of certain assets acquired by him and his wife but not recorded in his books - In pursuance of settlement before Commissioner unaccounted assets were quantified, and after deducting income already returned for relevant years, balance of income was spread over those years - Said settlement further indicated levy of penalties at 40 per cent of concealed income - Penalties were accordingly levied - Tribunal, however, held that substantial moiety of amount agreed for settlement being recorded in assessee's books, it was incomprehensible that assessee should have accepted settlement in respect of such assets - Whether in view of Tribunal taking this view of facts, any interference in its order cancelling penalties was called for - Held, no

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1965-66 - Whether where ITO initiated penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c) in December 1967, maximum penalty that could be imposed was one and half times of amount of tax which would have been avoided and ITO was not right in imposing penalty at rate of 150 per cent of concealed income - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 28(1)(c) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1946-47 - ITO levied penalty under section 28(1)(c) for concealment of income from business in form of deposits appearing in Amanat khatta of assessee in which names of depositors were not available nor any evidence had been given to explain nature and service of amount - AAC confirmed addition and no further appeal was filed which meant that assessee had acquiesced to department’s decision that it was concealed income of assessee from business - Whether there is no essential difference between tax and penalty and liability for payment of both is imposed as part of machinery of assessment and penalty is merely additional tax imposed in certain circumstances on account of assessee’s conduct - Held, yes - Whether if there is material justifying finding that assessee has concealed particulars of income for assessment purposes it could not be said that it was not sufficient to justify imposition of penalty and, therefore, view that penalty proceedings require different or stricter standard of evidence than assessment proceedings or that evidence that is sufficient for assessment purposes may fall short of that required for imposition of penalty was not correct - Held, yes - Whether it is only when income-tax authorities base their earlier finding not on falsity of claim made by assessee about nature of receipt but on their mere holding it not proved, or on their being in doubt whether it was correct or not, that materials they had before them in assessment proceedings can be said to be not sufficient to justify finding adverse to assessee in penalty proceedings - Held, yes - Whether income-tax authorities cannot assess all receipts; they can assess only those receipts that amount to income and, therefore, before they assess particular receipt, they must find it to be income which they cannot do unless they have some material to justify their finding - Held, yes - Whether, since nature of particular receipt is within personal or special knowledge of assessee, onus lies upon him to prove real nature of receipt and not to prove that it is not income and if materials that he produces satisfy income-tax authorities that it is not income, they will not assess it and no question of imposition of penalty will arise at all, but if same are found to be false or not accepted as true by them, it may be sufficient circumstance to justify inference that it does not belong to any kind of non-assessable receipt - Held, yes - Whether onus of proof lies on party and not on Tribunal that has to give finding and, therefore, there cannot be any question of income-tax authorities leading evidence to prove any fact and what is required under law in order to levy penalty is that they must have material to justify their finding of concealment of particulars or deliberate furnishing of inaccurate particulars - Held, yes - Whether where a receipt is income but it is disguished in accounts or in return as non-assessable receipt, as in instant case, it is clearly case of concealment of particulars or of furnishing inaccurate particulars of income and penalty under section 28(1)(c) can be imposed on assessee - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1960-61 - Whether where revised return was filed only after ITO discovered concealed income, quantum of penalty had to be worked out on basis of total assessed figure minus amount originally returned and not on basis of revised return - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c), read with section 256, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1984-85 - Assessee-firm stated to have contracted loans from seven persons who were found by tax authorities as well as Tribunal, as street hawkers, for whom it was very difficult to make out their livelihood by their profession and they did not have required capacity to lend money - Tribunal upheld penalty imposed by assessing authority for concealment of income - Whether Tribunal’s finding being finding of fact, no referable question of law arose from Tribunal’s order - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1969-70 - Assessee’s returned income was less than 80 per cent of assessed income - He, however, did not discharge burden showing that no case for imposition of penalty was made out - Whether, in aforesaid circumstances, imposition of penalty was justified - Held, yes

facts.text:
For the assessment year 1968-69, the assessee filed his original return without showing the income from sale of land, but when required to produce the sale deed in respect of the land sold by him, the assessee filed a revised return showing therein capital gains and business income on estimate basis. The ITO passed the assessment order and also issued notice under section 274 read with section 271 for failure to furnish the return within the stipulated time and also for concealment of income. Later, he levied penalty only under section 271(1)(c) of an amount equal to 100 per cent of the concealed income.

On writ, the assessee challenged the constitutional validity of section 271(1)(c) on two grounds: (1) that section 271(1)(c) is violative of Article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as there is no classification at all even though there is a difference between various types of tax evasions; and (2) that the impugned provisions are a colourable exercise of legislative power inasmuch as in the guise of levying penalty the legislature had enacted for expropriation of the whole of the property of the citizen.

The petitioners, some of whom had been imposed penalty under section 271(1)(c) of the 1961 Act and others under section 18(1)(a) of the 1957 Act, challenged the constitutional validity of these provisions on the ground that they are discriminatory and violative of article 14 of the Constitution of India besides being unreasonable restriction on the fundamental rights guaranteed under article 19(1)(f ) thereof. They further urged that the penalty based on the concealed income on wealth prescribed under the impugned sections is arbitrary and unjust and cannot be regarded as incidental to the levy of tax.

On writ :

The assessee’s failure to file any return provoked the Department to carry out search action under section 132. For the assessment year 1989-90, it was found that assessee had earned a substantial income on the sale of shares. The assessee, in response to notice under section 148, filed the return declaring income, and the assessment was completed on an income of Rs. 4,98,200. In response to the show-cause notice as to why penalty for concealment should not be imposed on the assessee, the assessee contended that there was no mala fide intention to conceal the particulars of income as the sum of Rs. 1,02,000 was paid by way of advance tax attributable to the capital gain and further tax was deducted at source on salary and dividend income. The Assessing Officer levied penalty under section 271(1)(c) by rejecting the assessee’s explanation on the ground that it was only the search action and subsequent issue of notice which forced the assessee to file his return and that mere payment of advance tax did not confer the right on the assessee not to file the return.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the levy of penalty holding that the non-furnishing of the return would tantamount to concealment of particulars of income. The contention of the assessee that such construction would render the provisions of Explanation 3 to section 271(1)(c) redundant was also rejected by the Commissioner (Appeals) who held that Explanation 3 to section 271(1)(c) is applicable to new assessees while the old assessees would be covered by the main provision of section 271(1)(c).

On second appeal :

The assessee-petitioner was a yarn dealer. The ITO holding that the assessee had deliberately furnished false particulars regarding his income made some additions. Assessments for years 1944-45 and 1945-46 were confirmed by the Tribunal while the revision for the assessment years 1946-47 and 1947-48 were dismissed by the Commissioner. Thereafter, ITO initiated proceedings under section 28(1)(c) of 1922 Act. On writ challenging the penalty proceedings the assessee submitted that (1) section 28 of the 1922 Act which enables the ITO and other income-tax authorities to levy a penalty in certain circumstances was not within the legislative competence of the Central Legislature under the Government of India Act, 1935. (2) The procedure for the levy of a penalty for concealment of particulars of the income of an assessee which was an alternative to the launching of a prosecution under sections 51 and 52 of the 1922 Act vested an arbitrary and unguided discretion in the IAC to direct either proceedings for levy of a penalty or for the initiation of a prosecution and that the same was, therefore, violative of article 14 of the Constitution and that on that ground section 28(1)(c) of the 1922 Act ought to be struck down. (3) On a proper construction of section 28 of the 1922 Act the ITO should be satisfied that there has been a deliberate concealment of the income of an assessee during the pendency of the assessment proceedings and as in the instant case the assessment proceedings were completed in regard to the first two years by the dismissal of the assessee's appeals by the Tribunal, and in respect of the later two years by the disposal of the revision by the Commissioner, the orders passed subsequent thereto, levying penalties were illegal and not in conformity with the requirements of the section.

The assessment of the petitioner for the assessment year 1960-61 was completed under section 23(3) of the 1922 Act on 27-2-1965, and thereafter a show cause notice under section 274/271 of the 1961 Act proposing to levy penalty for concealment of income was issued to the petitioner.

On writ, the petitioner contended (1) that the provisions of section 297(2)( g) were ultra vires, being violative of article 14 of the Constitution, and (2) that, in any event, even assuming that the 1961 Act was applicable, no penalty could be imposed under section 271 as the Income-tax Officer could not have been satisfied that there had been any non-disclosure by the assessee in the course of any proceedings under that Act.

In view of certain discrepancies in accounts, the ITO made three additions to the income returned by the assessee. The ITO also levied penalty under section 28(1)(c) of 1922 Act. The AAC confirmed the penalty. On appeal, the Tribunal held that only one item of concealment had been established and that the other items could not be taken to be items of concealment. It, however, held that penalty under section 28(1)(c) of the 1922 Act was justified. As regards the quantum of penalty, the Tribunal held that it would be quite proper to take into account the tax actually avoided in so far as it was referable to the actual concealed income and, in that view, the Tribunal ultimately reduced the penalty.

On reference :

The assessee had constructed four shops and he had shown the cost of construction as per books in a sum of Rs. 15,337. The ITO, however, was of the view that the cost of construction he had shown in the books of account was on the lower side. Later on, the assessee submitted a report from the approved valuer who had estimated the cost of construction in a sum of Rs. 35,900. He produced before the ITO another valuation report showing the cost of construction in a sum of Rs. 21,000. In view of the difference, the ITO had valuation through a valuer of the Department, who estimated the cost of construction at Rs. 24,000. The officer was of the view that the difference between the cost of construction shown as per the books of account and the first estimated value given by the assessee should be taken as income concealed from the Department. On that view, penalty was levied under section 271(1)(c). On second appeal the Tribunal while confirming the view of the authorities below that there was concealment of income on the part of the assessee, fixed the penalty by taking the difference between the second valuation report given by the assessee and the actual cost of construction shown in the books of account.

On reference :

The assessee was a firm dealing in hessian, twines, gunny bags, etc., on wholesale basis. For the relevant assessment year, the ITO added two items as profits and income from undisclosed sources which had been concealed by the assessee and imposed penalty within the maximum limits provided by section 28(1)(c) 1922 Act.

The AAC in appeal held that only the first item be treated as concealed income and the other amount could not be treated as such for the purpose of imposing a penalty. In his opinion maximum penalty payable under section 28(1)(c) of Act 1922 came to Rs. 30,000 and taking into consideration all the circumstances he imposed a penalty of Rs. 20,000 only on the assessee. In appeal the Appellate Tribunal agreed with the order of AAC as regards concealment. However it was held by the Tribunal that, as there had been concealment of profit, it was wholly immaterial whether one item or more than one item had been concealed and the quantum had to be computed under section 28(1)(c) not on the basis of tax on the items proved to have been concealed but on the difference between the tax on the assessee's income as finally assessed and the tax which would have been avoided if the return filed by him had been accepted as correct. The Tribunal restored the order of the ITO imposing a penalty of Rs. 62,000.

On reference, the High Court was of the view that the expression "income as returned" occurring in section 28(1)(c) meant income disclosed by an assessee in the return and not income computed or assessed by the income-tax authorities minus the income added on the ground of concealment. The High Court, while appreciating that the penalty imposed appeared to be disproportionately heavy to the amount concealed, returned the answer against the assessee.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

After completion of the assessment of the assessee under section 23(4) of 1922 Act, the ITO issued a notice to the assessee calling upon him to show cause why a penalty should not be imposed on him in addition to the income-tax payable by him inasmuch as he had concealed the particulars of his income and deliberately furnished inaccurate particulars of such income. The ITO was of the opinion that the assessee deserved a tribute for his acuteness exercised in a wrong direction and that it was difficult to discover the devices of the assessee which were adopted in an ingenious and clever manner. He, therefore, imposed a penalty in the hope that it would be a sufficient warning to the assessee in future. The Assistant Commissioner agreed with the ITO and thought that the circumstances of the case called for the prosecution of the assessee and the assessee should consider himself fortunate in escaping with a penalty.

On an application under section 66(3) of 1922 Act :

The assessee filed its return for the assessment year 1966-67 after 1-4-1968. For concealment of income, which was eventually established, the IAC levied penalty on the basis of the difference between the assessed income and returned income, in accordance with section 271(1)(c) as amended from 1-4-1968. The Tribunal, however, held that penalty had to be levied in accordance with the law prevalent on the first day of the relevant assessment year, and directed that the penalty should be reduced to 25 per cent of the tax sought to be avoided.

On reference :

For the assessment year 1970-71, the assessee filed the return on 26-02-1971 declaring an income of Rs. 1,20,992. The ITO, however, determined the taxable income at Rs. 1,61,180 vide his order, dated 1-03-1972 and referred the penalty proceedings initiated under section 271(1)(c) to the IAC under section 274(2). The IAC held that the concealed income was Rs. 8,657 only and he levied a penalty of Rs. 9,000 vide his order, dated 4-03-1974. On appeal, the Tribunal sustained the penalty order. It held (i) that the IAC had jurisdiction to pass penalty order even though the concealed income was less than Rs. 25,000 ; and (ii) that the penalty order was not barred by limitation as the amendment, effected in section 275 by the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 1970, was retrospective and was applicable to the present proceedings.

On reference :

The search was carried out in case of the assessee under section 132. Pursuant thereto, the assessee was issued a notice under section 158BC, requiring him to file block return in respect of undisclosed income.

The assessee filed the same, declaring total income for block period of Rs. 20.36 lakhs. However, the tax payable on the aforesaid income was worked out at Rs. 12.83 lakhs.

The assessee filed block return with proof of payment of tax, to the tune of Rs. 7.36 lakhs.

The Assessing Officer held that since assessee had failed in making full payment of tax, therefore penalty was impugned under section 158BFA(2).

The Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the appeal filed by the assessee in part.

However, the Tribunal deleted the penalty by holding that since, the assessee had paid tax of more than 60 per cent of the total demand by the revenue and balance demand was paid by the assessee in instalments with interest, no fact of concealment of income had been proved by the department. Thus, the assessee could not be penalised under section 158BFA(2).

On revenue appeal:

In the course of the assessment proceedings, the ITO was satisfied that the assessee had concealed particulars of his income and, consequently, he initiated proceedings under section 271(1)(c). The IAC levied a penalty. On appeal, the Tribunal, while concurring with the finding of the IAC interfered with the order and reduced the penalty entering a finding that concealment of the particulars of income could be only in respect of reduced sum.

On reference:

Two of the partners of the assessee-firm introduced Rs. 19,500 and Rs. 30,000, respectively, as part of their share capital in the firm. It was explained that the amounts had been introduced out of their agricultural income. (a)Engineering contract rate of profit applied 15 per cent

(b)Coal handling contract rate of profit applied 12.5 per cent

(c)Foundry clinckers rate of profit applied 14 per cent

The petitioner made on appeal to the AAC of Income-tax with the result that his total income was reduced by a sum of Rs. 4,172.00. As the total income disclosed by the petitioner in the return, i.e., Rs. 23,968.00 was less than 80 per cent of the income assessed, i.e., Rs. 47,845.00, the ITO started penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c) Explanation. As the minimum penalty leviable in the petitioner's case exceeded one thousand rupees, the ITO, opposite party No. 2, referred the case to the IAC, opposite Party No. 1, under section 274(2) of the Act. The notice was contested, but ultimately opposite party No, 1 held that the provisions of section 271(1)(c) read with the Explanation to that section were applicable to the petitioner's case and thus a penalty of Rs. 2,100 was imposed on the difference between the petitioner on account of the alleged concealment of income based on the difference between the income returned by the petitioner and the income assessed by the ITO and the amount was directed to be recovered by the opposite party No. 2 from the petitioner. It is against this order that this writ petition had been riled, and the relier claimed was that a writ of certiorari be issued for the quashing of the order or assessment, the notice for the imposing of the penalty and the order or the imposition of penalty.

The assessee a Chilean national, at the relevant point of time, was employed with a Switzerland based company (TP-Swiss). In the course of employment he was deputed under an international assignment agreement to an Indian company associated with the employer as a group company ('TP-India'), for the purpose, inter alia, of maintaining uniform standard in quality, processes, and to provide technical support. All the taxes were to be borne by the employer. He was compensated for the services so rendered in India, in addition to the salary, bonus, pension contribution and spouse pension paid by TP-Swiss, by way of salaries and perquisites, such as accommodation, car and utilities, etc., provided by TP-India. While computing the assessee's tax liability in India, the compensation received for aforesaid services was not included in his taxable income for the reasons that (i) the services were for the benefit of TP-Swiss and its group companies other than TP-India, and, as such, TP-India was in no way connected with those services; (ii) the compensation so paid to the assessee was not charged to the profits of any Indian entity; and (iii) the compensation was out of accruals which had no link with TP-India. However, later on, TP-Swiss was advised that the stand so taken by it might not be free from doubt. Therefore, TP-Swiss revised its computation of taxable income in the hands of the assessee, and paid additional taxes. The taxes were paid on 30-8-2006, and the revised statement showing computation of tax liabilities of the employee was filed by TP-Swiss on 4-9-2006. All the requisite information regarding the income was, thus, duly furnished to the Indian tax authorities on 4-9-2006. The income, on the basis of said declaration submitted by TP-Swiss to the Indian tax authorities was recomputed at Rs. 1,23,34,537, as against an income of Rs. 35,47,950 disclosed in the original return. On 17-11-2006, a notice under section 148 for reopening the assessment proceedings so as to bring the income escaping assessment to tax, was issued. A revised income-tax return was filed disclosing a revised income of Rs. 1,23,34,573. The assessment was completed on the basis of the revised return and without making any adjustments thereto.

The Assessing Officer was of the view that the assessee had deliberately concealed an income of Rs. 87,86,620 in his original return, and, it was only after initiating the reassessment proceedings to bring such income to tax that the assessee offered concealed income to tax. He, thus, required the assessee to show cause as to why this lapse on the part of the taxpayer should not be visited with concealment penalty under section 271(1)(c). In response, it was explained that TP-Swiss had suo motu filed all the information about the income subsequently offered to tax on 4-9-2006; that TP-Swiss also proceeded on the basis that there was, to that extent, a short deduction of tax at source; that the tax so short deducted, i.e., tax withholding liability under section 201(1), along with interest on delayed deposit was duly deposited by TP-Swiss; and that the reassessment of income was on the basis of declaration made by TP-Swiss, which was suo motu given by the TP-Swiss. The Assessing Officer, however, was of the view that the assessee was under an obligation to disclose all incomes taxable in India to Indian employer, so that the same could be taken into account while estimating his taxable income in India and taxes at source be properly deducted thereon. According to the Assessing Officer, the assessee should have considered such receipts as his income and he should have also paid due advance tax thereon. The Assessing Officer thus concluded that the intention of the assessee was to conceal the said income and, accordingly penalty was to be imposed under section 271(1)(c). On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the action of the Assessing Officer.

held.text:
As regards the challenge on the basis of Article 14 of the Constitution, it is well-settled that while article 14 forbids class legislation, it does not forbid reasonable classification for the purposes of legislation. In order, however, to pass the test of permissible classification, two conditions must be fulfilled, namely : (i) that the classification must be founded on an intelligible differentia which distinguishes persons or things that are grouped together from others left out of the group ; and (ii ) that that differentia must have a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved by the statute in question.

In deciding whether a taxation law is discriminatory or not it is necessary to bear in mind that the State has a wide discretion in selecting the persons or objects it would tax, and that a statute is not open to attack on the ground that it taxes some persons and objects and not others. It is only when within the range of its selection, the law operates unequally, and that cannot be justified on the basis of any valid classification, that it would be violative of article 14. It is for the person who assails a legislation as discriminatory to establish that it is not based on a valid classification and it is well-settled that this burden is all the heavier when the legislation under attack is a taxing statute. In taxation even more than in other fields, legislatures possess the greatest freedom in classification. The burden is on the one attacking the legislative arrangement to negative every conceivable basis which might support it. Thus, unless the petitioner succeeds in establishing that there was a clear and hostile discrimination by virtue of the impugned legislation, the challenge on the ground of article 14 can not be sustained.

In the instant case, the challenge of the assessee, on the ground of article 14 must fail because in this piece of taxing statute he had not been able to point out any hostile discrimination against a particular type of taxpayer. The fact that the penalty with effect from 1-4-1968, is linked up with the income concealed rather than with the tax evaded shows the gravity which the legislature attaches to such tax evasions. The fact that under section 27l(1)(a)(i ) the penalty for not filing a return is correlated to the amount of the tax evaded as against the correlation of penalty to concealed income under the impugned provisions of section 271(1)(c)( iii) is totally beside the point because, so far as concealed income is concerned, the penalty for concealed income proceeds on altogether a different footing from penalty for omission to file a return in time. The history of legislation shows that Parliament has progressively moved more and more stringent measures of penalty obviously with a view to deter people from evading tax by concealing their income.

The object of the legislation behind all these penalty provisions, whether in section 28 of the 1922 Act or in section 271(1) of the 1961 Act is to provide a deterrent against tax evasion and the provisions are intended to be by way of an effective deterrent to put a stop to the practice which the legislature considers to be against the public interest.

The penalties imposed by the legislature to enforce the tax laws embrace both civil and criminal sanctions. Invocation of one does not exclude resort to the other. Thus, merely because a penalty is provided for concealing income and that penalty is correlated to the income concealed rather than to the tax evaded, it cannot be said that the provision is a piece of hostile legislation or hostile discrimination. The apparent harshness of the provision in the case of evaders of small income arises merely because at the lower levels of taxation the tax imposed is on a much lesser basis than on the higher slabs of income. Therefore, the higher the slab and the greater the extent of the income concealed, the lesser will be the ratio of the penalty, maximum and minimum, to the tax actually evaded as a result of concealment of such income. But this result has been brought about by the higher rates of taxation in the upper brackets of income. In any particular case the actual proportion between the penalty imposed and the tax evaded will depend upon the rate of tax applicable to the assessee concerned and again the penalty is to be levied on the basis of the concealed income and not on the basis of the entire income.

Under these circumstances it was obvious that the impugned provisions of section 271(1)(c)(iii ) could not be said to violate article 14 of the Constitution. As regards the challenge on the grounds of article 19(1)(f ), it could not be said that the provisions are expropriatory. After all, all kinds of punishment and penalties can be said to be ex-proprietary in the sense that some part of the property of the delinquent concerned goes to the State. But, the power to impose punishment and penalties is incidental to the power for vindicating the main purpose of that power.

The object of the legislature in the impugned provision is not to provide for any confiscation but to provide a penalty for concealment of income and that too by providing a deterrent penalty. Deterrence is the main theme or object behind the imposition of penalty and the whole object as shown by the history to this scheme of provisions is to provide gradually more and more deterrent penalties with a view to see that tax evasion does not take place and result in detriment to society as a whole. Therefore, it was not possible to say that the provisions of section 271(1)(c)( iii) infringe article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. Therefore, each of the special civil applications was dismissed.
