The Hon’ble Supreme Court held that payment of differential duty, whether before or after the show-cause notice is issued, cannot alter liability for penalty, the conditions for which are clearly spelled out in section 11AC. From section 11A(1) read with its proviso, it is clear that in case the short-payment, non-payment or erroneous refund of duty is unintended and not attributable to fraud, collusion or any wilful mis-statement or suppression of facts, or contravention of any of the provisions of the Act or of the rules made under it, with an intent to evade payment of duty then the revenue can give notice for recovery of the duty to the person in default within one year from the relevant date. In other words, in the absence of any element of deception or malpractice, the recovery of duty can only be for a period not exceeding one year but in case the non-payment, etc., of duty is intentional and by adopting any means as indicated in the proviso, then the period of notice and the period for which duty can be demanded, gets extended to five years.

The Supreme Court further held that sub-section (2B) of section 11A provides that in case the person-in-default makes payment of the escaped amount of duty before the service of notice, then the revenue will not give him the notice under sub-section (1). This, perhaps, is the basis of the common, though erroneous view that no penalty would be leviable if the escaped amount of duty is paid before the service of notice. It, however, overlooks the two Explanations qualifying the main provision. Explanation 1 makes it clear that the payment would, nevertheless, be subject to imposition of interest under section 11AB. Explanation 2 makes it further clear that in case the escapement of duty is intentional and by reason of deception, the main provision of sub-section (2B) will have no application.

5. Section 80 of the Act provides that penalty should not be imposed if the assessee proves that he has reasonable cause for failure. Earlier, section 80 comprised of only one part. It was broken into two parts, comprising of sub-sections (1) & (2) w.e.f. 28-5-2012. Meaning of reasonable cause

6. In S. Raghbir Singh Sandhawalia v. CIT AIR 1958 Punj. 250, it was held that the expression 'reasonable' means 'rational' according to the dictates of reason and not excessive or immoderate. An act is reasonable when it is comfortable or agreeable to reasons, having regard to the facts of the particular controversy.

This phrase has been interpreted in a number of decisions, including under the I.T. Act. In the case of Municipal Corpn. of Delhi v. Jagan Nath Ashok Kumar, AIR 1987 SC 2316, the SC interpreted the expression 'reasonable cause' as follows:—

"…Stroud's Judicial Dictionary, Fourth Edition, page 2258, states that it would be unreasonable to expect an exact definition of the word 'reasonable'. Reason varies in its conclusions according to the idiosyncrasy of the individual, and the times and circumstances in which he thinks. The reasoning, which built up the old scholastic logic sounds now like the jingling of a child's toy. But mankind must be satisfied with the reasonableness within reach and in cases not covered by authority, the verdict of a jury or the decision of a judge sitting as a jury usually determines what is 'reasonable'…."

Reasonable cause can be reasonably said to be a cause which prevents a man of average intelligence and ordinary prudence, acting under normal circumstances, without negligence or inaction or want of bona fides [Azadi Bachao Andolan v. Union of India [2001] 116 Taxman 249/252 ITR 471 (Delhi)].

Lack of funds or financial crisis has not been held to tantamount to reasonable cause. In Trans (India) Shipping (P) Ltd. v. CCE [2005] 2 STT 82 (Chennai), it has been observed that a delay in payment or non-payment of service tax within the prescribed time due to the cash crisis or financial hardship is generally not approved as falling within the scope of 'reasonable cause'.

Briefly speaking, reasonable cause means an honest belief founded upon reasonable grounds of the existence of a state of circumstances, which (assuming them to be true) would reasonably lead any ordinary prudent and cautious man (placed in the position of the person concerned) to come to the conclusion that the same was the right thing to do. The cause shown has to be considered and only if it is found to be frivolous, without substance or foundation, the aforesaid penalty can be imposed [see Woodward Governors India (P) Ltd. v. CIT [2001] 118 Taxman 433 (Delhi)].

(a)

Legislature's Unpleasant Encounters with Penalty Under Section 271(1)(c)

Matters of penalty levied in the past under section 271(1)(c) had been the subject matter of intense litigation on various technical super technical grounds which may, inter alia, be listed briefly hereunder:

(a)

That penalty was not initiated during the course of assessment.

(b)

That 'satisfaction' as to the initiation of penalty has not been recorded in the assessment order and penalty notice has straightway been issued.

(c)

That 'satisfaction' as to the charge of 'concealment of particulars of income' or 'furnishing inaccurate particulars of income' has not been recorded or is not discernible from the assessment order.

(d)

That there was no definiteness in the 'charge' or 'satisfaction' recorded in the assessment order.

(e)

That penalty notice issued is vague and does not strike off the inapplicable clause of 'concealment of particulars of income' or 'furnishing inaccurate particulars of income'

(f)

That in the penalty order, conclusion is also vague and penalty has been imposed on both the above mentioned charges.

(g)

That penalty was initiated for one charge in the assessment order whereas while passing penalty order, penalty has come to be levied for other charge.

(b)

Legislature's Attempt to be Wiser while Drafting new Penalty Section 270A

Under the new penalty regime, legislature has sought to draft the law in section 270A in such a manner so as to do away with all the possibilities of the above grounds available with the tax payers while contesting the levy of penalty under section 270A.Phraseology used in sub section (1) of section 271(1)(c) and the present penalty provision of sub section (1), (8) other sub sections of section 270A are materially different in this regard which is evident from the plain reading of the referred sub sections of the both the penalty provisions.

Anxiety of the legislature to do away with such pre-requisite of 'recording satisfaction' etc. can be well understood. 'Not recording the satisfaction' or 'recording the satisfaction inappropriately' or the above mentioned variety of technical super-technical grounds raised by the tax payers in the appeals against the penalty levied, had cost the Revenue very dearly in the past, had been the source of the severe body blow profuse bleeding to the exchequer. At the same time, such penalties lost the deterrence effect too due to such penalties having been deleted on these short legal grounds, even when there was enough justification for their levy sustenance on merit. Language of section 270A has thus been so drafted by the legislature as not to admit any such interpretation requiring the initiation of penalty proceeding recording of the 'satisfaction' in the assessment order or meeting the other technical aspects as discussed above, on the lines of the language of section 271(1)(c) its judicial interpretations placed by the Courts.

On the first blush on bare reading of section 270A, there appears to be no legal necessity of initiation or 'satisfaction' and that too for 'recording' of such 'satisfaction' by the assessing officer in the assessment order as to the existence of the 'charge' of penalty under section 270A which used to be there in section 271(1)(c). New dispensation of penalty regime as is evident from the plain literal reading of sub section (1) of section 270A requires assessing officer merely to 'direct' to pay penalty on the 'under reported income'. 5. The following observations of the Court in the case of Baldev Krishna Sahi v. Shipping Corpn. of India Ltd. with reference to section 630 of the Companies Act aptly apply to the suggested amendments also : "Black’s Law Dictionary defines the term "penal" as punishable, inflicting a punishment, containing a penalty or relating to a penalty. The dominant intention embodied by the Legislature in section 630 of the Companies Act is an order for restoration or possession of the property, which is why the punishment provided is only token and incidental. It was for this reason and, to my mind, very rightly that Agarwal, J. used the expression "not purely criminal". I would prefer to describe the section as being quasi-criminal to the extent that the dominant relief permissible and, in fact, the main one, is the restoration is quite obvious that the legislative intent behind this provision was that in the case of a company, it would become virtually impossible for it to continue functioning if its property were to be wrongfully withheld by its employees. Such a situation could obviously lead to economic consequences and to the total collapse of the unit in a given situation. Obviously, therefore, it was essential to bring in a provision whereby such property could be speedily restored, for which purpose, a special provision has been incorporated. There is a definite and rational justification and need for such a provision, which cannot, therefore, be wrongly defined, as an act of favouritism of the property and the punishment for withholding it is the incidental part. Such provisions, though few and far between, are not foreign to criminal law and can be found for instance in section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.

Towards this end, if the Legislature provided for the resort to the jurisdiction of a criminal court, one can never categorise the provision to be devoid of containing a rational nexus to the objective. It was quite clear that the normal civil remedies which are complex and time-consuming were not intended to be resorted to in the case of company property and in sum and substance, the provision of an expeditious remedy for retrieval of the company property, to my mind, completely establishes the rationality between the provisions of law and the object sought to be achieved."

7. The mooting of an amnesty scheme for service-tax evaders is totally misconceived one and a wrong strategy. Amnesties cannot be solutions to the problems of non-compliance. The deleterious impacts of VDISs in the report on the study on 'Aspects of the Black Economy in India', carried out by the National Institute of Public Finance & Policy in 1984-85 have been mentioned in the following words in this report:- "Basically, these schemes seek to coax errant tax evaders to disclose their concealed income and wealth in return for taxation at concessional rates and immunity from penalties and prosecution."

ii.

The view that such schemes permit errant taxpayers to continue on their wayward paths is not supported by the large number of "repeat" beneficiaries of these schemes;

7. Difference between Underreporting and Misreporting

Underreporting of income entails ignoring or just partially declaring the real income obtained, and misreporting of income refers to knowingly submitting inaccurate or misleading information regarding income.

| Particulars | Under reporting of Income | Misreporting of Income |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nature | While underreporting of income entails ignoring or just partially declaring the real income obtained | Misreporting of income refers to knowingly submitting inaccurate or misleading information regarding income |
| Intent | While underreporting may result from ignorance, negligence, or a failure to understand the reporting requirements, | Misreporting suggests an intentional act of submitting inaccurate data to deceive or manipulate. |
| Scope of Inaccuracy | underreporting entails an inadequate or partial income statement with/without any manipulation. | Misreporting sometimes entails falsifying income projections or inflating deductions to reduce tax payments significantly. |
| Penalties | While underreporting can result in penalties that are usually 50% of the tax due | Penalties for misreporting are typically more severe., income reporting errors can result in larger fines of up to 200% of the tax due. |
| Legal Treatment | Tax authorities usually handle underreporting as a civil tax concern and levy penalties and fines. | Misreporting is often considered a more severe offense and may occasionally be subject to criminal prosecution. |
| Detection | underreporting can make it difficult for tax officials to spot differences between reported and real income. | Misreporting might be harder to spot since it includes deliberate manipulation and the fabrication of misleading records. |

3. Quantifying under-reported income: Where income is assessed for the first time and ITR was furnished by the assessee the difference between the income assessed and income determined under section 143(1)(a) would be the under-reported income.

Where no ITR is furnished or where it is furnished in response to notice under section 148 then (i) the amount of income assessed would be treated as under-reported income in the case of company, firm or local authority; and (ii) the difference between the income assessed and the basic exemption limit would be the under-reported income for other taxpayers.

Where it is not a case of the income being assessed for the first time the difference between the income reassessed or recomputed less the amount of income assessed or reassessed or recomputed previously would be the quantum of under-reported income.

4. Instances where it is not under-reporting of income: Section 270A(6) says that the following shall not be treated as under-reported income:

(i)

Where the assessee offers an explanation and the Assessing Officer or the Commissioner (Appeals) or the Commissioner or the Principal Commissioner, as the case may be, is satisfied that the explanation is bona fide and the assessee has disclosed all material facts to substantiate the explanation offered by him, the income so enhanced shall not be treated as under-reporting of income.

(ii)

The amount of under-reported income determined on the basis of an estimate shall not be treated as under-reported income if the accounts are correct and complete to the satisfaction of the Assessing Officer or Commissioner (Appeals) or the Commissioner or the Principal Commissioner provided the method employed is such that the income cannot properly be deduced therefrom.

(iii)

The amount of under-reported income determined on the basis of estimate and the assessee on his own estimated a lower amount of addition or disallowance of the same but has included such amount in the computation of his income and has disclosed all the facts material to the addition or disallowance.

(iv)

The amount of under-reported income represented by any addition made with reference to ALP determined by the TPO in case where the assessee has maintained information and documents prescribed under section 92E and declared the international transaction under Chapter X and disclosed all the material facts relating to the transaction.

(v)

The amount of undisclosed income which is dealt with in section 271AAB.

3. The chasm between the taxable income and the accountant’s or legal concept of income is very wide, more because of the numerous deeming provisions in the tax statute, which nullify them. Tax on capital gains itself is a glaring example of taxing what is not income. Deeming provisions even in respect of salary income treating terminal benefits as normal income, subject, no doubt, to measured relief and various other provisions like anti-compete fee under section 28 of the Act besides such income as from lotteries under section 56, are again other capital receipts, which are treated as revenue receipts, contrary to accepted understanding of revenue as against capital receipts. Provisions for deemed dividend and deeming accrual on receipt basis are other instances.

Some items of revenue expenditure are deemed to be capital expenditure allowed to be amortised over the years as in the case of expenses on mergers and demergers under section 35DD of the Act or VRS payments under section 35DDA of the Act. What makes the taxable income even more distorted making a sweeping departure from real income is the deeming provision like disallowance of what is deemed to be illegal under Explanation to section 37(1) of the Act. Expenditure from which tax is failed to be deducted at source is disallowed under section 40(a) of the Act. Even where mercantile system is followed, cash system is substituted under section 43B, so as to legitimise hybrid system to revenue’s advantage in the matter of taxes, interest to banks and financial institutions and welfare dues. What is worse is the provision to treat cash expenditure above the limit of Rs. 20,000 under section 40A(3) of the Act with minor exceptions on the understanding, that expenditure would include purchases. Apart from what is collected as tax, penalty is collected on deposits and repayments in cash under section 269SS and 269T of the Act, unless reasonable cause is established. Both sections 40A(3) and 269SS and 269T would strangely target genuine transactions, because expenditure, which is not genuine and deposits which are not genuine are taxable as income. The complexity of our laws is more evident in the matters of cross-border transactions with Double Tax Avoidance Agreements hardly touching the existing problems with transfer pricing adding to the existing confusion. Almost every Finance Act would add to the list of deeming provisions.

DISCRIMINATORY TREATMENT OF CORPORATE SECTOR

4. Our system of corporate taxation is highly discriminatory making corporations liable for additional burden by way of book profits tax on one hand and dividend distribution tax on the other. Tax on dividend is a double taxation of corporate income, whether the dividends are assessed in the hands of shareholder or company. Loans and advances are deemed as dividend income of the shareholder or a concern in which the shareholder is interested under section 2(22)( e) of the Act. Right of set off on actual distributed dividend in a later year as provided in the section makes no sense, when such dividend is taxed in the hands of an interested concern, so that it is another instance of double taxation in shareholder’s hands once as deemed dividend and again in the hands of the interested concern, when there is actual distribution of dividend. Deeming loss under the head ‘Capital gains’ on share transactions as speculative under Explanation to section 73 of the Act is a special provision targetting corporations. Fringe Benefits Tax though not limited to corporations imposes further burden especially on manufacturing companies with a large work force.

'Under reported Income'

'Under reported income' has been explained under sub section (3) with the help of various situations of return filing, income shown in the returns filed processed under section 143(1)(a), and assessments reassessments made. Situations have been almost similarly explained about the 'person' who can be considered to have 'under reported income' under sub section (2).

It is noteworthy that penalty under section 270A is leviable on 'under reported income' which, if simply put, is the difference between the income assessed and amount of the income determined under section 143(1)(a) where the return has been furnished. If return of income has not been furnished or return has been furnished under section 148 for the first time, difference between the income assessed and basic exemption limit shall be the amount of 'under reported income'. Since in case of a company, firm or local authority, there is no basic exemption limit, thus the amount of 'under reported income' would be equal to the income assessed where the return of income has been filed by them for the first time. Certain other situations of the 'under reported income' too have been envisaged under sub section (3) of section 270A where income processed assessed was on deemed basis under section 115JB/115JC, or post-assessment assessed income has the effect of reducing the loss or converting the loss into income.

Without going into the fine nitty-gritty of these provisions putting simply, we would not be wrong if we say, that the 'under reported income' would be the difference between the income assessed income processed under section 143(1)(a). If it is a case of reassessment under section 147 or under section 153A, 'under reported income' would be the difference between the reassessed income and the earlier assessed income.

At the cost of repetition, we would urge that we have sought to simplify the meaning of 'under reported income' or else, we would also have landed in the similar complex maze, labyrinths round-about of situations mentioned in sub section (2) (3) of section 270A. Thus, it would be sufficient to say that there is in a way automatic 'under reported income' the moment there is difference between the assessed income and processed income subject to the exclusions given in sub section (6) of section 270A.

But, there may well be a situation whereby assessing officer while passing the assessment order finds that the 'under reported income' or part thereof is covered under any one or more of the clauses (a) to (e) of sub section (6). Detailed discussion in this regard has been made under the following caption titled 'Exceptions to or Exclusions from the 'Under reported Income'. In such a scenario, the assessing officer may reduce the amount of 'under reported income' by the amounts of additions/disallowances so covered by clause (a) to (e) of sub section (6).If after excluding such amounts covered under clause (a) to (e) of sub section (6), there remains no 'under reported income', the assessing officer may not even initiate the penalty proceeding under section 270A, in the assessment order.

That is why whenever there would be additions/disallowances made in the assessment order which would make the income assessed more than the income processed, all that the assessing officer has to do is to initiate penalty under section 270A, as there is 'under reported income' on the face of the assessment order.

5. Such schemes have been adversely commented upon by tax economists and policymakers. Some observations were as follows:—

Policy of leniency in tax matters has not been favoured. Shri A.M. Nremner, while giving evidence before the Royal Commission on Income Tax had said as early as in the year 1920:—

"The real way to prevent fraud …. Is that fraud should be punished by terms of imprisonment; that is the way to stop it. It will never be stopped in any other way; the temptation is so great now. Expert Committees on taxes in the past have disfavoured such schemes for tapping black money with immunities. The Wanchoo Committee has said:—

"We consider that a disclosure scheme is an extraordinary measure, meant for abnormal situations such as after a war or at a time of national crisis. The taxpayer can use section 270A(6)(a) to press his stand that he has offered bona fide explanation and it is for the income-tax authority to record why he is not satisfied with the explanation of the taxpayer.

(b) Placement of section 270A(6):Section 270A(1) gives the overall scope of the provision empowering the income-tax authorities to levy penalty for under-reported income which could include under-reported income as such or due to misreporting of income. Sub-section (6) is meant for the entire section 270A and not for under-reported income simpliciter. Unfortunately, it is placed after describing the under-reported income simpliciter but much before the misreporting of income dealt with in sections 270A(8) and 270A(9). Ideally, section 270A(6) must have been placed after explaining both under-reported and misreported incomes so that its applicability / coverage would not have created confusion and ambiguity.

(c) Misrepresentation or suppression of facts: Under-reporting of income due to misreporting of income is one of the instances covered in section 270A(9). The expression 'misrepresentation' could be found in section 245D(6) (relating to settlement of cases) and in section 245T (relating to advance ruling). In both, settlement of cases and in advance ruling the taxpayer is given opportunity of being heard. Only on representing the case before the prescribed authority, there could be a possibility of misrepresentation.

Where there is no query from the income-tax authority and no reply from the taxpayer, any addition made could not be called as 'misrepresentation'. It could be argued that misrepresentation is implicit by submitting incorrect ITR with details of income chargeable to tax and thus when wrong claims in the ITR when negatived, it amounts to misrepresentation of income.

The other aspect 'suppression of facts' entails a deliberate act of not revealing the facts and not necessarily twisting of facts. Not furnishing the facts could amount to suppression of facts.

The expression "misrepresentation and suppression of facts" could create great hardship to the taxpayers as any addition made otherwise than by way of estimated addition would be construed as misrepresentation or suppression of facts by the tax authorities.

(d) Failure to record investments in the books of account: This expression would cover unrecorded investments of the taxpayers chargeable to tax as income. But usage of the expression "recording investments in the books of account" seems to provide a leeway in cases where the investments do not belong to the business. Obviously, in such cases, the unrecorded investment would belong to the family of incomes which are chargeable to tax under section 115BBE with resultant penal consequence under section 271AAC of 10% of the unrecorded investments, which is less severe than 200% penalty envisaged in section 270A(8) read with section 270A(9).

(e) Claim of expenditure not substantiated by any evidence: Where the assessee incurs expenditure, which is not substantiated would be treated as misreporting of income. For example, if the assessee has incurred expenditure by way of salary to employees and did not maintain vouchers or the payment was not incurred through banking channel a confirmation from the employees would be adequate for allowance of claim. Where the expenditure claim is not substantiated by any evidence that could only lead to the claim of expenditure treated as misreporting of income.

(f) Recording of false entry in the books of account: This would cover making of accounting entries in the books of account for the purpose of under-reporting of income through misreporting. Where the income is not impacted even if the entry is a false entry for example a journal entry between two suppliers account or inter se customers accounts will not fall in this category. Further one has to take notice of section 271AAD which penalizes false entry in the books of account and which is independent of any other provision in the Act. It includes not only a false entry but also omission of any entry which can impact the total income chargeable to tax under the Act. For example, purchase not recorded in the books of account is not a false entry but it is an omission of entry which is covered by section 271AAD.

Thus recording false entry /omission of entry in the books of account would attract penalty under section 270A(8) @ 200% plus penalty under section 271AAD @ 100%.

Background Introduction

Section 270A has been inserted under the Income Tax Act, 1961 to take effect from 1.4.2017 i.e. from assessment year 2017-18, to provide for the levy of penalty on the 'under-reported income'. Hon'ble Finance Minister while presenting the Finance Bill, 2016 mentioned about his resolve to reduce the litigation and provide certainty in taxation including in the matter of penalty. Memorandum explaining the provisions of the Finance Bill, 2016 gave an insight into the amendment in penalty provision by terming the proposal to introduce section 270A as 'Rationalisation of penalty provisions' emphasizing further that in order to rationalize and bring objectivity, certainty and clarity in the penalty provisions, it is proposed that section 271 shall not apply to and in relation to any assessment for the assessment year commencing on or after the 1stday of April, 2017 and subsequent assessment years and penalty be levied under the newly inserted section 270A with effect from 1stApril, 2017. The new section 270A provides for levy of penalty in cases of underreporting and misreporting of income.

Section 270A

Since section 270A is quite lengthy section, hence we have put this section at the end of this article so that reference to various provisions of this section can be easily made for better comprehension. Also, Section 270AA, section 271(1)(c) section 275 too have been similarly appended.

Provisions in Brief

According to the plain provision of sub section (1) of section 270A, the Assessing Officer or the Commissioner (Appeals) or the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner may 'direct', 'during the course of any proceeding' under the Income Tax Act, 1961, to levy the penalty on a person who has 'under reported' his income such penalty shall be in addition to tax, if any, and would be on the 'under reported income'.

Sub section (2) provides as to who can be a person considered to have 'under reported income' whereas sub section (3) provides as to how 'underreported income' shall be computed.

Sub sections (4) (5) speak for the 'under reported income' the preceding year(s) to which such 'under reported income' would relate, in respect of the amount of intangible additions made in the past where no penalty was levied on such intangible additions, if any deposit, receipt or investment made in the current year is sought to be explained with the help of such past intangible additions and. In fact, sub section (4) (5) of section 270A are on the lines of Explanation 2 to section 271(1)(c).

Sub section (6) of section 270A provides five exhaustive situations in which additions/disallowances mentioned thereunder made in the assessment order may not constitute 'under reported income'.

Thereafter, sub section (7) provides the rate of penalty in respect of the 'under reported income' equal to 50% of the tax payable on such 'under reported income'.

Subsection (8) provides for the levy of penalty equal to 200% of the tax payable on the 'under reported income' if such 'under reported income is in consequence of misreporting of income' instances of which have been exhaustively listed in the form of six cases (a) to (f) under sub section (9).

Sub section (10) provides for the methodology for computing tax payable in respect of the 'under reported income'.

Sub section (11) is to provide that there would be no penalty on any addition or disallowance made if such addition or disallowance has already formed the basis of imposition of penalty on a person either in this year or in any other year.

Sub section (12) mandates the passing of penalty order in writing.

So, this is the new penalty section 270A in place of section 271where there used to be in all 8 live sub sections (count wise) and 7 Explanations, as against 12 sub sections 1 Explanation engrafted now in section 270A. Thus, reincarnated penalty provision under section 270A is 'simplified' at least in that respect and extent.

9. The problem is not only with the law, it is as much from erratic interpretations of law, which distort ‘income’. No attempt is made to clarify the controversial interpretations on any of the issues. Under the Income-tax Act, certain categories of income are taxed at the Maximum Marginal Rate (MMR) rather than the normal slab rates or other rates otherwise applicable to the assessee. The concept of MMR was introduced as an anti-avoidance measure to discourage high-income taxpayers from reducing their tax burden by distributing income among multiple entities, such as private trusts, Associations of Persons (AOPs), or Bodies of Individuals (BOIs), that might otherwise be eligible for lower tax rates.

By taxing such income at the MMR, the Act seeks to ensure tax neutrality and discourage tax avoidance, particularly in cases where the shares of beneficiaries or members are indeterminate or where the legislature considers taxation at the highest rate appropriate.

The provisions relating to MMR apply to specified entities and circumstances, including certain trusts, AOPs/BOIs, business trusts, Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs), and registered Non-Profit Organisations (NPOs). Introduction

1. Aiming to kick the tax criminals, the new Finance Minister has tightened the penalty clauses in the new budget, to give the baddies a run for their money. If one plays with the law, one would have to pay. From exorbitant fines to special financial reporting institutions, the Finance Minister has announced a slew of penalty measures.

Understanding Penalty

2. Let us first know what penalty exactly means. The word "penalty" has not been defined anywhere in the Income-tax Act. It is a punishment for offence commited, in realm of income-tax law. There have been arguments against the imposition of penalty itself. In Hindustan Steel Ltd. v. State of Orissa [1972] 83 ITR 26 (SC) case it was held that penalty should not be imposed just because it was lawful to do so. In CIT v. Suresh Chandra Mittal [2001] 251 ITR 9/119 Taxman 433 (SC) case held that the burden of proving necessity of penalty was on the tax department's shoulders.

New penalty provisions

3. The fiscal budget 2014-15 has made novel changes in the penalty provisions, which have been analysed hereunder:

3.1 AIR substituted with "Statement of Financial Transaction or Reportable Account" :- Section 271FA of the Income-tax Act, which related to penalty for failure to furnish Annual Information Return (AIR) has been drastically amended. The words 'annual information return' has been substituted by the word "statement of financial transaction or reportable account." Both, in marginal heading and body, the annual information return has been struck off. Not only this, the budgetary amendment has specified that wherever the word "return" occurs, it should be replaced by "statement." The meaning of all these changes is that there would be no penalty, if annual information return is not furnished. Only if statements of financial transactions or reportable accounts are not submitted penalty would be imposed.

The income-tax department can now-a-days find about an individual's bank deposits, sale or purchase of property mutual fund shares or credit card purchases through it's extensive information system or just PAN card. To put pressure on assessees to file annual information return and then impose penalty clause for non-submission was harsh till now. The new step is a healthy innovation.

3.2 Pay through the nose now - A new section 271FAA has been introduced in the Income-tax Act, which has taken up cudgels against errant taxpayers. Where a person who is required to furnish a statement under section 285BA (i)(k) provides inaccurate information and where inaccuracy is due to failure to comply with due diligence requirement under section 285BA(7) or is deliberate, or person knows of inaccuracy at time of filing but does not inform the concerned authority or discovers inaccuracy after statement is furnished and does not inform and furnish correct information in 10 days, he would have to pay 50,000 rupees, by way of penalty.

The strict penalty has been devised to bring tax dodgers tottering down on their knees. The penalty has been hiked from 100 rupees for each day of default to a staggering 50,000 rupees, at one go. Small doses are not enough; the department seems to have felt. That is why big, bitter medicinal syrup has been administered. The measure would be a deterrent for falsification of accounts by unscrupulous tax evaders.

The due diligence requires that the statement of financial transactions is certified by a renowned authority like ICAI or a chartered accountant on behalf of ICAI.

Any deliberate furnishing of inaccurate information, knowledge of inaccuracy or discovery of inaccurate facts and non-intimation to income-tax authorities would entangle defaulters seriously.

The only relief now available is that if a person discovers inaccurate facts after filing financial statement or reportable account, he can, within 10 days inform the income-tax department and render correct information. This grace period is given, because the penalty amount is so high. An assessee should take advantage of the 10 days time slot available to set things right.

All cases viz. clause (a) to (f) of sub section (9) ought to lead to addition to income or disallowance of a claim resulting into the difference between assessed income and processed income. This is so because if there is no such difference, that would mean that there is no 'under reported income' and when there is no 'under reported income', there would not be 'under reported income in consequence to 'misreporting of income'. In other words, this can be put like this that even if 'charge' is there but if quantification or machinery fails, no pecuniary consequence in the form of penalty under section 270A would follow.

For instance, even if there was 'failure to report international transaction' or 'specified domestic transaction' but during the course of assessment, there may not result any addition/adjustment on this account as assessee may have proved that such transaction was entered into at arm's length price. In that situation, 'failure to report' such transaction was though ostensibly a case of 'misreporting of income' under clause (f) of subsection (9), yet in so far as the penalty under section 270A is concerned, no penalty can be imposed under that section since there was no addition/adjustment made in the assessment order and thus there was no difference on that account resulting between the assessed income and processed income and accordingly, there was thus no 'under reported income'. (g)

Similarly, not all the 'misrepresentation' or 'suppression' of facts as mentioned in clause (a) of sub section (9) may lead to the addition of income or disallowance of a claim, which means that in the absence of such addition or disallowance made in the assessment order to the returned income, there would not be 'under reported income' and since there would be no 'under reported income' in such a case, there would be no question of penalty under section 270A.

For instance, if a closely-held company having accumulated profits had given a loan to a shareholder who was holding more than 10% shareholding. But in order to camouflage real character of this transaction so that it can avoid the glare of applicability of section 2(22)(e), such company misrepresented this fact by terming and showing this transaction as not in the nature of loan but in the nature of advance in the course of business. Such transaction its real nature when exposed in the assessment of the company would obviously not lead to the addition of income in the hands of the company as the deemed dividend can be taxed in the hands of the shareholder. The fact of the matter is that there would be no addition in the hands of the company on this score. There would thus be no difference between the assessed income and processed income on this account in the hands of the company and thus, there would be no 'under reported income' and accordingly, there would be no penalty on the company under section 270A. Therefore, this is a classic case where despite such rank 'misrepresentation of facts', there may not be 'under reported income' in the hands of the company with no penal consequence under section 270A.

'Penalties and Prosecutions'

35. Need clarity on the levy of multiple penalties under the ITA 2025

The ITA 2025 has omitted the expression "without prejudice" from several penalty provisions, e.g., Sections 440, 441, 443, 444, 460, 462, and 463 (corresponding to Section 271A, 271AA, 271AAD, 271AAE, 271H, 271J, and 271K of the ITA 1961). These sections deal with serious defaults, such as failure to maintain books, false entries, incorrect reporting, TDS/TCS statement defaults and incorrect certifications, etc. In the absence of this phrase, it has become unclear and ambiguous whether any other provisions of the ITA 2025 are still fully effective or whether these provisions will override or conflict with any other penalty provision of the ITA 2025.

This omission has created ambiguity, as taxpayers may contend that only one specific penalty should apply for a particular contravention, thereby precluding other penalties arising from the same transaction or its consequences. This is especially relevant where the same default can trigger dual penalties. The lack of explicit statutory guidance increases the risk of interpretational disputes, inconsistent enforcement, and litigation.

It is therefore recommended that the ITA 2025 be suitably amended or clarified to explicitly state the legislative intent on whether multiple penalties can be levied for the same default. Clear drafting will ensure certainty, uniform application of penalty provisions, and effective deterrence, while avoiding unnecessary litigation.

36. Start-ups may be penalised for not fulfilling conditions after claiming the deduction

Section 140 of ITA 2025 [Corresponds to Section 80-IAC of ITA 1961] does not contain any provision to withdraw the deduction if the start-up fails to fulfil the prescribed conditions. It is apprehended that an amendment could be made to Section 140 to withdraw the deduction if the assessee company fails to comply with the conditions prescribed in the DPIIT's notification.

37. Prosecution for wilful attempt to evade payment of tax should be contingent upon assessment

Section 478 of ITA 2025 [corresponding to Section 276C of ITA 1961] is widely used to initiate prosecution proceedings. The basic difference between sub-section (1) and sub-section (2) of Section 478 is that the former is attracted in cases where there is a wilful attempt to evade any tax, penalty or interest, whereas the latter is attracted when there is a wilful attempt to evade the payment of tax, penalty or interest.

The logical corollary is that to attract the provision of Section 478(2), there should be an already determined tax, the payment of which is wilfully evaded by the assessee. However, the existence of a pre-determined tax is not a condition to be satisfied for attracting the provision of Section 478(1).

It is also stated that both sections use the word "wilfully". However, the word 'wilfully' is not defined and is thus left to the officer's discretion. Thus, to remove the ambiguity, the following changes should be proposed under Section 478.

(a)

A provision should be inserted that sub-section (2) of Section 478 shall not apply unless the assessment determining the tax demand is made.

(b)

A provision should be inserted that sub-section (2) of Section 478 shall not apply if the appellate authority has provided the relief to the assessee in regard to the alleged tax evaded as referred to in sub-section (1) of Section 478.

In other words, the prosecution under Section 478(2) should be linked with the assessment outcome.

38. Prosecution on failure to furnish the return of income should be launched only in proven cases

A prosecution is launched under Section 479 [Corresponds to Section 276CC of ITA 1961] if a person fails to furnish the return of income, which he is required to furnish under Section 263(1)(a) [Corresponds to Section 139(1) of ITA 1961] or in pursuance of a notice issued by the Income-tax authorities. Such an offence is punishable with rigorous imprisonment of 3 months to 7 years and with a fine.

Section 273B of the Act – Shelter of "reasonable cause" not available for penalties under Section 270A of the Act

As we are aware, section 273B of the Act provides for non-levy of penalty, levied under the specific provisions mentioned therein, if the taxpayer proves that there was a reasonable cause for the failure.

Immunity under Section 270AA of the Act not available for misreporting of income

To reduce instances of levy of penalty inter-alia in cases where the addition(s) made in the assessment /re-assessment proceedings (leading to the levy of penalty) has(ve) been accepted, section 270AA of the Act has been introduced by the Finance Act, 2017 to provide the taxpayer an opportunity to seek, from the Assessing Officer, immunity from imposition of penalty under section 270A of the Act.

This is subject to fulfillment of the following conditions:

(a)

Payment of tax and interest within the specified time.

(b)

Non filing of any appeal against the order of assessment/reassessment.

An important point to note here is that the aforesaid immunity provisions are applicable for penalty levied/sought to be levied under section 270A only vis-à-vis cases related to "underreporting of income". In other words, no immunity can be sought in cases of "misreporting of income".

In addition to above, the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT), vide Circular No. 05/2018 dated 16 August 2018, has clarified that an application made by an assessee under section 270AA of the Act seeking immunity, will not bar the assessee from contesting the same issue in any earlier assessment year. This circular also clarifies that the tax authority shall not take an adverse view in penalty proceedings for earlier assessment year(s) under the old penalty regime merely because the taxpayer has applied for immunity under the new penalty regime.

Interplay between Section 271G of the Act and Section 270A of the Act – Double blow?

Section 270A of the Act inter-alia provides for the levy of penalty for underreporting of the income, if information prescribed under Section 92D of the Act is not maintained.

Section 271G of the Act seeks to levy a penalty of 2 percent of the value of international transaction for failure to furnish any information as required under section 92D (3) of the Act. The said section is an independent section.

Accordingly, a literal interpretation of the above sections may seemingly lead to a double blow to taxpayer by levy of the penalty in both the sections. However, one point of difference could be that penalty under section 270A of the Act may only be sustained if the transfer pricing adjustment is upheld before the higher authorities whereas the penalty under section 271G of the Act is usually independent of the fate of transfer pricing adjustments; though there are contradicting decisions on the subject.

(viii)

Thin line of difference exists between the term 'suppression of fact' (misreporting of income) and 'disclosure of material facts' (underreporting of income)

There is a thin line of difference between the term 'suppression of fact' as mentioned under misreporting of income and 'disclosure of material facts' as contemplated under underreporting of income. Given that either of the terms are not defined under the Act, it may open up the doors for prolonged litigation as penalty under the head 'underreporting' is lower than what is contemplated under 'misreporting of income'.

Evidence for developing countries is more limited however and this is well discussed in (Fuest & Riedel 2012). The lack of reliable and consistent data is often one of the most significant constraints faced by researchers. The current global financial recession and the associated policies for fiscal consolidation have made tax evasion and avoidance a prominent issue for developed countries. However, the effects of tax avoidance and evasion are probably more significant for developing economies. While tax revenues in OECD countries represent around 35 per cent of their gross domestic product (GDP), developing countries obtain on average only 13 per cent according to (International Development Committee 2012). The low amount of tax raised by developing countries often leads to a situation where governments cannot obtain the financial resources required to guarantee citizens' access to essential services, such as healthcare, clean water and sanitation, and education. In addition, low tax revenues often imply the need for governments to increase debt and aid levels, which in turn can skew accountability towards creditors and donors.

The low level of tax revenues raised in developing countries is caused by a number of reasons. The existence of large informal sectors, high levels of poverty and the consequent inability of poorer citizens to pay taxes, the abuse of tax incentives (e.g. tax holidays) to attract foreign direct investment, and tax avoidance and evasion by corporations and individuals can be identified as the most relevant causes, coupled with the existence of weak institutional capacity to expand the tax base and enforce taxpayers' compliance.

Determining the economic and social impact of each of these factors is not an easy task to accomplish, not even at a national level. Nonetheless, research available provides useful insights. In relation to the losses caused by the existence of a shadow economy, (Schneider 2005) estimated that developing countries could lose as much as US$ 285bn (£188.6bn). As for the revenue foregone because of tax incentives, (Government of India 2012) indicated that losses could have represented in 2011 as much as 5 per cent of GDP. Similar staggering figures were suggested in recent research by (Tax Justice Network-Africa & ActionAid International 2012)on the use of tax incentives in east and central Africa. Finally, (Gurría 2008), the head of the OECD has stated that developing countries could be losing three times the amount they receive in aid because of tax evasion and avoidance through tax havens.

This statement would justify why tax havens have been incorporated into the analysis as one of the fundamental elements of the systems and strategies associated with tax evasion and avoidance practices. Two main reasons may explain why tax havens play an important role:

1.

Tax havens offer nil or low tax rates, so they can produce an important incentive for corporations and individuals to shift income from high-tax jurisdictions.

2.

Tax havens often offer secrecy provisions (e.g. banking secrecy, lack of exchange of tax information with other jurisdictions, disguise of beneficial ownership, etc.), so they enable tax evasion and avoidance practices, allowing the taxpayer to remain hidden from tax authorities elsewhere.

Both elements – low tax rates and secrecy – combine to increase the capacity of tax havens to attract foreign capital, which is much easier to move between countries as a result of intensive globalisation and financial de-regulation since the 1970s. However, secrecy jurisdictions should not be seen as just geographical locations. Because of their connectedness to major international financial centres, tax havens need to be understood as a fundamental element of a broader system and industry that supports tax evasion and avoidance, as argued, for example, by (Shaxson 2011).

One of the research avenues in past years has focused on estimating the wealth stock deposited in tax havens' bank accounts and its associated tax losses for developing countries. A recent report by Tax Justice Network by (Henry 2012), for instance, estimates that as much as US$ 32tn (£21.2tn) could be held offshore. The same report states that developing countries could be losing US$ 189bn (£125.1bn) in associated tax revenue every year.

The importance of and role played by tax havens in today's world economy becomes clear by looking at some Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) figures. According to (OECD 2013a), in 2010 Barbados, Bermuda and the British Virgin Islands received more FDI (combined 5.11 per cent of global FDI) than Germany (4.77 per cent) or Japan (3.76 per cent).

During the same year, these three jurisdictions made more investments into the world (combined 4.54 per cent) than Germany (4.28 per cent). On a country-by-country position, in 2010 the British Virgin Islands were the second largest investor into China (14 per cent) after Hong Kong, while Mauritius is the top investor into India (24 per cent).

4.3 Penalties under sections 76 and 78 are for different offences - The court further observed that the penalty imposable under section 76 is for failure to pay service tax by the person liable to pay the same in accordance with the provisions of section 68 and the rules made thereunder, whereas section 78 relates to penalty for suppression of the value of taxable service. Of course, these two offences may arise in the course of the same transaction, or from the same act of the person concerned. But the incidence of penalty is distinct and separate and even if the offences are committed in the course of same transaction or arise out of the same act, the penalty is imposable for ingredients of both the offences. There can be a situation where even without suppressing value of taxable service, the person liable to pay service tax fails to pay. Therefore, penalty can certainly be imposed on erring persons under both the above sections, especially since the ingredients of the two offences are distinct and separate. Perhaps invoking powers under section 80 the appropriate authority could have decided not to impose penalty on the assessee if the assessee proved that there was reasonable cause for the said failure in respect of one or both of the offences. However, no circumstances were either pleaded or proved for invocation of the said section also. In any event it could not be held that an assessee who was guilty of suppression deserved such sympathy. As such, the Single Judge was not correct in directing the appellant (the revenue) to modify the demand withdrawing penalty under section 76. The writ petitions were liable to be dismissed.

Thus, it is evident that when a person fails to pay tax even without suppressing the value of a taxable service, thus invoking the penalty under section 76, he would be penalized for a separate offence of suppressing the value of a taxable service under section 78.

Case I

Example 1. Payment of penalty under section 73(4A)

Assessee ‘A’ has been found to have short-paid Rs. 1 lakh during audit. The transactional details as available in the specified records are true and complete. Example 2. Payment of penalty under section 78(1)

Assessee ‘B’ has short-paid the tax by Rs. 1 lakh by suppressing the records. Anti-evasion files a case after 3 years. A notice is issued to him under section 73(1) proviso. The true and complete transactional details are available in specified records. He pays Rs. 1 lakh along with interest and 25 per cent of penalty within 30 days of the order.

Assessee ‘A’ has short-paid without any established intent. Assessee ‘B’ has short-paid by suppression of facts. The mere fact that section 73(4A) states in the context of an audit or an investigation doesn’t mean it is found to be a short payment by reason of fraud or wilful default. A. Preview

Over the years, transfer pricing adjustments have become a common phenomenon for multinational companies engaged in voluminous cross border transaction(s) with related parties. Hitherto, the trend has been that tax authorities have initiated penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (the Act) in almost every case where a transfer pricing adjustment has been made. Penalty has even been levied in a number of cases pending at various stages in the appellate hierarchy.

Based on data available in the public domain, instances of penalty levied being sustained at the appellate stage, is significantly low. One such instance, where the levy of penalty was confirmed by the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) is in the case of Genom Biotech (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [2016] 67 taxmann.com 219 (Mum. - Trib.). This was a case where penalty was levied for the failure on the part of the taxpayer to adopt Comparable Uncontrolled Price Method for benchmarking the transaction of sale of goods and for not benchmarking it separately. While confirming the levy of penalty, the ITAT observed that the assessee was silent in the explanations on both the 'due diligence' and 'good faith' issues. However, in a later decision the ITAT in the case of Mitsui Prime Advanced Composites India (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2016] 70 taxmann.com 123 (Delhi - Trib.), refused to accept the proposition laid out by the Revenue - addition on account of transfer pricing adjustment invariably means absence of good faith and due diligence; then each and every case involving transfer pricing adjustment would call for imposition of penalty. While doing so the ITAT has held that "the proposition so propounded on behalf of the Revenue is too wide and clearly unacceptable inasmuch as the intention of the legislature is to impose penalty due to addition on account of transfer pricing adjustment only when good faith and due diligence are lacking and not because of a genuine and valid difference of opinion in the determination of ALP of an international transaction". This view of the ITAT has subsequently been affirmed by the Delhi High Court in the appeal filed by the Tax Department in the case of Pr. CIT v. Mitsui Prime Advanced Composites India (P.) Ltd. [2017] 79 taxmann.com 283/392 ITR 280 (Delhi).

Finance Act, 2016 made a significant amendment to the Act in relation to rationalisation of the erstwhile penalty provisions under section 271(1)(c) of the Act. The Hon'ble Finance Minister in his Budget speech mentioned, "Levy of heavy penalty for concealment of income has over the years resulted in large number of disputes despite a number of decisions of the Apex court on interpretation of statutory provisions and principles guiding imposition of penalty. …. I propose to modify the entire scheme of penalty by providing different categories of misdemeanor with graded penalty and thereby substantially reducing the discretionary power of the tax officers."1

Accordingly, Finance Act, 2016 inserted a new section 270A effective from 1 April 2017 to rationalise the penalty provisions. In this article, an attempt is made to demystify the impact of new penalty regime in transfer pricing assessments.

C. Section 270A – Potential transfer pricing exposure in the new penalty regime

Having looked at the provisions of law, let us now test the common issues which have come up in transfer pricing assessments in the past for a potential exposure to the new penalty regime:

(i)

Transfer pricing adjustment for difference in opinion – can it be said to be underreporting of income?

Typically, difference of opinion has arisen on the following issues:

(a)

Characterisation of the entity;

(b)

Aggregation vs segregation;

(c)

Comparability factors;

(d)

Method of benchmarking; etc.

The law provides that no penalty for underreporting of income shall be levied in cases where:

(a)

Information and documents as prescribed under section 92D are maintained;

(b)

Relevant international transaction under Chapter X is disclosed in Form 3CEB, and

(c)

Material facts relating to the transaction are disclosed

The taxpayer in the above cases may maintain the information and documents under section 92D of the Act as per its bona fide belief; however, tax authorities may have an opinion contrary to the taxpayer's.

Accordingly, in such cases, it will be imperative for the taxpayer to demonstrate before the authorities, from documentation and other supporting evidences, that the position taken by it, be it for classifying its activities or for justifying its transfer pricing approach, leads to a possible view on the subject. A view against it, on merits, is not due to non-furnishing or disability to explain any evidence, but a purely interpretational issue.

(ii)

Transactions where there is ambiguity over applicability of transfer pricing provisions – Can it be construed to be misreporting of income?

Another thought provoking situation may arise when there is a dispute between the taxpayer and tax authorities over the applicability of the transfer pricing provisions. These are typically cases where the taxpayers have historically denied of any international transaction(s). For example, incurring of advertising, marketing and promotion expenses, giving of interest-free loans and/or extending of guarantees to associated enterprises, etc.

In such cases, a question may arise as to whether penalty on account of misreporting of income be levied? This question would arise as such transactions are generally not disclosed and hence one needs to be careful vis-à-vis disclosures in respect thereof.

(iii)

Disclosure of 'material facts' a subjective concept

As mentioned above, for a taxpayer to be safeguarded against the penal provisions of underreporting of income, it has to disclose all material facts relating to the transaction under question. However, as we all know, the term 'material facts' is a subjective concept and may involve different meaning(s) for different stakeholders. It may also be interpreted differently in different situations based on the transaction involved and hence disclosure of material facts still continues to remain a very important self-defense tool even in the new penalty regime.

(iv)

Misrepresentation or suppression of fact – Not defined in the Act

One of the conditions for treating a transaction as misreporting of income is 'misrepresentation' or 'suppression of facts'. The tax authorities, in order to initiate and/or levy the penalty, may highlight/harp on some instances to prove the so-called misrepresentation or suppression and hence monumental burden of proof is thereafter cast on the taxpayers to demonstrate with appropriate evidences, to negate the stand.

It is pertinent to note that the said term has not been defined under the Act thereby leading to different interpretations in different situations. Hence one needs to fall back on the dictionary meaning of these terms.

The dictionary meaning of these terms are:

Duhaime's law dictionary defines "misrepresentation" as a "false and material statement which induces a party to enter into a contract". Further, it also defines "suppression" as "the intentional non-disclosure by the prosecution of evidence favorable to an accused and asked for by the accused, where that evidence is material either to guilt or punishment".

The penalty (for concealment of income, which is substituted) is consi-dered of penal nature, as held by Supreme Court, in the following cases, and it is observed as follows:

(i)

CIT v. Anwar Ali [1970] 76 ITR 696 (SC) 'The first point which falls for determination is whether the imposition of penalty is in the nature of a penal provision. The determination of the question of burden of proof will depend largely on the penalty proceedings being penal in nature or being merely meant for imposition of an additional tax, the liability to pay such tax having been designated as penalty under section 28. One line of argument which has prevailed particularly with the Allahabad High Court in Lal Chand Gopal Das case (supra) is that there was no essential difference between tax and penalty because the liability for payment of both was imposed as a part of the machinery of assessment and the penalty was merely an additional tax imposed in certain circumstances on account of the assessee's conduct. The justification of this view was founded on certain observations in C.A. Abraham v. Income-tax Officer, Kottayam [1961] 41 ITR 425/2 SCR 765 (SC). It is true that penalty proceedings under section 28 are included in the expression "assessment" and the true nature of penalty has been held to be additional tax. But one of the principal objects in enacting section 28 is to provide a deterrent against recurrence of default on the part of the assessee. The section is penal in the sense that its consequences are intended to be an effective deterrent which will put a stop to practices which the legislature considers to be against the public interest. It is significant that in C.A. Abraham's case (supra) this court was not called upon to determine whether penalty proceedings were penal or of quasi-penal nature and the observations made with regard to penalty being an additional tax were made in a different context and for a different purpose. It appears to have been taken as settled by now in the sales tax law that an order imposing penalty is the result of quasi-criminal proceedings [Hindustan Steel Ltd. v. State of Orissa CA Nos. 883-892 of 1965 dt. 4-8-1969 (Since reported in [1970] 25 STC 211 (SC))]. In England also it has never been doubted that such proceedings are penal in character: Fattorini (Thomas) (Lancashire) Ltd. v. Inland Revenue Commissioners [1942] AC 643/[1942] 1 All ER 619/24 TC 328/[1943] 11 ITR (Supp.) 50.'

(ii)

Hindustan Steel Ltd. v. State of Orissa [1972] 83 ITR 26 (SC)

"Under the Act penalty may be imposed for failure to register as a dealer: section 9(1), read with section 25(1)(a) of the Act. But the liability to pay penalty does not arise merely upon proof of default in registering as a dealer. An order imposing penalty for failure to carry out a statutory obligation is the result of a quasi-criminal proceeding, and penalty will not ordinarily be imposed unless the party obliged, either acted deliberately in defiance of law or was guilty of conduct contumacious or dishonest, or acted in conscious disregard of its obligation. Penalty will not also be imposed merely because it is lawful to do so. Whether penalty should be imposed for failure to perform a statutory obligation is a matter of discretion of the authority to be exercised judicially and on a consideration of all the relevent circumstances. Even if a minimum penalty is prescribed, the authority competent to impose the penalty will be justified in refusing to impose penalty, when there is a technical or venial breach of the provisions of the Act or where the breach flows from a bona fide belief that the offender is not liable to act in the manner prescribed by the statute. Those in charge of the affairs of the company in failing to register the company as a dealer acted in the honest and genuine belief that the company was not a dealer. Granting that they erred, no case for imposing penalty was made out."

Interpretation of penalty provisions - Law relating to penalty should be construed strictly in favour of the assessee, more stringent the law, stricter the construction that is required in favour of the assessee.

3.

Penalty proceedings are independent proceedings - Since penalty proceedings are independent proceedings, the matter has to be considered afresh in the light of the law applicable to penalty.

The word 'concealed' is derived from the latin expression 'concelare' which implies contcelare meaning 'to hide'. In Webster's New International Dictionary its meaning is equated 'to hide or withdraw from observation; to cover or keep from sight; to prevent the discovery of; to withhold knowledge of'.

♦♦

India Cine Agencies v. Dy. CIT [2005] 275 ITR 430 (Mad.)

The word 'conceal' as defined in the Concise Oxford Dictionary means—not allowed to be seen; hide; keep secret; prevent from doing known. Concealment implies the existence of a deliberate intent to prevent relevant facts from becoming known.

♦♦

ITO v. R.B.G.M. Modi & Ors. (P.) Ltd. [1988] 31 TTJ (Delhi - Trib.) 550

The expressions 'conceal' has been judicially noticed in several cases by the High Courts and the Supreme Court. In its plain meaning, the word 'conceal' means to hide, to keep secret. The phrase 'concealed the particulars of his income' would, therefore, involve a knowledge on the part of the assessee of income which, though real, is not shown.

♦♦

Ram Saran Gupta v. Asstt. CIT [1997] 58 TTJ (Jp. - Trib.) 599

The word 'conceal' is derived from the Latin word 'concelare' which implies 'con+celare = to hide'. Webster's New International Dictionary equates its meaning 'to hide or withdraw from observation; to cover or keep from sight; to prevent the discrepancy of; to withhold knowledge'. The offence of concealment is thus a direct attempt to hide an item of income or a portion thereof from the knowledge of the income-tax authorities. It is implicit in the word 'concealed' that there has been a deliberate act on the part of the assessee.

♦♦

Yeshwant B. Chigteri v. Asstt. CIT [2000] 75 ITD 377 (Pune - Trib.)

The word 'concealment' or 'conceal' have not been defined in the Income-tax Act, 1961. The words 'conceal' and 'concealment', according to their dictionary meaning, can be used by the Legislature in the widest possible sense. It may include the act of commission as well as the act of omission. But it is a well settled legal position that words in a given statute are to be construed in the context in which they are used. The word 'concealment' is qualified by the words 'of particulars of income'. So one can be said to have concealed the particulars of income if he is under an obligation to disclose the same. The reason is obvious. Penal provisions are to be construed very strictly. No person can be penalised unless he is found guilty on account of his failure to perform his statutory obligation.

♦♦

Sanjay D. Gupta v. Asstt. CIT [2004] 90 ITD 776 (Mum. - Trib.)

Notwithstanding the difference in the expressions 'has concealed the particulars of income' and 'has furnished inaccurate particulars of income', it is well-established that they lead to the same effect, namely, keeping off a portion of the income from the return. The word 'concealment' inherently carries with it the element of mens rea.

♦♦

The dictionary meaning of 'concealment' is to hide, to keep secret. The Explanation does not alter or extend this meaning. It only assumes it to exist if the assessee fails to prove that disclosure was not due to fraud or wilful conduct. Between fraud and innocence, carefulness and gross or wilful conduct, there may be numerous stages. One may not be innocent, yet he may not be a fraud. An action may not be careful but for that reason only it cannot be considered gross or wilful. The assessee may lead evidence in penalty proceedings or may rely on circumstances on records to show that the disclosure was not due to fraud or wilful conduct.

1-6a AGGREGATION OF PENALTY IN CASE OF THE TOTAL INCOME [115JB/115JC] - To provide for aggregation, in section 271(1), Explanation 4 was inserted by the Finance Act, 2015 and the reasons for the introduction of the same were explained as follows:

'Amount of tax sought to be evaded for the purposes of penalty for concealment of income under clause (iii) of sub-section (1) of section 271 Under the existing provision contained in clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271 of the Act penalty for concealment of income or furnishing inaccurate particulars of income is levied on the "amount of tax sought to be evaded", which has been defined, inter alia, as the difference between the tax due on the income assessed and the tax which would have been chargeable had such total income been reduced by the amount of concealed income. Problems have arisen in the computation of amount of tax sought to be evaded where the concealment of income or furnishing inaccurate particulars of income occurs in the computation of income under provisions of section 115JB or 115JC of the Act and also under the provisions other than the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC of the Act (hereafter referred as general provisions). Further, courts have held that penalty under section clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271 cannot be levied in cases where the concealment of income occurs under the income computed under general provisions and the tax is paid under the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC of the Act. Tax paid under the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC over and above the tax liability arising under general provisions is available as credit for set off against future tax liability. Under-statement of income and the tax liability thereon under general provisions results in larger amount of such credit becoming available to the assessee for set off in future years. Therefore, where concealment of income, as computed under the general provisions, has taken place, penalty under clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271 should be leviable even if the tax liability of the assessee for the year has been determined under provisions of section 115JB or 115JC of the Act. Accordingly, it is proposed to amend section 271 of the Act so as to provide that the amount of tax sought to be evaded shall be the summation of tax sought to be evaded under the general provisions and the tax sought to be evaded under the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC. However, if an amount of concealment of income on any issue is considered both under the general provisions and provisions of section 115JB or 115JC then such amount shall not be considered in computing tax sought to be evaded under provisions of section 115JB or 115JC. Further, in a case where the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC are not applicable, the computation of tax sought to be evaded under the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC shall be ignored. This amendment will take effect from 1st April, 2016 and will accordingly apply, in relation to the assessment year 2016-17 and subsequent assessment years. [Clause 68]'.

New sections 273B, 278AA and 278E, were inserted, shifting the burden on the assessee to prove that the failure or omission or commission is with ‘reasonable cause’ or ‘excuse’ or the absence of the existence of culpable mental state. Explaining reasons for these amendments and insertion of new sections, the Explanatory Memorandum1 states that one of the reasons for the unsatisfactory performance of Income-tax Department in the matter of successfully levying penalty and of prosecuting the defaulters is that invariably appellate authorities and the courts have cast upon the Department the near impossible burden of proving the existence of a culpable state of mind on the part of the defaulters. On a consideration of the relevant factors in this regard, it was announced by the Long Term Fiscal Policy that in order to effectively tackle the problem of tax evasion, the Income-tax Department will implement a strategy consisting, inter alia, of removing weaknesses in the law which hinder effective prosecution of tax evaders and that it was intended to incorporate certain provisions in the direct tax laws similar to those which already exist in the Customs Act and the Gold (Control) Act. For example, under section 123(1) of the Customs Act, 1962, when any gold, diamonds or any other class of specified goods are seized in the reasonable belief that they are smuggled goods, the burden of proving that they are not smuggled goods shall be on the person from whose possession, the goods were seized and any person claiming to be the owner of such seized goods. Similarly, under section 98B of the Gold (Control) Act, 1968 in any prosecution for an offence under that Act which requires a culpable mental state on the part of the accused, the court shall presume the existence of such mental state but it shall be open to the accused to prove the fact that he had no such mental state with respect to the offence. Accordingly, the intention of the Government was announced by the Long Term Fiscal Policy to amend the direct tax laws also to provide similar provisions so that once evasion is proved, the intention to evade need not be proved by the Department.

Apart from the above, in the context of the existing scheme of accepting returns without scrutiny, which is based on trust, it is only logical that the burden should be cast on the assessee to prove his innocence if he has concealed the particulars of his income or to prove the existence of reasonable cause if he has committed any other default under the tax laws.

By omitting the words “without reasonable cause” from penalty provisions, it has been provided that default by itself will attract penalty. At the same time, it has been provided by a new section 273B, inserted by the Amendment Act, that notwithstanding anything contained in these provisions, no penalty shall be imposable on the person or the assessee, as the case may be, for any failure referred to in the said provisions if he proves that there was reasonable cause for the said failure. By this amendment, the onus of proving the existence of reasonable cause for the defaults referred to in these provisions has been cast on the taxpayer. In this context, reference may be made to section 123(1) of the Customs Act, 1962.
