On appeal to the Supreme Court, the assessee submitted that the Tribunal having arrived at a finding of fact, the impugned judgment of the High Court could not be sustained and that in any event, no specific question having been referred as to whether the Tribunal’s findings were perverse or not, the High Court committed a manifest error in differing with the findings of fact arrived at by the Tribunal. HELD: Reference of the question to the High Court was general in nature. No question was referred as to whether the finding of the Tribunal was perverse or not. Existence of mens rea is essentially a question of fact. The Tribunal alone, as the highest authority empowered to determine the question of fact, would be entitled to go thereinto. However, the same would not mean that the High Court will have no jurisdiction in this behalf. The High Court, it is well-known, should not ordinarily disturb the finding of fact arrived at by the Tribunal. Question of law should generally arise only accepting the finding of fact to be correct. [Para 9]

It is trite that if an explanation given by the assessee with regard to the mistake committed by him has been treated to be bona fide and it has been found as of fact that he had acted on the basis of wrong legal advice, the question of his failure to discharge his burden in terms of Explanation appended to section 271(1)(c ) would not arise. [Para 13]

The expression ‘conceal’ signifies a deliberate act of omission on the part of the assessee. Such deliberate act must be either for the purpose of concealment of income or furnishing of inaccurate particulars. [Para 15]

The term ‘inaccurate particulars’ is not defined. Furnishing of an assessment of value of the property may not by itself be furnishing of inaccurate particulars. Even if the Explanations are taken recourse to, a finding has to be arrived at having regard to clause (A) of Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c) that the explanation offered by an assessee, in the event, he offers one was false. He must be found to have failed to prove that such explanation is not only not bona fide but all the facts relating to the same and material to the income were not disclosed by him. Thus, apart from his explanation being not bona fide, it should be found as of fact that he has not disclosed all the facts which was material to the computation of his income. [Para 16]

The explanation, having regard to the decision of the Supreme Court, must be preceded by a finding as to how and as to in what manner he furnished the particulars of his income. It is beyond any doubt or dispute that for the said purpose the ITO must arrive at its satisfaction in this behalf. [Para 17]

The order imposing penalty is quasi-criminal in nature and, thus, burden lies on the department to establish that the assessee had concealed his income. Since burden of proof in penalty proceeding varies from that in the assessment proceeding, a finding in an assessment proceeding that a particular receipt is income cannot automatically be adopted, though a finding in the assessment proceeding constitute good evidence in the penalty proceeding. In the penalty proceedings, thus, the authorities must consider the matter afresh as the question has to be considered from a different angle. [Para 18]

It is now a well-settled principle of law that the more is the stringent law, more strict construction thereof would be necessary. Even when the burden is required to be discharged by an assessee, it would not be as heavy as in the prosecution case. [Para 19]

The omission of the word ‘deliberate’ in the amended provision of section 271(1)(c) thus, may not be much significance. [Para 20]

Section 271(1)(c ) remains a penal statute. Rule of strict construction shall apply thereto. Ingredients of imposing penalty remains the same. The purpose of the Legislature that it is meant to be deterrent to tax evasion is evidenced by the increase in the quantum of penalty, from 20 per cent under the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 to 300 per cent in 1985. [Para 21]

‘Concealment of income’ and ‘furnishing of inaccurate particulars’ carry different connotations. Concealment refers to deliberate act on the part of the assessee. A mere omission or negligence would not constitute a deliberate act of suppressio veri or suggestio falsi. [Para 22]

The instant case was not a case where penalty had been imposed for breach of contravention of a commercial statute where lack of or intention to contravene or existence of bona fide might not be of much importance. It was also not a case where penalty was mandatorily impossible. It was, therefore, not a case where the enabling provision should have been invoked. [Para 29]

For the reasons aforementioned, the impugned judgment could not be sustained which was to be set aside accordingly. The appeal was to be allowed. [Para 30]

the assessee and held that there was deliberate concealment which had been fully established and, thus, imposed penalty under section 271(1)(c). On appeal, the Tribunal set aside the order of penalty and held that mere estimate of income without any definite basis did not account for any penalty action. Applying the decision of the Supreme Court in CIT v. Anwar Ali [1970] 76 ITR 696 , the Tribunal cancelled the penalty imposed upon the assessee.

On reference: HELD: In the instant case the assessment was completed on 23-3-1967. On the same date penalty proceedings had been initiated. The satisfaction of the ITO that there was concealment of income thus solidified on 23-3-1967. The penalty was, therefore, to be levied in terms of the law applicable on 23-3-1967. The Tribunal was, thus, in error in cancelling the penalty on the basis of the authority laid down in the case of Anwar Ali (supra). There being obvious discrepancy of more than 20 per cent, the obligation to explain the difference was squarely upon the assessee. The assessee did not produce any material to show that his explanation was correct. There was no explanation as to why the assessee showed a figure of sale before the income-tax authority, lower than what he had stated before the sales tax authority. There was, thus, an obvious concealment. Secondly, in regard to assessed income although it was based on estimate, but the estimate was based upon the assessee's own percentage of income from the records of the earlier years. If the rate of sale was higher in earlier years, the income-tax authority was fully justified in holding that the income could not be lower in a subsequent year, as the rate of sale of coal had not come down. These were sufficient to hold that there had been concealment of income. In fact, the Tribunal did not consider these matters with any seriousness, but merely held that the revenue had not brought anything on record to show that the assessee had concealed any income. The concealment of income was writ large on the record. Moreover, even if one brushed aside the Explanation to section 271(1)(c), the concealment would be obvious even upon the authority of the case of Anwar Ali (supra). Thus, the Tribunal was not correct in cancelling the penalty imposed by the IAC under section 271(1)(c) upon the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 297, read with section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 28(1)(c) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Repeals and savings - Assessment year 1959-60 - Whether for purposes of penalty, there is no doubt classification under section 297(g) between assessees who had filed returns of income before 1-4-1962, and whose assessments were completed before that date and assessees who had filed returns of income before 1-4-1962, but whose assessments were completed on or after 1-4-1962 and, this is an intelligible classification - Held, yes - Whether clauses (f) and (g) of section 297(2) is not to discriminate against those assessees whose assessments for year ending on 31-3-1962, or any earlier year had not been completed before 1-4-1962, but to bring them in line with other assessees whose assessments are completed on or after 1-4-1962, in matter of imposition of penalty - Held, yes - Whether, in view of aforesaid, it could be concluded that section 297 (2)(g) was not violative of Article 14 of Constitution of India - Held, yes

FACT: The petitioner, assessee took forest contracts. It ran a saw-mill and also manufactured and sold furniture. It also did stone quarrying business. For the assessment year 1959-60 the petitioner filed a return of its income under section 22(2) of Act, 1922, on 21-10-1959, showing an income of Rs. 7,896. In the assessment proceedings the ITO noticed some discrepancies in the accounts and registers maintained by the assessee of its business and called upon the assessee to explain the discrepancies and furnish certain particulars. Thereupon, the assessee filed a revised return of its income on 17-1-1964, disclosing its total income as Rs. 50,605. The ITO finalized the assessment on 19-3-1964, after taking into consideration the revised return and issued a notice to the petitioner under section 271(1)(c) for concealment of income. The ITO referred the matter to the AAC as penalty intended to imposed by him exceeded Rs. 1,000.

The Inspecting Assistant Commissioner, finding that the assessee had concealed the particular of its income, made the impugned order imposing a penalty of Rs. 25,000 on the petitioner. The petitioner then preferred an appeal before the Tribunal which was dismissed. In the instant writ petition. It was contended by the petitioner that section 297(2)(g) being violative of article 14 of the Constitution is invalid and, therefore, no penalty could be imposed on the petitioner under section 271 and, that under section 271(1) a penalty can be imposed by the Income-tax Officer or the Appellate Assistant Commissioner only if he, in the course of any proceedings under the Act of 1961, is satisfied that any person has committed any of the acts enumerated in clauses (a), (b) or (c) of section 271(1); that, as the assessment against the petitioner was made under the Act of 1922, and not under the Act of 1961, the Income-tax Officer or the Appellate Assistant Commissioner had no jurisdiction to impose any penalty under section 271(1).

HELD: The effect of clauses (a), (f) and (g) of section 297(2) is that where the assessee files a return of income before the commencement of the Act of 1961, that is before 1-4-1962, for any assessment year, then the assessment of that person for that year is under the 1922 Act; any proceeding for the imposition of a penalty in respect of any assessment completed before 1-4-1962, can be initiated and penalty can be imposed under the 1922 Act; any proceedings for the imposition of a penalty in respect of any assessment for the year ending on 31-3-1962 or any earlier year which is completed on or after 1-4-1962 can be initiated and penalty can be imposed under the 1961 Act. In the present case, the petitioner filed a return of income before 1-4-1962, but the assessment was completed on 19-3-1964, that is after 1-4-1962, therefore, clause (g) of section 297(2) was plainly attracted for the initiation of proceedings for imposition of penalty under the Act of 1961.

. An. appellate authority in the case of an assessee whose assessment is completed before 1-4-1962, can reached a finding that there is a concealment of income and such a finding can be reached even after 1-4-1962. Thus, if the completion of assessment has any relevance in determining whereunder and in which circumstances the penal proceedings should be initiated or carried out, it date, 1-4-1962, does not play any important part. It is true that before the classification made by the legislature could be struck down, it is to be established that it is either arbitrary or fanciful or capricious or unjust. The argument that the classification was necessary because initiation of proceedings could not be taken before the assessment was completed was not acceptable. It is true that the ITO or the AAC as the case may be, is required to determine the quantum of penalty with reference to the tax which is determined as payable. But from that circumstances it cannot be held that the very initiation of proceedings is held over until after the completion of the assessment.

Thus, the event which gives a cause of action for initiation of penalty proceedings is not held over until after the completion of assessment proceedings. If the completion of assessment proceedings, therefore, is not relevant to determine whether or not the ITO or the AAC should initiate penalty proceedings, the date on which the assessment is completed in a particular case cannot have any bearing is determining whether the assessment should be governed by one set of provisions of one case and a different set of provisions in the matter of penalty in another case.

If the date of completion of assessment is not a relevant factor in determining whether or not penal proceedings should be initiated or whether the assessee has or has not committed one of the other wrong, there is nothing dividing the two classes of assessee with reference to the date of completion of the assessment proceedings.

The provisions of either sec tion 28 of the 1922 Act or section 271 of the Act of 1961 will show that the infraction of the provisions of the Act takes place as soon as the return is filed.

That such satisfaction is entered by the ITO at a later date shows that the adjudication of the Act or omission of the deliquent assessee is postponed to the date of recording such finding. But, from that it cannot be inferred or legitimately urged that the infraction has not taken place when the returns were filed. Some time must necessarily elapse between the filing of the return and commencement of proceedings for assessment, and during such proceedings the income-tax authority records satisfaction whether there has been failure to comply with the provisions of the Act in respect of matters provided in section 28 of the old Act or section 271 of the new Act.

The date of completion of the assessment makes no difference so far as this aspect of concerned. In fact, it has no impact either on incurring of the liability or for imposition of penalty. Therefore, the classification made by section 297(2)(g) of the Act of 1961 cannot be justified either as relevant or having any relation to the object with which it is concerned. So far as making a provision for imposing a penalty is concerned, there is no difference between the assessees who have filed returns but in whose cases the assessment was completed prior to 1-4-1962, and assessees who have filed returns but in whose cases assessment was not completed or could not be completed till 1-4-1962.

The mere fact that the legislation divides assessees into two classes cannot be itself be its justification. Justification has to be found somewhere else, namely, in a rational nexus between the classification and the object to be achieved. If the respondents are not able to show that nexus, then it is not possible to uphold the contention that classification is rational or just.

That it is arbitrary is obvious when the date of coming into force of the Act is found to have no bearing on the division of assessees into two classes, one governed by one set of provisions and the other governed by anther set of provisions.

The contention that in the instant case, there was no rational nexus between the object with which the provision has been made for imposing penalty and selecting the date for differentiating as to this provision of law by which the proceedings should be governed, was well founded and had not been satisfactorily answered by the respondents.

The contention on behalf of the revenue that if there was no provision like clause (g) of sub-section (2) of section 297, the Income-tax authorities would have no power to initiate penal proceedings for imposition of penalty by having recourse to the provisions of the old Act had no force with regard to assessments completed after 1-4-1962. Assuming that the provisions like clause (g) of sub-section (2) of section 297 were not to be made by the legislature, the provisions of sub-clause (c) of (d) or (e ) of section 6 of the General Clauses Act would have applied and proceedings for imposition of penalty could have been initiated and penalty imposed under the provisions of the repealed Act, i.e., the Income-tax Act, 1922.

HEADNOTE: Explanation-I to section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1972-73 - Since returned income of assessee was less than 80 per cent of assessed income, in penalty proceedings Explanation to section 271(1)(c) became applicable - As assessee failed to furnish any explanation, penalty was imposed under section 271(1)(c) - Whether even though provisions of main section 271(1)(c) were not specifically invoked, penalty was rightly imposed as Explanation to section 271(1)(c) did not give rise to a separate charge as distinguished from substantive provisions of section 271(1)(c) - Held, yes

FACT: For the assessment year 1972-73, since the returned income of the assessee was less than 80 per cent of the assessed income, in penalty proceeding's Explanation to section 271(1)(c) became applicable. Since the assessee was not able to furnish any explanation, penalty was imposed under section 271(1)(c). On appeal, the assessee contended before the Tribunal that Explanation to section 271(1)(c) gave rise to a separate charge as distinguished from the substantive provisions of section 271(1)(c) and that the provisions of the main section 271(1)(c) having not been specifically invoked, penalty could not be levied. The Tribunal rejected the assessee's contention and upheld the imposition of penalty.

On reference:

HELD: The penalty provision is contained in section 271 and on different counts penalty of different amounts is imposable, wherever there is concealment of income. If the concealment is beyond 20 per cent of the returned income, then the Explanation becomes applicable and presumption has to be raised against the assessee which he can rebut but in case concealment does not exceed 20 per cent. the penalty is still leviable but in this situation the onus lies on the department to prove concealment. Therefore, the Explanation has to be read with section 271(1)(c ) and there is no question of considering the Explanation as separate or distinct from it. The law has to be applied to the given facts. Even if in the order specific reference to Explanation is not mentioned but Explanation is applied and onus is placed on the assessee because the returned income is less than 80 per cent of the assessed income, from this inference has to be drawn that the assessing authorities were conscious of the fact that Explanation was applicable. The Tribunal had, therefore, rightly rejected the assessee's claim.

duty to adopt measures to strike at the evil of tax evasion and it must have freedom to choose the class of persons through whom such evasion can be effectively combated and subject such class to a special procedure or treatment. Such legislation cannot be struck down on the ground that it meets out hostile unequal treatment. The petitioners had failed to discharge the heavy burden which laid upon them to sustain the challenge to the impugned provision based on article 14 and the contention urged in that behalf must be rejected. The other argument was that the impugned provision could not be treated as incidental or ancillary to the main provisions and that, therefore, it could not be said to have any rational nexus with the main provisions of the statute.

This is not the case where on the basis of any presumption made by the legislature a penalty such as seizure or confiscation or penalty in lieu of confiscation is sought to be levied. The impugned provision is made on the basis of a well-known fact which is a matter of common knowledge and common report and all that it requires a building contractor to do is to furnish prescribed particulars within the stipulated time limit on the span of penalty with a view to detecting evasion of tax. Such a provision is clearly incidental or ancillary to the power to levy tax because the power to enact a provision for preventing evasion of tax is always an incidental power. In fact, the challenge levelled to the impugned provision on the ground of legislative incompetence has not even been pressed in the instant case. In these circumstances, it could hardly be contended that the impugned provision being not incidental or ancillary to the main power to tax income which is conferred by the Act, it had no nexus with the statute in question.

The petition was, therefore to be dismissed.

Note: The case was decided in favour of the Department.

HEADNOTE: Section 256, read with section 271(1)(c), of the income-tax act, 1961-Reference-question of fact-Ito imposed penalty for concealment of income on assessee on ground that certain household expenses had been underestimated and certain other expenses had not been shown properly-On appeal, penalty was cancelled on ground that as particulars of concealment had not been disclosed to assessee, he was not in position to defend himself and as such he could not be said to have been granted reasonable opportunity of being heard-Tribunal upheld cancellation of penalty-Whether any question of law arose from tribunal's order-Held, no

Section 274(1) of the income-tax act, 1961-Penalty-Opportunity of hearing-Whether where particulars of concealment are not disclosed to assessee while imposing penalty, it would mean that assesses has not been given reasonable opportunity of being heard-Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was assessed by the ITO at an income higher than that declared in the return filed. The ITO held that the assessee had certain concealed income which could be determined from the fact that household expenses had been underestimated and travelling expenses of family and club expenses as well as medical expenses which had been reimbursed, had not been shown properly. The ITO also imposed penalty under section 271(1)(c). On appeal, the penalty was cancelled on the ground that the basis of the penalty proceedings had not been disclosed to the assessee who was put in a difficult position to defend the matter under section 274(1) and was not granted a reasonable opportunity of being heard. On further appeal, the Tribunal confirmed the order cancelling the penalty and rejected the application for reference under section 256(1), holding that the finding regarding lack of reasonable opportunity was a finding of fact.

On application for reference under section 256(2):

HELD: In order to constitute a penalty under section 271(1)(c ) what is required is a concealment, either of the income or of the particulars thereof. In order to enable such a penalty to be imposed, it is necessary to determine which is the income concealed or which are the particulars not disclosed. If a person is accused of a particular offence of which particulars are given to him, he has a chance of giving his defence thereto. If he is generally accused of some offence of an unknown type, he cannot easily defend himself. The additions which were made during the assessment proceedings in the instant case were based on certain surmises and conjectures. In penalty proceedings, it was not only necessary to inform the assessee of the particular concealment but also necessary for the department to prove positively that there was such a concealment. It was the duty of the department to inform the assessee of the particular concealment that had taken place so that he could defend the case. The failure to do so had led to the cancellation of the penalty. No question of law, therefore, arose from the Tribunal's decision since the question whether penalty had been imposed in accordance with proper procedure or in consonance with natural justice, was one of fact.

IT CASE NO. 39 OF 1981.

HEADNOTE: Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (Corresponding to section 28 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922) - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1954-55 - Whether ITO does not cease to have power to impose a penalty under section 28 of 1922 Act once an appeal has been filed before AAC against assessment which gives rise to initiation of penalty proceedings - Held, yes
Interpretation of statute:
(i) Legislative intent
(ii) Beneficial interpretation

FACT: For the assessment year 1954-55, the ITO made an addition as estimated income for low gross profits and for business income kept outside the account books, and the assessment was completed .Prior to this ITO issued a notice under section 28 in regard to concealment of income.

On appeal, against the quantum assessment, the AAC reduced the addition, and the reduction was confirmed by the Tribunal. Thereafter, the ITO pursued the penalty proceedings initiated earlier and levied penalty.

On second appeal, the Tribunal upheld the penalty.

On reference, the question refereed was as to whether ITO ceased to have power to impose a penalty under section 28, once an appeal had been filed before the AAC against the assessment which gave rise to the initiation of penalty proceedings.

HELD: Tax and penalty, like tax and penal interest, are distinct and different concepts under the Act. Penalty is in addition to the tax determined as payable by the assessee. Penalty, cannot be taken as additional tax for all purposes. The penalty and assessment proceedings are not one and the same proceedings. The findings given in the assessment proceedings would only be relevant and admissible but not final and conclusive in penalty proceedings. In penalty proceedings, further evidence can be led to rebut the findings given in the assessment proceedings. Even in matters which are processed by the ITO, the assessee might not place all the materials before the ITO, with the result he might not be able to detect or find out concealment of income. The AAC, during his enquiry, may come to know additional facts, which are either not disclosed to the ITO, or which escape the attention of the ITO, and those facts might reasonably lead the AAC to a finding that the assessee had concealed income. In such a case, if the AAC has no powers to impose a penalty, the assessee would altogether escape penalty. Therefore, the law has wisely given powers to the AAC and also the Tribunal to impose penalty on the assessee. When the law empowers more than one authority to impose penalty, it would be unreasonable to expect that each one of them would, in his own turn, invoke and impose penalty. At any rate, the assessee can be punished only once in respect of concealment of income and not by all the three authorities simultaneously or one after the other and for the same offence.

It would, therefore, be reasonable to think that when the ITO, having original jurisdiction, and the appellate authorities, i.e. , AAC and the Tribunal, are also invested with powers to impose penalties, it would be wise for the inferior officer to exercise that jurisdiction or power. If section 28 is interpreted in a different manner it would be disadvantageous to the assessee. If the penalty is imposed by the ITO, the assessee would have two opportunities to test the correctness of that penalty order by filing appeals to the AAC and if necessary to the Tribunal. If the power to impose penalty is exercised by the AAC, then the assessee would lose the benefit of one appeal because he could in that case file an appeal only to the Tribunal. If the power to impose penalty is exercised by the Tribunal, then the assessee would altogether lose the right of filing an appeal against the penalty order. If section 28 of the Act is at all to be construed, such construction should be placed on it which would be more advantageous to the assessee.

The language used in section 28 is clear and unambiguous. The section does not under any circumstances oust the jurisdiction of the ITO to impose penalty. If the AAC or the Tribunal imposes penalty on an assessee under section 28(1)(c), he or it is bound under sub-section (5) of section 28, to send a copy thereof to the ITO so that he could not once again impose a penalty upon the assessee for the same concealment.

If the legislature had intended to oust the jurisdiction of the ITO to impose a penalty on an assessee if an appeal was filed against the assessment before the AAC, nothing prevented the legislature from saying so in express language in section 28. There is a general presumption in law against an intention to disturb or oust the jurisdiction or interfere with the jurisdiction, which is given to an officer.

of the business but at the same time to evade income-tax which he would have otherwise been liable to pay. The Income-tax Enquiry Commission of 1936 made certain recommendations to prevent evasion of tax in such cases. The Legislature accepted those recommendations and the loopholes were sought to be plugged by enacting the said sub-section. Sub-section (3)(a)(i) and (ii) was, therefore, enacted for preventing evasion of tax and was well within the competence of the Federal Legislature. The constitutional validity of the said provision was next questioned on the ground that it violated the doctrine of equality before the law enshrined in article 14 of the Constitution. Under the impugned sub-section, an individual is taxed on the income of his wife or his minor children, if he carries on business in partnership with his wife or if he admits his minor sons to the benefits of the partnership, whereas an individual, if he carries on business in partnership with a third party, whether a man or a woman, or even with his major children or if he and his wife or children carry on business separately, will be liable only to pay tax on his share of the partnership income, that, is, for the purpose of this sub-section, the former is put in a category different from the latter. It could not be said that there was no differentia between the two groups. The object of the legislation was to prevent evasion of tax. A similar device would not ordinarily be resorted to by individuals by entering into partnership with persons other than those mentioned in the sub-section, as it would involve a risk of the third party turning round and asserting his own rights. The Legislature, therefore, selected for the purpose of classification only that group of persons who in fact are used as a cloak to perpetrate fraud on taxation.

It was then said that there might be genuine partnerships between an individual and his wife and, therefore, there was no reasonable relation between the classification and the object sought to be achieved, at any rate to the extent of those genuine cases. But there was no classification between genuine and non-genuine cases: the classification was between cases of partnership between husband, wife and/or minor children, whether genuine or not, and partnerships between others. In demarcating, a group, the net was cast a little wider, but it was necessary, as any further sub-classification as genuine and non-genuine partnerships might defeat the purpose of the Act. Hence that contention was rejected.

As to the validity of the provisions based upon article 19(1)(f) and (g) of the Constitution, A combined and plain reading of the provisions of articles 13 and 265 makes it abundantly clear that a law which is inconsistent with any of the provisions of Part III is void. It cannot be denied that a law providing for levy and collection of taxes is a law within the meaning of Part III of the Constitution, and therefore it must stand the test laid down by article 13 of the Constitution. The "law" in article 265 of the Constitution must be a valid law. A law to be valid must not only be one passed by the Legislature in exercise of power conferred on it, but must also be one that does not infringe the fundamental rights declared by the Constitution.

Section 16(3)(a) of 1922 Act must, therefore, pass both the tests and if it violates any of the provisions of article 19, to the extent it is inconsistent with the said provisions, it will be void.

HEADNOTE: Section 140A of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Assessment - Self-assessment - Whether section 140A(3) which provides for levy of penalty for failure to pay self-assessment tax, does not in any way infringe article 19(1)(f) of Constitution of India - Held, yes

FACT: The petitioner did not pay tax due in accordance with the return of income filed by him within stipulated time and, consequently, proceedings for levying penalty under section 140A(3) were commenced by issuing a show-cause notice, to which the petitioner replied contending that inasmuch as on the assessment being completed he had paid the entire tax due, no penalty could be levied under section 140A(3). However, the ITO levied a penalty, which was affirmed in appeal. On writ, the petitioner challenged the constitutional validity of section 140A(3).

HELD: Section 140A which provides for payment of tax due in accordance with the return of income filed by an assessee, within 30 days of the filing of the return is one of the modes/stages of collection of tax devised by Parliament in exercise of its power of taxation.

The principle behind section 140A is that if at the end of the year the assessee is liable to pay any tax according to his own estimate of his income, he shall pay the same within 30 days of the filing of the return. If an assessee is liable to pay advance tax, he would normally pay almost the entire tax in the shape of advance tax, and if he still finds any further tax due at the end of the year, he has to pay it under sub-section (1) of section 140A. In the case of an assessee or in the case of income not liable for payment of advance-tax, the tax due has to be paid within the said 30 days. Obviously, the finalisation of the assessment may take some time and on that occasion, the excess or deficit can be paid or refunded. It is reasonable to presume that every person earning taxable income knows approximately the tax due from him and is expected to and has to pay the same in accordance with law. In other words, the portion of his income due towards income-tax would not be deemed by a prudent and reasonable person to be his "income", properly speaking. In the earlier days, the entire tax was payable, only after the assessment was completed. But when the theory of advance tax was introduced, he had to pay it in certain (now three) instalments as and when he is earning his income. Now, another step is introduced under section 140A, namely, that he has to pay the admitted tax due (i.e., the tax due from him as per his own return) within 30 days of the filing of the return. All these payments towards advance tax and under section 140A(1) are liable to be adjusted at the time of the finalisation of the assessment. There are provisions in the Act providing for levy of penalties for non-compliance with the provisions relating to filing of return, non-furnishing of accounts or particulars, failure to pay advance tax, concealment or evasion of income-tax, etc. Criminal prosecution is also pro-provided for by Chapter 22 in certain cases which, inter alia, include failure to file a return of income, failure to produce accounts and documents, making of false statements and declaration, failure to deduct and pay tax when required to do so. These provisions relating to levy of penalties and criminal prosecutions are twin sanctions provided by law for ensuring compliance with law on the part of the assessees. The object of the two sets of provisions, namely, one levying penalties and the other providing for criminal prosecution, are entirely different.

The provisions made in sub-section (3) is only a measure enacted for ensuring compliance with sub-section (1) of section 140A. The said sub-section merely makes the assessee liable for a penalty which may go up to 50% of the tax payable under sub-section (1). A discretion is conferred upon the ITO in the matter of levying the penalty. In a proper case, he may decline to levy any penalty. The said provision do not compel the ITO to levy such a penalty in each and every case and/or up to the maximum limit. An appeal and a second appeal are provided against his orders and a further reference to the High Court. Further, one cannot assume the case of an assessee "who is not able to pay his taxes". Every person earning taxable income has to provide for payment of taxes. However, certain situations may arise where the assessee may not be able to pay the taxes within 30 days as required by section 140A. But in such cases, if he properly explains the circumstances to the satisfaction of the ITO, he would not levy the penalty.

HEADNOTE: Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessee returned income at Rs. 14,768 but ITO and AAC estimated the same at Rs. 30,000 and imposed penalty of Rs. 15,230 - Tribunal computed total income at Rs. 25,000 but estimated concealed income at Rs. 3,000 with consequential reduction of penalty to Rs. 4,500 - Whether tribunal justified - Held, on facts, yes

FACT: For the assessment year 1970-71, the assessee engaged in the business of assembling pumping sets and manufacturing of canal gates returned its income at Rs. 14,768. The ITO found that in addition to other defects,, the assessee had not incorporated accounts relating to 27 vouchers in his books of account and that, Rs. 2,000 paid in cash to M on 17-3-1970 was recorded in books on 18-3-1970. He consequently estimated income at Rs. 30,000 and levied penalty of Rs. 15,230 for default under section 271(1)( c). The AAC confirmed the ITO's order. On further appeal, the Tribunal held (i) that the recording of cash payment of Rs. 2,000 on a subsequent date was not due to any fraud or gross or wilful neglect on his part; and (ii) that while 12 vouchers were satisfactorily reconciled, the value of Rs. 2,500 represented by the remaining 15 vouchers was not recorded in his books. It, therefore, calculated the concealed income at Rs. 3,000 even though it had estimated the assessee's total income at Rs. 25,000, and reduced the penalty to Rs. 4,500 being 150 per cent of the concealed income.

On reference:

HELD: 1. It is settled that proceedings for penalty are of quasi-criminal nature. While adjudicating on the offence of concealment, the Tribunal is not to be guided by the findings given in the quantum appeal and has to examine the facts afresh to determine the assessee's guilt of concealment and the amount of concealed income for computing the quantum of penalty.

2. The Explanation to section 271(1 )(c) does not have the effect of fixing the quantum of concealment for imposing penalty. The function of fiction created by the Explanation is to convert a case where the assessed income exceeds 80 per cent of the returned income into a case which was covered by section 271 (1)(c), unless the assessee proves that he was not guilty of any fraud or any gross or wilful neglect in filing his return of income. The Explanation exhausts itself once this purpose is achieved. It does not create any further fiction for taking the assessed income as the correct income for levy of penalty under section 271(1)(c)(iii) for which purpose the concerned authority has to independently find the amount of concealed income and may or may not accept the assessed amount as the concealed income. Any other interpretation would make the penalty proceedings completely subservient to the assessment proceedings which does not appear to be the scheme of the Act.

3. Hence, the Tribunal was justified in estimating concealed income at Rs. 3,000, even though the total income had been computed at Rs. 25,000 against returned income of Rs. 14,768 and consequently reducing the quantum of penalty.

Editor's note

The revenue had also argued (i) that the Tribunal had omitted to consider relevant facts while estimating the concealed income at Rs. 3,000 only; and (ii) that, apart from the fact that the assessee had made purchases not shown in the vouchers, there were other irregularities in the accounts to show that he had been carrying on business outside the books: The High Court did not consider these aspects because the question referred did not solicit an enquiry into the validity of the finding regarding estimated concealed income on those scores.

R.K. Gulati and A. Gupta for the Applicant.

Bharatjee Agrawal for the Respondent.

2.

Merely because the legislature in its wisdom decided to give a different treatment to proceedings relating to penalty it is difficult to find discrimination with regard to the classification which has been made in clauses (f) and (g ) which are independent of clauses (a ) and (b). Although penalty has been regarded as an additional tax in a certain sense and for certain purposes it is not possible to hold that penalty proceedings are essentially a continuation of the proceedings relating to assessment where a return has been filed. Further, it is well-settled that in fiscal enactments the legislature has a larger discretion in the matter of classification so long as there is no departure from the rule that persons included in a class are not singled out for special treatment. It cannot be said that while applying the penalty provisions contained in the Act of 1961 to cases of persons whose assessments are completed after 1-4-1962, any class has been singled out for special treatment. It is obvious that for the imposition of penalty it is not the assessment year or the date of the filing of the return which is important but it is the satisfaction of the Income-tax authorities that a default has been committed by the assessee which would attract the provisions relating to penalty. Whatever the stage at which the satisfaction is reached, the scheme of sections 274(1) and 275 of the Act of 1961, is that the order imposing penalty must be made after the completion of the assessment. The crucial date, therefore, for purposes of penalty, is the date of such completion.

As regards the argument that because it rests with the Income-tax Officer to complete the assessment by a particular date it will depend on his fiat whether the penalty should be imposed under the Act of 1922 or under the Act of 1961. It cannot be presumed that officers or authorities who are entrusted with responsible duties under the taxation laws would not discharge them properly and in a bona fide manner. If in a particular case any mala fide action is taken that can always be challenged by an assessee in appropriate proceedings but the mere possibility that some officer may intentionally delay the disposal of a case can hardly be a ground for striking down clause (g) as discriminatory under article 14.

The classification made is based on intelligible differentia having reasonable relation to the object intended to be achieved. The object essentially was to prevent the evasion of tax.

It is true that clause (a) of sub-section (1) of section 271 mentions the corresponding provisions of the Act of 1961 and does not mention provisions of Act of 1922 but that will not make the part relating to payment of penalty inapplicable once it is held that section 297(2)(g ) governs the case. Both sections 271(1) and 297(2)(g) have to be read together and in harmony and so read the only conclusion possible is that for the imposition of a penalty in respect of any assessment for the year ending on 31-3-1962, or any earlier year which is completed after first day of April, 1962, the proceedings have to be initiated and the penalty imposed in accordance with the provisions of section 271 of the Act of 1961. Thus the assessee would be liable to a penalty as provided by section 271(1) for the default mentioned in section 28(1) of the Act of 1922 if his case falls within the terms of section 297(2)(g).

The provision of section 271 of the Act of 1961 will apply mutatis mutandis to proceedings relating to penalty initiated in accordance with section 297(2)(g) of that Act.

As regards challenge to section 271(2) of the Act of 1961 on the ground of contravention of article 14 of the Constitution, it was open to the legislature to say that once a registered firm committed a default attracting penalty, it should be deemed or considered to be an unregistered firm for the purpose of its imposition. No question of discrimination under article 14 can arise in such a situation. There was nothing to prevent the legislature from giving the benefit of a reduced rate to a registered firm for the purpose of tax but withhold the same when it committed a default and became liable to imposition of penalty.

The appeal was dismissed.

Note : The decision was in favour of the revenue.

HEADNOTE: Section 271(1)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment years 1961-62 and 1962-63 - Whether penalty is in nature of a punishment for act of concealment, and, therefore, quantum of penalty must be determined with reference to law prevailing on day when act of concealment was committed and not when proceedings are initiated or order is passed - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, where act of concealment in respect of assessment years 1961-62 and 1962-63 took place long before 1-4-1968, quantum of penalty would have to be regulated with reference to provisions of section 271(1)(c) before amendment on 
1-4-1968 - Held, yes

FACT: For the assessment years 1961-62 and 1962-63, the assessee had shown income from house properties in respect of two houses only. After the completion of the original assessment proceedings, the assessments were reopened and during the course of the reassessment proceedings the ITO made certain additions to the income of the house properties, which had been omitted from the original returns filed by the assessee. The ITO issued notice under section 271(1)(c). Since according to the ITO, the minimum penalty which could be imposed under the Act exceeded Rs. 1,000, he, referred the matter to the IAC, who came to the conclusion that the assessee was guilty of concealment and he, therefore, imposed a penalty of Rs. 5,020 in respect of the assessment year 1961-62 and Rs. 7,020 in respect of the assessment year 1962-63. On appeal, before the Tribunal the assessee contended that penalty, if any, must be computed in accordance with the provisions of section 271 as it stood before the amendment and that as the minimum penalty under section 271(1)(c) as it stood before the amendment fell below Rs. 1,000, the ITO had jurisdiction to proceed with the penalty proceedings. These contentions were upheld by the Tribunal. It accordingly, set aside the orders of the Assistant Commissioner in respect of these years and directed that the matter would go back to the ITO for fresh decision according to law.

On reference:

HELD: A comparison of the provisions of section 271 before and after amendment shows that the penalty provisions for concealment of income have been made very stringent and the amount of penalty leviable has been much enhanced. The point for consideration in this case is whether the amended provisions would be applicable to penalty proceedings in respect of assessment years 1961-62 and 1962-63, even though the amendment came into effect on 1-4-1968.

Liability for penalty is incurred by an assessee for concealment of income. The provisions relating to penalty are of a penal character and their object is to punish the assessee so as to deter him from concealing his income in future. Thus, penalty is in the nature of a punishment for the act of concealment, and, therefore, the quantum of penalty must be determined with reference to the law prevailing on the day when the act of concealment was committed and not when the proceedings are initiated or the order is passed.

The provisions of article 20(1) of the Constitution provides that no person shall be subject to a penalty greater than that which might have been inflicted under the law in force at the time of the commission of the offence. Although imposition of penalty under the Income-tax Act is not a punishment for any offence so as to attract article 20 of the Constitution, the principle underlying article 20 would be applicable to instant case, in the absence of any express provision to the contrary.

It is also a settled rule of construction that an amending statute must be given effect to prospectively and not restrospectively unless there in an express provision to that effect. Since, the imposition of penalty is directly related to the act of concealment of the income of the assessee, the material date for the purpose is the date of concealment, and, therefore, the question of penalty must be determined with reference to the law in force on such date.
