Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1983-84 - Assessee’s books of account were seized by department and assessee was not given sufficient time for filing return - Assessee filed provisional return declaring income of Rs. 1,60,000 and after inspecting documents and making copies of accounts, filed another return declaring income of Rs. 2,44,760 - Income was assessed at Rs. 2,57,820 making certain additions relating to cash credits and sales tax liability and latter sale tax addition was deleted on appeal - Assessing Officer initiated penalty proceedings and levied penalty on basis of discrepancy between provisional return and income assessed by department - Whether where Assessing Officer himself had not considered provisional return as valid for assessment purpose, it could not be treated as valid for purpose of levying penalty - Held, yes - Whether mere fact that assessee did not file appeal against cash credit addition, would not automatically mean that penalty could be levied under section 271(1)(c) unless concealment was clearly established by Assessing Officer - Held, yes - Whether since difference between valid return and income assessed by department was only on account of certain petty additions and such additions did not indicate any concealment of income or furnishing of inaccurate particulars of income within meaning of section 271(1)(c), penalty levied was unjustified - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c), read with section 256, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1979-80 - Whether to find out whether any case as contemplated in section 271(1)(c) is made out, one has primarily to see nature of concealment, explanation offered by assessee, his conduct, etc. - Held, yes - Assessing Officer while disallowing assessee’s claim for sales tax, made addition to income and imposed penalty for concealment of income - Tribunal examined entire facts and came to a conclusion that no case of concealment as contemplated under section 271(1)(c) was made out and, accordingly, set aside penalty - Whether any referable question of law arose from Tribunal’s order - Held, no

Section 271(1)(c), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of Income - Assessment year 1968-69 - Assessee-firm filed return showing loss of Rs. 2 lakhs - ITO completed assessment under section 144 on total income of Rs. 50,000/-as against returned loss of Rs. 2 lakhs - IAC considered concealed income at Rs. 2,50,000 and imposed penalty under section 271(1)(c) - Tribunal reduced penalty holding that for purposes of imposition of penalty under section 271(1)(c), income concealed was income actually determined, i.e., Rs. 50,000 - Whether view taken by Tribunal was correct and it was justified in reducing quantum of penalty accordingly - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Whether grant of imposition of penalty on assessee is essentially a question of discussion and if proper explanation is offered and same is accepted by Tribunal, High Court would not disturb such finding in exercise of its jurisdiction conferred under section 256(1) - Held, yes

Section 18(1)(a)  of the Wealth-tax Act, 1957 - Penalty - For failure to furnish returns - Assessment years 1968-69 and 1969-70 - Whether object of section 18(1)(a) is to prevent concealment of wealth and thus, classification of persons, who has failed without reasonable cause to furnish return of net wealth within time, in one category in respect of levy of penalty at uniform rate of one-half per cent on net wealth assessed was an intelligible differentia based on rational relation to object sought to be achieved by statute and, therefore, section 18(1)(a) does not violate article 14 of Constitution - Held, yes - Whether section 18(1)(a) being penal provision intended to prevent evasion of tax and concealment of wealth, it is saved under article 19(5) of Constitution as reasonable restriction on fundamental right of petitioner under article 19(1)(f) of Constitution, in interest of general public and therefore, section 18(1)(a) does not infringe article 19(1)(g) - Held, yes - Whether Parliament lacks legislative competence to enact section 18(1)(a) - Held, no

Section 271(1)(c) , read with section 256 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 28(1), read with section 66 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Penalty - For concealment of income - Whether in matter of imposition of penalty, unless it can be shown that discretion vested in income-tax authorities has been exercised arbitrarily, with no regard to judicial considerations, Court can not require Commissioner to state a case - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 28(1)(c) of Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1960-61 - ITO levied penalty under section 271(1)(c) - Tribunal held that assessment year being 1960-61, provisions of 1922 Act applied and as under relevant provision no minimum penalty had been prescribed, application of provisions of 1961 Act would offend provisions of article 20 of Constitution - Tribunal, therefore, applying section 28(1)(c) of 1922 Act restricted penalty to sum which was less than minimum penalty provided for under section 271(1)(c) of 1961 Act - Whether when penalty proceedings were initiated in 1965, those proceedings would be governed by provisions of 1961 Act - Held, yes - Whether article 20(1) of Constitution is not applicable to proceedings imposing penalty under Act - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, levy of penalty of amount which was less than minimum prescribed under section 271(1)(c) of 1961 Act was not justified - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(iii) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Whether during the period between 1-4-1968 to 31-3-1976 when in place of amount of tax sought to be avoided or evaded the amount of income was made the basis for quantification of the amount of penalty, the term 'income' did not contemplate gross income but contemplated taxable income - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, penalty was to be computed with reference to net capital gains after allowing deductions and not with reference to gross amount of capital gains - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section  28(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1930-31 - Whether maximum penalty that can be imposed under section 28(1) of 1922 Act is a sum representing difference between tax on income declared by assessee and tax on income ascertained under Act in respect of which assessment has been made - Held, yes - Whether in an inquiry under section 28 of 1922 Act, evidence adduced by assessee purporting to disclose real income of assessee is relevant and admissible, not for purpose of varying or affecting assessment made for purpose of imposing tax under Act, but in order to show either that no penalty ought to be imposed, or that amount of penalty ought to be less than maximum prescribed under section 28 - Held, yes

Section 27(1)(c), read with section 256 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1983-84 - Whether question of bona fide mistake in original return of income, rectified in revised return before completion of assessment, could not be termed to be question of law requiring reference to High Court for adjudication under section 256 - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessee voluntarily put in an application for settlement of his tax liability in view of certain assets acquired by him and his wife but not recorded in his books - In pursuance of settlement before Commissioner unaccounted assets were quantified, and after deducting income already returned for relevant years, balance of income was spread over those years - Said settlement further indicated levy of penalties at 40 per cent of concealed income - Penalties were accordingly levied - Tribunal, however, held that substantial moiety of amount agreed for settlement being recorded in assessee's books, it was incomprehensible that assessee should have accepted settlement in respect of such assets - Whether in view of Tribunal taking this view of facts, any interference in its order cancelling penalties was called for - Held, no

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1965-66 - Whether where ITO initiated penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c) in December 1967, maximum penalty that could be imposed was one and half times of amount of tax which would have been avoided and ITO was not right in imposing penalty at rate of 150 per cent of concealed income - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 28(1)(c) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1946-47 - ITO levied penalty under section 28(1)(c) for concealment of income from business in form of deposits appearing in Amanat khatta of assessee in which names of depositors were not available nor any evidence had been given to explain nature and service of amount - AAC confirmed addition and no further appeal was filed which meant that assessee had acquiesced to department’s decision that it was concealed income of assessee from business - Whether there is no essential difference between tax and penalty and liability for payment of both is imposed as part of machinery of assessment and penalty is merely additional tax imposed in certain circumstances on account of assessee’s conduct - Held, yes - Whether if there is material justifying finding that assessee has concealed particulars of income for assessment purposes it could not be said that it was not sufficient to justify imposition of penalty and, therefore, view that penalty proceedings require different or stricter standard of evidence than assessment proceedings or that evidence that is sufficient for assessment purposes may fall short of that required for imposition of penalty was not correct - Held, yes - Whether it is only when income-tax authorities base their earlier finding not on falsity of claim made by assessee about nature of receipt but on their mere holding it not proved, or on their being in doubt whether it was correct or not, that materials they had before them in assessment proceedings can be said to be not sufficient to justify finding adverse to assessee in penalty proceedings - Held, yes - Whether income-tax authorities cannot assess all receipts; they can assess only those receipts that amount to income and, therefore, before they assess particular receipt, they must find it to be income which they cannot do unless they have some material to justify their finding - Held, yes - Whether, since nature of particular receipt is within personal or special knowledge of assessee, onus lies upon him to prove real nature of receipt and not to prove that it is not income and if materials that he produces satisfy income-tax authorities that it is not income, they will not assess it and no question of imposition of penalty will arise at all, but if same are found to be false or not accepted as true by them, it may be sufficient circumstance to justify inference that it does not belong to any kind of non-assessable receipt - Held, yes - Whether onus of proof lies on party and not on Tribunal that has to give finding and, therefore, there cannot be any question of income-tax authorities leading evidence to prove any fact and what is required under law in order to levy penalty is that they must have material to justify their finding of concealment of particulars or deliberate furnishing of inaccurate particulars - Held, yes - Whether where a receipt is income but it is disguished in accounts or in return as non-assessable receipt, as in instant case, it is clearly case of concealment of particulars or of furnishing inaccurate particulars of income and penalty under section 28(1)(c) can be imposed on assessee - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1960-61 - Whether where revised return was filed only after ITO discovered concealed income, quantum of penalty had to be worked out on basis of total assessed figure minus amount originally returned and not on basis of revised return - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c), read with section 256, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1984-85 - Assessee-firm stated to have contracted loans from seven persons who were found by tax authorities as well as Tribunal, as street hawkers, for whom it was very difficult to make out their livelihood by their profession and they did not have required capacity to lend money - Tribunal upheld penalty imposed by assessing authority for concealment of income - Whether Tribunal’s finding being finding of fact, no referable question of law arose from Tribunal’s order - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1969-70 - Assessee’s returned income was less than 80 per cent of assessed income - He, however, did not discharge burden showing that no case for imposition of penalty was made out - Whether, in aforesaid circumstances, imposition of penalty was justified - Held, yes

facts.text:
For the assessment year 1968-69, the assessee filed his original return without showing the income from sale of land, but when required to produce the sale deed in respect of the land sold by him, the assessee filed a revised return showing therein capital gains and business income on estimate basis. The ITO passed the assessment order and also issued notice under section 274 read with section 271 for failure to furnish the return within the stipulated time and also for concealment of income. Later, he levied penalty only under section 271(1)(c) of an amount equal to 100 per cent of the concealed income.

On writ, the assessee challenged the constitutional validity of section 271(1)(c) on two grounds: (1) that section 271(1)(c) is violative of Article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as there is no classification at all even though there is a difference between various types of tax evasions; and (2) that the impugned provisions are a colourable exercise of legislative power inasmuch as in the guise of levying penalty the legislature had enacted for expropriation of the whole of the property of the citizen.

The petitioners, some of whom had been imposed penalty under section 271(1)(c) of the 1961 Act and others under section 18(1)(a) of the 1957 Act, challenged the constitutional validity of these provisions on the ground that they are discriminatory and violative of article 14 of the Constitution of India besides being unreasonable restriction on the fundamental rights guaranteed under article 19(1)(f ) thereof. They further urged that the penalty based on the concealed income on wealth prescribed under the impugned sections is arbitrary and unjust and cannot be regarded as incidental to the levy of tax.

On writ :

The assessee’s failure to file any return provoked the Department to carry out search action under section 132. For the assessment year 1989-90, it was found that assessee had earned a substantial income on the sale of shares. The assessee, in response to notice under section 148, filed the return declaring income, and the assessment was completed on an income of Rs. 4,98,200. In response to the show-cause notice as to why penalty for concealment should not be imposed on the assessee, the assessee contended that there was no mala fide intention to conceal the particulars of income as the sum of Rs. 1,02,000 was paid by way of advance tax attributable to the capital gain and further tax was deducted at source on salary and dividend income. The Assessing Officer levied penalty under section 271(1)(c) by rejecting the assessee’s explanation on the ground that it was only the search action and subsequent issue of notice which forced the assessee to file his return and that mere payment of advance tax did not confer the right on the assessee not to file the return.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the levy of penalty holding that the non-furnishing of the return would tantamount to concealment of particulars of income. The contention of the assessee that such construction would render the provisions of Explanation 3 to section 271(1)(c) redundant was also rejected by the Commissioner (Appeals) who held that Explanation 3 to section 271(1)(c) is applicable to new assessees while the old assessees would be covered by the main provision of section 271(1)(c).

On second appeal :

The assessee-petitioner was a yarn dealer. The ITO holding that the assessee had deliberately furnished false particulars regarding his income made some additions. Assessments for years 1944-45 and 1945-46 were confirmed by the Tribunal while the revision for the assessment years 1946-47 and 1947-48 were dismissed by the Commissioner. Thereafter, ITO initiated proceedings under section 28(1)(c) of 1922 Act. On writ challenging the penalty proceedings the assessee submitted that (1) section 28 of the 1922 Act which enables the ITO and other income-tax authorities to levy a penalty in certain circumstances was not within the legislative competence of the Central Legislature under the Government of India Act, 1935. (2) The procedure for the levy of a penalty for concealment of particulars of the income of an assessee which was an alternative to the launching of a prosecution under sections 51 and 52 of the 1922 Act vested an arbitrary and unguided discretion in the IAC to direct either proceedings for levy of a penalty or for the initiation of a prosecution and that the same was, therefore, violative of article 14 of the Constitution and that on that ground section 28(1)(c) of the 1922 Act ought to be struck down. (3) On a proper construction of section 28 of the 1922 Act the ITO should be satisfied that there has been a deliberate concealment of the income of an assessee during the pendency of the assessment proceedings and as in the instant case the assessment proceedings were completed in regard to the first two years by the dismissal of the assessee's appeals by the Tribunal, and in respect of the later two years by the disposal of the revision by the Commissioner, the orders passed subsequent thereto, levying penalties were illegal and not in conformity with the requirements of the section.

The assessment of the petitioner for the assessment year 1960-61 was completed under section 23(3) of the 1922 Act on 27-2-1965, and thereafter a show cause notice under section 274/271 of the 1961 Act proposing to levy penalty for concealment of income was issued to the petitioner.

On writ, the petitioner contended (1) that the provisions of section 297(2)( g) were ultra vires, being violative of article 14 of the Constitution, and (2) that, in any event, even assuming that the 1961 Act was applicable, no penalty could be imposed under section 271 as the Income-tax Officer could not have been satisfied that there had been any non-disclosure by the assessee in the course of any proceedings under that Act.

In view of certain discrepancies in accounts, the ITO made three additions to the income returned by the assessee. The ITO also levied penalty under section 28(1)(c) of 1922 Act. The AAC confirmed the penalty. On appeal, the Tribunal held that only one item of concealment had been established and that the other items could not be taken to be items of concealment. It, however, held that penalty under section 28(1)(c) of the 1922 Act was justified. As regards the quantum of penalty, the Tribunal held that it would be quite proper to take into account the tax actually avoided in so far as it was referable to the actual concealed income and, in that view, the Tribunal ultimately reduced the penalty.

On reference :

The assessee had constructed four shops and he had shown the cost of construction as per books in a sum of Rs. 15,337. The ITO, however, was of the view that the cost of construction he had shown in the books of account was on the lower side. Later on, the assessee submitted a report from the approved valuer who had estimated the cost of construction in a sum of Rs. 35,900. He produced before the ITO another valuation report showing the cost of construction in a sum of Rs. 21,000. In view of the difference, the ITO had valuation through a valuer of the Department, who estimated the cost of construction at Rs. 24,000. The officer was of the view that the difference between the cost of construction shown as per the books of account and the first estimated value given by the assessee should be taken as income concealed from the Department. On that view, penalty was levied under section 271(1)(c). On second appeal the Tribunal while confirming the view of the authorities below that there was concealment of income on the part of the assessee, fixed the penalty by taking the difference between the second valuation report given by the assessee and the actual cost of construction shown in the books of account.

On reference :

The assessee was a firm dealing in hessian, twines, gunny bags, etc., on wholesale basis. For the relevant assessment year, the ITO added two items as profits and income from undisclosed sources which had been concealed by the assessee and imposed penalty within the maximum limits provided by section 28(1)(c) 1922 Act.

The AAC in appeal held that only the first item be treated as concealed income and the other amount could not be treated as such for the purpose of imposing a penalty. In his opinion maximum penalty payable under section 28(1)(c) of Act 1922 came to Rs. 30,000 and taking into consideration all the circumstances he imposed a penalty of Rs. 20,000 only on the assessee. In appeal the Appellate Tribunal agreed with the order of AAC as regards concealment. However it was held by the Tribunal that, as there had been concealment of profit, it was wholly immaterial whether one item or more than one item had been concealed and the quantum had to be computed under section 28(1)(c) not on the basis of tax on the items proved to have been concealed but on the difference between the tax on the assessee's income as finally assessed and the tax which would have been avoided if the return filed by him had been accepted as correct. The Tribunal restored the order of the ITO imposing a penalty of Rs. 62,000.

On reference, the High Court was of the view that the expression "income as returned" occurring in section 28(1)(c) meant income disclosed by an assessee in the return and not income computed or assessed by the income-tax authorities minus the income added on the ground of concealment. The High Court, while appreciating that the penalty imposed appeared to be disproportionately heavy to the amount concealed, returned the answer against the assessee.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

After completion of the assessment of the assessee under section 23(4) of 1922 Act, the ITO issued a notice to the assessee calling upon him to show cause why a penalty should not be imposed on him in addition to the income-tax payable by him inasmuch as he had concealed the particulars of his income and deliberately furnished inaccurate particulars of such income. The ITO was of the opinion that the assessee deserved a tribute for his acuteness exercised in a wrong direction and that it was difficult to discover the devices of the assessee which were adopted in an ingenious and clever manner. He, therefore, imposed a penalty in the hope that it would be a sufficient warning to the assessee in future. The Assistant Commissioner agreed with the ITO and thought that the circumstances of the case called for the prosecution of the assessee and the assessee should consider himself fortunate in escaping with a penalty.

On an application under section 66(3) of 1922 Act :

The assessee filed its return for the assessment year 1966-67 after 1-4-1968. For concealment of income, which was eventually established, the IAC levied penalty on the basis of the difference between the assessed income and returned income, in accordance with section 271(1)(c) as amended from 1-4-1968. The Tribunal, however, held that penalty had to be levied in accordance with the law prevalent on the first day of the relevant assessment year, and directed that the penalty should be reduced to 25 per cent of the tax sought to be avoided.

On reference :

For the assessment year 1970-71, the assessee filed the return on 26-02-1971 declaring an income of Rs. 1,20,992. The ITO, however, determined the taxable income at Rs. 1,61,180 vide his order, dated 1-03-1972 and referred the penalty proceedings initiated under section 271(1)(c) to the IAC under section 274(2). The IAC held that the concealed income was Rs. 8,657 only and he levied a penalty of Rs. 9,000 vide his order, dated 4-03-1974. On appeal, the Tribunal sustained the penalty order. It held (i) that the IAC had jurisdiction to pass penalty order even though the concealed income was less than Rs. 25,000 ; and (ii) that the penalty order was not barred by limitation as the amendment, effected in section 275 by the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 1970, was retrospective and was applicable to the present proceedings.

On reference :

The search was carried out in case of the assessee under section 132. Pursuant thereto, the assessee was issued a notice under section 158BC, requiring him to file block return in respect of undisclosed income.

The assessee filed the same, declaring total income for block period of Rs. 20.36 lakhs. However, the tax payable on the aforesaid income was worked out at Rs. 12.83 lakhs.

The assessee filed block return with proof of payment of tax, to the tune of Rs. 7.36 lakhs.

The Assessing Officer held that since assessee had failed in making full payment of tax, therefore penalty was impugned under section 158BFA(2).

The Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the appeal filed by the assessee in part.

However, the Tribunal deleted the penalty by holding that since, the assessee had paid tax of more than 60 per cent of the total demand by the revenue and balance demand was paid by the assessee in instalments with interest, no fact of concealment of income had been proved by the department. Thus, the assessee could not be penalised under section 158BFA(2).

On revenue appeal:

In the course of the assessment proceedings, the ITO was satisfied that the assessee had concealed particulars of his income and, consequently, he initiated proceedings under section 271(1)(c). The IAC levied a penalty. On appeal, the Tribunal, while concurring with the finding of the IAC interfered with the order and reduced the penalty entering a finding that concealment of the particulars of income could be only in respect of reduced sum.

On reference:

Two of the partners of the assessee-firm introduced Rs. 19,500 and Rs. 30,000, respectively, as part of their share capital in the firm. It was explained that the amounts had been introduced out of their agricultural income. The assessee could not produce evidence regarding sale of agriculture produce and, therefore, amounts were treated as the assessee’s concealed income. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed some reduction. In penalty order, the Assessing Officer held that the assessee had not produced the correct particulars of its income and, thus, concealed the income of Rs. 34,500. Accordingly, penalty under section 271(1)(c) was imposed. On appeal, the assessee contended that the mere fact that the Assessing Officer had not accepted the explanation furnished was not sufficient ground for levy of penalty. The Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the penalty.

On the revenue’s appeal and cross-objection by the assessee, the assessee besides opposing the penalty order, also took preliminary objection to the maintainability of the appeal in the light of Instruction No. 1979, dated 27-3-2000, issued by the Central Board of Direct Taxes, asking all officers of the Income-tax Department under their control not to file appeals before the Tribunal in cases where the tax effect involved in appeal did not exceed Rs. 1.00 lakh. On the other hand, it was contended on behalf of the Department that the instructions were by way of guidelines and could not override the specific provisions of the Act and that these instructions were not in the nature of ‘benevolent Circulars’ for the benefit of the assessee. Thus, it was urged that the preliminary objection raised was not legally sustainable.

The petitioner was a railway contractor. He filed an income-tax return for the assessment year 1964-65 before the ITO, indicating an income of Rs. 23,968.00.

It would appear that no actual accounts of income and expenditure were filed, but the income was assessed at certain rates of estimated profits. The return was not accepted by the ITO concerned and the returned income enhanced to Rs. 52,017.00, the ITO applying the following rates :

(a)Engineering contract rate of profit applied 15 per cent

(b)Coal handling contract rate of profit applied 12.5 per cent

(c)Foundry clinckers rate of profit applied 14 per cent

The petitioner made on appeal to the AAC of Income-tax with the result that his total income was reduced by a sum of Rs. 4,172.00. A second appeal had been filed before the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal which was pending decision. As the total income disclosed by the petitioner in the return, i.e., Rs. 23,968.00 was less than 80 per cent of the income assessed, i.e., Rs. 47,845.00, the ITO started penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c) Explanation. As the minimum penalty leviable in the petitioner's case exceeded one thousand rupees, the ITO, opposite party No. 2, referred the case to the IAC, opposite Party No. 1, under section 274(2) of the Act. A show cause notice was thereafter issued by the opposite party No. 1 to the petitioner under section 274(2) read with section 271 of the Act charging the petitioner with concealment of the particulars of his income. The notice was contested, but ultimately opposite party No, 1 held that the provisions of section 271(1)(c) read with the Explanation to that section were applicable to the petitioner's case and thus a penalty of Rs. 2,100 was imposed on the difference between the petitioner on account of the alleged concealment of income based on the difference between the income returned by the petitioner and the income assessed by the ITO and the amount was directed to be recovered by the opposite party No. 2 from the petitioner. It is against this order that this writ petition had been riled, and the relier claimed was that a writ of certiorari be issued for the quashing of the order or assessment, the notice for the imposing of the penalty and the order or the imposition of penalty.

The assessee-company was a manufacturer of tea chest fitting from tin plates imported under licence. It had deposited with a bank some tin sheets on 3-11-1959 as security for loan and the bank released them between 12-3-1960 to 14-5-1960. On 26-11-1965, the assessee produced its account books for the year ended 31-5-1960 and the ITO found considerable manipulations therein by short crediting sales culminating in their being impounded. When asked to explain such irregularities, the assessee replied that fittings manufactured prior to 14-5-1960 were out of tin sheets cuttings taken on loan from two parties who were summoned by the ITO for examination. On 29-12-1969, the assessee requested the ITO not to examine the witness and enclosed a revised return of income including therein the amounts of unaccounted stock. The IAC, accordingly, imposed a penalty under section 271(1)(c) which was upheld by the Tribunal but the quantum was reduced to the extent of 100 per cent of the tax avoided. The assessee challenged the proceedings on the grounds (i) that mere concealment of income would not suffice and there must be a finding that there was a conscious concealment by it, and (ii) that the fact of its having filed a revised return under section 139(5) had not been taken into account.

On reference :

The assessee filed the return showing an income of Rs. 3,958. The ITO completed the assessment on a total income of Rs. 39,790 and initiated penalty proceedings for concealment of income under section 271(1)( c) read with Explanation thereto. The Tribunal, however, reduced the addition and determined the taxable income at Rs. 29,790. In penalty proceedings, the IAC levied a penalty of Rs. 21,000 on account of assessee's failure to prove that the difference between the returned income and the assessed income was not on account of any fraud or gross or wilful neglect on his part. The assessee's appeal before the Tribunal was unsuccessful.

On reference :

The assessee filed a return disclosing an income of Rs. 4,560. The ITO, assessing the income at Rs. 40,000, initiated penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c). The IAC to whom the matter was referred dismissed the explanation submitted by the assessee and held that the assessee had concealed income to the extent of Rs. 35,440. He, accordingly, levied a penalty of Rs. 35,500 on the assessee. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the penalty imposed was excessive inasmuch as, from the material on record, concealment of income of Rs. 10,440 alone was proved beyond doubt. Therefore, the Tribunal reduced the quantum of penalty.

On reference, the revenue contended that the Tribunal could not reduce penalty to an amount less than the difference between the assessed and the returned income.

The assessee used to earn commission in foreign exchange and out of this commission received, it used to transfer part of foreign exchange within the permissible limit prescribed by Reserve Bank of India to dollar account maintained with Hong Kong Bank where it was held by the bank as term deposit. The Assessing Officer from the perusal of the balance-sheet for the assessment year 1998-99 noticed that the assessee had shown balance of Rs. 81.83 lakhs with Hong Kong Bank representing dollar account. It was required to show earnings out of this account on interest and exchange rate. Information was also called from the bank. The bank informed that as per the conversion rate of US $ on 31-3-1998, the value of dollars in Indian currency was Rs. 92.98 lakhs as against Rs. 81.83 lakhs shown by the assessee. The difference of Rs. 11.15 lakhs was taxed as income from other sources. No appeal against same was filed by the assessee. The Assessing Officer, thereafter, initiated penalty proceedings and levied penalty of Rs. 3.08 lakhs for concealment of income. The Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the penalty order. However, the Tribunal set aside the order of Commissioner (Appeals) and deleted the penalty.

On appeal :

As the income returned by the assessee, or firm of contractors, fell short of the assessed income by more than 20 per cent. the ITO levied penalty under section 271(1)(c) on the ground that the assessee wilfully concealed the particulars of its income. The AAO allowed the assessee's appeal and the Tribunal dismissed the revenue's appeal.

On reference:

The assessee declared its income at Rs. 8,200 both in the original return filed before completion of regular assessment on 21-09-1965 and the return filed on 18-09-1969 in response to notice under section 148. The reassessment was completed at Rs. 21,807 and the IAC levied penalty of Rs. 5,000 under section 271(1)(c) for concealment of income of Rs. 5,000 under the provisions as amended with effect from 1-04-1968. The Tribunal held that since the assessee's default was attributable to the original return filed prior to 1-04-1968, the penalty provisions at that time would apply. It, accordingly, directed recomputation of penalty with reference to the tax sought to be avoided.

On reference :

For concealment of income the ITO imposed penalty upon the assessee under section 271(1)(c) read with Explanation thereto. The Tribunal, however, cancelled the penalty imposed upon the assessee. It, inter alia, followed the judgment of the Punjab and Haryana High Court in Addl. CIT v. Karnail Singh V. The assessee a Chilean national, at the relevant point of time, was employed with a Switzerland based company (TP-Swiss). In the course of employment he was deputed under an international assignment agreement to an Indian company associated with the employer as a group company ('TP-India'), for the purpose, inter alia, of maintaining uniform standard in quality, processes, and to provide technical support. All the taxes were to be borne by the employer. He was compensated for the services so rendered in India, in addition to the salary, bonus, pension contribution and spouse pension paid by TP-Swiss, by way of salaries and perquisites, such as accommodation, car and utilities, etc., provided by TP-India. While computing the assessee's tax liability in India, the compensation received for aforesaid services was not included in his taxable income for the reasons that (i) the services were for the benefit of TP-Swiss and its group companies other than TP-India, and, as such, TP-India was in no way connected with those services; (ii) the compensation so paid to the assessee was not charged to the profits of any Indian entity; and (iii) the compensation was out of accruals which had no link with TP-India. However, later on, TP-Swiss was advised that the stand so taken by it might not be free from doubt. Therefore, TP-Swiss revised its computation of taxable income in the hands of the assessee, and paid additional taxes. The taxes were paid on 30-8-2006, and the revised statement showing computation of tax liabilities of the employee was filed by TP-Swiss on 4-9-2006. All the requisite information regarding the income was, thus, duly furnished to the Indian tax authorities on 4-9-2006. The income, on the basis of said declaration submitted by TP-Swiss to the Indian tax authorities was recomputed at Rs. 1,23,34,537, as against an income of Rs. 35,47,950 disclosed in the original return. On 17-11-2006, a notice under section 148 for reopening the assessment proceedings so as to bring the income escaping assessment to tax, was issued. A revised income-tax return was filed disclosing a revised income of Rs. 1,23,34,573. The assessment was completed on the basis of the revised return and without making any adjustments thereto.

The Assessing Officer was of the view that the assessee had deliberately concealed an income of Rs. 87,86,620 in his original return, and, it was only after initiating the reassessment proceedings to bring such income to tax that the assessee offered concealed income to tax. He, thus, required the assessee to show cause as to why this lapse on the part of the taxpayer should not be visited with concealment penalty under section 271(1)(c). In response, it was explained that TP-Swiss had suo motu filed all the information about the income subsequently offered to tax on 4-9-2006; that TP-Swiss also proceeded on the basis that there was, to that extent, a short deduction of tax at source; that the tax so short deducted, i.e., tax withholding liability under section 201(1), along with interest on delayed deposit was duly deposited by TP-Swiss; and that the reassessment of income was on the basis of declaration made by TP-Swiss, which was suo motu given by the TP-Swiss. The Assessing Officer, however, was of the view that the assessee was under an obligation to disclose all incomes taxable in India to Indian employer, so that the same could be taken into account while estimating his taxable income in India and taxes at source be properly deducted thereon. According to the Assessing Officer, the assessee should have considered such receipts as his income and he should have also paid due advance tax thereon. The Assessing Officer thus concluded that the intention of the assessee was to conceal the said income and, accordingly penalty was to be imposed under section 271(1)(c). On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the action of the Assessing Officer.

held.text:
As regards the challenge on the basis of Article 14 of the Constitution, it is well-settled that while article 14 forbids class legislation, it does not forbid reasonable classification for the purposes of legislation. In order, however, to pass the test of permissible classification, two conditions must be fulfilled, namely : (i) that the classification must be founded on an intelligible differentia which distinguishes persons or things that are grouped together from others left out of the group ; and (ii ) that that differentia must have a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved by the statute in question.

In deciding whether a taxation law is discriminatory or not it is necessary to bear in mind that the State has a wide discretion in selecting the persons or objects it would tax, and that a statute is not open to attack on the ground that it taxes some persons and objects and not others. It is only when within the range of its selection, the law operates unequally, and that cannot be justified on the basis of any valid classification, that it would be violative of article 14. It is for the person who assails a legislation as discriminatory to establish that it is not based on a valid classification and it is well-settled that this burden is all the heavier when the legislation under attack is a taxing statute. In taxation even more than in other fields, legislatures possess the greatest freedom in classification. The burden is on the one attacking the legislative arrangement to negative every conceivable basis which might support it. Thus, unless the petitioner succeeds in establishing that there was a clear and hostile discrimination by virtue of the impugned legislation, the challenge on the ground of article 14 can not be sustained.

In the instant case, the challenge of the assessee, on the ground of article 14 must fail because in this piece of taxing statute he had not been able to point out any hostile discrimination against a particular type of taxpayer. The fact that the penalty with effect from 1-4-1968, is linked up with the income concealed rather than with the tax evaded shows the gravity which the legislature attaches to such tax evasions. The fact that under section 27l(1)(a)(i ) the penalty for not filing a return is correlated to the amount of the tax evaded as against the correlation of penalty to concealed income under the impugned provisions of section 271(1)(c)( iii) is totally beside the point because, so far as concealed income is concerned, the penalty for concealed income proceeds on altogether a different footing from penalty for omission to file a return in time. The history of legislation shows that Parliament has progressively moved more and more stringent measures of penalty obviously with a view to deter people from evading tax by concealing their income.

The object of the legislation behind all these penalty provisions, whether in section 28 of the 1922 Act or in section 271(1) of the 1961 Act is to provide a deterrent against tax evasion and the provisions are intended to be by way of an effective deterrent to put a stop to the practice which the legislature considers to be against the public interest.

The penalties imposed by the legislature to enforce the tax laws embrace both civil and criminal sanctions. Invocation of one does not exclude resort to the other. Thus, merely because a penalty is provided for concealing income and that penalty is correlated to the income concealed rather than to the tax evaded, it cannot be said that the provision is a piece of hostile legislation or hostile discrimination. The apparent harshness of the provision in the case of evaders of small income arises merely because at the lower levels of taxation the tax imposed is on a much lesser basis than on the higher slabs of income. Therefore, the higher the slab and the greater the extent of the income concealed, the lesser will be the ratio of the penalty, maximum and minimum, to the tax actually evaded as a result of concealment of such income. But this result has been brought about by the higher rates of taxation in the upper brackets of income. In any particular case the actual proportion between the penalty imposed and the tax evaded will depend upon the rate of tax applicable to the assessee concerned and again the penalty is to be levied on the basis of the concealed income and not on the basis of the entire income.

Under these circumstances it was obvious that the impugned provisions of section 271(1)(c)(iii ) could not be said to violate article 14 of the Constitution. As regards the challenge on the grounds of article 19(1)(f ), it could not be said that the provisions are expropriatory. After all, all kinds of punishment and penalties can be said to be ex-proprietary in the sense that some part of the property of the delinquent concerned goes to the State. But, the power to impose punishment and penalties is incidental to the power for vindicating the main purpose of that power.

Deterrence is the main theme or object behind the imposition of penalty and the whole object as shown by the history to this scheme of provisions is to provide gradually more and more deterrent penalties with a view to see that tax evasion does not take place and result in detriment to society as a whole. Article 14 of the Constitution guarantees to every citizen equality before the law and for the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.

An applicant pleading that article 14 has been violated must make out that not only he had been treated differently from others, but he has been so treated from persons similarly circumstances without any reasonable basis, and such differential treatment is unjustifiably made. Section 271(1) consists of three clauses. The first two clauses deal with a case of the failure of the assessee to furnish the return of total income either initially or within the time allowed under the provisions of law referred to therein and also with the failure to comply without reasonable cause with a notice under certain provisions of law mentioned therein and if these conditions are satisfied, i.e., of the failure to file the return or complying with the notice, then penalty is provided for in accordance with clauses (i) and (ii ) following these three clauses. But if it is a case of concealment of a particular income or furnishing inaccurate particulars of income, then the penalty as contemplated under the following clause (iii ) becomes liable to be imposed on the defaulting assessee. The penalty contemplated in the case of a person covered by clause (a ), i.e., who has failed to furnish his returns under the provisions referred to in that clause is that in addition to the amount of tax if any payable by him, he becomes liable to a sum equal to two per cent, of the tax for every month during which the default continued but not exceeding in the aggregate fifty per cent, of the tax by way of penalty. In case he fails to comply with notices contemplated under clause (b), he becomes liable to pay, in addition to any tax payable by him, by way of penalty a sum which shall not be less than ten per cent, but which shall not exceed fifty per cent of the amount of the tax, if any, which would have been avoided if the income returned by such person had been accepted as the correct income. In the case of clause (c ), namely, of concealing of particulars of his income or furnishing inaccurate particulars of such income, a person becomes liable to pay by way of penalty, in addition to any tax payable by him, a sum which shall not be less than twenty per cent but which shall not exceed one and a half time the amount of the tax, if any, which would have been avoided if the income had been accepted as the correct income.

Three classes of persons are thus covered by clauses (a ), (b) and (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271, but on account of their default under clauses (a) and (b) and deliberate act under clause (c) they are liable to pay varying amounts of penalty. The legislature views with disfavour the three types of assessees and considers the case of those covered by clause (c ) to be more serious, Under the Explanation what is contemplated by the legislature is that if an assessment has been made in the case of a person who has concealed the particulars of his income or has furnished inaccurate particulars and the return that he has shown is less than 80 per cent of the total income to which he is assessed, he will be deemed to have concealed the particulars of his income or has furnished inaccurate particulars thereof for the purpose of the penalty unless he proves that the failure to return the correct income did not arise from any fraud or wilful neglect on his part. The purpose of the clauses is to discourage concealing the particulars of one's income or furnishing inaccurate particulars of such income in the course of filing the returns. Such persons are looked upon with disfavour. If the concealment is a large amount or the inaccuracy in the furnishing of the particulars is large, the test of which is that it is less than 80 per cent of the amount for which the assessee has been ultimately assessed, the legislature thinks that there would be a presumption of such concealment having been made or inaccurate particulars having been supplied arising out of fraud or gross or wilful neglect on the part of the assessee. The purpose of the Explanation, therefore, is to discourage concealment of particulars in the filing of the returns of income and the furnishing of inaccurate particulars in the return and the more serious the concealment of the particulars or the furnishing of inaccurate particulars is, the more serious view is taken of the matter. This Explanation applies to all persons similarly placed, i.e., placed in a position covered by clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271 of the Act in whose case the return of income is less than 80 per cent of the income assessed. No doubt, such persons have been treated differently from others but they have not been so treated from persons similarly circumstanced. All persons placed in the same circumstances have been equally treated by the Explanation . The Explanation does create a class of persons. But the class of persons to whom the Explanation applies is a rational classification and has nexus with the object intended to be achieved, namely, of discouraging the concealment of the particulars of one's income or the furnishing of inaccurate particulars of such income during the course of assessment. In the circumstances, it cannot be said that the impugned provision of law violated the provisions of article 14 of the Constitution and is ultra vires.

What article 14 of the constitution requires is that the State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws. But it has been held by the Supreme Court in a number of cases that it shall not prevent the State from making a law based on a reasonable classification founded on an intelligble differentia having a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved by the law.

Section 18(1)(a), was substituted for the original section 18(1)(a) by Finance Act of 1969 which came into force on 1-4-1969. The Finance Act has increased the scale of penalty imposable on persons who failed without reasonable cause to furnish the return of net wealth within the time allowed and for non-compliance with the notice to produce evidence, etc. It is intended to provide an effective deterrent against faults without reasonable cause in the matter of furnishing the return of wealth or the production of accounts and documents called for by notice. Failure to furnish a return and failure to furnish a return within the time specified without reasonable cause amounts to concealment or temporary concealment of wealth. The object of the provision is thus intended to prevent concealment of wealth. So far as these persons are concerned they form a class by themselves. The gravamen of the offence is failure to submit the return without reasonable cause. Whether a person is richer comparatively than the other has no relevance to this classification. Having regard to the object of this provision, the classification of all these defaulters, so to say, into one category is an intelligible differentia based on a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved by the statute. Therefore, it could not be said that section 18(1)(a) infringes article 14 of the Constitution.

The purpose of section 18(1)(a ) is to render evasion or concealment unprofitable and of securing to the State compensation for damages caused by attempted evasion. Evasion or concealment is quasi-criminal in nature and character and, therefore, the levy of penalty need not be compensatory but it could be penal as to prevent the offence effectively.

Any concealment of the wealth and evasion of tax is a loss to the exchequer, and consequently, a loss to the public, that is, the community in general. Any provision intended against such evasion is, therefore, eminently a provision in the interest of the general public. Section 18(1)(a ) being a penal provision intended to prevent evasion of tax and concealment of wealth, it is saved under article 19(5) as a reasonable restriction on the fundamental right of the petitioner under article 19(1)(f ) of the Constitution, in the interest of the general public. Therefore, the contention of the petitioner that section 18(1)(a) offends article 19(1)(f) was untenable.

Equally untenable was the contention that Parliament lacks legislative competence to enact section 18(1)(a). The contention was based on a wrong assumption that a power to levy penalty is not incidental or ancillary to the power to legislate on taxes on the capital value of assets under entry 86, List I, of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution.

In the result, the writ petition failed and was dismissed.

Note : The case has been decided in favour of the revenue.

The legislation in question as to penalty may be prohibitine in nature, but there is no hostile discrimination against any particular taxpayer. The tax evaders are classified into different categories. The persons grouped in each category are treated alike in the matter of imposition of penalty. History of the legislation indicates that the Legislature has been trying the trial and error method to minimise the avoidance of tax, if not altogether eliminating it. The impugned provisions made from time to time are directed to practical problems faced by the Government in a highly complex economic field. They we preventive in nature although penal in character. They are not directed against honest taxpayers but only against the deliberate tax dodgers. There may be credities and inequities but on that ground alone the legislation cannot be struck down as invalid. Therefore, the said sections are not violative of article 14 or unreasonable restriction on the existing right guaranteed under article 19( 1)(f).

Chapter XIV-B consists of sections 158B to 158BH which was inserted by the Finance Act, 1995 so as to provide for an assessment of the undisclosed income detected as a result of search, and devised to operate in the separate field of undisclosed income and in addition to the regular assessments covering previous years in the block period. In the instant case, the contention of the assessee that sub-section (2) of section 158BFA was oppressive or in any way violative of any article of the Constitution of India could not be accepted. There was no basis in that contention. [Para 7]

Section 158BFA has been introduced in Chapter XIV-B which deals with special procedure for assessment of search cases. The said provision is intended to act as an effective deterrent against evasion of tax and to put a stop to that practice which the Legislature considers to be against public interest. Merely, because heavy penalty is provided for concealing income and also disclosing of undisclosed and unexplained investment during search conducted, it cannot be said that such a provision is a piece of hostile legislation. Assuming that the provision is harsh since it is a deterrent against tax evaders, provision is not expropriatory. Power to levy tax on income is vested in the Parliament and power to impose penalties to vindicate that particular power of imposition of tax is also with the Parliament. Object and purpose of section 158BFA is to provide penalty for concealment of income and act as a deterrent against tax evaders. Heavy penalty is prescribed to check tax evasion. If Legislature in its wisdom felt that in the matter of search cases such a penalty should be imposed, it cannot be canvassed in a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution of India. [Para 8]

Therefore, there is no infirmity in the said provision. The prayer of the assessee to declare such provision as oppressive and violative of fundamental rights guaranteed under the Constitution could not be sustained.

Entry 54 of the Federal List in Schedule VII of the Government of India Act, 1935, empowers the Central Legislature to enact laws with respect to 'taxes on income' and entry 42 of the same list with respect to 'offences against laws with respect to any of the matters in this list.' The expression 'taxes on income' is of the widest import and would obviously include laws in relation to the taxation of evaded income. Such a law may take the form of an appropriation not merely of the income evaded but even more as the tax or as the reparation for damage caused to the State by such attempted evasion. In this connection it should be borne in mind that the court is interpreting the words in an organic instrument designed to endow sovereign legislative bodies with legislative power and the words should not be construed in any narrow or pedantic sense. Apart from this, the power to enact laws to prevent evasion and make it unremunerative to the evader could also be viewed as an incidental or ancillary power necessary to render effective the substantive power conferred by entry 54. Lastly it is legitimate and proper in determining the scope of the power to have regard to what is ordinarily embraced in the topic in the legislative practice both of the State which has conferred the power, viz., the United Kingdom, as well as of the State on whom the power is conferred viz., India. From the earliest times in every State including the United Kingdom as well as India, the law relating to income-tax has always included provisions for circumventing evasion by concealment and for the levy of penalty in such cases as well as for the prosecution of the offender for such concealment. In the light of this it would follow that the content of a law relating to income-tax would comprehend a law designed to prevent evasion of the tax by the levy of suitable penalties. The argument that the penalty which could lawfully be levied under section 28 of the 1922 Act, viz., one and half times the tax evaded, might in certain cases where the average rate of tax exceeds 10 annas in the rupee exceed the income, and was, therefore, not a proper tax legislation proceeded as a misapprehension, for the quantum of the penalty is one for the Legislature and is wholly irrelevant for determining the constitutional validity of the penalty provision.

As regards section 28 of the 1922 Act, offending against the equal protection of laws guaranteed by article 14 of the Constitution, under both the sections 28 and 51 and 52 of the 1922 Act, the IAC is the pivotal authority. When an ITO comes across an assessee about whom he is satisfied that he has concealed the particulars of his income or has deliberately furnished inaccurate particulars thereof, he transmits the information to the IAC for the purpose of levying a penalty, for under section 28(6) of 1922 Act he cannot do this except with the previous approval of this Officer. When the matter is thus before the IAC, there are two courses which are open to him. He might in the case of any particular assessee grant the request of the ITO and approve his proposal and permit him to levy a penalty on the assessee. In other cases he might make up his mind to prosecute the assessee under section 52 of the 1922 Act. Which course he shall pursue is left to his unfettered discretion. The enactment gives him no guidance and prescribes no standards. It is not indicated how that choice is to be determined or what circumstances he might take into account in arriving at his conclusion. The assessee is left to the mercy of the IAC who might pursue one of two alternative courses.

The provision concerned is a provision in a taxing statute. It is open to the Parliament to classify the taxpayers on any rational basis and also treat the different classes of taxpayers differently. It is also permissible for the Parliament to further classify in a rational and non-arbitrary manner the assessees in relation to their conduct. The Parliament can legislate with respect to the assessees who comply with the requirements of law and extend such concessions as it deems fit to such assessees, which concessions it may choose to deny to those who have violated the law and such violations have been established by reason of the action taken by the authorities. It is in that background and with the object of laying down a special procedure for the assessment of the assessees who fail to comply with the law by not disclosing in full their taxable income and by not paying the taxes properly due from them that Chapter XIV-B consisting of sections 158B to 158BH was inserted in the Act.

The assumption made in the Scheme of the Act that a person who comes forward with the return or with further information after a search, does so only on account of the detection already made under the search and the likelihood of further exposure is a reasonable assumption and it can in no way be regarded as arbitrary. The special procedure provided in Chapter XIV-B is meant to apply to all such cases notwithstanding anything contained in any other provisions of the Act as provided in section 158BA(1) and other provisions of the Act, therefore, cannot control the contents of this Chapter except to the extent provided for in Chapter XIV-B.

There is no fundamental right in an assessee to commit breaches of the law. The right that can be asserted by one who has chosen to violate the law is the right to be treated in a manner similar to that in which other similar offenders are treated. Chapter XIV-B accords similar treatment to all persons belonging to the class to whom that Chapter is to apply. There is no discrimination therein among those who suffer such searches.

The petitioner’s argument that in cases where the assessee had paid advance tax, such payment would clearly indicate his intention to disclose his income and it could not be said that such person would not have disclosed his income, cannot be accepted for the payment of advance tax by itself does not establish an intent to disclose the income. The disclosure is to be made by filing the return. Even in search cases, where the time for filing the return under section 139(1) has not expired, income disclosed in the books of account is not treated as undisclosed income. All that is denied to the assessee in search cases is the opportunity to file a return after the period specified in section 139(1) and to claim that the income that he would have disclosed in a belated return is not to be regarded as undisclosed income. The reason for denying such opportunity in search cases is obvious. After having suffered a search, the assessee is not to be enabled to escape the consequences of his failure to disclose all his income by filing a return after the search and after the expiry of the time prescribed under section 139(1) and by disclosing therein income which had remained undisclosed up to the date of the search. Therefore, section 158BB(1)(c ) is not in any way unconstitutional.
