Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1983-84 - Whether where Tribunal deleted addition made in respect of income from self-occupied property, penalty referable to that addition could be sustained - Held, no - Whether, where addition made had undergone valid fluctuations at various stages of estimation, it could not be made basis of levy of penalty under section 271(1)(c) - Held, yes - Whether, where certain book entries found in course of survey disclosed income receipts of assessee at a much higher figure than returned by assessee, this act of assessee amounted to conscious effort on his part to conceal his income and thus, penalty was leviable - Held, yes - Whether, where assessee had himself admitted that he was having 25 per cent share in a benami contract business though not disclosed by him in his return on view that it having been issued from unregistered firm was not includible in his hands, such an act of assessee amounted to concealment of income and penalty was imposable under section 271(1)(c) - Held, yes

HEADNOTE: Section 297, read with section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 28(1)(c) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Repeals and savings - Assessment year 1959-60 - Whether for purposes of penalty, there is no doubt classification under section 297(g) between assessees who had filed returns of income before 1-4-1962, and whose assessments were completed before that date and assessees who had filed returns of income before 1-4-1962, but whose assessments were completed on or after 1-4-1962 and, this is an intelligible classification - Held, yes - Whether clauses (f) and (g) of section 297(2) is not to discriminate against those assessees whose assessments for year ending on 31-3-1962, or any earlier year had not been completed before 1-4-1962, but to bring them in line with other assessees whose assessments are completed on or after 1-4-1962, in matter of imposition of penalty - Held, yes - Whether, in view of aforesaid, it could be concluded that section 297 (2)(g) was not violative of Article 14 of Constitution of India - Held, yes

FACT: The petitioner, assessee took forest contracts. It ran a saw-mill and also manufactured and sold furniture. It also did stone quarrying business. For the assessment year 1959-60 the petitioner filed a return of its income under section 22(2) of Act, 1922, on 21-10-1959, showing an income of Rs. 7,896. In the assessment proceedings the ITO noticed some discrepancies in the accounts and registers maintained by the assessee of its business and called upon the assessee to explain the discrepancies and furnish certain particulars. Thereupon, the assessee filed a revised return of its income on 17-1-1964, disclosing its total income as Rs. 50,605. The ITO finalized the assessment on 19-3-1964, after taking into consideration the revised return and issued a notice to the petitioner under section 271(1)(c) for concealment of income. The ITO referred the matter to the AAC as penalty intended to imposed by him exceeded Rs. 1,000.

The Inspecting Assistant Commissioner, finding that the assessee had concealed the particular of its income, made the impugned order imposing a penalty of Rs. 25,000 on the petitioner. The petitioner then preferred an appeal before the Tribunal which was dismissed. In the instant writ petition. It was contended by the petitioner that section 297(2)(g) being violative of article 14 of the Constitution is invalid and, therefore, no penalty could be imposed on the petitioner under section 271 and, that under section 271(1) a penalty can be imposed by the Income-tax Officer or the Appellate Assistant Commissioner only if he, in the course of any proceedings under the Act of 1961, is satisfied that any person has committed any of the acts enumerated in clauses (a), (b) or (c) of section 271(1); that, as the assessment against the petitioner was made under the Act of 1922, and not under the Act of 1961, the Income-tax Officer or the Appellate Assistant Commissioner had no jurisdiction to impose any penalty under section 271(1).

HELD: The effect of clauses (a), (f) and (g) of section 297(2) is that where the assessee files a return of income before the commencement of the Act of 1961, that is before 1-4-1962, for any assessment year, then the assessment of that person for that year is under the 1922 Act; any proceeding for the imposition of a penalty in respect of any assessment completed before 1-4-1962, can be initiated and penalty can be imposed under the 1922 Act; any proceedings for the imposition of a penalty in respect of any assessment for the year ending on 31-3-1962 or any earlier year which is completed on or after 1-4-1962 can be initiated and penalty can be imposed under the 1961 Act. In the present case, the petitioner filed a return of income before 1-4-1962, but the assessment was completed on 19-3-1964, that is after 1-4-1962, therefore, clause (g) of section 297(2) was plainly attracted for the initiation of proceedings for imposition of penalty under the Act of 1961.

. An. appellate authority in the case of an assessee whose assessment is completed before 1-4-1962, can reached a finding that there is a concealment of income and such a finding can be reached even after 1-4-1962. Thus, if the completion of assessment has any relevance in determining whereunder and in which circumstances the penal proceedings should be initiated or carried out, it date, 1-4-1962, does not play any important part. It is true that before the classification made by the legislature could be struck down, it is to be established that it is either arbitrary or fanciful or capricious or unjust. The argument that the classification was necessary because initiation of proceedings could not be taken before the assessment was completed was not acceptable. It is true that the ITO or the AAC as the case may be, is required to determine the quantum of penalty with reference to the tax which is determined as payable. But from that circumstances it cannot be held that the very initiation of proceedings is held over until after the completion of the assessment.

Thus, the event which gives a cause of action for initiation of penalty proceedings is not held over until after the completion of assessment proceedings. If the completion of assessment proceedings, therefore, is not relevant to determine whether or not the ITO or the AAC should initiate penalty proceedings, the date on which the assessment is completed in a particular case cannot have any bearing is determining whether the assessment should be governed by one set of provisions of one case and a different set of provisions in the matter of penalty in another case.

If the date of completion of assessment is not a relevant factor in determining whether or not penal proceedings should be initiated or whether the assessee has or has not committed one of the other wrong, there is nothing dividing the two classes of assessee with reference to the date of completion of the assessment proceedings.

The provisions of either sec tion 28 of the 1922 Act or section 271 of the Act of 1961 will show that the infraction of the provisions of the Act takes place as soon as the return is filed.

That such satisfaction is entered by the ITO at a later date shows that the adjudication of the Act or omission of the deliquent assessee is postponed to the date of recording such finding. But, from that it cannot be inferred or legitimately urged that the infraction has not taken place when the returns were filed. Some time must necessarily elapse between the filing of the return and commencement of proceedings for assessment, and during such proceedings the income-tax authority records satisfaction whether there has been failure to comply with the provisions of the Act in respect of matters provided in section 28 of the old Act or section 271 of the new Act.

The date of completion of the assessment makes no difference so far as this aspect of concerned. In fact, it has no impact either on incurring of the liability or for imposition of penalty. Therefore, the classification made by section 297(2)(g) of the Act of 1961 cannot be justified either as relevant or having any relation to the object with which it is concerned. So far as making a provision for imposing a penalty is concerned, there is no difference between the assessees who have filed returns but in whose cases the assessment was completed prior to 1-4-1962, and assessees who have filed returns but in whose cases assessment was not completed or could not be completed till 1-4-1962.

The mere fact that the legislation divides assessees into two classes cannot be itself be its justification. Justification has to be found somewhere else, namely, in a rational nexus between the classification and the object to be achieved. If the respondents are not able to show that nexus, then it is not possible to uphold the contention that classification is rational or just.

That it is arbitrary is obvious when the date of coming into force of the Act is found to have no bearing on the division of assessees into two classes, one governed by one set of provisions and the other governed by anther set of provisions.

The contention that in the instant case, there was no rational nexus between the object with which the provision has been made for imposing penalty and selecting the date for differentiating as to this provision of law by which the proceedings should be governed, was well founded and had not been satisfactorily answered by the respondents.

The contention on behalf of the revenue that if there was no provision like clause (g) of sub-section (2) of section 297, the Income-tax authorities would have no power to initiate penal proceedings for imposition of penalty by having recourse to the provisions of the old Act had no force with regard to assessments completed after 1-4-1962. Assuming that the provisions like clause (g) of sub-section (2) of section 297 were not to be made by the legislature, the provisions of sub-clause (c) of (d) or (e ) of section 6 of the General Clauses Act would have applied and proceedings for imposition of penalty could have been initiated and penalty imposed under the provisions of the repealed Act, i.e., the Income-tax Act, 1922.

In view of the decision in state of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar [1952] SCR 284 that article 14 of the Indian Constitution does not insist that every piece of legislation must have universal application and it does not take away from the State the power to classify persons for the purposes of legislation, but the classification must be rational, and in order to satisfy this test (i) the classification must be founded on an intelligible differentia which distinguished those that are grouped together from others, and (ii ) that differentia must have a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved by the Act. The differentia which is the basis of the classification and the object of the Act are distinct things and what is necessary is that there must be a nexus between them.

Applying those tests it seemed that the progressive graduation of income-tax with different rates applying to different income groups or to different slabs of income far form being discriminatory was a just practical and reasonable system of classification. Obviously a flat rate applicable to different groups of income would be the most inequitable arrangement. In the instant case, the scheme of the graduation of the rates so far as the income-tax was concerned was based on such slabs as the exempted limit of the first Rs. 1,500, the next Rs. 3,500, with one rate, the next Rs. 5,000 on a higher rate, the next Rs. 5,000 on a still higher rate and thereafter the balance of the total income on a still further higher rate. Rates increased with the increase of incomes. It was a reasonable classification and could be justified both on the ground of ability to pay as well as by the objective of reducing disparity of incomes in society. With each group or slabs of income, the rates applied uniformly and there was no discrimination. That being so, the scheme and the rates could not be called unconstitutional or in violation of the constitutional clause of equal protection of laws or equality before the law.

Similarly again the scheme and rates of super-tax, in the instant case were based on reasonable classification of income on the basis of higher and higher slabs of income. It was not necessary that the basis of the scheme for the income-tax should also be the same as the basis of the scheme for the super-tax in order to be reasonable. The constitutional doctrine of equality before the law or the equal protection of the law was not violated by a reasonable classification and there was no limit as to the classification so long as it had and observed a rational basis. There was no constitutional inhibition in the Indian Constitution to suggest that once a class has been reasonably made, that class cannot be further divided into reasonable sub-classes for achieving particular legislative policies and therefore, there was no reason why the classification or classes made reasonably for purpose of income-tax cannot equally reasonably be re-classified or subdivided for the purposes of super-tax.

Therefore, the Finance Act, 1951, as applicable to the Finance Act, 1954, under section 2 of the Finance Act, 1954, was not ultra virus the Constitution and did not infringe the right of equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws. Further, the Finance Act was not ultra virus the Constitution and the rates imposed thereunder were neither discriminatory nor arbitrary.

For these reasons the application failed and was dismissed.

Note : Decision was in favour of revenue.

HEADNOTE: Explanation-I to section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1972-73 - Since returned income of assessee was less than 80 per cent of assessed income, in penalty proceedings Explanation to section 271(1)(c) became applicable - As assessee failed to furnish any explanation, penalty was imposed under section 271(1)(c) - Whether even though provisions of main section 271(1)(c) were not specifically invoked, penalty was rightly imposed as Explanation to section 271(1)(c) did not give rise to a separate charge as distinguished from substantive provisions of section 271(1)(c) - Held, yes

FACT: For the assessment year 1972-73, since the returned income of the assessee was less than 80 per cent of the assessed income, in penalty proceeding's Explanation to section 271(1)(c) became applicable. Since the assessee was not able to furnish any explanation, penalty was imposed under section 271(1)(c). On appeal, the assessee contended before the Tribunal that Explanation to section 271(1)(c) gave rise to a separate charge as distinguished from the substantive provisions of section 271(1)(c) and that the provisions of the main section 271(1)(c) having not been specifically invoked, penalty could not be levied. The Tribunal rejected the assessee's contention and upheld the imposition of penalty.

On reference:

HELD: The penalty provision is contained in section 271 and on different counts penalty of different amounts is imposable, wherever there is concealment of income. If the concealment is beyond 20 per cent of the returned income, then the Explanation becomes applicable and presumption has to be raised against the assessee which he can rebut but in case concealment does not exceed 20 per cent. the penalty is still leviable but in this situation the onus lies on the department to prove concealment. Therefore, the Explanation has to be read with section 271(1)(c ) and there is no question of considering the Explanation as separate or distinct from it. The law has to be applied to the given facts. Even if in the order specific reference to Explanation is not mentioned but Explanation is applied and onus is placed on the assessee because the returned income is less than 80 per cent of the assessed income, from this inference has to be drawn that the assessing authorities were conscious of the fact that Explanation was applicable. The Tribunal had, therefore, rightly rejected the assessee's claim.

When the proviso to section 139(1), which is a departure from the earlier Act, was inserted, the legislature applied its mind and in its wisdom thought of a special classification by treating defaulting registered firms as a class by itself. When it imposed such stringent conditions for the exercise of the discretion to extend the time for filing of returns, the legislature bore in mind the privileges enjoyed by the registered firm in the matter of exemption, rates of tax, etc., and this was possibly the basis for the differentia which was thought of. On a fair reading of the above provisions it cannot be doubted that the classification created in the above situation subserves the object of sustaining the privileges which a registered firm could claim under the Act and also to act as a deterrent against delayed submission of returns. There is, therefore, a nexus between the object with which the provision has been made and the differentia projected in the proviso to section 139(1).

So long as the firm does not admit that there was wilful abstention from the submission of returns, the firm is conscious of its laches in having delayed such returns and, therefore, it invokes the discretion of the ITO to excuse such delay after showing sufficient cause. If the delay is excused, then the conduct of the assessee ceases to be contumacious, which, if found, is liable to attract section 271. Hence, the assessee who sets the proviso to section 139(1) into motion cannot ignore all these implications including the effect of the proviso thereto and in such a situation he has to be dealt with under section 139 and not under any other provision of the Act.

No doubt, by reason of the classification the defaulting registered firm suffers in effect a higher quantum of income-tax, in the garb of interest the classification is intended to subserve a particular purpose, namely, to compel the registered firms to be cautious and prompt in the matter of submission of their returns lest they should suffer a higher quantum of tax and the object so projected has an intelligible nexus with the differentia that is thought of.

The true intent and scope of article 14 of the Constitution appears to be that no one should be denied equality before law or equal protection of the law provided, however, that nothing could prevent the State from designing a law based on or involving a classification which is founded on an intelligible differentia which distinguishes persons or things that are grouped together from those left out of the group and such a differentia must have a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved by the statute in question. If, thus, therefore, there is a methodology in classification, then the resultant differentia would be maintained as valid. If there is total absence of any connection whatsoever between the object sought to be achieved and that of the legislation in question, then such a law would lead to invidious discrimination. But, if the basis of the classification is made for any reason, may be historical or otherwise, or difference in the nature, trade, calling or occupation of a person sought to be affected by the legislation, or even the difference in the position or nature of different business concerns, then such a classification which is referable to occupation, point of time, locality, etc., may be sustained as an intelligible classification. It is indeed very difficult to exhaust the circumstances under which a classification could be thought of or made. It is by now well-settled that article 14 does not envisage a fanatical approach to the problem of equality before law. Unless a well instructed person on a study of the law impugned comes to a reasonable conclusion that there is total lack of rational classification, then the methodology adopted is open to challenge. If the classification is intended to lay down a policy and incidentally exercise effective control over persons for whom certain privileges and exemptions are granted under the taxing law and in case they are classified for the particular purpose of imposing a heavier quantum of liability in a particular situation, then it cannot be said that the discrimination achieved is hopelessly unguided and not prompted by any public interest or based upon rational principles. Such a difference, as was made in the instant case, is on an intelligible differentia and has a rational relationship to the purpose of the statute.

The Explanation to section 271(1)(c) can be applied only when the Assessing officer has invoked the same at the time of issuing the notice itself. In the instant case, the notices issued by the department did not mention the Explanation in question.

There could not be any dispute about the legal contention of the revenue that the power of the Commissioner (Appeals) is co-terminous with that of the Assessing Officer, but this power is subject to limitations and restrictions placed by the statutory provisions. A reading of section 271 showed that it required the satisfaction of that authority regarding the concealment of particulars of income or furnishing of inaccurate particulars of income which had to levy the penalty. This satisfaction of the authority levying the penalty could not, therefore, be substituted by any other authority. The restriction on the powers of the Commissioner (Appeals) was implicit in the provisions of section 271 itself. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) was not justified in invoking the Explanation.

Penalty proceedings being quasi-criminal in nature, the onus lay on the revenue to prove that there was concealment of the particulars of the income by the assessee. As regards the question as to whether their respective burdens had been discharged by the concerned parties, where a fact is in the special knowledge of a particular person and he hides or withholds the same from the knowledge of other, he can be said to have concealed the said fact. Hence a person can be said to have concealed the particulars of income only when he is under obligation to disclose the same and withholds the same from the knowledge of the Assessing Officer.

In the instant case, since it was the duty of the assessee to disclose the basic and primary facts which were within his special knowledge, he should have disclosed the relevant details in respect of increase in the share capital and unsecured loans either in the return or in the course of the assessment proceedings. Even if the same were not disclosed and the additions had been confirmed by the Tribunal, the assessee had also a chance to disclose them in the course of penalty proceedings to show prima facie that receipts in question were not the income of the assessee. The details furnished before the Commissioner (Appeals) were never available with the Assessing Officer who levied the penalties and, therefore, the Assessing Officer had no opportunity to consider these details. Even the Commissioner (Appeals)’s original order dated 17-8-1990 did not indicate about these details being filed by the assessee. It was only the rectification order of the Commissioner (Appeals) under section 154 which indicated that these details were filed by the assessee. But that order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was subsequent to the order of penalty passed by the Assessing Officer. Therefore, the Assessing Officer had no knowledge of the said details filed before the Commissioner (Appeals), and thus the onus had been discharged by the revenue by showing the conduct of the assessee in withholding the basic and primary facts which the assessee was under obligation to disclose, these being within its special knowledge. Such withholding of facts by the assessee itself amounted to concealment.

Such legislation cannot be struck down on the ground that it meets out hostile unequal treatment. The petitioners had failed to discharge the heavy burden which laid upon them to sustain the challenge to the impugned provision based on article 14 and the contention urged in that behalf must be rejected. The other argument was that the impugned provision could not be treated as incidental or ancillary to the main provisions and that, therefore, it could not be said to have any rational nexus with the main provisions of the statute.

This is not the case where on the basis of any presumption made by the legislature a penalty such as seizure or confiscation or penalty in lieu of confiscation is sought to be levied. The impugned provision is made on the basis of a well-known fact which is a matter of common knowledge and common report and all that it requires a building contractor to do is to furnish prescribed particulars within the stipulated time limit on the span of penalty with a view to detecting evasion of tax. In these circumstances, it could hardly be contended that the impugned provision being not incidental or ancillary to the main power to tax income which is conferred by the Act, it had no nexus with the statute in question.

The petition was, therefore to be dismissed.

HEADNOTE: Section 256, read with section 271(1)(c), of the income-tax act, 1961-Reference-question of fact-Ito imposed penalty for concealment of income on assessee on ground that certain household expenses had been underestimated and certain other expenses had not been shown properly-On appeal, penalty was cancelled on ground that as particulars of concealment had not been disclosed to assessee, he was not in position to defend himself and as such he could not be said to have been granted reasonable opportunity of being heard-Tribunal upheld cancellation of penalty-Whether any question of law arose from tribunal's order-Held, no

Section 274(1) of the income-tax act, 1961-Penalty-Opportunity of hearing-Whether where particulars of concealment are not disclosed to assessee while imposing penalty, it would mean that assesses has not been given reasonable opportunity of being heard-Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was assessed by the ITO at an income higher than that declared in the return filed. The ITO held that the assessee had certain concealed income which could be determined from the fact that household expenses had been underestimated and travelling expenses of family and club expenses as well as medical expenses which had been reimbursed, had not been shown properly. The ITO also imposed penalty under section 271(1)(c). On appeal, the penalty was cancelled on the ground that the basis of the penalty proceedings had not been disclosed to the assessee who was put in a difficult position to defend the matter under section 274(1) and was not granted a reasonable opportunity of being heard. On further appeal, the Tribunal confirmed the order cancelling the penalty and rejected the application for reference under section 256(1), holding that the finding regarding lack of reasonable opportunity was a finding of fact.

On application for reference under section 256(2):

HELD: In order to constitute a penalty under section 271(1)(c ) what is required is a concealment, either of the income or of the particulars thereof. In order to enable such a penalty to be imposed, it is necessary to determine which is the income concealed or which are the particulars not disclosed. If a person is accused of a particular offence of which particulars are given to him, he has a chance of giving his defence thereto. If he is generally accused of some offence of an unknown type, he cannot easily defend himself. The additions which were made during the assessment proceedings in the instant case were based on certain surmises and conjectures. In penalty proceedings, it was not only necessary to inform the assessee of the particular concealment but also necessary for the department to prove positively that there was such a concealment. It was the duty of the department to inform the assessee of the particular concealment that had taken place so that he could defend the case. The failure to do so had led to the cancellation of the penalty. No question of law, therefore, arose from the Tribunal's decision since the question whether penalty had been imposed in accordance with proper procedure or in consonance with natural justice, was one of fact.

IT CASE NO. 39 OF 1981.

HEADNOTE: Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (Corresponding to section 28 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922) - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1954-55 - Whether ITO does not cease to have power to impose a penalty under section 28 of 1922 Act once an appeal has been filed before AAC against assessment which gives rise to initiation of penalty proceedings - Held, yes
Interpretation of statute:
(i) Legislative intent
(ii) Beneficial interpretation

FACT: For the assessment year 1954-55, the ITO made an addition as estimated income for low gross profits and for business income kept outside the account books, and the assessment was completed .Prior to this ITO issued a notice under section 28 in regard to concealment of income.

On appeal, against the quantum assessment, the AAC reduced the addition, and the reduction was confirmed by the Tribunal. Thereafter, the ITO pursued the penalty proceedings initiated earlier and levied penalty.

On second appeal, the Tribunal upheld the penalty.

On reference, the question refereed was as to whether ITO ceased to have power to impose a penalty under section 28, once an appeal had been filed before the AAC against the assessment which gave rise to the initiation of penalty proceedings.

HELD: Tax and penalty, like tax and penal interest, are distinct and different concepts under the Act. Penalty is in addition to the tax determined as payable by the assessee. Penalty, cannot be taken as additional tax for all purposes. The penalty and assessment proceedings are not one and the same proceedings. The findings given in the assessment proceedings would only be relevant and admissible but not final and conclusive in penalty proceedings. In penalty proceedings, further evidence can be led to rebut the findings given in the assessment proceedings. Even in matters which are processed by the ITO, the assessee might not place all the materials before the ITO, with the result he might not be able to detect or find out concealment of income. The AAC, during his enquiry, may come to know additional facts, which are either not disclosed to the ITO, or which escape the attention of the ITO, and those facts might reasonably lead the AAC to a finding that the assessee had concealed income. In such a case, if the AAC has no powers to impose a penalty, the assessee would altogether escape penalty. Therefore, the law has wisely given powers to the AAC and also the Tribunal to impose penalty on the assessee. When the law empowers more than one authority to impose penalty, it would be unreasonable to expect that each one of them would, in his own turn, invoke and impose penalty. At any rate, the assessee can be punished only once in respect of concealment of income and not by all the three authorities simultaneously or one after the other and for the same offence.

It would, therefore, be reasonable to think that when the ITO, having original jurisdiction, and the appellate authorities, i.e. , AAC and the Tribunal, are also invested with powers to impose penalties, it would be wise for the inferior officer to exercise that jurisdiction or power. If section 28 is interpreted in a different manner it would be disadvantageous to the assessee. If the penalty is imposed by the ITO, the assessee would have two opportunities to test the correctness of that penalty order by filing appeals to the AAC and if necessary to the Tribunal. If the power to impose penalty is exercised by the AAC, then the assessee would lose the benefit of one appeal because he could in that case file an appeal only to the Tribunal. If the power to impose penalty is exercised by the Tribunal, then the assessee would altogether lose the right of filing an appeal against the penalty order. If section 28 of the Act is at all to be construed, such construction should be placed on it which would be more advantageous to the assessee.

The language used in section 28 is clear and unambiguous. The section does not under any circumstances oust the jurisdiction of the ITO to impose penalty. If the AAC or the Tribunal imposes penalty on an assessee under section 28(1)(c), he or it is bound under sub-section (5) of section 28, to send a copy thereof to the ITO so that he could not once again impose a penalty upon the assessee for the same concealment.

If the legislature had intended to oust the jurisdiction of the ITO to impose a penalty on an assessee if an appeal was filed against the assessment before the AAC, nothing prevented the legislature from saying so in express language in section 28. There is a general presumption in law against an intention to disturb or oust the jurisdiction or interfere with the jurisdiction, which is given to an officer.

As per section 297(2)(g) the proceedings for imposition of penalty in respect of any assessment for the year ending on 31-3-1962, or any earlier year which is completed on or after the 1-4-1962, shall be under the Act. As the assessment was for the assessment year 1954-55, and as it was completed after April, 1962, the proceeding for imposition of penalty under the Act was perfectly competent. Therefore, the proceedings for the imposition of penalty under section 271 of the Act were not open to attack.

As regards violation of article 20(1) of the Constitution, the argument was that as this article prohibited the imposition of a penalty greater than that which might have been imposed upon the petitioner under the law in force on the date of the commission of the offence, she was not liable to be prosecuted, as a penalty had already been imposed upon her on the same facts, and that the petitioner stood in danger of being prosecuted for an offence under section 277 of the Act of 1961.

From section 277 it is clear that, unless a person makes a statement in any verification under the Act or under any rules made thereunder or delivers an account or statement which is false and which he either knows or believes to be false or does not believe to be true, he shall not be punishable. The act of the petitioner was not an offence under the Act. Therefore, a prosecution on the basis that she committed an offence under the provisions of section 277 would not lie. Hence the apprehension of the petitioner that she would be prosecuted under the new Act was an idle one.

The maximum penalty being the same in both the enactments, there was no substance in the contention that the petitioner was being subjected to a greater penalty under the new Act because a minimum is specified in section 271 of the 1961 Act, Penalty is nothing but compensation for damages collected by the State for attempting to evade the provisions of the Act. No conviction for any offence is involved in the imposition of a penalty. Article 20(1) of the Constitution will have application only when a person is subjected to a penalty greater than that which might to have been inflicted under the law in force at the time of the commission of the offence. This would indicate that commission of an offence and a conviction thereof are necessary in order that the provisions of the Article may be attracted.

Although the concealment of the particulars of the income was made an offence under section 52 of the 1922 Act and is also made an offence under section 277 of the new Act, it couldnot be said that the penalty imposed under section 28 of the 1922 Act or under section 271 of the 1961 Act was or is imposed on the basis that it was or is an offence. For the offence punishment was or is prescribed such as imprisonment, fine or both. The imposition of penalty on the basis of an act or omission by an assessee is not because the act or omission constitutes an offence, but because that act or omission would constitute an attempt at evasion. Therefore penalty is exacted not because an act or omission is an offence but because it is an attempt at evasion of tax on the part of the assessee. Article 20(1) of the Constitution can have no application to a case where a penalty is imposed not as punishment for an offence but for some other collateral purpose.

So, even assuming that the penalty has been enhanced under the new Act, that would not attract the constitutional inhibition of article 20(1) of the Constitution because the penalty is imposed not as punishment for the commission of an offence, even though the act for which the penalty is imposed is an offence liable to be punished.

In view of above, the instant petition failed and was to be dismissed.

Note : The decision was in favour of revenue.

No case for interference in exercise of court’s extraordinary powers under article 226 of the Constitution had been made out by the petitioners. Any order of penalty that may be passed under the new Act will be appealable under section 246 thereof and it will be open to the petitioners to ventilate their grievances, if any, by an appeal to appropriate authority. Eventually, the case can be brought before this Court on a reference under section 256 of the new Act. The exceptional circumstances under which the High Court may be persuaded to interfere at the inception of the proceedings pursuant to the notice dated 19-4-1963, have not been made out in the instant case.

As regards violation of article 20(1) of the Constitution, this article hits at the infliction of a penalty greater than the one that could be inflicted at the time the act was done. The maximum limit of penalty is obviously not enhanced by the new Act and then it is discretionary under the new Act also that the ITO may choose not to inflict any penalty in the circumstances of a case. However, if he chooses to do so, then a yardstick for the determination of the penalty based on each month of the default is prescribed. This rather results in rationalizing the exercise of discretion by the ITO by providing a criterion when there was no such corresponding criterion prescribed under the old Act. Under the old Act the ITO was free to determine any penalty within the maximum limit prescribed. In the circumstances, article 20(1) of the Constitution had not been infringed in any manner.

As regards violation of article 14 of the Constitution, in enacting section 297(2)(g) of the new Act, in construing the validity of a statute impugned under this article, courts have to bear in mind the well-established principle that the legislature can make class legislation, provided the classification on which it purports to be based is rational and has a reasonable nexus with the object intended to be achieved by it, and so, on the failure of the party to show that the said classification is irrational, or has no nexus with the object intended to be achieved by the impugned Act, the initial presumption of constitutionality would help the state to urge that the failure of the party challenging the validity to rebut the initial presumption goes against his claim that the Act is invalid. In all cases where the material adduced before the court in matters relating to article 14 is unsatisfactory, the court may have to allow the state to lean on the doctrine of initial presumption of constitutionality.

In the instant case no material had been placed to show that this provision had been abused or was capable of being abused in any manner by the taxation authorities. It also could not be said that the legislature had not made a valid classification in drawing a line between assessments which had been completed before the coming into force of the new Act, and those which were completed thereafter. The penalties prescribed under the Income-tax Act for failure to submit returns of income in time are not in the nature of punishment imposed for conviction of an offence. Such penalties are more or less compensatory in character to make good the loss that may be caused to the state revenues on account of late submission of returns of income and in consequence late realization of the tax. Therefore, the provision relating to imposition of penalties can be said to form integral parts of the proceedings relating to assessment. It was, therefore, open to the legislature to make a distinction regarding assessments which were completed before the coming into force of the new Act and those which are to be completed after the coming into force of the new Act. Thus, the distinction made by the legislature was a valid one, and therefore, the provisions were not invalid.

As regards the question as to whether the notice issued under section 22(2) of the old Act could be deemed to be a notice under the new act, reference may be made to section 297 (2)(k) of the new Act. This saving provision applies to the case and the legislature could not have intended that the notices already issued under section 22(1) of the old Act should be taken to be wiped out with the coming into force of the new Act. Section 297(2)(k ) covers agreements, appointments, approval given, recognition granted, direction and instructions, besides the notification, orders or rules issued under any of the old Act. These provisions will, therefore, cover administrative orders and notices and the words "order or rule issued under any provisions" will cover a notice issued under section 22(1) of the old Act. Thus, the notice issued under the old Act can legitimately be considered as good as a notice issued under the new Act for purposes of invoking sections 271 and 274 of the new Act.

Consequently, the instant petition was to be dismissed.

Note : The decision was in favour of revenue.

In the instant case the assessment was completed on 23-3-1967. On the same date penalty proceedings had been initiated. The satisfaction of the ITO that there was concealment of income thus solidified on 23-3-1967. The penalty was, therefore, to be levied in terms of the law applicable on 23-3-1967. The Tribunal was, thus, in error in cancelling the penalty on the basis of the authority laid down in the case of Anwar Ali (supra). There being obvious discrepancy of more than 20 per cent, the obligation to explain the difference was squarely upon the assessee. The assessee did not produce any material to show that his explanation was correct. There was no explanation as to why the assessee showed a figure of sale before the income-tax authority, lower than what he had stated before the sales tax authority. There was, thus, an obvious concealment. Secondly, in regard to assessed income although it was based on estimate, but the estimate was based upon the assessee's own percentage of income from the records of the earlier years. If the rate of sale was higher in earlier years, the income-tax authority was fully justified in holding that the income could not be lower in a subsequent year, as the rate of sale of coal had not come down. These were sufficient to hold that there had been concealment of income. In fact, the Tribunal did not consider these matters with any seriousness, but merely held that the revenue had not brought anything on record to show that the assessee had concealed any income. The concealment of income was writ large on the record. Moreover, even if one brushed aside the Explanation to section 271(1)(c), the concealment would be obvious even upon the authority of the case of Anwar Ali (supra). Thus, the Tribunal was not correct in cancelling the penalty imposed by the IAC under section 271(1)(c) upon the assessee.

The Income-tax Enquiry Commission of 1936 made certain recommendations to prevent evasion of tax in such cases. The Legislature accepted those recommendations and the loopholes were sought to be plugged by enacting the said sub-section. Sub-section (3)(a)(i) and (ii) was, therefore, enacted for preventing evasion of tax and was well within the competence of the Federal Legislature. The constitutional validity of the said provision was next questioned on the ground that it violated the doctrine of equality before the law enshrined in article 14 of the Constitution. Under the impugned sub-section, an individual is taxed on the income of his wife or his minor children, if he carries on business in partnership with his wife or if he admits his minor sons to the benefits of the partnership, whereas an individual, if he carries on business in partnership with a third party, whether a man or a woman, or even with his major children or if he and his wife or children carry on business separately, will be liable only to pay tax on his share of the partnership income, that, is, for the purpose of this sub-section, the former is put in a category different from the latter. It could not be said that there was no differentia between the two groups. The object of the legislation was to prevent evasion of tax. A similar device would not ordinarily be resorted to by individuals by entering into partnership with persons other than those mentioned in the sub-section, as it would involve a risk of the third party turning round and asserting his own rights. The Legislature, therefore, selected for the purpose of classification only that group of persons who in fact are used as a cloak to perpetrate fraud on taxation.

It was then said that there might be genuine partnerships between an individual and his wife and, therefore, there was no reasonable relation between the classification and the object sought to be achieved, at any rate to the extent of those genuine cases. But there was no classification between genuine and non-genuine cases: the classification was between cases of partnership between husband, wife and/or minor children, whether genuine or not, and partnerships between others. In demarcating, a group, the net was cast a little wider, but it was necessary, as any further sub-classification as genuine and non-genuine partnerships might defeat the purpose of the Act. Hence that contention was rejected.

As to the validity of the provisions based upon article 19(1)(f) and (g) of the Constitution, A combined and plain reading of the provisions of articles 13 and 265 makes it abundantly clear that a law which is inconsistent with any of the provisions of Part III is void. It cannot be denied that a law providing for levy and collection of taxes is a law within the meaning of Part III of the Constitution, and therefore it must stand the test laid down by article 13 of the Constitution. The "law" in article 265 of the Constitution must be a valid law. A law to be valid must not only be one passed by the Legislature in exercise of power conferred on it, but must also be one that does not infringe the fundamental rights declared by the Constitution.

Section 16(3)(a) of 1922 Act must, therefore, pass both the tests and if it violates any of the provisions of article 19, to the extent it is inconsistent with the said provisions, it will be void.

Where the returned income is negative or less than zero, clause (a ) is applicable. In cases falling under clause (c), the expression 'amount of tax 'sought to be evaded' means the difference between the tax on the total income assessed and the tax calculated on the returned income. [Para 10] If a person conceals income in the sense one understand it, he becomes liable to pay penalty. The concealment triggers the liability to penalty. Once the liability arises, the only other thing to do is to quantify the amount of penalty. The minimum and maximum penalty amounts have been specified. In all cases of concealment where the concealed amount exceeds the total income assessed (or, in other words, where the declared or returned income is negative), clause (a) of Explanation 4 will apply and in all other cases (i.e., where the declared or returned income is greater than or equal to zero), clause (c) would apply. Clause (b), would apply in the special case specified under Explanation 3. All the instant appeals were in respect of cases falling under clause (a) of Explanation 4. The assessees in all the appeals wanted to read clause (a) as excluding those cases where, although the returned income is negative and there is established concealment, the total income assessed is negative and no tax is payable thereon. One cannot discern any such intention on the part of the Legislature in making any such exception. On the contrary, the only classification made by the Legislature is between the cases where the returned income is negative [clause (a )] and where the returned income is greater than or equal to zero [clause (c )] and, of course, the special case of clause (b). The meaning of the provisions and in particular Explanation 4 are very clear. The legislative intent, is that in respect of imposition of a penalty for concealment, the issue of the total assessed income being positive or negative does not arise at all. [Para 12]

The expression 'in addition to any tax payable' in the context it is used, does not and cannot mean that there must be a tax payable before a penalty under the provision can be levied. It only means that the penalty amount will be over and above 'any tax payable'. The event that triggers a liability for penalty is entirely different and distinct from the taxable event. The changing section for tax under the Act is section 4 under Chapter II. Penalties, including the penalty for concealment of income, fall under Chapter XXI 'Penalties Imposable'. There are several penalties where liability of tax is not even mentioned such as section 271A (Failure to keep, maintain or retain books of account, documents, etc.), 271B (Failure to get accounts audited), 271F (Penalty for failure to furnish return of income), etc., Therefore, as a general statement it cannot be said - 'When there is no tax payable, the question of any penalty does not arise'. The context of the words must be seen. The words must be construed to the context in which they appear. The expression 'in addition to any tax payable' merely signifies that the penalty payable is over and above the tax that may be payable. It does not mean that tax being payable is a condition precedent for the penalty being payable. [Para 13]

Under section 2(24) 'income' has been given an inclusive meaning. It includes items such as profits and gains, dividends, capital gains, value of perquisites, etc. Obviously, the total income is computed by aggregating the 'incomes' under each head of income. Even if one goes by the definition, if the totalling of the income results in a negative figure (a loss), it would still be regarded as 'total income'. The context in which the expression 'total income' is used is also of vital importance. This is the legislative mandate. The general meaning, therefore, ascribed to 'total income' includes both income or loss. Specific mention of both 'income or loss' in a provision must be seen in the context of that provisions. Taking the textual and contextual meaning of 'total income' appearing in clause (a ) of Explanation 4 to section 271(1), it is found that the meaning is the same - it includes both a positive figure as well as a negative figure. Thus, for the purpose of imposition of penalty under section 271(1)(c), it is not at all necessary that any tax is payable on the total income assessed. If it were linked to the payment of tax, then it would be relevant to differentiate between positive income or negative income (loss). But, as penalty is not linked to the factum of payment of tax, it is not necessary to specify as to whether total income assessed refers to positive income or negative income (loss). Therefore, the text as well as the context required to construe "total income" appearing in clause (a ) of the Explanation 4 to section 271(1) as including loss also. [Para 14]

Hence, the Tribunal was not right in deleting the penalty imposed under section 271(1)(c) merely on the ground that the total income of the assessee had been assessed at a minus figure/loss. [Para 18]

The assessment of the total income and the computation of tax liability is a proceeding which, for that purpose, is governed by entirely different considerations from a proceeding for penalty imposed for concealment of income. And this is so notwithstanding that the income concealed is the income assessed to tax. In the case of assessment of income and the determination of consequent tax liability, the relevant law is the law which rules during the assessment year in respect of which the total income is assessed and the tax liability determined. The rate of tax is determined by the relevant Finance Act. The penalty is, however, imposed on account of the commission of a wrongful act, and would be determined by law operating on the date on which such wrongful act is committed. Where penalty is imposed for concealment of particulars of income, it is the law ruling on the date when the act of concealment takes place, which is relevant. It is wholly immaterial that the income concealed was to be assessed in relation to an assessment year in the past.

2. Under section 139, although the statute itself prescribes the date for filing the return, power has been conferred on the ITO to extend this date. A return filed within the extended period is a good return in the sense that the ITO is bound to take it into consideration. But nowhere section 139 declares that where a return is filed within the extended period, it will be deemed to have been filed within the period originally prescribed by the statute. On the contrary, the section contains a pro vision for payment of interest where the return is filed beyond the prescribed date even though within the extended period. That is evidence of the fact that the return filed during the extended period is not regarded by the statute as filed within the time originally prescribed.

3. Section 271(1)(iii), as substituted by the Finance Act, 1968 with effect from 1-4-1968, would, therefore, govern the penalty imposed in this case.

The assessee’s failure to file any return provoked the Department to carry out search action under section 132. For the assessment year 1989-90, it was found that assessee had earned a substantial income on the sale of shares. The assessee, in response to notice under section 148, filed the return declaring income, and the assessment was completed on an income of Rs. 4,98,200. In response to the show-cause notice as to why penalty for concealment should not be imposed on the assessee, the assessee contended that there was no mala fide intention to conceal the particulars of income as the sum of Rs. 1,02,000 was paid by way of advance tax attributable to the capital gain and further tax was deducted at source on salary and dividend income. The Assessing Officer levied penalty under section 271(1)(c) by rejecting the assessee’s explanation on the ground that it was only the search action and subsequent issue of notice which forced the assessee to file his return and that mere payment of advance tax did not confer the right on the assessee not to file the return.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the levy of penalty holding that the non-furnishing of the return would tantamount to concealment of particulars of income. The contention of the assessee that such construction would render the provisions of Explanation 3 to section 271(1)(c) redundant was also rejected by the Commissioner (Appeals) who held that Explanation 3 to section 271(1)(c) is applicable to new assessees while the old assessees would be covered by the main provision of section 271(1)(c).

HEADNOTE: Section 140A of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Assessment - Self-assessment - Whether section 140A(3) which provides for levy of penalty for failure to pay self-assessment tax, does not in any way infringe article 19(1)(f) of Constitution of India - Held, yes

FACT: The petitioner did not pay tax due in accordance with the return of income filed by him within stipulated time and, consequently, proceedings for levying penalty under section 140A(3) were commenced by issuing a show-cause notice, to which the petitioner replied contending that inasmuch as on the assessment being completed he had paid the entire tax due, no penalty could be levied under section 140A(3). However, the ITO levied a penalty, which was affirmed in appeal. On writ, the petitioner challenged the constitutional validity of section 140A(3).

HELD: Section 140A which provides for payment of tax due in accordance with the return of income filed by an assessee, within 30 days of the filing of the return is one of the modes/stages of collection of tax devised by Parliament in exercise of its power of taxation.

The principle behind section 140A is that if at the end of the year the assessee is liable to pay any tax according to his own estimate of his income, he shall pay the same within 30 days of the filing of the return. If an assessee is liable to pay advance tax, he would normally pay almost the entire tax in the shape of advance tax, and if he still finds any further tax due at the end of the year, he has to pay it under sub-section (1) of section 140A. In the case of an assessee or in the case of income not liable for payment of advance-tax, the tax due has to be paid within the said 30 days. Obviously, the finalisation of the assessment may take some time and on that occasion, the excess or deficit can be paid or refunded. It is reasonable to presume that every person earning taxable income knows approximately the tax due from him and is expected to and has to pay the same in accordance with law. In other words, the portion of his income due towards income-tax would not be deemed by a prudent and reasonable person to be his "income", properly speaking. In the earlier days, the entire tax was payable, only after the assessment was completed. But when the theory of advance tax was introduced, he had to pay it in certain (now three) instalments as and when he is earning his income. Now, another step is introduced under section 140A, namely, that he has to pay the admitted tax due (i.e., the tax due from him as per his own return) within 30 days of the filing of the return. All these payments towards advance tax and under section 140A(1) are liable to be adjusted at the time of the finalisation of the assessment. There are provisions in the Act providing for levy of penalties for non-compliance with the provisions relating to filing of return, non-furnishing of accounts or particulars, failure to pay advance tax, concealment or evasion of income-tax, etc. Criminal prosecution is also pro-provided for by Chapter 22 in certain cases which, inter alia, include failure to file a return of income, failure to produce accounts and documents, making of false statements and declaration, failure to deduct and pay tax when required to do so. These provisions relating to levy of penalties and criminal prosecutions are twin sanctions provided by law for ensuring compliance with law on the part of the assessees. The object of the two sets of provisions, namely, one levying penalties and the other providing for criminal prosecution, are entirely different.

The provisions made in sub-section (3) is only a measure enacted for ensuring compliance with sub-section (1) of section 140A. The said sub-section merely makes the assessee liable for a penalty which may go up to 50% of the tax payable under sub-section (1). A discretion is conferred upon the ITO in the matter of levying the penalty. In a proper case, he may decline to levy any penalty. The said provision do not compel the ITO to levy such a penalty in each and every case and/or up to the maximum limit. An appeal and a second appeal are provided against his orders and a further reference to the High Court. Further, one cannot assume the case of an assessee "who is not able to pay his taxes". Every person earning taxable income has to provide for payment of taxes. However, certain situations may arise where the assessee may not be able to pay the taxes within 30 days as required by section 140A. But in such cases, if he properly explains the circumstances to the satisfaction of the ITO, he would not levy the penalty.

Reference of the question to the High Court was general in nature. No question was referred as to whether the finding of the Tribunal was perverse or not. Existence of mens rea is essentially a question of fact. The Tribunal alone, as the highest authority empowered to determine the question of fact, would be entitled to go thereinto. However, the same would not mean that the High Court will have no jurisdiction in this behalf. The High Court, it is well-known, should not ordinarily disturb the finding of fact arrived at by the Tribunal. Question of law should generally arise only accepting the finding of fact to be correct. [Para 9]

It is trite that if an explanation given by the assessee with regard to the mistake committed by him has been treated to be bona fide and it has been found as of fact that he had acted on the basis of wrong legal advice, the question of his failure to discharge his burden in terms of Explanation appended to section 271(1)(c ) would not arise. [Para 13]

The expression ‘conceal’ signifies a deliberate act of omission on the part of the assessee. Such deliberate act must be either for the purpose of concealment of income or furnishing of inaccurate particulars. [Para 15]

The term ‘inaccurate particulars’ is not defined. Furnishing of an assessment of value of the property may not by itself be furnishing of inaccurate particulars. Even if the Explanations are taken recourse to, a finding has to be arrived at having regard to clause (A) of Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c) that the explanation offered by an assessee, in the event, he offers one was false. He must be found to have failed to prove that such explanation is not only not bona fide but all the facts relating to the same and material to the income were not disclosed by him. Thus, apart from his explanation being not bona fide, it should be found as of fact that he has not disclosed all the facts which was material to the computation of his income. [Para 16]

The explanation, having regard to the decision of the Supreme Court, must be preceded by a finding as to how and as to in what manner he furnished the particulars of his income. It is beyond any doubt or dispute that for the said purpose the ITO must arrive at its satisfaction in this behalf. [Para 17]

The order imposing penalty is quasi-criminal in nature and, thus, burden lies on the department to establish that the assessee had concealed his income. Since burden of proof in penalty proceeding varies from that in the assessment proceeding, a finding in an assessment proceeding that a particular receipt is income cannot automatically be adopted, though a finding in the assessment proceeding constitute good evidence in the penalty proceeding. In the penalty proceedings, thus, the authorities must consider the matter afresh as the question has to be considered from a different angle. [Para 18]

It is now a well-settled principle of law that the more is the stringent law, more strict construction thereof would be necessary. Even when the burden is required to be discharged by an assessee, it would not be as heavy as in the prosecution case. [Para 19]

The omission of the word ‘deliberate’ in the amended provision of section 271(1)(c) thus, may not be much significance. [Para 20]

Section 271(1)(c ) remains a penal statute. Rule of strict construction shall apply thereto. Ingredients of imposing penalty remains the same. The purpose of the Legislature that it is meant to be deterrent to tax evasion is evidenced by the increase in the quantum of penalty, from 20 per cent under the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 to 300 per cent in 1985. [Para 21]

‘Concealment of income’ and ‘furnishing of inaccurate particulars’ carry different connotations. Concealment refers to deliberate act on the part of the assessee. A mere omission or negligence would not constitute a deliberate act of suppressio veri or suggestio falsi. [Para 22]

The instant case was not a case where penalty had been imposed for breach of contravention of a commercial statute where lack of or intention to contravene or existence of bona fide might not be of much importance. It was also not a case where penalty was mandatorily impossible. It was, therefore, not a case where the enabling provision should have been invoked. [Para 29]

For the reasons aforementioned, the impugned judgment could not be sustained which was to be set aside accordingly. The appeal was to be allowed. [Para 30]

The penalty provision is contained in section 271 and on different counts penalty of different amounts is imposable, wherever there is concealment of income. If the concealment is beyond 20 per cent of the returned income, then the Explanation becomes applicable and presumption has to be raised against the assessee which he can rebut but in case concealment does not exceed 20 per cent. the penalty is still leviable but in this situation the onus lies on the department to prove concealment. Therefore, the Explanation has to be read with section 271(1)(c ) and there is no question of considering the Explanation as separate or distinct from it. The law has to be applied to the given facts. Even if in the order specific reference to Explanation is not mentioned but Explanation is applied and onus is placed on the assessee because the returned income is less than 80 per cent of the assessed income, from this inference has to be drawn that the assessing authorities were conscious of the fact that Explanation was applicable. The Tribunal had, therefore, rightly rejected the assessee's claim.

HEADNOTE: Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessee returned income at Rs. 14,768 but ITO and AAC estimated the same at Rs. 30,000 and imposed penalty of Rs. 15,230 - Tribunal computed total income at Rs. 25,000 but estimated concealed income at Rs. 3,000 with consequential reduction of penalty to Rs. 4,500 - Whether tribunal justified - Held, on facts, yes

FACT: For the assessment year 1970-71, the assessee engaged in the business of assembling pumping sets and manufacturing of canal gates returned its income at Rs. 14,768. The ITO found that in addition to other defects,, the assessee had not incorporated accounts relating to 27 vouchers in his books of account and that, Rs. 2,000 paid in cash to M on 17-3-1970 was recorded in books on 18-3-1970. He consequently estimated income at Rs. 30,000 and levied penalty of Rs. 15,230 for default under section 271(1)( c). The AAC confirmed the ITO's order. On further appeal, the Tribunal held (i) that the recording of cash payment of Rs. 2,000 on a subsequent date was not due to any fraud or gross or wilful neglect on his part; and (ii) that while 12 vouchers were satisfactorily reconciled, the value of Rs. 2,500 represented by the remaining 15 vouchers was not recorded in his books. It, therefore, calculated the concealed income at Rs. 3,000 even though it had estimated the assessee's total income at Rs. 25,000, and reduced the penalty to Rs. 4,500 being 150 per cent of the concealed income.

On reference:

HELD: 1. It is settled that proceedings for penalty are of quasi-criminal nature. While adjudicating on the offence of concealment, the Tribunal is not to be guided by the findings given in the quantum appeal and has to examine the facts afresh to determine the assessee's guilt of concealment and the amount of concealed income for computing the quantum of penalty.

2. The Explanation to section 271(1 )(c) does not have the effect of fixing the quantum of concealment for imposing penalty. The function of fiction created by the Explanation is to convert a case where the assessed income exceeds 80 per cent of the returned income into a case which was covered by section 271 (1)(c), unless the assessee proves that he was not guilty of any fraud or any gross or wilful neglect in filing his return of income. The Explanation exhausts itself once this purpose is achieved. It does not create any further fiction for taking the assessed income as the correct income for levy of penalty under section 271(1)(c)(iii) for which purpose the concerned authority has to independently find the amount of concealed income and may or may not accept the assessed amount as the concealed income. Any other interpretation would make the penalty proceedings completely subservient to the assessment proceedings which does not appear to be the scheme of the Act.

3. Hence, the Tribunal was justified in estimating concealed income at Rs. 3,000, even though the total income had been computed at Rs. 25,000 against returned income of Rs. 14,768 and consequently reducing the quantum of penalty.

Editor's note

The revenue had also argued (i) that the Tribunal had omitted to consider relevant facts while estimating the concealed income at Rs. 3,000 only; and (ii) that, apart from the fact that the assessee had made purchases not shown in the vouchers, there were other irregularities in the accounts to show that he had been carrying on business outside the books: The High Court did not consider these aspects because the question referred did not solicit an enquiry into the validity of the finding regarding estimated concealed income on those scores.

Bharatjee Agrawal for the Respondent.

Merely because the legislature in its wisdom decided to give a different treatment to proceedings relating to penalty it is difficult to find discrimination with regard to the classification which has been made in clauses (f) and (g ) which are independent of clauses (a ) and (b). Although penalty has been regarded as an additional tax in a certain sense and for certain purposes it is not possible to hold that penalty proceedings are essentially a continuation of the proceedings relating to assessment where a return has been filed. Further, it is well-settled that in fiscal enactments the legislature has a larger discretion in the matter of classification so long as there is no departure from the rule that persons included in a class are not singled out for special treatment. It cannot be said that while applying the penalty provisions contained in the Act of 1961 to cases of persons whose assessments are completed after 1-4-1962, any class has been singled out for special treatment. It is obvious that for the imposition of penalty it is not the assessment year or the date of the filing of the return which is important but it is the satisfaction of the Income-tax authorities that a default has been committed by the assessee which would attract the provisions relating to penalty. Whatever the stage at which the satisfaction is reached, the scheme of sections 274(1) and 275 of the Act of 1961, is that the order imposing penalty must be made after the completion of the assessment. The crucial date, therefore, for purposes of penalty, is the date of such completion.

As regards the argument that because it rests with the Income-tax Officer to complete the assessment by a particular date it will depend on his fiat whether the penalty should be imposed under the Act of 1922 or under the Act of 1961. It cannot be presumed that officers or authorities who are entrusted with responsible duties under the taxation laws would not discharge them properly and in a bona fide manner. If in a particular case any mala fide action is taken that can always be challenged by an assessee in appropriate proceedings but the mere possibility that some officer may intentionally delay the disposal of a case can hardly be a ground for striking down clause (g) as discriminatory under article 14.

The classification made is based on intelligible differentia having reasonable relation to the object intended to be achieved. The object essentially was to prevent the evasion of tax.

It is true that clause (a) of sub-section (1) of section 271 mentions the corresponding provisions of the Act of 1961 and does not mention provisions of Act of 1922 but that will not make the part relating to payment of penalty inapplicable once it is held that section 297(2)(g ) governs the case. Both sections 271(1) and 297(2)(g) have to be read together and in harmony and so read the only conclusion possible is that for the imposition of a penalty in respect of any assessment for the year ending on 31-3-1962, or any earlier year which is completed after first day of April, 1962, the proceedings have to be initiated and the penalty imposed in accordance with the provisions of section 271 of the Act of 1961. Thus the assessee would be liable to a penalty as provided by section 271(1) for the default mentioned in section 28(1) of the Act of 1922 if his case falls within the terms of section 297(2)(g).

The provision of section 271 of the Act of 1961 will apply mutatis mutandis to proceedings relating to penalty initiated in accordance with section 297(2)(g) of that Act.

As regards challenge to section 271(2) of the Act of 1961 on the ground of contravention of article 14 of the Constitution, it was open to the legislature to say that once a registered firm committed a default attracting penalty, it should be deemed or considered to be an unregistered firm for the purpose of its imposition. No question of discrimination under article 14 can arise in such a situation. There was nothing to prevent the legislature from giving the benefit of a reduced rate to a registered firm for the purpose of tax but withhold the same when it committed a default and became liable to imposition of penalty.

The appeal was dismissed.

Note : The decision was in favour of the revenue.

The word 'conceal' is derived from the Latin word 'concelare' which implies concelare, i.e., to hide. The offence of concealment is, thus, a direct attempt to hide an item of income or a portion thereof from the income or a portion thereof from the knowledge of the income-tax authorities. In the present case, the order under section 132 was passed after contest. It was important to note that the said order was passed before the date of filing the income-tax return. It would be irrational and illegal for any reasonable person to hold that the assessee should have disclosed in the return, furnished by him, unmindful of the facts and circumstances, that these amounts represented his income and so by the same token it was not possible to hold that the failure to do so, was concealment of income or omission in that regard, would amount to concealment or furnishing inaccurate particulars of such income.

Further, question as to whether the concealment to make the penalty exigible in a given case, is a question of fact ; question as to whether the burden of proof in a given case has been discharged is also a question of fact and question as to whether the presumption under the Explanation to section 271(1)(c) has been rebutted, by evidence, is also a question of fact. In the instant case, the Tribunal, on the facts, had found that the assessee had not concealed any particulars of income or furnished inaccurate particulars of such income. On these findings, the conclusion of the Tribunal in cancelling the penalty was justified.
