Clarification on amendment to section 271 by Finance Bill, 2008 - In view of the apprehension raised on the retrospective amendment to section 271 of the Income-tax Act, proposed in the Finance Bill, 2008, empowering the Assessing Officer to, inter alia, levy penalty in case of concealment of income, the Ministry of Finance has issued the following clarification:

In the context of levy of penalty under section 271, there has been an ongoing dispute between the Income-tax department and taxpayers on whether an Assessing Officer is required to record his satisfaction before initiating penalty proceedings. The Income-tax department has held the view that no separate satisfaction is required to be recorded before initiating penalty proceedings. In the case of Commissioner of Income-tax v. S.V. Angidi Chettiar [1962] 44 ITR 739, the Supreme Court has, while dealing with penalty under section 28 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, held that "satisfaction before conclusion of proceeding under the Act, and not the issue of a notice or initiation of any step for imposing penalty is a condition for the exercise of the jurisdiction". The same matter came up once again before the Calcutta High Court in the case of Becker Gray and Company (1930) Ltd. v. ITO, Central Circle-I, Calcutta [1977] 112 ITR 503. Relying on the Supreme Court decision in the above case, the Calcutta High Court held that "It is true that the Income-tax Officer should be prima facie satisfied before the penalty notice is issued, but it does not mean that he is required to record such satisfaction in writing in every case." Following these decisions, wherever additions are made, Assessing Officers have, without separately recording any satisfaction, been issuing directions for initiating penalty proceedings.

However, interpreting the aforesaid Supreme Court decision, the Delhi High Court has, in the case of CIT v. Ram Commercial Enterprises Ltd. [2000] 246 ITR 568/[2002] 122 Taxman 620 held that "It is the assessing authority which has to form its own opinion and record its satisfaction before initiating penalty proceedings."

Subsequently, the Allahabad High Court went into this issue in the case of Shyam Biri Works Pvt. Ltd. v. CIT [2003] 259 ITR 625/131 Taxman 253. After considering the above Calcutta High Court decision and the Delhi High Court decision, it has held that "With profound respect to the Delhi High Court decision, we are unable to agree…. We are, therefore, of the opinion that although the Assessing Officer must have satisfaction as required under section 273 of the Act, it is not necessary for him to record that satisfaction in writing before initiating penalty proceedings under section 273 of the Act.".

In view of conflicting judicial opinion on this issue, it was necessary to make legislative intervention and settle the matter. Therefore, clause 48 of the Finance Bill, 2008 proposes to insert a new sub-section (1B) in section 271 so as to unambiguously provide that where any amount is added or disallowed in computing the total income or loss of an assessee in any order of assessment or reassessment, and such order contains a direction for initiating of penalty proceedings under sub-section (1) of section 271, such an order of assessment or reassessment shall be deemed to constitute satisfaction of the Assessing Officer for initiating penalty proceedings under sub-section (1) of that section.

As regards the contention that section 44AB is discriminatory vis-a-vis big assessees, the Karnataka High Court observed : “Section 44AB provides for audit of accounts if bigger cases fulfil the twin-tests of a valid classification. The object of choosing bigger cases or bigger assessees for specialised audit by a special class of persons, that have qualifications to audit them facilitate the prevention of evasion of taxes, administrative convenience in the quick and proper completion of assessment under the Act, has rational nexus to the object of the Act. On the principles enunciated by the Supreme Court in Balaji v. ITO [1961] 43 ITR 393, Pooran Mal v. Director of Inspection (Investigation) [1974] 93 ITR 505 (SC) and Hiralal Rattan Lal v. STO [1973] 31 STC 178, section 44AB that fulfils the object of the Act cannot be condemned as violative of article 14 of the Constitution at all.” (p. 117)

As for ITPs contention that article 14 violates their rights, the High Court observed:

“What emerges from the discussion is that the ITPs who belong to a separate class, cannot compare themselves with the class of Chartered Accountants that have special qualifications and expertise to do the job of audit more efficiently. Article 14 of the Constitution guarantees equal treatment to equal and not unequals. On this conclusion the challenge of the petitioners based on article 14 of the Constitution is liable to be rejected.” (p. 117)

“We have earlier found that the provision had been enacted to prevent evasion of taxes and facilitate administration. If that is so, it is undoubtedly a reasonable provision that furthers the object and purpose of the Act.” (p. 118)

“On the application of the principles enunciated in cases noted by us earlier, we are of the view that section 44AB places a reasonable restriction in the interests of the general public and is saved by article 19(6) of the Constitution.” (p. 119)

The twin objects of section 44AB are administrative convenience and prevention of tax evasion and avoidance. There is no hostile discrimination between one class of assessees having total sales/turnover, gross receipts being less than the prescribed limit and the other class, having more. If there is any, the difference in treatment is capable of being explained in the light of the aforesaid twin objects for which the legislation was undertaken. If there is equality and uniformity with each group, the law would not be condemned as discriminatory though due to some fortuitous circumstances arising out of a peculiar situation, some included in a class get an advantage over others, so long as they are not singled out for special treatment. Taxation laws are not exception to this doctrine.1 But in the application of the principles, the Courts in view of the inherent complexity of fiscal adjustment of diverse elements permit a larger discretion to the Legislature in the matter of classification, so long as it adheres to the fundamental principles underlying the said doctrine. The power of legislation to classify is of “wide range of flexibility” so that it can adjust its system of taxation in all proper and reasonable ways. In Murthy Match Works v. Asstt. Collector of Central Excise1, G.K. Krishnan v. State of Tamil Nadu2, R.K. Garg v. Union of India3, the Supreme Court noticing the case of Twyford Tea Co. Ltd. v. State of Kerala4 has only reiterated the above statement of law. Administrative convenience is a valid ground for classification in a taxation measure.5 Differentiation made to check evasion or avoidance of tax is also a valid ground.6

10.3 Section 271(1) of the Act empowers the Assessing Officer to levy penalty for the following offences :

Failure to comply with notice for assessment (of total income or fringe benefits); or

Failure to comply with direction under section 142 for the audit; or

Concealment of particulars of income or furnishing inaccurate particulars of income ['concealment penalty']; or

Concealment of particulars of fringe benefits or furnishing inaccurate particulars of fringe benefits.

The sub-section requires the Assessing Officer to record satisfaction about initiation of the penalty proceedings. It reads as follows :

"If the Assessing Officer or the Commissioner (Appeals) or the Commissioner in the course of any proceedings under this Act, is satisfied that any person ... he may direct that such person shall pay by way of penalty ...".

10.3-1 Amendment and reasons therefor - Sub-section (1B) is inserted in section 271, with retrospective effect from 1-4-1989 providing for deemed satisfaction of the Assessing Officer, if a direction is contained in the Assessment Order about initiation of penalty proceedings with respect to any disallowance. The Memorandum explains the reasons thereof as follows:

"It is a requirement that the Assessing Officer is required to be satisfied before such a penalty is levied.

There is a considerable variance in the judicial opinion on the issue as to whether the Assessing Officer is required to record his satisfaction before issue of penalty notice under this sub-section. Some judicial authorities have held that such a satisfaction need not be recorded. However, Hon'ble Delhi High Court in the case of CIT v. Ram Commercial Enterprises Ltd. [2000] 246 ITR 568 has held that such a satisfaction must be recorded by the Assessing Officer."

"Given the conflicting judgments on the issue and the legislative intent, it is imperative to amend the Income-tax Act to unambiguously provide that where any amount is added or disallowed in computing the total income or loss of an assessee in any order of assessment or reassessment; and such order contains a direction for initiation of penalty proceedings under sub-section (1), such an order of assessment or reassessment shall be deemed to constitute satisfaction of the Assessing Officer for initiation of penalty proceedings under sub-section (1)."

For the purpose of its decision, Delhi High Court (in the above referred case) had applied earlier Supreme Court decision in CIT v. D.M. Manasvi [1972] 86 ITR 557 and had relied on the following observations of the Supreme Court in CIT v. S.V. Angidi Chettiar [1962] 44 ITR 739, 745 :

"... the power to impose penalty under section 28 depends upon the satisfaction of the Income-tax Officer in the course of proceedings under the Act; it cannot be exercised if he is not satisfied about the existence of conditions specified in clauses (a), (b) or (c) before the proceedings are concluded. The proceeding to levy penalty has, however, not to be commenced by the Income-tax Officer before the completion of the assessment proceeding by the Income-tax Officer. Satisfaction before conclusion of the proceeding under the Act, and not the issue of the notice for initiation of any step for imposing penalty is a condition for the exercise of the jurisdiction ...". (p. 745)

At this stage, it may also be noted that Supreme Court approved Delhi High Court decision in Dilip N. Shroff v. Joint Commissioner of Income-Tax [2007] 161 Taxman 218/291 ITR 519 (SC), in the following words :

"46. The explanation, having regard to the decisions of this court, must be preceded by a finding as to how and in what manner he furnished the particulars of his income. It is beyond any doubt or dispute that for the said purpose the Income-tax Officer must arrive at a satisfaction in this behalf. (See CIT v. Ram Commercial Enterprises Ltd. [2002] 122 Taxman 620/[2000] 246 ITR 568 (Delhi) and Diwan Enterprises v. CIT [2000] 246 ITR 571 (Delhi))." (p. 243)

It may, thus, be noted that, as such, there was no difference of judicial opinion about the stage at which the satisfaction is required to be reached.

Further, the amendment itself makes it clear that the satisfaction must be for the purpose of initiation of the penalty proceedings.

Further, Supreme Court in Commissioner of Income-tax v. Tara Agencies [2007] 162 Taxman 337/292 ITR 444 explained legislative intent in the following manner :

2.

Interpretation of penalty provisions - Law relating to penalty should be construed strictly in favour of the assessee, more stringent the law, stricter the construction that is required in favour of the assessee.

3.

Penalty proceedings are independent proceedings - Since penalty proceedings are independent proceedings, the matter has to be considered afresh in the light of the law applicable to penalty.

4. Burden on initiation of the proceedings - The burden of proof placed on the assessee under the Explanation is subject to conditions therein. It is necessary that there should be an inference of concealment at the time of initiation of the proceedings.

5.

Extent of burden on taxpayer - Even where a burden is placed on the taxpayer, such burden cannot be the same as that of prosecution as was decided in Krishna Lal (P.N.) v. Government of Kerala (1995) Supp 2 SCC 187.

Where there was a false verification in the return filed by a firm and the partner against whom prosecution was launched, the defence was a plea, that the signature attributed to the partner was not his, but it was found that partner had not disputed his signature either during assessment nor during penalty proceedings, there is no burden on the prosecution to prove the signature was that of the partner.1

6.

Relevance of mens rea - Inference of mens rea, that is necessary for concealment penalty, is essentially based on facts. Penalty has two components, one prescribing conditions for imposition and the other for computation.

7.

Relevance of assessment to penalty proceedings - A finding in the assessment proceedings, that there is an omission in income does not by itself lead to the inference that there is concealment, notwithstanding the fact, that the omission may constitute a good evidence for concealment, but it is not conclusive.

8.

Effect of omission of requirement of deliberateness - The omission of the word "deliberate" in the penalty provision is not of much significance, so as to change the law on penalties.

9.

Deliberately is not to be lightly inferred - A mere omission or negligence does not constitute a deliberate act of suppressioveri or suggestiofalsi even after the amendment to section 271(1)(c) made in the year 1964. There is no material change as to the nature of proceedings.2 Penalty provisions under the income-tax law is not the same as provisions in commercial statute, where a breach or contravention is liable for punishment irrespective of the bona fide as provided in some cases of absolute liability, so that levy of penalty is not mandatory.

10.

Legal advice can be a shield - Where an assessee acts on legal advice, though wrong, the omission should be treated as bona fide with no deliberateness involved."

The Finance Bill 2016, the penalty regime in income-tax law is creates insomnia among the Tax Payers. Earlier mechanism in Income Tax Act 1961 provided for a levy of penalty, for concealment of income or furnishing inaccurate particulars of income u/s 271(1) ( c ), of an amount between 100% to 300% of the tax sought to be evaded. for the imposition of penalty, taken against an assessee under Income-tax Act are distinct from the criminal complaints filed against him. They can, therefore, continue simultaneously. The offences punishable under section 277 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1961, and section 193 of the Indian Penal Code may be somewhat similar, but they are not identical.1 There is no legal bar on the prosecution of the accused for both these offences in view of section 26 of the General Clauses Act. It is well known that the Legislature can impose both a criminal as well as a civil sanction for the same act or omission. In Helvering v. Mitchell,2 it was held that civil sanctions are provided primarily as a safeguard for the prosecution of the revenue and to reimburse the Government for the heavy expenses of investigation and the loss resulting from the taxpayers’ fraud. Similarly, Jackson, J., said in Murray R. Spies v. United States3 that the civil sanction consists of addition to the tax upon determination of facts by an administrative agency and with no burden upon the Government to prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt; whereas criminal sanction consists of penal offences enforced by the criminal process in the familiar manner. Invocation of one does not exclude resorting to the other.

Penalties are not in the nature of offences. The framers of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1961, have chosen to make a difference between the two - while section 271 thereof relates to penalty proceedings, sections under Chapter XXII prescribe what are offences under the Act and what punishment has to be imposed for the said offences. Therefore, penalty proceedings cannot be equated to criminal proceedings attracting punishment. The objects of the two provisions appear to be different. The one entailing the prosecution and punishment, is to vindicate public justice by punishing the offender, whereas the object of the penalty proceedings is to render evasion unprofitable and to secure to the State, the compensation for the damages or attempted evasions. As pointed out in P. Ummali Umma v. IAC4, they are mutually exclusive remedies and under the 1961 Act, both the proceedings are available, though under the 1922 Act, penalty proceedings would have been a bar on the launching of a prosecution. This does not make a difference to the distinction drawn.

These are concurrent remedies and the invocation of one does not necessarily dispense with, obviate or oust the other. The imposition of penalties under the Act by the authorities, and the conviction in a Court of law for an offence created by the Act, do not attract the principle of double jeopardy either. Ordinarily, the decision to prosecute an assessee or a person, who may be deemed to be an assessee under the various penal provisions of the Act, is a decision taken by the officer empowered to initiate action on being satisfied on the objective material before him that there is a case for prosecution without judicial determination under the Act, as to taxability, quantification of liability, or liability to any penalty, etc.

The view that the proceedings entailing penalty under the Income-tax Act are to be equated to the prosecution attracting the punishments is not correct as no conviction for any offence is involved in the imposition of penalty. From a reading of the provision of article 20(1) of the Constitution, it is evident that the first limit and the second limit are interlinked and have to be read together, and that while the first limit refers to a conviction for an offence, the second limit refers to the punishment that has to be inflicted with regard to an offence. Penalty is, on the other hand, levied for an act or omission of the assessee, not because it is an offence but because it is an attempt at evasion in the payment of the tax. In such a situation, article 20(1) of the Constitution is not attracted.1

There are a large number of cases where criminal law and civil law can run side by side. The object of the criminal law is to punish an offender who commits an offence against a person, property or the State for which the accused, on proof of the offence, is deprived of his liberty and in some cases even his life. This does not, however, affect the civil remedies at all for suing the wrongdoer in cases like arson, accident, etc. It is an anathema to suppose that when a civil remedy is available, criminal prosecution is completely barred. The two types of actions are quite different in content, scope and import.2

Concealed or furnished inaccurate particulars of income

The word "concealed" contemplates the element of mens rea [Yashwant Singh v. CIT [1995] 212 ITR 207 (Raj.)]. The expressions "has concealed particulars of income" or "has furnished inaccurate particulars of income" are not identical in detail, although they may have the same effect, namely, keeping off a certain portion of income. The former is direct and the latter is indirect in its execution. The word "concealed" is derived from the Latin word "concelare" which implies to hide. The offence of concealment is a direct attempt to hide an item of income or a portion thereof from the knowledge of the income-tax authorities. In furnishing the return an assessee is required to furnish particulars and accounts on which such income has been arrived at. These may be particulars as per its books of account, if it has maintained them, or any other basis upon which it had arrived at the returned figure of income. Any inaccuracy made in such books of account or otherwise which resulted in keeping or hiding a portion of income is punishable as furnishing inaccurate particulars of its income [CIT v. Indian Metals & Ferro Alloys Ltd. [1995] 211 ITR 35 (Ori.)]

(ii)The contention that such a provision brings in an oppressive restriction is also liable to be rejected as auditing of accounts is a specialized job. It may be true that some income-tax practitioners may also acquire that skill by sheer practice without passing the necessary examination. But that does not preclude the Parliament from prescribing special qualifications with reference to the auditing of accounts. (iii)Legal practitioners and chartered accountants are equal for the purpose of representation of the assessee before assessing authority, but they are not equals for the purpose of compulsory audit. The preferential treatment given to the chartered accountants for the purpose of compulsory audit does not militate against the rule of equality under article 14. The terms ‘audit’, ‘auditing’ and the ‘functions of auditor’ clearly bring about the difference between the chartered accountants and others. The object and purpose in providing compulsory audit is to facilitate the prevention of evasion of taxes, administrative convenience in quick and proper completion of assessments, etc. In the light of this object, chartered accountants and others cannot be said to be similarly situate. The qualifications and eligibility to be enrolled as income-tax practitioners are entirely different from those of chartered accountants from the point of view of auditing.

(iv)Merely because apart from dealers whose turn over is more than 40 lakhs, dealers in liquor trade have also to get their accounts audited does not make the provision arbitrary. Such dealers are a class by themselves as they are carrying on a trade which is res extra commercium. They constitute a class by themselves and if the Legislature in its wisdom has provided that their accounts should be audited, it is neither unreasonable nor treating them as a class arbitrary. The classification in the instant case is reasonable and has a nexus with the object which is to direct a class of dealers getting their accounts audited by a specialized agency so that there is no tax evasion.

Section 61 - Whether opposed to article 19(1)(g)

7. Considering section 82 of the VAT Act, the persons who are excluded from the ambit of Explanation of section 61 are not denied their right of appearance before the authorities under the Act. They are not prohibited from carrying on their profession. It is further provided that nothing in clause (6) shall prevent the State from making any law relating to professional or technical qualification necessary for practising the profession, trade or business as the case may be. In other words, apart from the power conferred on the State to impose reasonable restrictions under article 19(6), there is a further power conferred under article 19(6) of laying down professional or technical qualifications necessary for practising the profession as in the instant case. In the matter of carrying out audit, the State has chosen to confer that right only on a class of persons having expertise in the field. This cannot be said to be arbitrary or excessive in nature so as to go beyond the requirement of the interest of the general public. That would be yet another reason as to why the challenge under article 19(1)(g) must fail.

If the phrase ‘practice the profession of law’ is equated to appearance before the sales tax authority, in that event, a chartered accountant or a cost accountant or even a relative or an employee of an assessee will not be entitled to appear before a sales tax authority after the Advocates Act came into force. Not only that if the contention of the appellant is accepted, after the appointed date, the sales tax practitioner who does not have a degree in law will not be entitled to be enrolled as an advocate, will not be able to practise the profession of law and, consequently, will not be able to appear before any sales tax authority notwithstanding the provisions of section 71 of the Bombay Sales Tax Act. Section 29 of the Advocates Act till date has not been brought into force. The act of maintaining accounts is neither pleading, practice nor acting. Therefore, the challenge to the constitutional validity of the legislation with reference to articles 14 and 19 at the instance of the Bar Council will also have to be rejected.

As long as the twin tests of reasonableness of the classification and nexus with the object are satisfied, wisdom of legislation cannot be substituted. The State Legislature is free to decide in its wisdom as to how best to safeguard the State revenue. Different States may adopt different standards and policy of one Legislature may not be adopted by another Legislature as the matter lies in the domain of policy making. Because some States have permitted sales tax practitioners to carry on audit it need not necessarily mean that as the Legislature of the State of Maharashtra has not so provided, that would be arbitrary or that the classification considering the nexus of the object is arbitrary. It is for the State Legislature to decide how to protect its revenue and this is more true with regard to economic legislation.

Non obstante clause is to be understood as operating to set aside as no longer valid anything contained in relevant existing law which is inconsistent with the new enactment; and

The enacting parts of the statute must, where it is clear, be taken to control the non obstante clause, where both cannot be read harmoniously. As discussed above, section 115JB(1) only seeks to substitute the income-tax payable by SPT. This is the only and limited objective. Thus, the non obstante clause will override only those provisions which are in conflict with the objective of providing for the payment of SPT. In other words, the other provisions would not be affected or rather cannot be considered as in conflict with the provision. The inference is based on the following reasoning:

Broadly stated, section 115JB lays down:

Substitution of SPT for income-tax payable [sub-section (1)];

Providing machinery for computation of book profit [sub-section (2)];

Saving determination of unabsorbed losses, etc. [sub-section (3)];

Requires obtaining and furnishing Accountant's Report [sub-section (4)]; and

Application of the other provisions of the Act [sub-section (5)].

It would be appreciated that the section provides for the levy; machinery for computation; compliance with certain conditions, etc. How-ever, it does not provide for the charge, collection and recovery, assessment, etc. Accordingly, it makes the other provisions of the Act applicable. Accordingly, it's a complete code. The substantive provision is sub-section (1). Effectively, it seeks to create a fiction, limited to levy of SPT.

The non obstante clause, read with sub-section (5), and in particular, the first limb thereof, namely, 'save as otherwise provided in this section' and the limited object of levying SPT, seems to have only a limited overriding effect; but otherwise it relies on the other provisions of the Act, for the effective levy and recovery of tax.

The fiction, thus, has a limited field, namely

Substitution of tax payable by SPT; and

Computation of book profit.

Otherwise, it appears that all the provisions of the Act including the provisions relating to charge, definitions, recovery, payment, assessment, etc., would apply in construing the provisions of section 115JB.

10 lakhs by cheque or 1 lakh by cash against credit card. Do the honest taxpayers need to worry? The answer is an emphatic no. It is a beneficial reminder to them to include the payments that they have made from their legitimately earned taxed income. It is an assistance to make their tax compliance easier and error free. At the same time, it is strong message of deterrence and obviation for those, who have used tax evaded income to undertake such high value transactions. The faceless income tax assessment is a pioneering initiative. It is not an established practice of tax audit and collection anywhere in the world, although in Australia and Singapore randomised jurisdictions for tax audits have been experimented with. How will this new paradigm play out in practice? The income tax department is confident that the architectural structure and digital systems as well as sufficiently trained manpower are available for effective implementation. Yet, it would need a sustained collaborative effort by all the stakeholders to make a success out of it. Nobel laureate Elinor Ostrom, one of the most astute analysts of trust and reciprocity in public action points out that individual behaviour in any social dilemma is strongly impacted by the context in which interactions take place. It is not simply a result of individual differences. And payment or evasion of income tax is a significant social dilemma that confronts so many of us. All efforts ought to be made to tilt the balance of convenience in favour of payment and against avoidance or evasion of tax. So, the context and narrative in the society at large must change from lauding the tax evader to respecting the honest taxpayer. This requires passionate and active participation from all segments of the society; from the top social leadership that enjoys disproportionate leverage in setting the general conversation and agenda of the local communities, to the tax practitioners whose advice and guidance is typically sacrosanct for the taxpayers, to the income tax department that sets the rules of governance which lowers or enhances the cost of compliance for the honest taxpayers as well as layouts the quantum of penal actions for concealing income and wealth, and finally to the taxpayer, who is the best informed person among all the actors of his own true income and tax liability. The empirical research on trust and social action again offers a gateway of hope here. It shows that any individual would cooperate more, if he believes that others would reciprocate, and that mutuality of interest would benefit him as well as the others. His net benefit would feed into his learning loop to increase the level of cooperation in every succeeding round of interaction.

The Taxpayers' Charter announced along with initiation of faceless assessment scheme is aimed at this conundrum. The potential benefits to the taxpayers in terms of lower cost of compliance come with a set of duties and obligations cast on them. It is expected that taxpayers would be informed and responsive. They would maintain accurate record of their transactions and would ensure an honest and appraised representation of their financial affairs and pay their dues. The taxpayer is assumed to be guided by profits and his well-being but the conception of the taxpayer as exclusively a self-interested human is diluted. The economic doctrine arising from Adam Smith that is based on profit maximization as the sole driving force of human endeavour in business and profession is watered down by the Indian world view of 'PurusharthaChatushtaya', where the four objects of human pursuit simultaneously play out in individual and social action. Herein, 'Artha' or the goal of financial gain and economic prosperity does not completely override the other objects of desire and fulfilment, which also find ready and repeated reflection in both individual as well as community endeavours.

The assessee in this case admitted seizure of cash consequent to search under section 132 and the case of the assessee as regards quantum of assessment was dismissed by the court. As regards penalty the tribunal held that the onus to prove concealment of income is on the Department and it is not automatic. The Madras High Court took note of the apex court decision in MAK Data (Supra) and held that the burden is on the assessee to offer an explanation for taking out the case from penal consequences. It held that if the assessee has discharged onus by giving a cogent and reliable explanation and if the Department did not agree with the explanation the onus would be on the Department to prove that there was concealment of particulars of income or furnishing of inaccurate particulars of income.

Therefore in spite of the decision in the case of MAK Data (P) Ltd (Supra) if the assessee gives a cogent and proper explanation, the burden would be shifted on the Revenue for classifying the case as misreporting of income.

Conclusion

Presently, when the ITR is processed under section 143(1)(a) and there is enhancement of income no penalty is leviable. However, once the assessment is made under sections 143(3), 144 and 147 then any upward revision of income or reduction of loss would expose the taxpayers to penal consequence except in certain cases provided in section 270A(6). The penal consequence could be mitigated with regard to under-reporting of income simpliciter by having recourse to section 270AA. However, instance of under-reporting of income due to misreporting is a heavy burden cast on the taxpayers. The penal provisions are not only to penalize the errant assessees but also to have deterrent effect. The quantum of penalty seems to be too much and that would only pile up the cases for litigation. Section 270AA may have to be expanded by allowing misreporting also by limiting the relief for one or two times during the life time of the taxpayers so that the tax realization is quick to the exchequer and the tax disputes are also kept in check for better compliance and administration.

Lastly, any amount of 'undisclosed income' as referred to in explained through the Explanation (c) to section 271AAB would also not become 'under-reported income' as there is separate penalty provision under that section to deal with the penalty on the amount of such 'undisclosed income'. Therefore, out of the 'under reported income' being total difference between the assessed income and the processed income, the aggregate of the above amounts covered under clause (a) to (e) of sub section (6) would be excluded and balance, if any remaining, would thus be 'under reported income' on which penalty at the rate of 50% of the tax payable is visualized under sub section (7) unless the case is covered under sub section (8) (9) of section 270A for which higher penalty rate of 200% of the tax payable has been prescribed.

'Under reported income' in consequence of 'Misreporting of income'

There are sub section (8) and (9) of section 270A which prescribe that if 'under reported income is in consequence of misreporting of income', penalty would be 200% of the tax payable on such 'under reported income'. Six cases where such 'under reported income' can be said to be 'in consequence of misreporting of income' are given under sub section (9) which are numbered from clause (a) to (f) under that sub section.

There are however following issues which merit attention:

(a)

In a given case, even if there was a case of 'misreporting of income' due to which the addition/disallowance was made in the assessment order, the difference between the assessed income and processed income would nonetheless continue to be termed as 'under reported income' or at best 'under reported income in consequence to misreporting of income'.

This appears to have been done consciously by the legislature to avoid negotiate the possible argument coming at any stage that since assessing officer has failed to use the expression 'misreporting of income', jurisdiction to levy penalty under sub section (8) read with sub section (9) ought to fail. We have already opined that such stand of the Revenue may not stand to the test of law for the reasons elaborated by us in the earlier part of this article.

(b)

Burden to prove that the 'under reported income' includes such cases of income which can be called as 'under reported income in consequence to misreporting of income', would rest on the shoulders of the assessing officer. This situation is akin and identical to the old Explanation (1A) to section 271(1)(c) whereby also the burden to prove that the explanation furnished by the assessee in the matter of facts material to the computation of income was false, was rested on the shoulders of the assessing officer. It would therefore be incumbent for the assessing officer here also in the new penalty provision of sub section (9) of section 270A, to bring the case of the assessee under any of the clauses (a) to (f) of sub section (9) before penalty @ 200% of the tax payable is imposed. Show cause notice which would be issued by the assessing officer for eliciting the reply defence of the assessee, and the penalty order passed must clearly mention under which clause or clauses of sub section (9) of section 270A case of the 'under reported income' falls.

(c)

These clauses as mentioned in (a) to (f) of sub section (9) are exhaustive, meaning thereby that any situation other than the listed six would not make the addition/disallowance as 'misreporting of income'. This is different matter that hardly would there be any other situation which has been left out to be covered under these exhaustive six clauses except the ones discussed hereinafter.

(d)

These clauses (a) to (f) of sub section (9) are at times overlapping, meaning thereby that one situation of 'misreporting of income' may be covered under more than one such clauses/cases. 'Misreporting of income' may be due to 'suppression of facts' or 'misrepresentation of facts' or may result due to 'recording of false entry in the books of accounts', or due to 'claim of expenditure not substantiated by any evidence'. There may at times not exist any water tight compartments between various clauses enshrined under sub section (9).

For instance, an expense on account of commission on sale may remain unsubstantiated for want of evidence and at the same time, it may be found that such commission was in fact a 'false entry' recorded in the books of accounts as such. This too may have been done by 'misrepresenting the facts' and it is very well possible that it was on account of rather 'suppressing the correct facts'.

Introduction

1. It is common in enforcement provisions in a statute like levy of penalties to prescribe the minimum and maximum amount, setting forth the limits within which penalties can be imposed at the discretion of the officers authorized for the same taking into account the facts and circumstances of the cases where penalties are called for. In fiscal enactments like those relating to levy of taxes such as income-tax, wealth tax, service tax, etc., penalties are attracted for various defaults such as for delays in furnishing the returns, non-compliance of notices, failure to pay tax in time or for concealments, frauds, misrepresentations, etc. The legal provisions prescribing penalties mention the minimum and maximum amounts of penalties that can be imposed. For example, in the I.T. Act, 1961, section 271(1)(c) provides that for concealment of particulars of income or for furnishing inaccurate particulars thereof, penalties that can be imposed shall not be less than, but which shall not exceed three times the amount of tax sought to be evaded for such defaults. In other words, the penalty to be imposed cannot be less than 100% of the tax sought to be evaded, but shall not exceed 300% of such tax. Similarly, u/s 76 of the Finance Act, 1994 (Act) relating to levy of service tax from 8-4-2011, the amount of penalty leviable u/s 76 is not less than Rs.100 per day during which the failure continues or 1% of such tax per month, whichever is higher. The total amount of penalty leviable u/s 76, however, cannot exceed 50% of the service tax payable.

2. Whether in exercise of discretion, penalty can be imposed even below the minimum amount prescribed?

This issue came up for consideration of the Gujarat High Court in the case of CCE&C v. Port Officer [Tax Appeal No. 1367 of 2009, dated 8-7-2010]. The year for which the proceedings came up before the High Court section 76 of the Act provided for levy of penalty at Rs.200 for every day of default or equal to 2% of such tax a month, whichever was higher, not exceeding the amount of tax due. Similarly, penalties were imposable in respect of defaults mentioned in sections 77 to 79 also. Section 80 stipulated that despite sections 76 to 79, no penalty might be levied if the taxpayer proved that there was reasonable cause for failure.

2.1 Facts of the case - In the case that came up before the High Court, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the penalty imposed as per section 76 of the Act and the matter was taken to Tribunal - CESTAT - by the Central Excise Department. The Tribunal decided the issue by saying that penalty could be reduced below the minimum prescribed in view of section 80 of the Act. The issue was then taken to the High Court contending that the penalty could not be reduced below the minimum prescribed.

2.2 Arguments before the High Court - It was claimed before the Court that when the Act gives discretion to the authority of levying the penalty, the penalty amount could as well be below the minimum prescribed by the statute. It was argued that when section 80 of the Act (supra) gives discretion to the authority not to levy the penalty at all in cases of reasonable cause, the provision (section 80) could as well be construed to give power even to levy the penalty below the minimum prescribed, if the facts and circumstances of the case warrant such a decision on 'reasonable cause' ground.

2.3 Court's decision - The High Court observed that a plain reading of section 76 of the Act indicates that a person, who is liable to pay service tax and who has failed to pay such tax, is under an obligation to pay, in addition to the tax so payable and interest on such tax, a penalty for such failure. The quantum of penalty has been specified in the provision by laying down the minimum and the maximum limits, with a further rider for the maximum limit. The discretion vested in the authority is to levy minimum penalty as laid down in the section.

From the discretion it is not possible to read a further discretion being vested so as to entitle the authority to levy a penalty below the stipulated limit. The moment one reads such further discretion in the provision, it would amount to re-writing the provision, which is not permissible. It is not as if the provision is couched in a manner so as to lead to absurdity if it is read in a plain manner.

Decision of Income-tax Appellate Tribunal interpretating Dharamendra Textile Processors’ case 6.3 Based on the interpretation of Dharamendra Textile Processors’ case, department officials are of the view that the penalty is mandatory in each and every case of default. So the taxpayers were at the receiving end for some time. But taxpayers got some relief from some of the decisions of Income-tax Appellate Tribunals. In the case of Kanbay Software v. Dy. CIT [2009] 122 TTJ (Pune) 721 and ACIT v. VIP Industries [2009] 30 SOT 254 (Mum.), it was held that the judgment of the Supreme Court in Dharamendra Textiles Processors which holds that penalty under section 271(1)( c) is a civil liability and that wilful concealment and mens rea are not essential ingredients for imposing penalty cannot be read to mean that in all cases where addition is confirmed, penalty shall mechanically follow. In order to attract section 271(1)(c), there must be concealment the fact that the same is wilful or unintentional is irrelevant. But where an assessee genuinely claims a deduction after disclosing necessary facts, there is no concealment even if the claim is rejected. If penalty is imposed under such circumstances also there will remain no course open to an assessee to raise disputed claims and such proposition is beyond recognized canons of law. Similar types of decisions were also given under indirect taxes also.

Decision of Supreme Court in the case of Union of India v. Rajasthan Spg. & Wvg. Mills [2009] 20 STT 481

6.4 Proceedings were initiated against the assessees for non-payment and short-payment of excise duty. The demand for duty was confirmed on the assessees and penalty under section 11AC was also imposed. However, the Tribunal in its impugned orders had taken a view that there was no warrant for levy of penalty since the assessees had deposited the duty even before the show-cause notice was issued. In the instant appeal, the revenue relying upon the decision in Union of India v. Dharamendra Textile Processors [2008] 306 ITR 277/174 Taxman 571 (SC), contended that mere non-payment or short payment of duty would inevitably lead to imposition of penalty equal to the amount by which duty was short paid.

The Hon’ble Supreme Court held that payment of differential duty, whether before or after the show-cause notice is issued, cannot alter liability for penalty, the conditions for which are clearly spelled out in section 11AC. From section 11A(1) read with its proviso, it is clear that in case the short-payment, non-payment or erroneous refund of duty is unintended and not attributable to fraud, collusion or any wilful mis-statement or suppression of facts, or contravention of any of the provisions of the Act or of the rules made under it, with an intent to evade payment of duty then the revenue can give notice for recovery of the duty to the person in default within one year from the relevant date. In other words, in the absence of any element of deception or malpractice, the recovery of duty can only be for a period not exceeding one year but in case the non-payment, etc., of duty is intentional and by adopting any means as indicated in the proviso, then the period of notice and the period for which duty can be demanded, gets extended to five years.

The Supreme Court further held that sub-section (2B) of section 11A provides that in case the person-in-default makes payment of the escaped amount of duty before the service of notice, then the revenue will not give him the notice under sub-section (1). This, perhaps, is the basis of the common, though erroneous view that no penalty would be leviable if the escaped amount of duty is paid before the service of notice. It, however, overlooks the two Explanations qualifying the main provision. Explanation 1 makes it clear that the payment would, nevertheless, be subject to imposition of interest under section 11AB. Explanation 2 makes it further clear that in case the escapement of duty is intentional and by reason of deception, the main provision of sub-section (2B) will have no application.

Meaning of reasonable cause

6. In S. Raghbir Singh Sandhawalia v. CIT AIR 1958 Punj. 250, it was held that the expression 'reasonable' means 'rational' according to the dictates of reason and not excessive or immoderate. An act is reasonable when it is comfortable or agreeable to reasons, having regard to the facts of the particular controversy.

This phrase has been interpreted in a number of decisions, including under the I.T. Act. In the case of Municipal Corpn. of Delhi v. Jagan Nath Ashok Kumar, AIR 1987 SC 2316, the SC interpreted the expression 'reasonable cause' as follows:—

"…Stroud's Judicial Dictionary, Fourth Edition, page 2258, states that it would be unreasonable to expect an exact definition of the word 'reasonable'. Reason varies in its conclusions according to the idiosyncrasy of the individual, and the times and circumstances in which he thinks. The reasoning, which built up the old scholastic logic sounds now like the jingling of a child's toy. But mankind must be satisfied with the reasonableness within reach and in cases not covered by authority, the verdict of a jury or the decision of a judge sitting as a jury usually determines what is 'reasonable'…."

Reasonable cause can be reasonably said to be a cause which prevents a man of average intelligence and ordinary prudence, acting under normal circumstances, without negligence or inaction or want of bona fides [Azadi Bachao Andolan v. Union of India [2001] 116 Taxman 249/252 ITR 471 (Delhi)].

Lack of funds or financial crisis has not been held to tantamount to reasonable cause. In Trans (India) Shipping (P) Ltd. v. CCE [2005] 2 STT 82 (Chennai), it has been observed that a delay in payment or non-payment of service tax within the prescribed time due to the cash crisis or financial hardship is generally not approved as falling within the scope of 'reasonable cause'.

Briefly speaking, reasonable cause means an honest belief founded upon reasonable grounds of the existence of a state of circumstances, which (assuming them to be true) would reasonably lead any ordinary prudent and cautious man (placed in the position of the person concerned) to come to the conclusion that the same was the right thing to do. The cause shown has to be considered and only if it is found to be frivolous, without substance or foundation, the aforesaid penalty can be imposed [see Woodward Governors India (P) Ltd. v. CIT [2001] 118 Taxman 433 (Delhi)].

Legislature's Attempt to be Wiser while Drafting new Penalty Section 270A

Under the new penalty regime, legislature has sought to draft the law in section 270A in such a manner so as to do away with all the possibilities of the above grounds available with the tax payers while contesting the levy of penalty under section 270A.Phraseology used in sub section (1) of section 271(1)(c) and the present penalty provision of sub section (1), (8) other sub sections of section 270A are materially different in this regard which is evident from the plain reading of the referred sub sections of the both the penalty provisions.

Anxiety of the legislature to do away with such pre-requisite of 'recording satisfaction' etc. can be well understood. 'Not recording the satisfaction' or 'recording the satisfaction inappropriately' or the above mentioned variety of technical super-technical grounds raised by the tax payers in the appeals against the penalty levied, had cost the Revenue very dearly in the past, had been the source of the severe body blow profuse bleeding to the exchequer. At the same time, such penalties lost the deterrence effect too due to such penalties having been deleted on these short legal grounds, even when there was enough justification for their levy sustenance on merit. Language of section 270A has thus been so drafted by the legislature as not to admit any such interpretation requiring the initiation of penalty proceeding recording of the 'satisfaction' in the assessment order or meeting the other technical aspects as discussed above, on the lines of the language of section 271(1)(c) its judicial interpretations placed by the Courts.

7. Difference between Underreporting and Misreporting

Underreporting of income entails ignoring or just partially declaring the real income obtained, and misreporting of income refers to knowingly submitting inaccurate or misleading information regarding income.

| Particulars | Under reporting of Income | Misreporting of Income |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nature | While underreporting of income entails ignoring or just partially declaring the real income obtained | Misreporting of income refers to knowingly submitting inaccurate or misleading information regarding income |
| Intent | While underreporting may result from ignorance, negligence, or a failure to understand the reporting requirements, | Misreporting suggests an intentional act of submitting inaccurate data to deceive or manipulate. |
| Scope of Inaccuracy | underreporting entails an inadequate or partial income statement with/without any manipulation. | Misreporting sometimes entails falsifying income projections or inflating deductions to reduce tax payments significantly. |
| Penalties | While underreporting can result in penalties that are usually 50% of the tax due | Penalties for misreporting are typically more severe., income reporting errors can result in larger fines of up to 200% of the tax due. |
| Legal Treatment | Tax authorities usually handle underreporting as a civil tax concern and levy penalties and fines. | Misreporting is often considered a more severe offense and may occasionally be subject to criminal prosecution. |
| Detection | underreporting can make it difficult for tax officials to spot differences between reported and real income. | Misreporting might be harder to spot since it includes deliberate manipulation and the fabrication of misleading records. |

3. Quantifying under-reported income: Where income is assessed for the first time and ITR was furnished by the assessee the difference between the income assessed and income determined under section 143(1)(a) would be the under-reported income.

Where no ITR is furnished or where it is furnished in response to notice under section 148 then (i) the amount of income assessed would be treated as under-reported income in the case of company, firm or local authority; and (ii) the difference between the income assessed and the basic exemption limit would be the under-reported income for other taxpayers.

Where the assessee offers an explanation and the Assessing Officer or the Commissioner (Appeals) or the Commissioner or the Principal Commissioner, as the case may be, is satisfied that the explanation is bona fide and the assessee has disclosed all material facts to substantiate the explanation offered by him, the income so enhanced shall not be treated as under-reporting of income.

TAXABLE INCOME

3. The chasm between the taxable income and the accountant’s or legal concept of income is very wide, more because of the numerous deeming provisions in the tax statute, which nullify them. Tax on capital gains itself is a glaring example of taxing what is not income. Deeming provisions even in respect of salary income treating terminal benefits as normal income, subject, no doubt, to measured relief and various other provisions like anti-compete fee under section 28 of the Act besides such income as from lotteries under section 56, are again other capital receipts, which are treated as revenue receipts, contrary to accepted understanding of revenue as against capital receipts. Provisions for deemed dividend and deeming accrual on receipt basis are other instances.

Some items of revenue expenditure are deemed to be capital expenditure allowed to be amortised over the years as in the case of expenses on mergers and demergers under section 35DD of the Act or VRS payments under section 35DDA of the Act. What makes the taxable income even more distorted making a sweeping departure from real income is the deeming provision like disallowance of what is deemed to be illegal under Explanation to section 37(1) of the Act. Expenditure from which tax is failed to be deducted at source is disallowed under section 40(a) of the Act. Even where mercantile system is followed, cash system is substituted under section 43B, so as to legitimise hybrid system to revenue’s advantage in the matter of taxes, interest to banks and financial institutions and welfare dues. What is worse is the provision to treat cash expenditure above the limit of Rs. 20,000 under section 40A(3) of the Act with minor exceptions on the understanding, that expenditure would include purchases. Apart from what is collected as tax, penalty is collected on deposits and repayments in cash under section 269SS and 269T of the Act, unless reasonable cause is established. Both sections 40A(3) and 269SS and 269T would strangely target genuine transactions, because expenditure, which is not genuine and deposits which are not genuine are taxable as income. The complexity of our laws is more evident in the matters of cross-border transactions with Double Tax Avoidance Agreements hardly touching the existing problems with transfer pricing adding to the existing confusion. Almost every Finance Act would add to the list of deeming provisions.

DISCRIMINATORY TREATMENT OF CORPORATE SECTOR

4. Our system of corporate taxation is highly discriminatory making corporations liable for additional burden by way of book profits tax on one hand and dividend distribution tax on the other. Tax on dividend is a double taxation of corporate income, whether the dividends are assessed in the hands of shareholder or company. Loans and advances are deemed as dividend income of the shareholder or a concern in which the shareholder is interested under section 2(22)( e) of the Act. Right of set off on actual distributed dividend in a later year as provided in the section makes no sense, when such dividend is taxed in the hands of an interested concern, so that it is another instance of double taxation in shareholder’s hands once as deemed dividend and again in the hands of the interested concern, when there is actual distribution of dividend. Deeming loss under the head ‘Capital gains’ on share transactions as speculative under Explanation to section 73 of the Act is a special provision targetting corporations. Fringe Benefits Tax though not limited to corporations imposes further burden especially on manufacturing companies with a large work force.

Rationale of using the expression 'during the course of any proceeding' instead of using 'during the course of penalty proceeding'

Penalty is imposed during the course of penalty proceeding and therefore, legislature could have used the expression in sub section (1) of section 270A as to direction to pay penalty 'during the course of penalty proceeding'.

But as discussed above, there could be proceeding other than the penalty proceeding viz. quantum appeal proceeding under section 250 before Commissioner (Appeals) revision proceeding under section 263 before Principal Commissioner of Commissioner, during the course of which jurisdiction to impose penalty under section 270A would have to be assumed in respect of any addition made by these authorities. Therefore, different nature of proceedings other than the penalty proceeding alone, as explained above, during the course of which penalty may come to be initiated levied seems to be the reason for the legislature using the expression 'during the course of any proceeding' under sub section (1) of section 270A.

'Under reported Income'

'Under reported income' has been explained under sub section (3) with the help of various situations of return filing, income shown in the returns filed processed under section 143(1)(a), and assessments reassessments made. Situations have been almost similarly explained about the 'person' who can be considered to have 'under reported income' under sub section (2).

It is noteworthy that penalty under section 270A is leviable on 'under reported income' which, if simply put, is the difference between the income assessed and amount of the income determined under section 143(1)(a) where the return has been furnished. If return of income has not been furnished or return has been furnished under section 148 for the first time, difference between the income assessed and basic exemption limit shall be the amount of 'under reported income'. Since in case of a company, firm or local authority, there is no basic exemption limit, thus the amount of 'under reported income' would be equal to the income assessed where the return of income has been filed by them for the first time. Certain other situations of the 'under reported income' too have been envisaged under sub section (3) of section 270A where income processed assessed was on deemed basis under section 115JB/115JC, or post-assessment assessed income has the effect of reducing the loss or converting the loss into income.

Without going into the fine nitty-gritty of these provisions putting simply, we would not be wrong if we say, that the 'under reported income' would be the difference between the income assessed income processed under section 143(1)(a). If it is a case of reassessment under section 147 or under section 153A, 'under reported income' would be the difference between the reassessed income and the earlier assessed income.

At the cost of repetition, we would urge that we have sought to simplify the meaning of 'under reported income' or else, we would also have landed in the similar complex maze, labyrinths round-about of situations mentioned in sub section (2) (3) of section 270A. Thus, it would be sufficient to say that there is in a way automatic 'under reported income' the moment there is difference between the assessed income and processed income subject to the exclusions given in sub section (6) of section 270A.

But, there may well be a situation whereby assessing officer while passing the assessment order finds that the 'under reported income' or part thereof is covered under any one or more of the clauses (a) to (e) of sub section (6). Detailed discussion in this regard has been made under the following caption titled 'Exceptions to or Exclusions from the 'Under reported Income'. In such a scenario, the assessing officer may reduce the amount of 'under reported income' by the amounts of additions/disallowances so covered by clause (a) to (e) of sub section (6).If after excluding such amounts covered under clause (a) to (e) of sub section (6), there remains no 'under reported income', the assessing officer may not even initiate the penalty proceeding under section 270A, in the assessment order.

That is why whenever there would be additions/disallowances made in the assessment order which would make the income assessed more than the income processed, all that the assessing officer has to do is to initiate penalty under section 270A, as there is 'under reported income' on the face of the assessment order.

Penalty under section 270A is on 'under reported income' and even if such 'under reported income is in consequence to misreporting of income', yet the penalty would be levied quantified on income which is termed as 'under reported income' under the law. (b) Placement of section 270A(6):Section 270A(1) gives the overall scope of the provision empowering the income-tax authorities to levy penalty for under-reported income which could include under-reported income as such or due to misreporting of income. Sub-section (6) is meant for the entire section 270A and not for under-reported income simpliciter. Unfortunately, it is placed after describing the under-reported income simpliciter but much before the misreporting of income dealt with in sections 270A(8) and 270A(9). Ideally, section 270A(6) must have been placed after explaining both under-reported and misreported incomes so that its applicability / coverage would not have created confusion and ambiguity.

(c) Misrepresentation or suppression of facts: Under-reporting of income due to misreporting of income is one of the instances covered in section 270A(9). The expression 'misrepresentation' could be found in section 245D(6) (relating to settlement of cases) and in section 245T (relating to advance ruling). In both, settlement of cases and in advance ruling the taxpayer is given opportunity of being heard. Only on representing the case before the prescribed authority, there could be a possibility of misrepresentation.

Where there is no query from the income-tax authority and no reply from the taxpayer, any addition made could not be called as 'misrepresentation'. It could be argued that misrepresentation is implicit by submitting incorrect ITR with details of income chargeable to tax and thus when wrong claims in the ITR when negatived, it amounts to misrepresentation of income.

The other aspect 'suppression of facts' entails a deliberate act of not revealing the facts and not necessarily twisting of facts. Not furnishing the facts could amount to suppression of facts.

The expression "misrepresentation and suppression of facts" could create great hardship to the taxpayers as any addition made otherwise than by way of estimated addition would be construed as misrepresentation or suppression of facts by the tax authorities.

(d) Failure to record investments in the books of account: This expression would cover unrecorded investments of the taxpayers chargeable to tax as income. But usage of the expression "recording investments in the books of account" seems to provide a leeway in cases where the investments do not belong to the business. Obviously, in such cases, the unrecorded investment would belong to the family of incomes which are chargeable to tax under section 115BBE with resultant penal consequence under section 271AAC of 10% of the unrecorded investments, which is less severe than 200% penalty envisaged in section 270A(8) read with section 270A(9).

(e) Claim of expenditure not substantiated by any evidence: Where the assessee incurs expenditure, which is not substantiated would be treated as misreporting of income. For example, if the assessee has incurred expenditure by way of salary to employees and did not maintain vouchers or the payment was not incurred through banking channel a confirmation from the employees would be adequate for allowance of claim. Where the expenditure claim is not substantiated by any evidence that could only lead to the claim of expenditure treated as misreporting of income.

(f) Recording of false entry in the books of account: This would cover making of accounting entries in the books of account for the purpose of under-reporting of income through misreporting. Where the income is not impacted even if the entry is a false entry for example a journal entry between two suppliers account or inter se customers accounts will not fall in this category. Further one has to take notice of section 271AAD which penalizes false entry in the books of account and which is independent of any other provision in the Act. It includes not only a false entry but also omission of any entry which can impact the total income chargeable to tax under the Act. For example, purchase not recorded in the books of account is not a false entry but it is an omission of entry which is covered by section 271AAD.

Thus recording false entry /omission of entry in the books of account would attract penalty under section 270A(8) @ 200% plus penalty under section 271AAD @ 100%.

Background Introduction

Section 270A has been inserted under the Income Tax Act, 1961 to take effect from 1.4.2017 i.e. from assessment year 2017-18, to provide for the levy of penalty on the 'under-reported income'. Hon'ble Finance Minister while presenting the Finance Bill, 2016 mentioned about his resolve to reduce the litigation and provide certainty in taxation including in the matter of penalty. Memorandum explaining the provisions of the Finance Bill, 2016 gave an insight into the amendment in penalty provision by terming the proposal to introduce section 270A as 'Rationalisation of penalty provisions' emphasizing further that in order to rationalize and bring objectivity, certainty and clarity in the penalty provisions, it is proposed that section 271 shall not apply to and in relation to any assessment for the assessment year commencing on or after the 1stday of April, 2017 and subsequent assessment years and penalty be levied under the newly inserted section 270A with effect from 1stApril, 2017. The new section 270A provides for levy of penalty in cases of underreporting and misreporting of income.

Section 270A

Since section 270A is quite lengthy section, hence we have put this section at the end of this article so that reference to various provisions of this section can be easily made for better comprehension. Also, Section 270AA, section 271(1)(c) section 275 too have been similarly appended.

Provisions in Brief

According to the plain provision of sub section (1) of section 270A, the Assessing Officer or the Commissioner (Appeals) or the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner may 'direct', 'during the course of any proceeding' under the Income Tax Act, 1961, to levy the penalty on a person who has 'under reported' his income such penalty shall be in addition to tax, if any, and would be on the 'under reported income'.

Sub section (2) provides as to who can be a person considered to have 'under reported income' whereas sub section (3) provides as to how 'underreported income' shall be computed.

Sub sections (4) (5) speak for the 'under reported income' the preceding year(s) to which such 'under reported income' would relate, in respect of the amount of intangible additions made in the past where no penalty was levied on such intangible additions, if any deposit, receipt or investment made in the current year is sought to be explained with the help of such past intangible additions and. In fact, sub section (4) (5) of section 270A are on the lines of Explanation 2 to section 271(1)(c).

Sub section (6) of section 270A provides five exhaustive situations in which additions/disallowances mentioned thereunder made in the assessment order may not constitute 'under reported income'.

Thereafter, sub section (7) provides the rate of penalty in respect of the 'under reported income' equal to 50% of the tax payable on such 'under reported income'.

Subsection (8) provides for the levy of penalty equal to 200% of the tax payable on the 'under reported income' if such 'under reported income is in consequence of misreporting of income' instances of which have been exhaustively listed in the form of six cases (a) to (f) under sub section (9).

Sub section (10) provides for the methodology for computing tax payable in respect of the 'under reported income'.

Sub section (11) is to provide that there would be no penalty on any addition or disallowance made if such addition or disallowance has already formed the basis of imposition of penalty on a person either in this year or in any other year.

Sub section (12) mandates the passing of penalty order in writing.

So, this is the new penalty section 270A in place of section 271where there used to be in all 8 live sub sections (count wise) and 7 Explanations, as against 12 sub sections 1 Explanation engrafted now in section 270A. Thus, reincarnated penalty provision under section 270A is 'simplified' at least in that respect and extent.

8. The language of our law is antiquated and multiplicity of the amendments is mind-boggling. Mr. N.A. The bad provisions remain fossilised, while the new ones together have not integrated with other provisions making it extremely complicated. Mr. Palkhivala reasoned as under :

"Nothing is more detrimental to economic growth than uncertainty in business circles as to their tax liability which is still pretty high in India in the corporate sector."

His plea for stable law with clarity and certainty was never more in need than at the present. The constant refrain as justification given for such amendments as ‘rationalising and streamlining’ makes a mockery of the entire exercise.

Under the Income-tax Act, certain categories of income are taxed at the Maximum Marginal Rate (MMR) rather than the normal slab rates or other rates otherwise applicable to the assessee. The concept of MMR was introduced as an anti-avoidance measure to discourage high-income taxpayers from reducing their tax burden by distributing income among multiple entities, such as private trusts, Associations of Persons (AOPs), or Bodies of Individuals (BOIs), that might otherwise be eligible for lower tax rates.

By taxing such income at the MMR, the Act seeks to ensure tax neutrality and discourage tax avoidance, particularly in cases where the shares of beneficiaries or members are indeterminate or where the legislature considers taxation at the highest rate appropriate.

The provisions relating to MMR apply to specified entities and circumstances, including certain trusts, AOPs/BOIs, business trusts, Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs), and registered Non-Profit Organisations (NPOs). For instance, if a closely-held company having accumulated profits had given a loan to a shareholder who was holding more than 10% shareholding. The fact of the matter is that there would be no addition in the hands of the company on this score. There would thus be no difference between the assessed income and processed income on this account in the hands of the company and thus, there would be no 'under reported income' and accordingly, there would be no penalty on the company under section 270A. Therefore, this is a classic case where despite such rank 'misrepresentation of facts', there may not be 'under reported income' in the hands of the company with no penal consequence under section 270A.

35. Need clarity on the levy of multiple penalties under the ITA 2025

The ITA 2025 has omitted the expression "without prejudice" from several penalty provisions, e.g., Sections 440, 441, 443, 444, 460, 462, and 463 (corresponding to Section 271A, 271AA, 271AAD, 271AAE, 271H, 271J, and 271K of the ITA 1961). These sections deal with serious defaults, such as failure to maintain books, false entries, incorrect reporting, TDS/TCS statement defaults and incorrect certifications, etc. In the absence of this phrase, it has become unclear and ambiguous whether any other provisions of the ITA 2025 are still fully effective or whether these provisions will override or conflict with any other penalty provision of the ITA 2025.

This omission has created ambiguity, as taxpayers may contend that only one specific penalty should apply for a particular contravention, thereby precluding other penalties arising from the same transaction or its consequences. This is especially relevant where the same default can trigger dual penalties. The lack of explicit statutory guidance increases the risk of interpretational disputes, inconsistent enforcement, and litigation.

It is therefore recommended that the ITA 2025 be suitably amended or clarified to explicitly state the legislative intent on whether multiple penalties can be levied for the same default. Clear drafting will ensure certainty, uniform application of penalty provisions, and effective deterrence, while avoiding unnecessary litigation.

36. Start-ups may be penalised for not fulfilling conditions after claiming the deduction

Section 140 of ITA 2025 [Corresponds to Section 80-IAC of ITA 1961] does not contain any provision to withdraw the deduction if the start-up fails to fulfil the prescribed conditions. It is apprehended that an amendment could be made to Section 140 to withdraw the deduction if the assessee company fails to comply with the conditions prescribed in the DPIIT's notification.

37. Prosecution for wilful attempt to evade payment of tax should be contingent upon assessment

Section 478 of ITA 2025 [corresponding to Section 276C of ITA 1961] is widely used to initiate prosecution proceedings. The basic difference between sub-section (1) and sub-section (2) of Section 478 is that the former is attracted in cases where there is a wilful attempt to evade any tax, penalty or interest, whereas the latter is attracted when there is a wilful attempt to evade the payment of tax, penalty or interest.

The logical corollary is that to attract the provision of Section 478(2), there should be an already determined tax, the payment of which is wilfully evaded by the assessee. However, the existence of a pre-determined tax is not a condition to be satisfied for attracting the provision of Section 478(1).

It is also stated that both sections use the word "wilfully". However, the word 'wilfully' is not defined and is thus left to the officer's discretion. Thus, to remove the ambiguity, the following changes should be proposed under Section 478.

(a)

A provision should be inserted that sub-section (2) of Section 478 shall not apply unless the assessment determining the tax demand is made.

(b)

A provision should be inserted that sub-section (2) of Section 478 shall not apply if the appellate authority has provided the relief to the assessee in regard to the alleged tax evaded as referred to in sub-section (1) of Section 478.

In other words, the prosecution under Section 478(2) should be linked with the assessment outcome.
