(v)

Section 273B of the Act – Shelter of "reasonable cause" not available for penalties under Section 270A of the Act

As we are aware, section 273B of the Act provides for non-levy of penalty, levied under the specific provisions mentioned therein, if the taxpayer proves that there was a reasonable cause for the failure.

Interestingly and to an extent even surprisingly, the said shelter of "reasonable cause" has not been made available for penalty levied under section 270A of the Act.

(vi)

Immunity under Section 270AA of the Act not available for misreporting of income

To reduce instances of levy of penalty inter-alia in cases where the addition(s) made in the assessment /re-assessment proceedings (leading to the levy of penalty) has(ve) been accepted, section 270AA of the Act has been introduced by the Finance Act, 2017 to provide the taxpayer an opportunity to seek, from the Assessing Officer, immunity from imposition of penalty under section 270A of the Act.

This is subject to fulfillment of the following conditions:

(a)

Payment of tax and interest within the specified time.

(b)

Non filing of any appeal against the order of assessment/reassessment.

An important point to note here is that the aforesaid immunity provisions are applicable for penalty levied/sought to be levied under section 270A only vis-à-vis cases related to "underreporting of income". In other words, no immunity can be sought in cases of "misreporting of income".

In addition to above, the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT), vide Circular No. 05/2018 dated 16 August 2018, has clarified that an application made by an assessee under section 270AA of the Act seeking immunity, will not bar the assessee from contesting the same issue in any earlier assessment year. This circular also clarifies that the tax authority shall not take an adverse view in penalty proceedings for earlier assessment year(s) under the old penalty regime merely because the taxpayer has applied for immunity under the new penalty regime.

(vii)

Interplay between Section 271G of the Act and Section 270A of the Act – Double blow?

Section 270A of the Act inter-alia provides for the levy of penalty for underreporting of the income, if information prescribed under Section 92D of the Act is not maintained.

Section 271G of the Act seeks to levy a penalty of 2 percent of the value of international transaction for failure to furnish any information as required under section 92D (3) of the Act. The said section is an independent section.

Accordingly, a literal interpretation of the above sections may seemingly lead to a double blow to taxpayer by levy of the penalty in both the sections. However, one point of difference could be that penalty under section 270A of the Act may only be sustained if the transfer pricing adjustment is upheld before the higher authorities whereas the penalty under section 271G of the Act is usually independent of the fate of transfer pricing adjustments; though there are contradicting decisions on the subject.

(viii)

Thin line of difference exists between the term 'suppression of fact' (misreporting of income) and 'disclosure of material facts' (underreporting of income)

There is a thin line of difference between the term 'suppression of fact' as mentioned under misreporting of income and 'disclosure of material facts' as contemplated under underreporting of income. Given that either of the terms are not defined under the Act, it may open up the doors for prolonged litigation as penalty under the head 'underreporting' is lower than what is contemplated under 'misreporting of income'.

Taxpayers and professionals, need to gear up for the new penalty regime which will have its own set of propositions to be laid out and tested at the appellate fora. It will be interesting to see how they shape up specifically in the transfer pricing world which is more a fact driven exercise. Indeed, there are exciting times ahead!

The twin objects of section 44AB are administrative convenience and prevention of tax evasion and avoidance. There is no hostile discrimination between one class of assessees having total sales/turnover, gross receipts being less than the prescribed limit and the other class, having more. If there is any, the difference in treatment is capable of being explained in the light of the aforesaid twin objects for which the legislation was undertaken. If there is equality and uniformity with each group, the law would not be condemned as discriminatory though due to some fortuitous circumstances arising out of a peculiar situation, some included in a class get an advantage over others, so long as they are not singled out for special treatment. The words ‘in the case to which the appeal relates’ which appear in clauses (a) to (c ) of section 253(6) only refer to the proceedings relating to the assessee in whose case the penalty order has been passed. These words should not be understood in a restrictive sense and must be broadly construed so as to cover all appeals which are filed in the case of the assessee where the appeal is filed against an order which is based on the quantum of income assessed. An order levying penalty for concealment is undeniably connected with the assessment order or more particularly with the total income computed by the Assessing Officer. It may be that the penalty is levied only with reference to the tax sought to be evaded on the concealed income but the concealed income does form part of the assessed income as computed by the Assessing Officer and that is sufficient to establish the nexus between the amount of income assessed by the Assessing Officer and the concealed income and also establish the requisite relationship between the assessed income and the filing fee. The residuary clause takes care of all appeals, including appeals against certain penalties which have no nexus with the amount of income assessed. [Para 15]

The principle that assessment proceedings and penalty proceedings are different in nature is applicable for a limited and a different purpose. The settled legal position is that the penalty proceedings are quasi-criminal in nature, whereas the assessment proceedings are not so and that, therefore, any material gathered against the assessee during the assessment proceedings or findings recorded in the course of the assessment proceedings, though would constitute good evidence for purposes of levying penalty, would not be conclusive evidence against the assessee in penalty proceedings. The legal position is also that it is open to the income-tax authorities and the appellate authorities to make a reappraisal of the entire materials while judging the correctness or justification of the penalty imposed on an assessee for concealment of income and come to a different conclusion. The principle recognizing the distinction between the assessment and penalty proceedings cannot be extended, for determining a provision which prescribes the filing fee in respect of appeals filed before the Tribunal. Nor can it follow that penalty proceedings have no relation to the assessed income. Further, the requirement that the Assessing Officer should record the satisfaction that the assessee has concealed his income and such satisfaction should be reached in the course of the assessment proceedings, supports the view that there is a link or nexus or relationship between the assessment proceedings and the penalty proceedings. [Para 17]

For the above reasons, the view expressed in the dissenting opinion in the Special Bench decision in the case of Vinod Khatri was concurred in . [Para 18]

Therefore, the filing fee levying for an appeal to Tribunal against the order of penalty levied under section 271(1)(c) is governed by clauses (a) to (c) of section 253(6). [Para 19]

Non-monetary consequences

5. Such schemes have been adversely commented upon by tax economists and policymakers. Some observations were as follows:—

(i)

Policy of leniency in tax matters has not been favoured. Shri A.M. Nremner, while giving evidence before the Royal Commission on Income Tax had said as early as in the year 1920:—

"The real way to prevent fraud …. Is that fraud should be punished by terms of imprisonment; that is the way to stop it. It will never be stopped in any other way; the temptation is so great now. People must be made to understand that if they defraud the revenue, they are committing a mean and despicable offence against every one of their fellow taxpayers".

(ii)

Expert Committees on taxes in the past have disfavoured such schemes for tapping black money with immunities. The Wanchoo Committee has said:—

"We consider that a disclosure scheme is an extraordinary measure, meant for abnormal situations such as after a war or at a time of national crisis. Resorting to such a measure during normal times, and that too frequently, would only shake the confidence of the honest taxpayers in the capacity of the Govt. to deal with the law breakers and would invite contempt for its enforcement machinery. We are convinced that any more disclosure schemes would not only fail to achieve the intended purpose of unearthing black money but would have deleterious effect on the level of compliance among the taxpaying public and on the moral of the administration. We are, therefore, strongly opposed to the idea of the introduction of any general scheme of disclosure either now or in the future".

(iii)

In his dissenting judgment in the case of R.K. Garg/R. Karanjia/Madhu Mehta/P.K. Soi/S.S. Bedi v. Union of India [1982] 133 ITR 239/[1981] 67 Taxman 53 (SC), A.C. Gupta, J. of the Supreme Court, has said that -

The issues that arise in the context of amnesty are : Can fair minded, reasonable, unbiased and resolute men, who are not swayed by emotion or prejudice regard such scheme with equanimity and call it reasonable, just and fair, regard it as providing equal treatment and protection in the defence of the rights of being treated equally, which is expected of a sovereign democratic republic? The answers to these queries had to be obvious NO.

(iv)

The deleterious impacts of VDISs in the report on the study on 'Aspects of the Black Economy in India', carried out by the National Institute of Public Finance & Policy in 1984-85 have been mentioned in the following words in this report:—

"Basically, these schemes seek to coax errant tax evaders to disclose their concealed income and wealth in return for taxation at concessional rates and immunity from penalties and prosecution.

By offering de facto amnesty for tax evasion, such schemes blunt the deterrent provisions of the tax laws, including the provisions for prosecution. Voluntary Disclosure Schemes have been severely criticized by a number of reports of the Lok Sabha's Public Accounts Committee and the Wanchoo Committee. The main criticisms were as :-

(i)

The quantitative results have been disappointing in relation to even the lowest estimates of tax evasion;

(ii)

The view that such schemes permit errant taxpayers to forswear their wayward paths is not supported by the large number of "repeat" beneficiaries of these schemes;

(iii)

When such schemes are launched every few years, they reduce the incentives for voluntary compliance in the first place and weaken the morale of both honest taxpayers and the tax administration.

Even such un-favourable comments from eminent persons/Committees have not daunted the FM of India to refrain from doing so. He formulated another scheme, which too has proved to be a disaster from the angle of tax collection.

Further, such schemes bring down the credibility of the Govt. as a non-performing institution, unable to enforce its tax laws effectively. Hence, occasionally it has to go before the taxpayers with a begging bowl, asking them to pay taxes as per their initiative as a favour to the Govt., which is not able to collect these dues using its power under the Constitution of India.

If we closely examine 'Misrepresentation' and 'Suppression', we would end up in reaching traversing through the old concepts of 'furnishing inaccurately' 'concealment' of particulars of income. This is so because if there is no such difference, that would mean that there is no 'under reported income' and when there is no 'under reported income', there would not be 'under reported income in consequence to 'misreporting of income'. In other words, this can be put like this that even if 'charge' is there but if quantification or machinery fails, no pecuniary consequence in the form of penalty under section 270A would follow.

For instance, even if there was 'failure to report international transaction' or 'specified domestic transaction' but during the course of assessment, there may not result any addition/adjustment on this account as assessee may have proved that such transaction was entered into at arm's length price. In that situation, 'failure to report' such transaction was though ostensibly a case of 'misreporting of income' under clause (f) of subsection (9), yet in so far as the penalty under section 270A is concerned, no penalty can be imposed under that section since there was no addition/adjustment made in the assessment order and thus there was no difference on that account resulting between the assessed income and processed income and accordingly, there was thus no 'under reported income'. Since, there was no 'under reported income' resulting, there was no question of penalty under section 270A.This may be an altogether different matter that there may be other consequence for such non-disclosure, for instance, levy of penalty u/s 271AA for failure to report the international transaction or specified domestic transaction under section 92B/92BA. (g)

Similarly, not all the 'misrepresentation' or 'suppression' of facts as mentioned in clause (a) of sub section (9) may lead to the addition of income or disallowance of a claim, which means that in the absence of such addition or disallowance made in the assessment order to the returned income, there would not be 'under reported income' and since there would be no 'under reported income' in such a case, there would be no question of penalty under section 270A.

For instance, if a closely-held company having accumulated profits had given a loan to a shareholder who was holding more than 10% shareholding. But in order to camouflage real character of this transaction so that it can avoid the glare of applicability of section 2(22)(e), such company misrepresented this fact by terming and showing this transaction as not in the nature of loan but in the nature of advance in the course of business. Such transaction its real nature when exposed in the assessment of the company would obviously not lead to the addition of income in the hands of the company as the deemed dividend can be taxed in the hands of the shareholder. The fact of the matter is that there would be no addition in the hands of the company on this score. There would thus be no difference between the assessed income and processed income on this account in the hands of the company and thus, there would be no 'under reported income' and accordingly, there would be no penalty on the company under section 270A. Therefore, this is a classic case where despite such rank 'misrepresentation of facts', there may not be 'under reported income' in the hands of the company with no penal consequence under section 270A.

Substitution of SPT for income-tax payable [sub-section (1)];

Providing machinery for computation of book profit [sub-section (2)];

Substitution of tax payable by SPT; and

Computation of book profit.

The expression "misrepresentation and suppression of facts" could create great hardship to the taxpayers as any addition made otherwise than by way of estimated addition would be construed as misrepresentation or suppression of facts by the tax authorities.

(d) Failure to record investments in the books of account: This expression would cover unrecorded investments of the taxpayers chargeable to tax as income. But usage of the expression "recording investments in the books of account" seems to provide a leeway in cases where the investments do not belong to the business. Obviously, in such cases, the unrecorded investment would belong to the family of incomes which are chargeable to tax under section 115BBE with resultant penal consequence under section 271AAC of 10% of the unrecorded investments, which is less severe than 200% penalty envisaged in section 270A(8) read with section 270A(9).

(e) Claim of expenditure not substantiated by any evidence: Where the assessee incurs expenditure, which is not substantiated would be treated as misreporting of income. For example, if the assessee has incurred expenditure by way of salary to employees and did not maintain vouchers or the payment was not incurred through banking channel a confirmation from the employees would be adequate for allowance of claim. Where the expenditure claim is not substantiated by any evidence that could only lead to the claim of expenditure treated as misreporting of income.

(f) Recording of false entry in the books of account: This would cover making of accounting entries in the books of account for the purpose of under-reporting of income through misreporting. Where the income is not impacted even if the entry is a false entry for example a journal entry between two suppliers account or inter se customers accounts will not fall in this category. Further one has to take notice of section 271AAD which penalizes false entry in the books of account and which is independent of any other provision in the Act. It includes not only a false entry but also omission of any entry which can impact the total income chargeable to tax under the Act. For example, purchase not recorded in the books of account is not a false entry but it is an omission of entry which is covered by section 271AAD.

Thus recording false entry /omission of entry in the books of account would attract penalty under section 270A(8) @ 200% plus penalty under section 271AAD @ 100%.

7. Difference between Underreporting and Misreporting

Underreporting of income entails ignoring or just partially declaring the real income obtained, and misreporting of income refers to knowingly submitting inaccurate or misleading information regarding income.

| Particulars | Under reporting of Income | Misreporting of Income |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nature | While underreporting of income entails ignoring or just partially declaring the real income obtained | Misreporting of income refers to knowingly submitting inaccurate or misleading information regarding income |
| Intent | While underreporting may result from ignorance, negligence, or a failure to understand the reporting requirements, | Misreporting suggests an intentional act of submitting inaccurate data to deceive or manipulate. |
| Scope of Inaccuracy | underreporting entails an inadequate or partial income statement with/without any manipulation. | Misreporting sometimes entails falsifying income projections or inflating deductions to reduce tax payments significantly. |
| Penalties | While underreporting can result in penalties that are usually 50% of the tax due | Penalties for misreporting are typically more severe., income reporting errors can result in larger fines of up to 200% of the tax due. |
| Legal Treatment | Tax authorities usually handle underreporting as a civil tax concern and levy penalties and fines. | Misreporting is often considered a more severe offense and may occasionally be subject to criminal prosecution. |
| Detection | underreporting can make it difficult for tax officials to spot differences between reported and real income. | Misreporting might be harder to spot since it includes deliberate manipulation and the fabrication of misleading records. |

(a)

This is quite surprising that section 270A does not envisage any penalty on account of additions/disallowances/adjustments made to the returned income under section 143(1)(a). It may be recalled that section 143(1)(a) contains 6 different types of adjustments which can be made while processing the return. Such additions/disallowances/adjustments may be on account of any arithmetical error in the return, any incorrect claim if such incorrectness is apparent from any information in the return, disallowance of loss brought forward from earlier year and set off in this year which was not allowed to be carried forward as the return for that year was filed beyond the due date prescribed under section 139(1), disallowance of expenditures indicated in the audit report but not disallowed in the return, disallowance of deduction under section 10AA, 80IA, 80IAB, 80IB, 80IC, 80ID, 80IE if the return is furnished beyond the due date as prescribed under section 139(1). Legislature has not created any disincentive in the form of any additional tax on the lines of erstwhile section 143(1A), or any penalty under section 270A on account of the difference between the returned income and the processed income. Under section 271(1)(c), there was 'Explanation 6' which provided that no penalty under section 271(1)(c) would be levied in respect of prima facie adjustments made if as per the then existing provision under section 143(1A), additional tax had been charged which was equal to 20% of the tax payable on such adjustments. Under the existing provisions, there is no concept of additional tax on such adjustments except the normal tax levied on such difference. There does not seem to be any justification for not envisaging any disincentive or penalty in respect of such adjustments. Rationale for not envisaging the penalty under section 270A or some other disincentive on account of these adjustments seems to be that when such additions/disallowances are made in the intimation under section 143(1)(a) based on the information contained in the return of income itself, it means that there was no attempt to hide anything on the part of the assessee. But, if this is the rationale, it may not sound well. Contrarily, such additions/disallowances/adjustments made on account of patent and blatant errors in the return of income ultimately lead to under-reporting of income for no good reason or justification.

C. Section 270A – Potential transfer pricing exposure in the new penalty regime

Having looked at the provisions of law, let us now test the common issues which have come up in transfer pricing assessments in the past for a potential exposure to the new penalty regime:

(i)

Transfer pricing adjustment for difference in opinion – can it be said to be underreporting of income?

Typically, difference of opinion has arisen on the following issues:

(a)

Characterisation of the entity;

(b)

Aggregation vs segregation;

(c)

Comparability factors;

(d)

Method of benchmarking; etc.

The law provides that no penalty for underreporting of income shall be levied in cases where:

(a)

Information and documents as prescribed under section 92D are maintained;

(b)

Relevant international transaction under Chapter X is disclosed in Form 3CEB, and

(c)

Material facts relating to the transaction are disclosed

The taxpayer in the above cases may maintain the information and documents under section 92D of the Act as per its bona fide belief; however, tax authorities may have an opinion contrary to the taxpayer's.

Accordingly, in such cases, it will be imperative for the taxpayer to demonstrate before the authorities, from documentation and other supporting evidences, that the position taken by it, be it for classifying its activities or for justifying its transfer pricing approach, leads to a possible view on the subject. A view against it, on merits, is not due to non-furnishing or disability to explain any evidence, but a purely interpretational issue.

(ii)

Transactions where there is ambiguity over applicability of transfer pricing provisions – Can it be construed to be misreporting of income?

Another thought provoking situation may arise when there is a dispute between the taxpayer and tax authorities over the applicability of the transfer pricing provisions. These are typically cases where the taxpayers have historically denied of any international transaction(s). For example, incurring of advertising, marketing and promotion expenses, giving of interest-free loans and/or extending of guarantees to associated enterprises, etc.

In such cases, a question may arise as to whether penalty on account of misreporting of income be levied? This question would arise as such transactions are generally not disclosed and hence one needs to be careful vis-à-vis disclosures in respect thereof.

(iii)

Disclosure of 'material facts' a subjective concept

As mentioned above, for a taxpayer to be safeguarded against the penal provisions of underreporting of income, it has to disclose all material facts relating to the transaction under question. However, as we all know, the term 'material facts' is a subjective concept and may involve different meaning(s) for different stakeholders. It may also be interpreted differently in different situations based on the transaction involved and hence disclosure of material facts still continues to remain a very important self-defense tool even in the new penalty regime.

(iv)

Misrepresentation or suppression of fact – Not defined in the Act

One of the conditions for treating a transaction as misreporting of income is 'misrepresentation' or 'suppression of facts'. The tax authorities, in order to initiate and/or levy the penalty, may highlight/harp on some instances to prove the so-called misrepresentation or suppression and hence monumental burden of proof is thereafter cast on the taxpayers to demonstrate with appropriate evidences, to negate the stand.

It is pertinent to note that the said term has not been defined under the Act thereby leading to different interpretations in different situations. Hence one needs to fall back on the dictionary meaning of these terms.

'Under reported income' in consequence of 'Misreporting of income'

There are sub section (8) and (9) of section 270A which prescribe that if 'under reported income is in consequence of misreporting of income', penalty would be 200% of the tax payable on such 'under reported income'. Six cases where such 'under reported income' can be said to be 'in consequence of misreporting of income' are given under sub section (9) which are numbered from clause (a) to (f) under that sub section.

There are however following issues which merit attention:

(a)

In a given case, even if there was a case of 'misreporting of income' due to which the addition/disallowance was made in the assessment order, the difference between the assessed income and processed income would nonetheless continue to be termed as 'under reported income' or at best 'under reported income in consequence to misreporting of income'.

This appears to have been done consciously by the legislature to avoid negotiate the possible argument coming at any stage that since assessing officer has failed to use the expression 'misreporting of income', jurisdiction to levy penalty under sub section (8) read with sub section (9) ought to fail. We have already opined that such stand of the Revenue may not stand to the test of law for the reasons elaborated by us in the earlier part of this article.

(b)

Burden to prove that the 'under reported income' includes such cases of income which can be called as 'under reported income in consequence to misreporting of income', would rest on the shoulders of the assessing officer. This situation is akin and identical to the old Explanation (1A) to section 271(1)(c) whereby also the burden to prove that the explanation furnished by the assessee in the matter of facts material to the computation of income was false, was rested on the shoulders of the assessing officer. It would therefore be incumbent for the assessing officer here also in the new penalty provision of sub section (9) of section 270A, to bring the case of the assessee under any of the clauses (a) to (f) of sub section (9) before penalty @ 200% of the tax payable is imposed. Show cause notice which would be issued by the assessing officer for eliciting the reply defence of the assessee, and the penalty order passed must clearly mention under which clause or clauses of sub section (9) of section 270A case of the 'under reported income' falls.

(d)

These clauses (a) to (f) of sub section (9) are at times overlapping, meaning thereby that one situation of 'misreporting of income' may be covered under more than one such clauses/cases. 'Misreporting of income' may be due to 'suppression of facts' or 'misrepresentation of facts' or may result due to 'recording of false entry in the books of accounts', or due to 'claim of expenditure not substantiated by any evidence'. There may at times not exist any water tight compartments between various clauses enshrined under sub section (9).

For instance, an expense on account of commission on sale may remain unsubstantiated for want of evidence and at the same time, it may be found that such commission was in fact a 'false entry' recorded in the books of accounts as such. Interestingly, clause (b) of subsection (9) of section 270A speaks of a case where there is 'failure to record investment in the books of account'. But, such 'failure to record any investment in the books of account' may result into addition under section 69 which would though result into 'under reported income' but since income under section 69 is subject to higher tax rate under section 115BBE, penalty provision as prescribed under section 271AAC would come into being not penalty provision under section 270A. Therefore, there may be a case of 'misreporting' of such income resulting into 'under reported income' yet it is outside the scope of penalty under section 270A.

This situation would in fact emerge in all such cases where addition to the income is made in the assessment order under section 68,69, 69A to 69D, as in all such cases, penalty can be levied under section 271AAC and not under section 270A. Question arises as to when in such cases penalty under section 270A cannot be imposed, where was the necessity of enacting clause (b) to sub section (9) of section 270A.

In fact, this anomaly seems to have crept in the statute due to the reason that penalty provision of section 270A was brought into effect by the Finance Act, 2016 whereas section 271AAC was brought subsequently by the Taxation Laws (Second Amendment) Act, 2016 and legislature seems to have glossed over this 'lapse' creptor resulted subsequently in section 270A(9)(b). Following this settled law, non-fulfilment of such jurisdictional conditions precedent as deliberated above, in our considered view, would prove to be fatal to the very levy of the penalty under section 270A. Rationale of using the expression 'during the course of any proceeding' instead of using 'during the course of penalty proceeding'

Penalty is imposed during the course of penalty proceeding and therefore, legislature could have used the expression in sub section (1) of section 270A as to direction to pay penalty 'during the course of penalty proceeding'.

But as discussed above, there could be proceeding other than the penalty proceeding viz. quantum appeal proceeding under section 250 before Commissioner (Appeals) revision proceeding under section 263 before Principal Commissioner of Commissioner, during the course of which jurisdiction to impose penalty under section 270A would have to be assumed in respect of any addition made by these authorities. Therefore, different nature of proceedings other than the penalty proceeding alone, as explained above, during the course of which penalty may come to be initiated levied seems to be the reason for the legislature using the expression 'during the course of any proceeding' under sub section (1) of section 270A.

'Under reported Income'

'Under reported income' has been explained under sub section (3) with the help of various situations of return filing, income shown in the returns filed processed under section 143(1)(a), and assessments reassessments made. Situations have been almost similarly explained about the 'person' who can be considered to have 'under reported income' under sub section (2).

It is noteworthy that penalty under section 270A is leviable on 'under reported income' which, if simply put, is the difference between the income assessed and amount of the income determined under section 143(1)(a) where the return has been furnished. If return of income has not been furnished or return has been furnished under section 148 for the first time, difference between the income assessed and basic exemption limit shall be the amount of 'under reported income'. Since in case of a company, firm or local authority, there is no basic exemption limit, thus the amount of 'under reported income' would be equal to the income assessed where the return of income has been filed by them for the first time. Certain other situations of the 'under reported income' too have been envisaged under sub section (3) of section 270A where income processed assessed was on deemed basis under section 115JB/115JC, or post-assessment assessed income has the effect of reducing the loss or converting the loss into income.

Without going into the fine nitty-gritty of these provisions putting simply, we would not be wrong if we say, that the 'under reported income' would be the difference between the income assessed income processed under section 143(1)(a). If it is a case of reassessment under section 147 or under section 153A, 'under reported income' would be the difference between the reassessed income and the earlier assessed income.

At the cost of repetition, we would urge that we have sought to simplify the meaning of 'under reported income' or else, we would also have landed in the similar complex maze, labyrinths round-about of situations mentioned in sub section (2) (3) of section 270A. Thus, it would be sufficient to say that there is in a way automatic 'under reported income' the moment there is difference between the assessed income and processed income subject to the exclusions given in sub section (6) of section 270A.

But, there may well be a situation whereby assessing officer while passing the assessment order finds that the 'under reported income' or part thereof is covered under any one or more of the clauses (a) to (e) of sub section (6). Detailed discussion in this regard has been made under the following caption titled 'Exceptions to or Exclusions from the 'Under reported Income'. In such a scenario, the assessing officer may reduce the amount of 'under reported income' by the amounts of additions/disallowances so covered by clause (a) to (e) of sub section (6).If after excluding such amounts covered under clause (a) to (e) of sub section (6), there remains no 'under reported income', the assessing officer may not even initiate the penalty proceeding under section 270A, in the assessment order.

That is why whenever there would be additions/disallowances made in the assessment order which would make the income assessed more than the income processed, all that the assessing officer has to do is to initiate penalty under section 270A, as there is 'under reported income' on the face of the assessment order.

3. Quantifying under-reported income: Where income is assessed for the first time and ITR was furnished by the assessee the difference between the income assessed and income determined under section 143(1)(a) would be the under-reported income.

Where no ITR is furnished or where it is furnished in response to notice under section 148 then (i) the amount of income assessed would be treated as under-reported income in the case of company, firm or local authority; and (ii) the difference between the income assessed and the basic exemption limit would be the under-reported income for other taxpayers.

Where it is not a case of the income being assessed for the first time the difference between the income reassessed or recomputed less the amount of income assessed or reassessed or recomputed previously would be the quantum of under-reported income.

4. Instances where it is not under-reporting of income: Section 270A(6) says that the following shall not be treated as under-reported income:

(i)

Where the assessee offers an explanation and the Assessing Officer or the Commissioner (Appeals) or the Commissioner or the Principal Commissioner, as the case may be, is satisfied that the explanation is bona fide and the assessee has disclosed all material facts to substantiate the explanation offered by him, the income so enhanced shall not be treated as under-reporting of income.

(ii)

The amount of under-reported income determined on the basis of an estimate shall not be treated as under-reported income if the accounts are correct and complete to the satisfaction of the Assessing Officer or Commissioner (Appeals) or the Commissioner or the Principal Commissioner provided the method employed is such that the income cannot properly be deduced therefrom.

(iii)

The amount of under-reported income determined on the basis of estimate and the assessee on his own estimated a lower amount of addition or disallowance of the same but has included such amount in the computation of his income and has disclosed all the facts material to the addition or disallowance.

(iv)

The amount of under-reported income represented by any addition made with reference to ALP determined by the TPO in case where the assessee has maintained information and documents prescribed under section 92E and declared the international transaction under Chapter X and disclosed all the material facts relating to the transaction.

(v)

The amount of undisclosed income which is dealt with in section 271AAB.

The quantum of penalty shall be 50% of the amount payable on under-reported income.

The jurisdiction of the High Court under article 226 is not so wide as to resurrect a cause of action which has become unenforceable on account of the law of limitation. Further, the jurisdiction under article 226 cannot be invoked against express statutory provisions, however, harsh the effect of the provisions might be on an assessee or litigant.

Thus, article 226 does not empower any High Court to exceed an express statutory provision. 4.2 All the remedies of the respondents came to an end when their appeals were dismissed - All the remedies of the respondents had come to an end when their appeals were dismissed by the Commissioner (Appeals) on the ground of limitation. Even the further appellate authority or the High Court would not have the jurisdiction to entertain the claim on merits disregarding the limitation or condoning the delay. In any event, the appellants had not pleaded any extraordinary circumstances warranting interference, even if the court would have any jurisdiction to do so. Therefore, the respondents could not have raised their contentions regarding the imposition of penalty on merits notwithstanding the limitation prescribed under section 85(3) and dismissal of their appeals on the ground of limitation even in the writ petitions filed under article 226.

Thus, no court can ignore the provisions relating to limitation of time or powers to condone delay within the specified time-limit.

4.3 Penalties under sections 76 and 78 are for different offences - The court further observed that the penalty imposable under section 76 is for failure to pay service tax by the person liable to pay the same in accordance with the provisions of section 68 and the rules made thereunder, whereas section 78 relates to penalty for suppression of the value of taxable service. Of course, these two offences may arise in the course of the same transaction, or from the same act of the person concerned. But the incidence of penalty is distinct and separate and even if the offences are committed in the course of same transaction or arise out of the same act, the penalty is imposable for ingredients of both the offences. There can be a situation where even without suppressing value of taxable service, the person liable to pay service tax fails to pay. Therefore, penalty can certainly be imposed on erring persons under both the above sections, especially since the ingredients of the two offences are distinct and separate. Perhaps invoking powers under section 80 the appropriate authority could have decided not to impose penalty on the assessee if the assessee proved that there was reasonable cause for the said failure in respect of one or both of the offences. However, no circumstances were either pleaded or proved for invocation of the said section also. In any event it could not be held that an assessee who was guilty of suppression deserved such sympathy. As such, the Single Judge was not correct in directing the appellant (the revenue) to modify the demand withdrawing penalty under section 76. The writ petitions were liable to be dismissed.

Thus, it is evident that when a person fails to pay tax even without suppressing the value of a taxable service, thus invoking the penalty under section 76, he would be penalized for a separate offence of suppressing the value of a taxable service under section 78.

4.4 Sub-section (3) of section 85 of Finance Act, 1994, prescribing time-limit for condoning the delay in filing appeal was challenged - The court further observed that the writ petitions were filed challenging sub-section (3) of section 85 which prescribes a maximum period of three months as the period during which the Commissioner (Appeals) could condone the delay in filing the appeals. They also challenged, inter alia, the imposition of penalty under section 76. On those grounds the respondents prayed for quashing of orders in appeal passed by the Commissioner of Central Excise (Appeals). However, since the writ petitioners had not chosen to file any appeal against the judgment of the learned Single Judge in which this question was not considered, impliedly rejecting the prayer, the court comprising the double Bench was not called upon to decide the same. Nor were any arguments advanced before the court on that aspect probably because that question was no more res integra in view of the decisions interpreting identical provisions in other taxing statutes.

4.5 Single Judge Bench confirmed the demand for service tax under section 68, interest under section 75 and penalty under section 78 but directed to withdraw penalty under section 76 - The Two-Judge Bench noted that the Single Judge by the impugned judgments in each of the writ petitions, confirmed the demand for service tax and interest under section 75, as also penalty under section 78. However, the learned Single Judge directed the first appellant (the revenue) herein to modify the demand by withdrawing the penalty under section 76. The revenue was aggrieved by that part of the judgment of the learned Single Judge.

As per section 281 of the Income Tax Act, during the pendency of any proceeding under this Act or after the completion thereof, but before the service of notice under rule 2 of the Second Schedule, if any assessee creates a charge on, or parts with the possession (by way of sale, mortgage, gift, exchange or any other mode of transfer whatsoever) of, any of his assets, such charge, transfer or any action will be void subject to such conditions.

In Model GST Law, where a person, after any tax has become due from him, creates a charge on or parts with the property belonging to him or in his possession by way of sale, mortgage, exchange, or any other mode of transfer whatsoever of any of his properties in favour of any other person with the intention of defrauding the Government revenue, such charge or transfer shall be void as against any claim in respect of any tax or any other sum payable by the said person.

If we understand the phrase "after any tax has become due" in general parlance, in any case tax will always be due once supply take place. Income Tax Act says if any proceeding due or any service of notice due after completion of such proceedings, but GST laws are differentiating from it and it covers almost all tax payers whether any proceeding is pending against taxpayer or not. With reference tax due in erstwhile sales tax act, the Calcutta High Court in case of Recols (India) Ltd., In re [1953] 4 STC 371, has held that as soon as there is a taxable turnover, the tax is due.

In case of CST v. Sri Jagatbandhu Mohanty, [1961] 12 STC 706, the Orissa High Court said that there are two important points of difference between the Bihar Sales Tax Act and the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922. (1) Whereas income-tax for the assessment year is assessed on the income of the previous year, sales tax becomes liable to be paid immediately after each sale is effected though, for facility of computation and payment of tax, provision has been made for the filing of returns at the. expiry of each quarter. (2) Whereas rates of income-tax vary in accordance with the amount of income and therefore no one can be certain of what income-tax he has to pay at least until the accounting year expires, the rate of sales tax does not vary on the amount of taxable turnover and a dealer, therefore, can always be certain of what sales tax he has to pay as soon as he effects a sale. In other words, sales tax becomes payable immediately after a sale is transacted. It said further that the words 'due' and 'payable' are separate. Eventually, honourable high court came to the conclusion that it is, therefore, clear that to the extent of liability admitted in a return the amount of tax is payable before the dealer submits that return. Thus, there is no doubt that the tax is payable since the sale is transacted and it is incumbent upon the registered dealer to state that amount in the return when submitted.

9. The nomenclature of this dispute resolution scheme i.e. 'Vivad se Vishwaas Scheme' suggests the 'trust-centric' philosophy and intent of the Law Makers behind bringing out this Tax Amnesty Scheme.

It has been asserted that this dispute resolution scheme would benefit primarily in the disputes concerning cash deposit cases in demonetisation period and penny stock cases.

In all such cases, the provisions of section 115BBE have been pressed into service by the Revenue Authorities and an effective tax rate of almost 78% (Basic Rate u/s 115BBE @ 60% plus surcharge @ 25%), has been levied on the additions.

Therefore, in all such cases, even the 'disputed tax' @ 78%, is very high and may not be persuasive enough to motivate the assessee to opt for this scheme.

Therefore, in order to bring fruitful results in such cases, under this scheme, the amount of 'disputed tax' to be paid by the appellant, should be reduced to the maximum marginal rate of tax of approximately 33.66% and not at the high rate of 78%. If at all, some differentiation is to be made between normal cases and such cases, then a higher rate of say 40% may be prescribed, so as to ensure fruitful tax realisation, in such cases, under the scheme.

There is a standing anomaly in restricting setting-off of carried forward unabsorbed depreciation on the basis of income-tax rate of depreciation even for a year of book profits tax under sub-section (3) of section 115JA/115JB of the Act by mixing up statutory and company law depreciation to taxpayer’s disadvantage, with tax credit being a poor substitute. ADDITIONAL TAX ON FRINGE BENEFITS

6. The tax on fringe benefits is claimed to be a new levy with the objective of plugging in the loopholes enabling tax avoidance by employees, so as to make good such loss. After giving small relief to employees by amending rule 3, a much larger burden is imposed on the employer. The Board Circular No. 8 of 2005 [2005] 277 ITR (St.) 20 has conceded that the actual amount expended on fringe benefits enjoyed by the employees out of the targetted expenditure will be of ‘no consequence or relevance’ admitting thereby that the professed objective is an unreal pretext. Liability is ultimately dependent upon classification of expenditure for which there are no set guidelines, as every case has seeds of potential litigation.

SERVICE TAX

7. Service tax among indirect taxes has spread its tentacles even more unevenly as between different classes of taxpayers and different classes of transactions. Services like employment, law and medicine are conspicuous by their absence, while minor services have been targetted. Even rent has been construed as service and this tax is most lopsided. Since service tax is a charge on the profits of the service-providers, when they bear it, either directly or as a part of price, service tax is another factor, which has uneven effect on income in economic sense.

TORRENT OF MINDLESS AMENDMENTS

8. The language of our law is antiquated and multiplicity of the amendments is mind-boggling. Mr. N.A. Palkhivala regretted the 3,000 amendments in the first thirty years of the Income-tax Act, describing it as ‘torrential spate of mindless amendments mistaking change for progress’ and called it ‘a tragedy of waste’ and a ‘national disgrace’. He did not live to see all the further spate of amendments in a faster track in much larger numbers in the further 17 years after his comment. The bad provisions remain fossilised, while the new ones together have not integrated with other provisions making it extremely complicated. Mr. Palkhivala reasoned as under :

"Nothing is more detrimental to economic growth than uncertainty in business circles as to their tax liability which is still pretty high in India in the corporate sector."

His plea for stable law with clarity and certainty was never more in need than at the present. The constant refrain as justification given for such amendments as ‘rationalising and streamlining’ makes a mockery of the entire exercise.

Tax statute, therefore, is a patchwork and a poor patchwork at that. Modern business with revolution in communications has given rise to a number of innovative methods of business transactions. These have to be dealt with by prompt clarifications. The fact that there is no definite yardstick for accounting for income as to whether an assessee is an investor or dealer or in respect of foreign exchange transactions on mark to market basis for foreign currency held by an exporter or for accounting of carbon credits has all to await precise solutions.

There is no reason why income recognised by accounting standards and accounting principles should not be accepted as a base for income-taxation, unless and until a precise measure of income in economic sense is devised.

ERRATIC INTERPRETATIONS

9. The problem is not only with the law, it is as much from erratic interpretations of law, which distort ‘income’. The Board circulars, which used to be benevolent in the light of the objectives of the amendments are no more to be seen, since even the annual circulars merely paraphrase the law. No attempt is made to clarify the controversial interpretations on any of the issues. Even the Board’s instructions, which are favourable are ignored with impunity and counsels for revenue are known to have questioned the validity of benevolent Board circulars. The officers are left to their own devices in the implementation of law with vigilance, audit and supervision ever ready to find fault with them. They would like to play safe. Remedy in appeal also suffers from the weakness arising out of absence of a definite reasonable stand on the part of revenue. Even the simpler law is thwarted in its application by ultra-technical interpretations both by the assessee and the income-tax department proliferating litigation.

TAXABLE INCOME

3. The chasm between the taxable income and the accountant’s or legal concept of income is very wide, more because of the numerous deeming provisions in the tax statute, which nullify them. Tax on capital gains itself is a glaring example of taxing what is not income. Deeming provisions even in respect of salary income treating terminal benefits as normal income, subject, no doubt, to measured relief and various other provisions like anti-compete fee under section 28 of the Act besides such income as from lotteries under section 56, are again other capital receipts, which are treated as revenue receipts, contrary to accepted understanding of revenue as against capital receipts. Provisions for deemed dividend and deeming accrual on receipt basis are other instances.

Some items of revenue expenditure are deemed to be capital expenditure allowed to be amortised over the years as in the case of expenses on mergers and demergers under section 35DD of the Act or VRS payments under section 35DDA of the Act. What makes the taxable income even more distorted making a sweeping departure from real income is the deeming provision like disallowance of what is deemed to be illegal under Explanation to section 37(1) of the Act. Expenditure from which tax is failed to be deducted at source is disallowed under section 40(a) of the Act. Even where mercantile system is followed, cash system is substituted under section 43B, so as to legitimise hybrid system to revenue’s advantage in the matter of taxes, interest to banks and financial institutions and welfare dues. What is worse is the provision to treat cash expenditure above the limit of Rs. 20,000 under section 40A(3) of the Act with minor exceptions on the understanding, that expenditure would include purchases. Apart from what is collected as tax, penalty is collected on deposits and repayments in cash under section 269SS and 269T of the Act, unless reasonable cause is established. Both sections 40A(3) and 269SS and 269T would strangely target genuine transactions, because expenditure, which is not genuine and deposits which are not genuine are taxable as income. The complexity of our laws is more evident in the matters of cross-border transactions with Double Tax Avoidance Agreements hardly touching the existing problems with transfer pricing adding to the existing confusion. Almost every Finance Act would add to the list of deeming provisions.

DISCRIMINATORY TREATMENT OF CORPORATE SECTOR

4. Our system of corporate taxation is highly discriminatory making corporations liable for additional burden by way of book profits tax on one hand and dividend distribution tax on the other. Tax on dividend is a double taxation of corporate income, whether the dividends are assessed in the hands of shareholder or company. Loans and advances are deemed as dividend income of the shareholder or a concern in which the shareholder is interested under section 2(22)( e) of the Act. Right of set off on actual distributed dividend in a later year as provided in the section makes no sense, when such dividend is taxed in the hands of an interested concern, so that it is another instance of double taxation in shareholder’s hands once as deemed dividend and again in the hands of the interested concern, when there is actual distribution of dividend. Deeming loss under the head ‘Capital gains’ on share transactions as speculative under Explanation to section 73 of the Act is a special provision targetting corporations. Fringe Benefits Tax though not limited to corporations imposes further burden especially on manufacturing companies with a large work force.

There is a standing anomaly in restricting setting-off of carried forward unabsorbed depreciation on the basis of income-tax rate of depreciation even for a year of book profits tax under sub-section (3) of section 115JA/115JB of the Act by mixing up statutory and company law depreciation to taxpayer’s disadvantage, with tax credit being a poor substitute.

Accounting Standards (AS) 22

Accounting for Taxes on Income

(This Accounting Standard includes paragraphs set in bold italic type and plain type, which have equal authority. Paragraphs in bold italic type indicate the main principles. This Accounting Standard should be read in the context of its objective and the General Instructions contained in part A of the Annexure to the Notification.)

Objective

The objective of this Standard is to prescribe accounting treatment for taxes on income. Taxes on income is one of the significant items in the statement of profit and loss of an enterprise. In accordance with the matching concept, taxes on income are accrued in the same period as the revenue and expenses to which they relate. Matching of such taxes against revenue for a period poses special problems arising from the fact that in a number of cases, taxable income may be significantly different from the accounting income. This divergence between taxable income and accounting income arises due to two main reasons. Firstly, there are differences between items of revenue and expenses as appearing in the statement of profit and loss and the items which are considered as revenue, expenses or deductions for tax purposes. Secondly, there are differences between the amount in respect of a particular item of revenue or expense as recognised in the statement of profit and loss and the corresponding amount which is recognised for the computation of taxable income.

Scope

1. This Standard should be applied in accounting for taxes on income. This includes the determination of the amount of the expense or saving related to taxes on income in respect of an accounting period and the disclosure of such an amount in the financial statements.

2. For the purposes of this Standard, taxes on income include all domestic and foreign taxes which are based on taxable income.

3. This Standard does not specify when, or how, an enterprise should account for taxes that are payable on distribution of dividends and other distributions made by the enterprise.

Definitions

4. For the purpose of this Standard, the following terms are used with the meanings specified:

4.1 Accounting income (loss) is the net profit or loss for a period, as reported in the statement of profit and loss, before deducting income-tax expense or adding income-tax saving.

4.2 Taxable income (tax loss) is the amount of the income (loss) for a period, determined in accordance with the tax laws, based upon which income-tax payable (recoverable) is determined.

4.3 Tax expense (tax saving) is the aggregate of current tax and deferred tax charged or credited to the statement of profit and loss for the period.

4.4 Current tax is the amount of income-tax determined to be payable (recoverable) respect of the taxable income (tax loss) for a period.

4.5 Deferred tax is the tax effect of timing differences.

4.6 Timing differences are the differences between taxable income and accounting income for a period that originate in one period and are capable of reversal in one or more subsequent periods.

4.7 Permanent differences are the differences between taxable income and accounting income for a period that originate in one period and do not reverse subsequently.

5. Taxable income is calculated in accordance with tax laws. In some circumstances, the requirements of these laws to compute taxable income differ from the accounting policies applied to determine accounting income. The effect of this difference is that the taxable income and accounting income may not be the same.

6. The differences between taxable income and accounting income can be classified into permanent differences and timing differences. Permanent differences are those differences between taxable income and accounting income which originate in one period and do not reverse subsequently. For instance, if for the purpose of computing taxable income, the tax laws allow only a part of an item of expenditure, the disallowed amount would result in a permanent difference.

Timing differences are those differences between taxable income and accounting income for a period that originate in one period and are capable of reversal in one or more subsequent periods. Timing differences arise because the period in which some items of revenue and expenses are included in taxable income do not coincide with the period in which such items of revenue and expenses are included or considered in arriving at accounting income. For example, machinery purchased for scientific research related to business is fully allowed as deduction in the first year for tax purposes whereas the same would be charged to the statement of profit and loss as depreciation over its useful life. The total depreciation charged on the machinery for accounting purposes and the amount allowed as deduction for tax purposes will ultimately be the same, but periods over which the depreciation is charged and the deduction is allowed will differ. Another example of timing difference is a situation where, for the purpose of computing taxable income, tax laws allow depreciation on the basis of the written down value method, whereas for accounting purposes, straight line method is used. Some other examples of timing differences arising under the Indian tax laws are given in Illustration 1.

Under the Income-tax Act, certain categories of income are taxed at the Maximum Marginal Rate (MMR) rather than the normal slab rates or other rates otherwise applicable to the assessee. The concept of MMR was introduced as an anti-avoidance measure to discourage high-income taxpayers from reducing their tax burden by distributing income among multiple entities, such as private trusts, Associations of Persons (AOPs), or Bodies of Individuals (BOIs), that might otherwise be eligible for lower tax rates.

By taxing such income at the MMR, the Act seeks to ensure tax neutrality and discourage tax avoidance, particularly in cases where the shares of beneficiaries or members are indeterminate or where the legislature considers taxation at the highest rate appropriate.

The provisions relating to MMR apply to specified entities and circumstances, including certain trusts, AOPs/BOIs, business trusts, Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs), and registered Non-Profit Organisations (NPOs). Evidence for developing countries is more limited however and this is well discussed in (Fuest & Riedel 2012). The lack of reliable and consistent data is often one of the most significant constraints faced by researchers. The current global financial recession and the associated policies for fiscal consolidation have made tax evasion and avoidance a prominent issue for developed countries. However, the effects of tax avoidance and evasion are probably more significant for developing economies. While tax revenues in OECD countries represent around 35 per cent of their gross domestic product (GDP), developing countries obtain on average only 13 per cent according to (International Development Committee 2012). The low amount of tax raised by developing countries often leads to a situation where governments cannot obtain the financial resources required to guarantee citizens' access to essential services, such as healthcare, clean water and sanitation, and education. In addition, low tax revenues often imply the need for governments to increase debt and aid levels, which in turn can skew accountability towards creditors and donors.

The low level of tax revenues raised in developing countries is caused by a number of reasons.
